s: Lucian's Philopseudes (c. 170 CE) has Eucrates overhear the Egyptian Pancrates' three-syllable incantation, animate a pestle to carry water, and then find it will not obey his order to stop until the house is full of water: the earliest form of the sorcerer's-apprentice story.

src.l: Lucian of Samosata, H. W. Fowler and F. G. Fowler (tr.), 1905, The Works of Lucian of Samosata, Vol. III
src.q: Stop: be water-carrier no longer, but pestle as heretofore. But the thing would take no notice of me: it went on drawing water the whole time, until at last the house was full of it.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. I
src.q: he discovered that he could not make it stop

s: In the same tale, cutting the disobedient pestle in two with an axe only yields two water-carriers; only the master, Pancrates, can turn them back into wood, and he then leaves the apprentice.

src.l: Lucian of Samosata, 1545, Loukianou Hapanta / Luciani Opera
src.q: He took an axe and cut the pestle into two parts, but each part took an amphora and fetched water, and instead of one, I had two servants.
src.qo: πτω τὸ ὕπερον εἰς δύο μέρη, τὰ δὲ ἑκάτερον τὸ μέ- ρος, ἀμφορέα λαβόντα, ὑδροφόρει, καὶ ἀνθ' ἑνὸς δύο μοι ἐγίνοντο οἱ διάκονοι.

s: Lucian frames the pestle story as one of the tall tales of credulous philosophers: the sceptic Tychiades rebukes the tellers for filling boys' heads with 'superstitious stuff'.

src.l: Lucian of Samosata, H. W. Fowler and F. G. Fowler (tr.), 1905, The Works of Lucian of Samosata, Vol. III
src.q: do not accustom them to listen to a tangle of superstitious stuff that will cling to them for the rest of their lives

s: Jacob Grimm (1844), describing a wax image that runs out and brings things back once its sender drips blood on it, compares it to the water-fetching broom of Goethe's Zauberlehrling.

src.l: Jacob Grimm, 1844, Deutsche Mythologie (2nd ed.)
src.q: Who does not remember the water-fetching broom in Goethe’s Zauberlehrling
src.qo: Wer erinnert sich nicht des wasserholenden besens in Göthes zauberlehrling?

s: Schopenhauer (Parerga, 1851) uses Goethe's Sorcerer's Apprentice as an image for the causal chain, which once started runs on without end.

src.l: Arthur Schopenhauer, 1862, Parerga und Paralipomena
src.q: We fare here like Goethe’s Sorcerer’s Apprentice … whose creation begins upon command but does not stop again.

s: Roskoff (1869) quotes an author on the witch period who says there will always be spirits one would like to take possession of and can no longer master, 'like in Goethe's Sorcerer's Apprentice'.

src.l: Gustav Roskoff, 1869, Geschichte des Teufels, Vol. II
src.q: spirits which one would like to take possession of, and of which one can no longer become master, like in Goethe's Sorcerer's Apprentice
src.qo: Geister, deren man sich bemächtigen möchte, und deren Herr man nicht mehr werden kann, wie Goethe's Zauberlehrling".

s: A conjuration printed by Reginald Scot (1584; 1886 reprint) binds the spirit Bealphares with explicit constraints: not to leave the operator's sight, not to change the shape it appeared in, and to have no power over the operator's body or soul.

src.l: Reginald Scot, 1886, The Discoverie of Witchcraft
src.q: that thou shalt not depart out of my sight, nor yet to alter thy bodilie shape, that thou art appeared in, nor anie power shalt thou have of our bodies or soules

s: The Goetia ends an operation with a formal 'license to the spirit that he may depart', ordering it back to its dwelling to obey the operator's law without terror to men or any creature.

src.l: Anonymous, S. L. MacGregor Mathers (ed.), L. W. de Laurence (publ.), 1916, The Lesser Key of Solomon: Goetia (de Laurence edition)
src.q: Descend unto thy dwelling, obey the law which I have made, without terror to the sons of men, creatures, all things upon the surface of the earth.

s: A 1707 German text (Allix) reports the convert's charge that some Jews shape a lump of clay like a man and whisper oaths into it so that it lives and walks; the respondent mocks him as made of such clay, able to walk but without sechel (reason).

src.l: Pierre Allix, 1707, Ausspruch der alten Jüdischen Kirchen
src.q: take a lump of clay, form it, and make it like a human being; afterward, one whispers … into it, from which the image lives and walks

s: Eisenmenger (1711) quotes the Talmud that Rav Hanina and Rav Oshaya studied the Book of Yetzirah every Sabbath eve and created a three-year-old calf, and reports the Jewish view that powerful things are done through this book by arranging the letters.

src.l: Johann Andreas Eisenmenger, 1711, Entdecktes Judenthum
src.q: studied in the Book of Yetzirah

s: Russell (2017) states the AI control problem as a failure of value alignment, quoting Wiener (1960) that we must be sure the purpose put into the machine is the one we really desire, and invoking King Midas.

src.l: Stuart Russell, 2017, Provably Beneficial Artificial Intelligence

s: Larsson and Viktorelius (2022), from an anthropological study of a machine-learning system for ship propulsion, define magic's function as reducing contingency and argue that ML shares this with oracles, while the distinction from magic still matters.

src.l: Simon Larsson, Martin Viktorelius, 2022, Reducing the contingency of the world: magic, oracles, and machine-learning technology
src.loc: section on magic and contingency; abstract

s: Hedged answer to Q3: the tradition's runaway-servant stories locate the danger in an operator who can start a servant but cannot revoke or correct it, and the ritual literature answers with written constraints and a formal dismissal; but its made beings (pestle, golem) are mindless, its spirits' power was never shown, so it offers a vocabulary of control, not a tested method.

src.l: Lucian of Samosata, H. W. Fowler and F. G. Fowler (tr.), 1905, The Works of Lucian of Samosata, Vol. III
Reginald Scot, 1886, The Discoverie of Witchcraft
Anonymous, S. L. MacGregor Mathers (ed.), L. W. de Laurence (publ.), 1916, The Lesser Key of Solomon: Goetia (de Laurence edition)
Pierre Allix, 1707, Ausspruch der alten Jüdischen Kirchen
Stuart Russell, 2017, Provably Beneficial Artificial Intelligence

s: Campolo and Crawford (2020) argue that describing deep learning as magical ('enchanted determinism') shields its creators from accountability and places the systems outside understanding, regulation and responsibility while they sit inside systems of capital and profit.

src.l: Alexander Campolo, Kate Crawford, 2020, Enchanted Determinism: Power without Responsibility in Artificial Intelligence
Alexander Campolo, Kate Crawford, 2020, Enchanted Determinism: Power without Responsibility in Artificial Intelligence

s: Elish and boyd (2018) problematize the myths that animate the supposed 'magic' of Big Data and AI and argue for grounding machine learning in methodological reflection rather than hype and fear.

src.l: M. C. Elish, danah boyd, 2018, Situating methods in the magic of Big Data and AI

s: Larsson and Viktorelius (2022) find that prior scholarship comparing technology to magic failed both to define magic adequately and to use research on magic, so the analogy is often drawn with an undefined term.

src.l: Simon Larsson, Martin Viktorelius, 2022, Reducing the contingency of the world: magic, oracles, and machine-learning technology

s: Pliny (Natural History 30.1) calls magic the most fraudulent of arts and explains its hold on mankind by its having absorbed three other arts: medicine, religion and astrology ('the mathematical arts').

src.l: Pliny the Elder, 1535, C. Plinii Secundi Naturalis Historiae, Vol. 3 (Venice: Aldus)
src.q: this most fraudulent of arts has flourished most extensively throughout the whole world ... since it is the only one of the arts to have gathered into itself three other most powerful disciplines

s: Pliny reports the agreed opinion that magic originated in Persia with Zoroaster, while admitting it is unclear whether there was one Zoroaster or more.

src.l: Pliny the Elder, 1535, C. Plinii Secundi Naturalis Historiae, Vol. 3 (Venice: Aldus)
src.q: Without doubt, it originated there in Persia with Zoroaster, as the authors agree. But whether this was one man, or another after him, is not sufficiently certain.
src.qo: Sine dubio illic orta in Perfide à Zoroastre, ut inter autores conuenit. Sed unus hic fuerit, an postea & alius, non satis constat.

s: Pliny names Osthanes, who accompanied Xerxes' invasion of Greece, as the first author on magic and blames him for spreading the 'monstrous art' among the Greeks.

src.l: Pliny the Elder, 1535, C. Plinii Secundi Naturalis Historiae, Vol. 3 (Venice: Aldus)
src.q: The first (as I find it) who wrote about it is Osthanes, who accompanied Xerxes, king of the Persians, in the war which he brought upon Greece; and he seems to have scattered the seeds of this monstrous art along the way
src.qo: Primus extat (ut equidem inuenio) commentatus de ea Osthanes Xerxem regem Persarum bello, quod is Græciæ intulit comitatus:

s: Pliny remarks that medicine and magic flourished in the same age, medicine illustrated by Hippocrates and magic by Democritus, around the Peloponnesian War.

src.l: Pliny the Elder, 1535, C. Plinii Secundi Naturalis Historiae, Vol. 3 (Venice: Aldus)
src.q: both arts flourished equally—I mean medicine and magic—at the same age, with Hippocrates illustrating the former, and Democritus the latter, around the time of the Peloponnesian War of Greece.

s: Pliny records 'another faction of magic' depending on Moses, Jannes and Jotape, the Jews, which he dates many thousands of years after Zoroaster.

src.l: Pliny the Elder, 1535, C. Plinii Secundi Naturalis Historiae, Vol. 3 (Venice: Aldus)
src.q: There is also another faction of magic, dependent upon Moses, Jannes, and Jotape, the Jews, but many thousands of years after Zoroaster.
src.qo: Est et alia magicæ factio, à Mose & Iamne et Iotape Iudæis pendens, sed multis milibus annorum post Zoroastre.

s: Pliny finds traces of magic among the Italian peoples in the Twelve Tables and dates a Senate decree forbidding human sacrifice to the 657th year of the city (97 BCE).

src.l: Pliny the Elder, 1535, C. Plinii Secundi Naturalis Historiae, Vol. 3 (Venice: Aldus)
src.q: there are traces of it even among the Italian peoples in our Twelve Tables, and in other arguments, which I set forth in the previous volume. Finally, in the 657th year of the city

s: Pliny counts the Druids of Gaul, suppressed under Tiberius, and the rites of Britain as instances of the same magic, which he says the whole world agrees on.

src.l: Pliny the Elder, 1535, C. Plinii Secundi Naturalis Historiae, Vol. 3 (Venice: Aldus)
src.q: For the principate of Tiberius Caesar abolished their Druids and this class of seers and physicians.
src.qo: Namque Tiberij Cæsaris principatus sustulit Druidas eorum, & hoc genus uatum medicorumq;.

s: Pliny, citing Osthanes, lists the kinds of magical divination: by water, spheres, air, stars, lamps, basins and axes, among others.

src.l: Pliny the Elder, 1535, C. Plinii Secundi Naturalis Historiae, Vol. 3 (Venice: Aldus)
src.q: As Osthanes related, there are many species of it. For it promises divine things by water, and spheres, and air, and stars, and lamps, and basins, and axes

s: Pliny presents Nero as a decisive test of magic: an emperor with unlimited wealth, talent and desire who studied it and found it vain and false.

src.l: Pliny the Elder, 1535, C. Plinii Secundi Naturalis Historiae, Vol. 3 (Venice: Aldus)
src.q: This is an immense and indubitable example of the false art which Nero left behind
src.qo: Immensum et indubitatum exemplum est falsæ artis, quam dereliquit Nero:

s: Pliny mocks the magi for prizing the mole above all animals, promising divination to whoever eats its fresh, palpitating heart.

src.l: Pliny the Elder, 1535, C. Plinii Secundi Naturalis Historiae, Vol. 3 (Venice: Aldus)
src.q: so that if someone devours its heart while it is fresh and palpitating, they promise divination and the success of things to be accomplished.
src.qo: ut si quis cor eius recens palpitansq; deuorarit, diuinationis & rerum efficiendarum euentus promittant.

s: Apuleius defends himself by citing authors who say 'magus' is the Persian word for priest, and Plato's account that the magic of Zoroaster taught to Persian princes is the worship of the gods.

src.l: Apuleius, H. E. Butler (tr.), 1909, The Apologia and Florida of Apuleius of Madaura
src.q: If what I read in a large number of authors be true, namely, that magician is the Persian word for priest, what is there criminal in being a priest

src.l: Apuleius, H. E. Butler (tr.), 1909, The Apologia and Florida of Apuleius of Madaura
src.q: And one of these teaches the boy the magic of Zoroaster the son of Oromazes ; and this magic is no other than the worship of the gods.

s: Apuleius cites Plato's account of Zalmoxis that magical charms are merely beautiful words.

src.l: Apuleius, H. E. Butler (tr.), 1909, The Apologia and Florida of Apuleius of Madaura
src.q: in another passage dealing with a certain Zalmoxis, a Thracian and also a master of this art, has written that ' magical charms are merely beautiful words '.

s: Apuleius gives the common definition of a magician as one who, by communion of speech with the gods, can do any marvel through incantation, and turns it against his accusers.

src.l: Apuleius, H. E. Butler (tr.), 1909, The Apologia and Florida of Apuleius of Madaura
src.q: define a magician as one who by communion of speech with the immortal gods has power to do all the marvels that he will, through a strange power of incantation

s: Apuleius says it is a common error of the uninitiated to call philosophers irreligious or magicians, naming Epimenides, Orpheus, Pythagoras and Ostanes as so labelled.

src.l: Apuleius, H. E. Butler (tr.), 1909, The Apologia and Florida of Apuleius of Madaura
src.q: So Epimenides, Orpheus, Pythagoras, and Ostanes were regarded as magicians

s: Apuleius answers the charge about buying fish by saying he sought remedies in fish, as a doctor or philosopher would, and adds that ancient doctors cured wounds with song.

src.l: Apuleius, H. E. Butler (tr.), 1909, The Apologia and Florida of Apuleius of Madaura
src.q: do you think it more the business of a magician than of a doctor, or indeed of a philosopher, to know and seek out remedies?

s: Apuleius cites Varro's story that at Tralles a boy gazing at an image of Mercury in a bowl of water foretold the outcome of the Mithridatic war.

src.l: Apuleius, H. E. Butler (tr.), 1909, The Apologia and Florida of Apuleius of Madaura
src.q: a boy who was gazing at an image of Mercury reflected in a bowl of water foretold the future in a hundred and sixty lines of verse.

s: Apuleius accepts Plato's view that divine powers midway between gods and men control all divination and the miracles of magicians.

src.l: Apuleius, H. E. Butler (tr.), 1909, The Apologia and Florida of Apuleius of Madaura
src.q: there are certain divine powers holding a position and possessing a character midway between gods and men, and that all divination and the miracles of magicians are controlled by them.

s: Apuleius argues that his wife Pudentilla's letter calling him a magician cannot by itself prove the charge.

src.l: Apuleius, H. E. Butler (ed.), A. S. Owen (ed.), 1914, Apulei Apologia sive Pro se de magia liber (with commentary)
src.q: You do not prove me a magician with so many arguments, so many witnesses, so much oratory: would she prove it with one word?
src.qo: uos tot argumentis, tot testibus, tanta oratione magum me non probatis: illa uno uerbo probaret?

s: A 1572 commentary on the Twelve Tables quotes Apuleius that magic is a matter for the law, forbidden by the Twelve Tables because of incantations against crops.

src.l: Anonymous commentator, 1572, Juris civilis initia et progressus. Ad leges XII. Tabularum brevis commentatio
src.loc: scan 22, on the XII Tables (quoting Apol. 47)
src.q: That magic, as far as I hear, is a matter delegated to the laws, already forbidden of old by the Twelve Tables on account of the incredible enticements of crops.
src.qo: iam inde antiquitus duodecim Tabulis propter incredundas frugum illicebras interdicta.

s: Butler and Owen's commentary argues that the lex Cornelia covered all magic practised for evil ends and quotes Paulus that those who perform nocturnal rites to bewitch or bind someone are crucified or thrown to the beasts.

src.l: Apuleius, H. E. Butler (ed.), A. S. Owen (ed.), 1914, Apulei Apologia sive Pro se de magia liber (with commentary)
src.loc: commentary on Apol. 2 [scan 176], quoting Paulus, Sententiae 5.23.15
src.q: Those who have performed or caused to be performed impious or nocturnal rites, in order to bewitch, bind, or fasten someone, are either crucified or thrown to the beasts.
src.qo: qui sacra impia nocturnaue, ut quem obcantarent defigerent obligarent, fecerint faciendave curauerint, aut cruci suffiguntur aut bestiis obiciuntur.

s: Plato's Laws distinguishes two kinds of poisoning: harm done bodily by drugs, and harm by sorceries, incantations and spells that persuade both the doer and the victim of their power.

src.l: Plato, R. G. Bury (tr.), 1926, Plato: Laws, Vol. 2 (Books 7-12) (Loeb)
src.q: Distinct from this is the type which, by means of sorceries and incantations and spells (as they are called), not only convinces those who attempt to cause injury that they really can do so

s: Plato says it is futile to tell suspicious people to disregard images of moulded wax found at doorways, crossroads or ancestors' tombs.

src.l: Plato, R. G. Bury (tr.), 1926, Plato: Laws, Vol. 2 (Books 7-12) (Loeb)
src.q: if they happen to see images of moulded wax at doorways, or at points where three ways meet, or it may be at the tomb of some ancestor

s: In Plato's law on sorcery, a prophet or diviner convicted of harm by bindings, incantations or spells is put to death, while a layman's penalty is set by the court.

src.l: Plato, R. G. Bury (tr.), 1926, Plato: Laws, Vol. 2 (Books 7-12) (Loeb)
src.q: But if he be thought to be acting in a manner similar to one who causes injury through bindings, incantations, spells, or any such

s: Audollent reports two explanations for curse tablets being made of lead: Saturn's deathly metal chosen for a deadly work (Huschke, Bouché-Leclercq, Wünsch), or simple convenience for writing (Hübner).

src.l: Auguste Audollent, 1904, Defixionum tabellae quotquot innotuerunt
src.q: the ancients deliberately used this cold, heavy, ash-colored metal, which is suffused with the deathly pallor of Saturn, to complete a death-dealing work.

src.l: Auguste Audollent, 1904, Defixionum tabellae quotquot innotuerunt
src.q: should, I think, be explained not so much by a peculiar superstition as by the easy and convenient use of that metal in writing.
src.qo: « Quod plumbum prae reliquis metallis devotionibus et obsecrationibus inserviret, non tam ex peculiari quadam superstitione quam ex facili et commodo eius metalli in scribendo usu explicandum puto. »

s: Audollent states that the victim's name had to be written on a curse tablet, otherwise the formula failed or recoiled on the curser.

src.l: Auguste Audollent, 1904, Defixionum tabellae quotquot innotuerunt
src.q: it is absolutely necessary that his name be inscribed on the plate; otherwise the formulas fall void or perhaps recoil upon the one performing the curse.

s: An Attic curse tablet in Audollent consigns a group of legal adversaries to Hermes katochos ('the binder').

src.l: Auguste Audollent, 1904, Defixionum tabellae quotquot innotuerunt
src.q: I curse to Hermes the <term>katochos</term> <gloss>binder/holder</gloss>

s: A Latin love curse in Greek letters from Hadrumetum asks secret powers to make a woman named Tottina love the writer; Audollent notes its barbarous names hide the divine name Iao.

src.l: Auguste Audollent, 1904, Defixionum tabellae quotquot innotuerunt
src.q: You will not deny that the divine name <term>Iao</term> lies hidden under <term>iaoth</term> and <term>ioth</term>.

s: The Great Paris magical papyrus, quoted by Audollent, prescribes a love-binding spell with two wax figures, an armed male like Ares and a bound, kneeling female carrying the woman's hair.

src.l: Auguste Audollent, 1904, Defixionum tabellae quotquot innotuerunt
src.q: Taking wax from a potter's wheel, mold two figures, male and female. Make the male as if armed like <term>Ares</term> <gloss>Greek god of war</gloss>, holding a sword in his left hand, threatening her at the right collarbone.

s: In the Headless One rite (PGM V), the practitioner asks the god to deliver a possessed person and then speaks in the god's person: 'I am the headless demon'.

src.l: Karl Preisendanz (ed.), 1928, Papyri Graecae Magicae, Vol. 1
src.q: I am the headless <margin>145</margin> demon with the face upon my feet; I am the strong one who possesses the immortal fire.

s: The Paris papyrus (PGM IV) uses single lines of Homer's Iliad as charms, for example one to banish anger.

src.l: Karl Preisendanz (ed.), 1928, Papyri Graecae Magicae, Vol. 1
src.q:
To banish anger:
> 'Will you dare to raise the mighty spear against Zeus?'

s: In the so-called Mithras Liturgy (PGM IV 475ff.) the speaker asks to be reborn in thought and to behold the immortal beginning, 'born mortal from a mortal womb'.

src.l: Karl Preisendanz (ed.), 1928, Papyri Graecae Magicae, Vol. 1
src.q: For I am about to behold today with immortal eyes—I, who was born mortal from a mortal womb

s: A love-compulsion spell in PGM IV invokes Hekate together with Persephone and the Mesopotamian underworld goddess Ereschigal.

src.l: Karl Preisendanz (ed.), 1928, Papyri Graecae Magicae, Vol. 1
src.q: Persephone, <margin>2750</margin> three-headed, fire-roamer, cow-eyed, heifer-feeder, all-feeder, Phorbara; Aktiōphi, Ereschigal

s: A lamp divination in the Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden summons a great god with Boel into a flame so that a boy medium sees and hears him and gives true answers.

src.l: F. Ll. Griffith, Herbert Thompson, 1904, The Demotic Magical Papyrus of London and Leiden
src.q: come into the midst of this flame with Boel, Aniel, and give strength to the eyes of Heu

s: In the Babylonian New Year ritual, the incantation priest (mašmašu) wipes the temple with a sheep's carcass, throws it into the river, and stays outside Babylon from the 5th to the 12th day.

src.l: F. Thureau-Dangin, 1921, Rituels accadiens
src.q:
With the carcass of the sheep, the <term>incantation-priest</term> <note>Akkadian: mašmašu</note> shall
wipe

src.l: F. Thureau-Dangin, 1921, Rituels accadiens
src.q: From the 5th day to the 12th day, they shall dwell in the countryside.

s: The New Year ritual's purification incantation names Marduk, Azag-sug and Nin-a-ha-du and expels all evil from the temple: 'O great demon, may Bêl destroy you!'

src.l: F. Thureau-Dangin, 1921, Rituels accadiens
src.q:
Whatever evil is present in the temple, go out!
> O great demon, may <term>Bêl</term> <note>Literally "Lord," the common title for Marduk</note> destroy you!

s: In Theocritus' second Idyll, Simaetha's love rite works by likeness: as the laurel burns and the wax melts, so may Delphis burn and melt with love.

src.l: Theocritus, 1515, Bucolica (Greek, early printed edition)
src.q:
As I melt this wax with divine help,
May the Myndian Delphis melt immediately with love.

s: Lucan's Thessalian witch Erictho prays to no god above, yet the gods grant every crime at the first word of her petition.

src.l: Lucan, J. D. Duff (tr.), 1928, Lucan: The Civil War (Loeb)
src.q: The gods grant every crime at the very first word of her petition, and they fear to hear a second song.

s: Thorndike reads the Apology as hinting that Roman law did not condemn a man for magic unless he was shown to have done harm or gained unjustly by it.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. I
src.q: This is significant as hinting that Roman law did not condemn a man for magic unless he were proved to have committed some crime or made some unjust gain thereby.

s: The word 'magic' in the ancient sources is often the accuser's term: Apuleius shows it applied to philosophers and pious men, so Pliny's hostile genealogy (and our use of 'magic' for Babylonian temple exorcism) must say whose label it is.

src.l: Apuleius, H. E. Butler (tr.), 1909, The Apologia and Florida of Apuleius of Madaura
src.q: Others call those magicians who bestow unusual care on the investigation of the workings of providence and unusual devotion on their worship of the gods

s: Tylor (1871) calls the belief in magic 'one of the most pernicious delusions' and places its main principle in 'the lowest known stages of civilization', surviving among modern nations as a survival.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: much may be learnt from the history of one of the most pernicious delusions that ever vexed mankind, the belief in Magic ... It belongs in its main principle to the lowest known stages of civilization

s: Tylor makes the 'Association of Ideas' the principal key to occult science: man wrongly inverted connections found in experience, concluding that association in thought must involve similar connection in reality.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: The principal key to the understanding of Occult Science is to consider it as based on the Association of Ideas ... and to conclude that association in thought must involve similar connexion in reality.

s: Tylor reports that peoples who themselves believe in magic regularly ascribe the stronger magic to races they consider less civilized, giving as an example the Malays' resort to the sorcerers of the Mintira.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: nations who believe with the sincerest terror in the reality of the magic art, at the same time cannot shut their eyes to the fact that it more essentially belongs to, and is more thoroughly at home among, races less civilized than themselves.

s: Tylor notes that Protestants in Scotland, England and Germany credited Catholic priests with power to cast out devils, lay ghosts and counter witchcraft that they denied their own clergy.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: Protestants get the aid of Catholic priests and monks to help them against witchcraft, to lay ghosts, consecrate herbs, and discover thieves

s: In the first edition of The Golden Bough (vol. II, 1890) Frazer argues that hunters used sympathetic magic before they worshipped game, and that 'sympathetic magic is one of the earliest means' by which man adapts nature to his needs.

src.l: James George Frazer, 1890, The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion, Vol. II
src.q: sympathetic magic is one of the earliest means by which man endeavours to adapt the agencies of nature to his needs.

s: Frazer collects cases in which eating an animal is believed to transfer its qualities: the Zaparo avoid heavy meats lest they become unwieldy, and the Namaquas avoid hare lest they become faint-hearted.

src.l: James George Frazer, 1890, The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion, Vol. II
src.q: The Namaquas abstain from eating the flesh of hares, because they think it would make them faint-hearted as a hare. But they eat the flesh of the lion, or drink the blood of the leopard or lion to get the courage and strength of these beasts.

s: Frazer's 'transference of ills' section gives cures in which a disease is believed to pass into a leaf, stick or animal that is then thrown away or beaten, e.g. epilepsy passed into leaves.

src.l: James George Frazer, 1890, The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion, Vol. II
src.q: The epilepsy is believed to have passed into the leaves, and to have been thrown away with them.

s: Codrington (1891) describes Melanesian mana as a power outside the common processes of nature whose presence 'is ascertained by proof': a stone resembling a fruit is buried in the garden, and a good crop shows it has mana.

src.l: Robert Henry Codrington, 1891, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore
src.q: the presence of it is ascertained by proof. A man comes by chance upon a stone which takes his fancy; its shape is singular, it is like something, it is certainly not a common stone, there must be mana in it.

s: Codrington writes that a charm of words is itself called a mana, and that this power, 'though itself impersonal, is always connected with some person who directs it'.

src.l: Robert Henry Codrington, 1891, The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-lore
src.q: certain forms of words, generally in the form of a song, have power for certain purposes; a charm of words is called a mana. But this power, though itself impersonal, is always connected with some person who directs it

s: Doutté (1909), following Frazer, Hubert and Mauss and Fossey, places magic at the base of religion and holds that 'in the beginning, religion, like sorcery, was magic', while granting that a forbidden magic (sorcery) probably existed even then.

src.l: Edmond Doutté, 1909, Magie et religion dans l'Afrique du Nord
src.q: With Frazer, Hubert and Mauss, Fossey, etc., we place magic at the base of religion, in the sense that for us, religion began by being essentially magical ... for in the beginning, religion, like sorcery, was magic.
src.qo: Avec Frazer, Hubert et Mauss, Fossey, etc. ... nous plaçons la magie à la base de la religion, en ce sens que pour nous la religion a commencé par être essentiellement magique ; mais il y avait aussi probablement dès cette époque une magie interdite, c'est-à-dire une sorcellerie(4) ; à Jevons, Lang, et aux théologiens nous concédons que plus tard la sorcellerie, issue de la magie, emprunta ses éléments à la religion et en arriva à se présenter comme une dégénérescence (ou plutôt une contrepartie) de celle-ci ; à Davies, que la sorcellerie est nécessairement distincte de la religion, mais nous estimons que la magie enveloppait les deux à l'origine(5) : car au commencement la religion, comme la sorcellerie, était une magie.

s: Doutté adopts Hubert and Mauss's definition of magic as 'the domain of desire', a system of a priori inductions made under the pressure of need by groups, and concludes that magic is above all a technique.

src.l: Edmond Doutté, 1909, Magie et religion dans l'Afrique du Nord (second SL copy, shelf dated 1908)
src.q: Magic is the domain of desire... Magic is a system of a priori ... inductions carried out under the pressure of need by groups of individuals

s: Doutté says that in many languages the word for magic comes from a root meaning 'to do' or 'to act', citing Assyrian, while noting that the Arabic words for magic come from different roots.

src.l: Edmond Doutté, 1909, Magie et religion dans l'Afrique du Nord (second SL copy, shelf dated 1908)
src.q: Magic is therefore, above all, a technique; in many languages, the word used to designate it comes from a root meaning “to do” or “to act.”
src.qo: La magie est donc avant tout une technique ; dans beaucoup de langues le mot qui la désigne vient de la racine signifiant « faire, agir » ;

s: Doutté, developing Hubert and Mauss, calls magic 'originally a collective creation' and says the magician exists as an individual only because his fellow tribesmen solicit and expect his magical acts.

src.l: Edmond Doutté, 1909, Magie et religion dans l'Afrique du Nord (second SL copy, shelf dated 1908)
src.q: Magic is, above all, originally a collective creation: it is the imagination of the entire clan at work
src.qo: La magie est avant tout à l'origine une création collective : c'est le clan tout entier dont l'imagination travaille,

s: Doutté objects to Frazer and Jevons that magic is not, in its origins, a 'false science': the 'primitive' lacks the notion of an invariable cause-effect relation, and magic is a practice 'felt rather than perceived'.

src.l: Edmond Doutté, 1909, Magie et religion dans l'Afrique du Nord (second SL copy, shelf dated 1908)
src.q: We therefore believe that one cannot say, alongside Frazer and Jevons, that magic is a "false science" (2), at least in its origins: it is merely a practice, poorly adapted to its goal and felt rather than perceived (3).
src.qo: Nous pensons donc qu'on ne peut pas dire avec Frazer et Jevons que la magie est une science fausse (2), au moins dans ses origines : elle n'est qu'une pratique, mal adaptée à son but et plutôt sentie que perçue (3).

s: Westermarck (1926), accepting Frazer's distinction, says magic deals with 'impersonal forces' and aims at control or constraint, not conciliation; when it addresses spirits it coerces them.

src.l: Edward Westermarck, 1926, Ritual and Belief in Morocco, Vol. 1
src.q: Magic, on the other hand, deals with “ impersonal forces ”, and aims at control or constraint, not conciliation.

s: Westermarck locates the difference between religion and magic in the practitioner's mental state: the religious attitude is 'respectful and humble', the magical 'domineering and self-assertive'.

src.l: Edward Westermarck, 1926, Ritual and Belief in Morocco, Vol. 1
src.q: The religious attitude is in its nature respectful and humble, the magical attitude is domineering and self-assertive.

s: Westermarck claims support from medieval conceptions: theologians mostly attributed magic's success to demons, but demons worked marvels largely through superior knowledge of the forces of nature (citing Thorndike).

src.l: Edward Westermarck, 1926, Ritual and Belief in Morocco, Vol. 1
src.q: the theologians mostly attributed the success of magic to demons, who were enticed by men to work marvels ; but the demons were able to do so largely through their superior knowledge of the forces of nature.

s: Catharine Cook Smith (1930) argues that Frazer misreads primitive mentality by transferring his own logical premise to the sorcerer, so that the magician appears as an unsuccessful scientist or a wilful deceiver.

src.l: Catharine Cook Smith, 1930, In Defense of Magic: The Meaning and Use of Symbol and Rite
src.q: If Fraser himself were performing a magic rite, he would have a logical premise and would look for a reasonable result. This attitude he transfers to the primitive sorcerer

s: Skeat (1900) describes the Malay Pawang as the accredited intermediary between men and spirits, a constituted village functionary who has 'nothing whatever to do' with the official Muhammadan religion of the mosque.

src.l: Walter William Skeat, 1900, Malay Magic: Being an Introduction to the Folklore and Popular Religion of the Malay Peninsula
src.q: It must be clearly understood that he has nothing whatever to do with the official Muhammadan religion of the mosque

s: Andrew Lang (1898) summarises the then-established Tylorian conclusion that 'the ideas of God and of the soul are the result of early fallacious reasonings about misunderstood experiences', in order to propose revising it.

src.l: Andrew Lang, 1898, The Making of Religion
src.q: Thus the ideas of God and of the soul are the result of early fallacious reasonings about misunderstood experiences.

s: The Arabic Picatrix defines magic (siḥr) as whatever has a cause hidden from most minds and a derivation hard to deduce.

src.l: Pseudo-Majriti, c. 1000, Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm (Arabic Picatrix), ed. Ritter
src.loc: p. 13, bk I ch. 2 (definition of magic)
src.q: In short, Magic is that whose cause is hidden from most minds and whose derivation is difficult to deduce.

s: The Ghāya distinguishes three operative arts by their subject: nīranj ("spirit within spirit"), the talisman ("spirit within a body") and alchemy ("body within a body").

src.l: Pseudo-Majriti, c. 1000, Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm (Arabic Picatrix), ed. Ritter
src.q: In contrast, the subject of a Talisman is "spirit within a body," and the subject of Alchemy is "body within a body."

s: The Ghāya holds that choosing an astrological moment (an election) is itself already the making of a talisman.

src.l: Pseudo-Majriti, c. 1000, Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm (Arabic Picatrix), ed. Ritter
src.q: Know that whoever makes a choice of timing has effectively created a talisman; this is an essential principle.

s: The Ghāya calls speech and gesture "the finest type of common magic", citing the prophetic hadith "Truly, some speech is magic".

src.l: Pseudo-Majriti, c. 1000, Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm (Arabic Picatrix), ed. Ritter
src.q: The finest type of common magic is speech and similar gestures, as indicated by the Prophetic saying: "Truly, some speech is magic."

s: For the Ghāya, practical magic works through the "specific properties" (khawāṣṣ) of minerals, plants and animals, i.e. planetary powers dispersed in the three kingdoms, used even by those who do not know their cause.

src.l: Pseudo-Majriti, c. 1000, Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm (Arabic Picatrix), ed. Ritter
src.q: Practical magic consists of understanding the three kingdoms of nature and the planetary powers dispersed within them. These are referred to as specific properties by those who believe in them, though they may not understand their cause

s: The Ghāya makes the operator's certainty a working condition: it strengthens the rational soul so that the will connects with the World Soul.

src.l: Pseudo-Majriti, c. 1000, Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm (Arabic Picatrix), ed. Ritter
src.q: This certainty strengthens the action of the Rational Soul, allowing the practitioner’s will to connect with the "World Soul" to achieve the desired result.

s: The Ghāya sets out the 28 lunar mansions for talismanic timing "according to the consensus of the Indian Sages", and forbids any work until the Moon is in the degree proper to it.

src.l: Pseudo-Majriti, c. 1000, Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm (Arabic Picatrix), ed. Ritter
src.loc: p. 17, bk I ch. 4 (mansions of the Moon)
src.q: do not perform any work until the Moon is in the specific degree that corresponds to that work.

s: The Ghāya says the masters agree that words spoken over a talisman are essential, quoting "Timaeus": speech is to the talisman what the soul is to the body.

src.l: Pseudo-Majriti, c. 1000, Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm (Arabic Picatrix), ed. Ritter
src.q: The speech used over talismans holds the same place as the soul does for the body; it is the mover of the spiritual powers.

s: The Ghāya opens its second treatise by citing pseudo-Ptolemy's Fruit (Centiloquium): images in the world of composition are subject to celestial images.

src.l: Pseudo-Majriti, c. 1000, Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm (Arabic Picatrix), ed. Ritter
src.q: I saw the virtuous Ptolemy saying in his famous book The Fruit: "The images in the world of composition are submissive to celestial images."

s: The Ghāya models the composite talisman on compound medicine: as physicians compound simples into electuaries, the talismanic body is compounded to receive a specific effect.

src.l: Pseudo-Majriti, c. 1000, Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm (Arabic Picatrix), ed. Ritter
src.q: This state is similar to the medicines that physicians prescribe for the treatment of diseases and pains.

s: The Ghāya gives rites for drawing down the Moon's power in each sign, e.g. for Taurus: a chosen place, a rooster, a censer, ritual washing and a linen garment.

src.l: Pseudo-Majriti, c. 1000, Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm (Arabic Picatrix), ed. Ritter
src.loc: p. 158, bk III (drawing down the power of the Moon)
src.q: When the Moon is in Taurus, seek out a location as previously described. Bring with you a rooster, as I mentioned to you, and a censer.

s: Ibn Khaldun distinguishes the prophetic miracle from a saint's karāma and from sorcery by the "challenge" (taḥaddī) the prophet issues in advance.

src.l: Ibn Khaldun, 1858, Muqaddima (Prolégomènes d'Ebn-Khaldoun, Arabic text ed. Quatremère, vol. 1)
src.loc: Muqaddima, Prolégomènes vol. 1, p. 182 [scan], ch. on prophecy
src.q: The challenge is what distinguishes it from the karamah miracle of a saint and sorcery, as there is no need for authentication in them
src.qo: والتحدي هو الفارق بينها وبين الكرامة والسحر اذ لا حاجة فيهما الى التصديق

s: Ibn Khaldun reports that for the philosophers (ḥukamāʾ) the prophetic soul has essential properties by which supernatural events issue from it and the elements obey it.

src.l: Ibn Khaldun, 1858, Muqaddima (Prolégomènes d'Ebn-Khaldoun, Arabic text ed. Quatremère, vol. 1)
src.q: The prophetic soul, according to them, has essential properties, among which is the issuing of these supernatural events by his power and the obedience of the elements to him in creation.
src.qo: وان النفس النبوية عندهم لها خواص ذاتية منها صدور هذه الخوارق بقدرته وطاعة العناصر له في التكوين

s: Ibn Khaldun explains soothsaying (kahāna) as a deficient power of the soul that leans on sensory media such as transparent bodies, animal bones, rhymed speech, or birds.

src.l: Ibn Khaldun, 1858, Muqaddima (Prolégomènes d'Ebn-Khaldoun, Arabic text ed. Quatremère, vol. 1)
src.q: they cling to partial, sensory, or imagined matters, such as transparent bodies, animal bones, rhymed speech, or whatever may occur of birds or animals.
src.qo: تشبث بامور جزئية محسوسة او متخيلة كالاجسام الشفافة وعظام الحيوان وسجع الكلام وما يسنح من طير او حيوان

s: Ibn Khaldun says he himself had "wondrous visions" by reciting dream-names, while arguing the recitation only prepares the soul and does not cause the vision.

src.l: Ibn Khaldun, 1858, Muqaddima (Prolégomènes d'Ebn-Khaldoun, Arabic text ed. Quatremère, vol. 1)
src.q: I have personally had wondrous visions using these names, and through them, I gained knowledge of matters I was seeking regarding my own conditions.
src.qo: وقد وقع لي انا بهذه الاسماء مراء عجيبة واطلعت بها على امور كنت اتشوف اليها من احوالي

s: Ibn Khaldun denies that the hadith "there was a prophet who would write lines" licenses geomancy (khaṭṭ al-raml) for knowing the unseen.

src.l: Ibn Khaldun, 1858, Muqaddima (Prolégomènes d'Ebn-Khaldoun, Arabic text ed. Quatremère, vol. 1)
src.q: It contains no evidence for the legitimacy of sand divination, nor the permissibility of adopting it to know the unseen
src.qo: وليس فيه دلالة على مشروعية خط الرمل ولا جواز انتحاله لتعرف الغيب

s: Ibn Khaldun allows geomancy only as a way to occupy the senses so that the soul turns to the spiritual world; used as a technique for knowing the unseen it is "nonsense of speech and action".

src.l: Ibn Khaldun, 1858, Muqaddima (Prolégomènes d'Ebn-Khaldoun, Arabic text ed. Quatremère, vol. 1)
src.q: If it is not so, and he only intended the knowledge of the unseen through this craft, then it is nonsense of speech and action
src.qo: وان لم يكن كذلك وانما قصد معرفة الغيب بهذه الصناعة فهذر من القول والعمل

s: Ibn Khaldun describes the "ḥisāb al-nīm", predicting the victor of two kings from the abjad value of their names, as attributed to the end of the pseudo-Aristotelian book on politics.

src.l: Ibn Khaldun, 1858, Muqaddima (Prolégomènes d'Ebn-Khaldoun, Arabic text ed. Quatremère, vol. 1)
src.q: which is mentioned at the end of the book on politics attributed to Aristotle.
src.qo: وهو مذكور في آخر كتاب السياسة المنسوب لارسطو

s: Macdonald (1912), paraphrasing the Muqaddima's chapter on siḥr, reports Ibn Khaldun's view that magicians have an inborn psychic power to influence things and draw down the spiritual force of the stars.

src.l: Duncan Black Macdonald, 1912, The Religious Attitude and Life in Islam
src.q: In magicians, on the other hand, there is a peculiar psychic power by which they influence these things and draw down and apply the spiritual force of the stars

s: Per Macdonald, Ibn Khaldun ranks three kinds of magic: by the soul alone, by aid of spheres/elements/numbers ("talismanic art", weaker), and by working on the imagination (conjuring).

src.l: Duncan Black Macdonald, 1912, The Religious Attitude and Life in Islam
src.q: This they call talismanic art, and this kind is weaker than the first.

s: Macdonald reports that Ibn Khaldun held the reality of the first two kinds of magic certain, citing the Qurʾān on Hārūt and Mārūt and the "blowers on knots".

src.l: Duncan Black Macdonald, 1912, The Religious Attitude and Life in Islam
src.q: On that point, Ibn Khaldūn has no doubt; all reasonable men admit it, and the Qur'ān speaks of it with perfect clearness.

s: Macdonald retells Ibn Khaldun's eyewitness account of a sorcerer who made a figure of the victim, knotted a cord and blew on it, an evil spirit going out with the saliva.

src.l: Duncan Black Macdonald, 1912, The Religious Attitude and Life in Islam
src.q: The idea was that an evil spirit went out from him when he blew, attached to his saliva, and fell upon his victim.

s: The Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ list among their epistles one "on the Essence of Magic and Incantations", covering the evil eye, omens, spells, talismans, and how jinn, devils and spiritual beings act on one another.

src.l: Ikhwan al-Safa, 1887, Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa (Epistles of the Brethren of Purity)
src.q: The Eleventh of them is on the Essence of Magic and Incantations. It concerns the essence of the evil eye, omens, portents, imagination, spells, and the manner of the operations of the remaining talismans
src.qo: الرسالة الحادية عشر منها فى ماهية السحر والعزائم وماهية العين والزجر والفال والوهم والرقى وكيفية اعمال الطلسمات الباقية

s: The Ikhwān compare the makers of talismans to physicians compounding remedies, giving the nine-cell square for easing childbirth as their example.

src.l: Ikhwan al-Safa, 1887, Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa (Epistles of the Brethren of Purity)
src.q: In similar fashion, the masters of tilsamat talismans worked in setting them up after their knowledge of the natures of things, their properties, their similarities, and the method of their composition and the ratios of their assembly.
src.qo: وعلى مثل ذلك عملوا اصحاب الطلسمات في نصبها بعد معرفتهم بطبائع الاشيا وخواصها ومشاكلتها وكيفية تركيبها ونسب تاليفها

s: In the Ikhwān's classification, "the science of magic, incantations" sits among the propaedeutic sciences beside divination, alchemy, mechanics and trades.

src.l: Ikhwan al-Safa, 1887, Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa (Epistles of the Brethren of Purity)
src.q: the science of divination and omens and the like, the science of magic, incantations, alchemy, mechanics and the like, the science of crafts and trades
src.qo: ومنها علم الزجر والفال وما يشاكله ومنها علم السحر والعزائم والكيمياء والحيل وما شاكلها ومنها علم الحرف والصنائع

s: Lane (writing in Egypt in the 1830s) reports that belief in magic is held by almost all Muslims and that one who denies it is regarded as a freethinker or infidel.

src.l: Edward William Lane, 1883, Arabian Society in the Middle Ages
src.q: An implicit belief in magic is entertained by almost all Muslims ; and him among them who denies its truth they regard as a freethinker or an infidel.

s: Lane reports that "spiritual magic" (rūḥānī) works through names of God, Qurʾān passages, angels and jinn, and is divided into Divine (raḥmānī) and Satanic (shayṭānī).

src.l: Edward William Lane, 1883, Arabian Society in the Middle Ages
src.q: It is of two kinds: High and Low ('Ilwee and Suflee), or Divine and Satanic

s: Lane reports that Muslims regard Babel as the fountainhead of magic, taught to mankind by the fallen angels Hārūt and Mārūt.

src.l: Edward William Lane, 1883, Arabian Society in the Middle Ages
src.q: Bábil, or Babel, is regarded by the Muslims as the fountain head of the science of magic

s: Lane reports that siḥr (enchantment) is almost universally counted a branch of satanic magic, though a few hold it can be practised with good jinn.

src.l: Edward William Lane, 1883, Arabian Society in the Middle Ages
src.q: Enchantment, which is termed es-Seḥr, is almost universally acknowledged to be a branch of satanic magic

s: Lane reports that natural magic (sīmiyāʾ) is regarded by enlightened Muslims as deceptive, like legerdemain, and that alchemy is counted a branch of it.

src.l: Edward William Lane, 1883, Arabian Society in the Middle Ages
src.q: Natural magic, which is called es-Seemiyà, is regarded by most persons of the more enlightened classes of Muslims as altogether a deceptive art, no more worthy of respect than legerdemain

s: The Shams al-Maʿārif text on SL teaches that numbers have a spiritual power and act on humans imperceptibly, which is why there are "secrets of benefit" in the letters.

src.l: Ahmad ibn Ali al-Buni (attrib.), 1700, Shams al-Maʿārif al-Kubrā (MS, c. 1700)
src.q: For numbers have an effect on humans that they do not perceive, for His power is glorified.
src.qo: وللإعداد ● فعال في البشر لا يدركون رتبها جلت قدرته

s: The Shams text promises that the angelic servants of two divine names will leave a gold dinar under the pillow nightly, on conditions of piety, grave-visiting and recitation.

src.l: Ahmad ibn Ali al-Buni (attrib.), 1700, Shams al-Maʿārif al-Kubrā (MS, c. 1700)
src.q: Know that the servants of these two noble names are among the believing angels
src.qo: واعلم ان خدام هذين الاسمين الشريفين من الملائكة المؤمنين

s: An Arabic Hermetic magical collection states, as Hermes's, that success depends on sound reports, sound intention, strong knowledge of spirituality (rūḥāniyya), and secrecy.

src.l: Hermes Trismegistus (attrib.), early 14th century, Collection of magical and other treatises ascribed to Hermes Trismegistus (Arabic MS)
src.q: I found in the Stored Book that the soundness of the secret is obtained from four aspects: the first is the correct reports found in the mentioned, known, and famous practices among us. The second aspect is the soundness of concern, determination, and intention.
src.qo: ...المذكورة ...الذي ...العقلي ...افضل قال هرمس وجدت في الكتاب المكنون ان صحة السر يحصل من اربعة اوجه احدها الاخبار الصحيحة التي يوجد على الموارس المذكورة المعلومة المشهورة عندنا والوجه الثاني صحة الهمة والعزم والنية

s: An Arabic geomancy manual (Ijtimāʿ al-shaml) names Thābit ibn Qurra al-Ḥarrānī among the masters who verified how to compose names from letters assigned to the four natures and the lunar mansions.

src.l: Anonymous, 1400, Ijtimāʿ al-shaml fī ṭarīq al-raml (geomancy)
src.loc: p. 89 [scan], table of the balance of letters
src.q: This is what the masters Ṭamṭam, al-Zanātī, al-Ghadāmisī, al-Ṭarābulusī, al-Hamadānī, and Thābit ibn Qurra al-Ḥarrānī agreed upon and verified regarding the manner of composing names from them.
src.qo: هَذَا مَا اتَّفَقَتْ عَلَيْهِ المَشَايِخ طَمْطَم وَالزَّنَاتِي وَالغَدَامِسِي وَالطَرَابُلُسِي وَالهَمَدَانِي وَثَابِت ابْن قُرَّه الحَرَّانِي وَصَحَّحُوهُ فِي كَيْفِيَّةِ تَرْكِيبِ الأَسْمَا مِنْهَا

s: The Kitāb al-Bulhān combines nativity lore credited to Abū Maʿshar with amulet prescriptions, e.g. the amulet (ḥirz) of Dajlah al-Anṣārī for women born under Capricorn.

src.l: Abd al-Hasan al-Isfahani, c. 1400, Kitāb al-Bulhān (Book of Wonders), Bodleian MS. Bodl. Or. 133
src.q: one should not fail to attach an amulet hirz of Dajlah al-Ansari upon them, for it suffices against their evil

s: Thorndike (1923) describes Thābit's Latin De imaginibus as opening with the need for astronomy in order to perform magic, its images made under prescribed constellations.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. I
src.loc: Vol. I, ch. XXVIII "Arabic Occult Science", p. 665 [scan 711]
src.q: The work begins by emphasizing the need of a knowl- edge of astronomy in order to perform feats of magic (praestigia).

s: Wellhausen (1897) reports that among the Arabs the practitioners of siḥr are men and women, with witches predominating, and that witches serve demons rather than command them.

src.l: Julius Wellhausen, 1897, Reste arabischen Heidentumes
src.q: The Arabic term for magic is sihr . There are people who practice it professionally, both men and women . Witches, however, predominate.
src.qo: Der arabische Ausdruck für Zauber ist سحر¹). Es gibt Leute, die ihn professionell betreiben, Männer und Weiber²). Die Hexen aber überwiegen.

s: Zwemer (1920), a missionary writer, asserts that no orthodox Muslim doubts that men can call forth demons and jinn by siḥr.

src.l: Samuel Marinus Zwemer, 1920, The Influence of Animism on Islam
src.q: No orthodox Moslem doubts that men are able to call forth the power of demons and Jinn by means of magic (sihr).

s: Thorndike judged the (Latin) Picatrix "a confused compilation" and "hodgepodge" of recipes, against reading it as a systematic theory of magic.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: In short, the work is a confused compilation of extracts from occult writings and a hodgepodge of innumerable magical and astrological recipes.

s: "Arabian Society in the Middle Ages" describes Egyptian practice observed in the 1830s (Lane notes "I write in 1837"), so its chapter on magic is not direct evidence for medieval belief.

src.l: Edward William Lane, 1883, Arabian Society in the Middle Ages
src.q: I write in 1837.

s: Bloomfield reports that a Brāhmaṇa passage (Śat. Br. X.5.2.20) presents yātu, 'sorcery', and the yātuvidaḥ, 'those skilled in sorcery', as the representatives of the fourth (Atharva) Veda, and that bheṣaja (healing charms) and yātu together make up what the name atharvāṅgirasaḥ embraces.

src.l: Maurice Bloomfield, 1897, Hymns of the Atharva-Veda (Sacred Books of the East 42)
src.q: the author presents yâtu, 'sorcery,' and the yâtuvidah, 'those skilled in sorcery,' as representatives of the fourth Veda. The bheshagâ of the Atharvan passage, and the yâtu of the present passage, make up together what is embraced in the name atharvâṅgirasaḥ

s: Bloomfield concludes that in the Vedic ritual texts witchcraft is blended with every sphere of religious thought and is judged useful or noxious only according to whom it is turned against.

src.l: Maurice Bloomfield, 1897, Hymns of the Atharva-Veda (Sacred Books of the East 42)
src.q: Witchcraft is blended with every sphere of religious thought and activity ... witchcraft blows hot and cold from the same mouth ; according as it is turned towards the inimical forces, human and demoniac, or is turned by others against oneself, it is regarded as useful, or noxious.

s: Bloomfield's arrangement of the Atharvaveda groups 'imprecations against demons, sorcerers, and enemies' under the native classes ābhicārikāṇi (hostile rites) and kṛtyāpratiharaṇāni (rites that turn back a kṛtyā, a spell or witchcraft), and opens with a hymn asking Agni to bring the self-vaunting sorcerer (yātudhāna) and make the sorcerers howl.

src.l: Maurice Bloomfield, 1897, Hymns of the Atharva-Veda (Sacred Books of the East 42)
src.q: IMPRECATIONS AGAINST DEMONS, SORCERERS, AND ENEMIES (ÂBHIKÂRIKÂNI AND KRITYÂPRATIHARANÂNI). I, 7. Against sorcerers and demons. 1. The sorcerer (yâtudhâna) that vaunts himself, and the Kimîdin do thou, O Agni, convey hither!

s: In Bloomfield's Atharvaveda the spell itself is addressed in the second person and threatened with dismemberment ('I shall hew off, O spell, thy neck, and thy feet: run away!'), with Indra and Agni called on to protect.

src.l: Maurice Bloomfield, 1897, Hymns of the Atharva-Veda (Sacred Books of the East 42)
src.q: I shall hew off, O spell, thy neck, and thy feet: run away! May Indra and Agni, to whom belong the children (of men), protect us!

s: Oldenberg argues that in Vedic practice magic and sacrifice mixed early: magical acts came to resemble or combine with sacrifices, magic's mode of action was transferred to the sacrifice, and the sacrificial setting, 'saturated with ideas of divine proximity and mysterious success', invited sorcery (Zauberei) like no other.

src.l: Hermann Oldenberg, 1894, Die Religion des Veda
src.q: Acts of sorcery were often similar to sacrificial acts, and became increasingly adapted to them ... where the manner of operation belonging to sorcery was then transferred to the sacrifice as well

s: Mahīdhara's Mantramahodadhi (1589) defines the six acts (ṣaṭkarman) of mantra practice: śānti for destroying diseases, vaśya for making others obey, stambhana for arresting hostile activity, dveṣa for creating dislike between lovers, uccāṭana for removal from one's place, and māraṇa for taking life.

src.l: Mahīdhara, Jibananda Vidyasagara (ed.), 1892, Mantramahodadhi (The Ocean of Mantras)
src.q: Now I shall state the six acts ... which provide success through their application: peace ... subjugation ... immobilization ... sowing discord ... driving away ... and killing

s: The Mantramahodadhi keys each of the six acts to a set of variables to be matched: deity, the deity's colour, season, direction, day, seat, arrangement (vinyāsa), maṇḍala, mudrā and letter.

src.l: Mahīdhara, Jibananda Vidyasagara (ed.), 1892, Mantramahodadhi (The Ocean of Mantras)
src.q: Deity, color of the deity, season, direction, day, seat, arrangement
src.qo: देवता देवता वर्णाः ऋतु दिक्दिवसासनम् ।

s: The Śāradātilaka gives the same six acts ('peace, subjection, paralysis, causing malice, driving away, and death') as yielding success 'according to all the tantras', defining śānti as the removal of diseases and decay and vaśya as making all people obedient.

src.l: Lakṣmaṇadeśika, 1100, Śāradātilaka Tantra
src.q: Now I will describe in this tantra the characteristics of the six acts, which yield success in practice according to all the tantras. (121) The wise speak of the six acts: peace, subjection, paralysis, causing malice, driving away, and death.
src.qo: अथाभिधास्ये तन्त्रेऽस्मिन् सम्यक् षट्कर्मलक्षणम् । सर्वतन्त्रानुसारण प्रयोगे फलसिद्धिदम् ॥ १२१ ॥ शान्तिर्वश्यस्तम्भनानि विद्वेषोच्चाटने ततः ।

s: The Śāradātilaka's hostile rite (abhicāra) to Kālī prescribes breaking an effigy of the enemy into seven parts and offering them into the kindled fire limb by limb (right foot, right hand, head, left hand ...) while reciting five ṛc verses.

src.l: Lakṣmaṇadeśika, 1100, Śāradātilaka Tantra
src.q: having broken the effigy into seven parts, one should offer [them] into the kindled fire while reciting the five ... (141) The first [part] is the right foot, followed by the right hand. The third is declared to be the head

s: A ritual in the Derge Tengyur (vol. 28) directs making an image of the victim from kuśa grass, smearing it with the three pungent spices, poison and mustard seed, and piercing it with a wooden stake.

src.l: Derge Tengyur (canonical collection), 1982–1985, bsTan 'gyur sde dge, rGyud 'grel, vol. 28 (Sha)
src.q: This is the ritual practice for that purpose: create an image of the victim ... Apply a mixture of the three pungent spices ... poison, and mustard seeds onto the image according to the rite. Pierce the image fully with a wooden stake

s: A Tengyur (vol. 48) rite for 'suppressing speech' (vāk-stambhana) has the practitioner draw two wheels (cakra) with the target's name inside and recite a formula built on the placeholder names Devadatta and Yajñadatta, framed by the seed syllable laṃ.

src.l: Derge Tengyur (canonical collection), 1982–1985, bsTan 'gyur sde dge, rGyud 'grel, vol. 48 (Tsi)
src.q: For those who desire to suppress speech: in the same manner, clearly draw two wheels ... with the name inserted inside.
src.qo: །།ངག་མནན་པར་འདོད་པས། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་མིང་ནང་དུ་བཅུག་པའི་འཁོར་ལོ་གཉིས་མངོན་པར་བྲིས་ཏེ།

s: In the Tantrāloka with its commentary, worship performed at the parva times fulfils one's desires 'even without specific astrological knowledge or yogic union', and the 'various tasks' it serves are glossed as acts such as pacification (śānti) or expulsion (uccāṭana).

src.l: Abhinavagupta, Jayaratha (comm.), 1000, Tantrāloka (with Jayaratha's Viveka)
src.q: during the ritual periods ... even without specific astrological knowledge or yogic union, one's desires may be fulfilled through worship alone.

s: Woodroffe argues that tantric seed-syllables (bīja) such as hrīṃ, śrīṃ, krīṃ, hūṃ and phaṭ only sound like 'gibberish' to outsiders: to the initiate each bīja is the own-form (svarūpa) of its deity, and every mantra is a particular sound-form of Brahman.

src.l: John Woodroffe (Arthur Avalon), 1927, Shakti and Shakta, 3rd ed.
src.q: the Tantras ... incurred the charge of "gibberish," for such the Bījas sound to those who do not know what they mean. Though a Mantra such as a Bīja-mantra may not convey its meaning on its face, the initiate knows that its meaning is the own form (Svarūpa) of the particular Devatā

s: The Kakṣapuṭa ascribed to Nāgārjuna prescribes writing a figure (an eight-petalled lotus) on birch bark to be worn on the head, adding that then 'one does not need to recite the mantra': the written object stands in for the spoken formula.

src.l: Nāgārjuna (attrib.), 1500, Kakṣapuṭa (shelf: The Manual of Secret Rituals)
src.q: an eight-petaled lotus on birch bark. ...having written it, one should wear it on the head; one does not need to recite the mantra.
src.qo: नीरनस्कनूर्जपत्रेमायावी॥नंदयेदले॥लिखित्वा धारयेन्मूर्ध्निमंत्रंनोजपेत्

s: The Kāmaratnam's appendix names eight yakṣiṇīs (Surasundarī, Manoharī, Kalāvatī, Kāmeśvarī, Raktakarī, Padminī, Naṭī, Anurāgiṇī) and gives the summoning mantra 'Om! Come, Surasundari, Svāhā!' with guggul incense and a thousand repetitions at the three junctions of the day.

src.l: Nityanātha (attrib.), 1899, Kāmaratnam
src.q: these are the eight Yakshinis ... "Om! Come, Surasundari, Svāhā!" This is the mantra. Having recited this, go home and offer

s: The Svara Tattva Udaya prints a four-by-four yantra 'for the destruction of ghosts (bhūta) and spirits (preta)' whose sixteen numbers form a magic square: every row, column and both diagonals sum to 34.

src.l: Anonymous, Unknown, Svara Tattva Udaya (The Rise of the Essence of Breath)
src.q: A protective diagram; a diagram that conquers the wicked and accomplishes all tasks. 16 9 4 5 3 6 15 10 13 12 1 8 2 7 14 11

s: Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra, a manual of statecraft, includes a section of 'medicinal and mantric operations for deception' in which a formula ending in svāhā serves for 'the opening of locks and the causing of sleep'.

src.l: Kauṭilya, 1919, Arthaśāstra
src.q: Medicinal and Mantric Operations for Deception ... you are the essence of bitterness, you are the moisture, ... this is the opening of locks and the causing of sleep.
src.qo: प्रलम्भने भैषज्यमन्त्रयोगः 423 चण्डालिकुम्भात्तुम्भकडुकसाराघः सनीरीभगोऽसि स्वाहा; 509·6 तालोद्घाटनं प्रस्वापनं च ।

s: The Mitākṣarā on the Yājñavalkya Smṛti explains that worship of the nine planets (graha-yajña) brings success by removing the obstructions that prevent the fruition of one's karma, and also brings good fortune (śrī).

src.l: Yājñavalkya, Vijñāneśvara (comm.), 1918, Yājñavalkya Smṛti with the Mitākṣarā
src.q: by the worship of the planets there results the success in all undertakings by the removal of obstructions which prevent the fruitions of Karmas

s: A Ming Daoist Canon text prescribes a talisman (fu) issued by the White Emperor to the Western Peak to avert the disaster of war in a given cyclical year, to be written in white ink on red silk.

src.l: Various (Daoist Canon), 1445, Zhengtong Daozang, vol. 5
src.q: The White Emperor issues the Middle Primordial Talisman to the Western Peak to deliver the people, controlling the heavenly distribution, eliminating the disaster of soldiers and weapons. Write in white ink on red silk
src.qo: 白書赤繪

s: De Groot reports from Amoy that sufferers from demoniacal fevers ate cakes on which men of letters had written exorcising characters, and that water in which a charm had been steeped, or mixed with the ashes of a burnt charm, was a still stronger medicine.

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1910, The Religious System of China, Vol. 6: Demonology and Sorcery
src.q: sufferers from fever or other demoniacal diseases eat cakes of flour on which schoolmasters or other men of letters have written exorcising characters ... A still more effective medicine for such patients is water in which a charm has been steeped or boiled, or which is mixed with ashes of a burnt charm.

s: De Groot quotes the Qing Code on ku (gu) poison-sorcery: the breeder's household is banished for life two thousand miles, a ward or village chief who knew and failed to report receives a hundred blows, and an informer is rewarded with twenty ounces of silver; he notes the Ming Code has the same terms.

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1907, The Religious System of China, Vol. 5: Demonology
src.q: receive one hundred blows with the long stick ... twenty ounces of silver ... These laws can boast of a respectable age, as we find them in the Code of the Ming dynasty

s: De Groot states that both the Ming and Qing dynasties considered ku (gu) the most common and typical mode of poisoning, and that the Code's notes list ku of snakes, geese, babies and gold caterpillars.

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1907, The Religious System of China, Vol. 5: Demonology
src.q: both dynasties considered k u to be the most common and typical mode of poisoning.

s: The Korean national code Taejŏn hoet'ong (1865) orders that those who create or keep gu poison be reported, rewards a proven informant with thirty pieces of cotton cloth, and gives false accusers the punishment intended for the accused.

src.l: Joseon court, 1865, Taejŏn hoet'ong (Comprehensive Collection of the National Code)
src.q: shall be reported; if the report is proven true, the informant shall be given thirty pieces of cotton cloth. ... False accusers shall receive the punishment intended for the accused.

s: De Groot's chapter on the wu (spirit-mediums) quotes a classical answer that 'anciently the functions with respect to the people and with regard to the gods were not exercised by the same persons', under his heading that the wu were possessed by spirits or gods.

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1910, The Religious System of China, Vol. 6: Demonology and Sorcery
src.q: THE WU WERE POSSESSED BY SPIRITS OR GODS.

s: Crooke records that the most famous and dreaded witch of the north Indian plains is Lona or Nona Chamārin, 'the salt one', a woman of the currier caste.

src.l: William Crooke, 1926, Religion and Folklore of Northern India
src.q: The most famous and dreaded witch in the northern plains is Lona or Nona Chamārin, ' the salt one ', a woman of the currier caste.

s: Waddell holds that magic, 'mostly of a sympathetic kind', crept into Indian Buddhism soon after the Buddha's death, citing irdhi (supernatural power) as an attribute of Arhats and the Paritta ('pirit') rite as essentially exorcism.

src.l: L. Austine Waddell, 1895, The Buddhism of Tibet, or Lamaism
src.q: Magic, and this mostly of a sympathetic kind, seems to have crept into Indian Buddhism soon after Buddha's death.

s: A Bhutanese bKa' brgyad ritual text repeats the command to repel curses of earth-lords, nāgas and yakṣas 'with this great red torma' and to turn their magical displays back upon the enemy.

src.l: Gangtey Monastery Collection, Unknown, bKa' brgyad yang bla med
src.q: Repel it! Repel it with this great red torma! Turn it! Turn the magical displays of the Nagas back upon the enemy!

s: A Bhutanese Lama-heart-practice text instructs the officiant to recite fierce mantras and hurl the torma-weapon (zor) so that 'enemies and obstructors' are 'destroyed like particles of ash'.

src.l: Gangtey Monastery Collection, Unknown, Bla ma'i thugs sgrub bar chad kun sel sogs
src.q: Let them be reduced to ruin without even a name remaining! Let them be destroyed like particles of ash! Recite the fierce mantras and hurl the torma-zor!

s: In Amoghavajra's Precious Casket Seal Dhāraṇī Sūtra the Buddha attributes the method's extraordinary merit to 'the divine power of this Precious Casket Seal Dharani', which contains the whole-body relic of all buddhas past, present and future.

src.l: Amoghavajra (Bukong, tr.), Tang, Yiqie rulai xin mimi quanshen sheli baoqieyin tuoluoni jing (Precious Casket Seal Dhāraṇī Sūtra)
src.q: The Buddha told Vajrapani: "It is because of the divine power of this Precious Casket Seal Dharani."

s: In Hearn's Japanese ghost story a priest gives a package of o-fuda to be pasted over every opening of the house, so that 'the power of the holy texts will prevent the dead from entering'.

src.l: Lafcadio Hearn, 1900, In Ghostly Japan
src.q: you must paste one of them over every opening of your house, — no matter how small. If you do this, the power of the holy texts will prevent the dead from entering.

s: Joly's dictionary describes Abe no Seimei, the most famous onmyōji, as court astrologer, son of a fox mother, who cured the emperor's illness by detecting a nine-tailed fox in the favourite concubine Tamamo no Mae.

src.l: Henri L. Joly, 1908, Legend in Japanese Art
src.q: Court Astrologer, son of Abe no Yasuna, occasionally shown with his fox mother Kuzunoha, who holds a writing brush in her mouth. He cured a grave illness of the Emperor TobA, proving that he was bewitched by no other than his own favorite concubine

s: Picart (1723) reports that the Japanese table of good and bad days was attributed to an astrologer named Seimei, learned in the influences of the stars and omens, whose supernatural birth from a fox was told to match his skill.

src.l: Bernard Picart, 1723, Cérémonies et coutumes religieuses des peuples idolâtres, tome second
src.q: The table of good and bad days is the invention of a certain Astrologer named ... very learned in Astrology and in everything concerning the influences of the Stars and Omens.

s: Esdaile reports performing surgery in Bengal on a patient in mesmeric trance, who woke only during the amputation and relapsed into a rigid, insensible trance with eyes open and pupils dilated.

src.l: James Esdaile, 1851, Mesmerism in India
src.q: he relapsed into the trance again in a few minutes, and remained for twenty minutes, quite rigid, and insensible, with his eyes wide open, and the pupils dilated

s: Doré reports that in China, in all the difficulties of life, people go to the pagoda to burn incense, to divine with blocks (pou-koa) or lots, to pray to a deity, or to buy a petition or talisman.

src.l: Henri Doré, 1915, Recherches sur les superstitions en Chine, vol. 10
src.q: In all the difficulties of life, one goes to the pagoda to burn incense, to perform the ... or the ... to pray to such and such a divinity, or to buy such a petition or talisman.

s: Critique: Bloomfield's reading of the Vedic ritual texts, that witchcraft was 'blended with every sphere of religious thought' and accepted with 'no evidence of repugnance or exclusiveness', tells against Oldenberg's model of two originally separate procedures, magic (Zauber) and sacrifice (Opfer), that later mixed; and against Frazer-style magic/religion staging generally.

src.l: Maurice Bloomfield, 1897, Hymns of the Atharva-Veda (Sacred Books of the East 42)
src.q: there is no evidence of repugnance or exclusiveness. ... Witchcraft is blended with every sphere of religious thought and activity

s: Critique: Woodroffe objects that the 'gibberish' charge against tantric bīja-mantras is an outsider's judgement by those who do not know what they mean; this tells against Waddell-style readings of tantric and lamaist mantra rites as charlatanism and against filing mantra under meaningless voces magicae.

src.l: John Woodroffe (Arthur Avalon), 1927, Shakti and Shakta, 3rd ed.
src.q: thus incurred the charge of "gibberish," for such the Bījas sound to those who do not know what they mean.

s: Frazer reduces the principles of thought behind magic to two: the Law of Similarity (like produces like) and the Law of Contact or Contagion (things once in contact go on acting on each other at a distance), whence 'Homoeopathic or Imitative' and 'Contagious' magic.

src.l: James George Frazer, 1922, The Golden Bough: A Study in Magic and Religion (abridged edition)
src.loc: ch. III, 'Sympathetic Magic', §1 The Principles of Magic

s: In Folk-Lore in the Old Testament Frazer explains the use of spittle in covenants as Contagious Magic: spittle, being part of a man, gives the spitter magical power over whoever swallows it.

src.l: James George Frazer, 1918, Folk-Lore in the Old Testament: Studies in Comparative Religion, Legend and Law
src.loc: Part II, ch. V 'Weeping as a salutation', p. 92 [scan 120]
src.q: spittle, being part of a man, confers on the spitter a magical power over him who has swallowed it. The case thus falls under the general head of Contagious Magic.

s: Rozin and Nemeroff (1990) report that, in University of Pennsylvania subjects, disgust objects such as cockroaches render a food inedible by contact with no sensory trace, and edible replicas of disgusting things are often refused; they read these as instances of Frazer's laws, which led to the 1986 study.

src.l: Paul Rozin, Carol Nemeroff, 1990, The laws of sympathetic magic: a psychological analysis of similarity and contagion
Paul Rozin, Linda Millman, Carol Nemeroff, 1986, Operation of the laws of sympathetic magic in disgust and other domains
src.loc: existence only (OpenAlex/Crossref); cited by the 1990 chapter

s: Rozin and Nemeroff (2002) treat the laws of sympathetic magic as a small, clearly defined subset of magical thinking that is abundant among contemporary people in developed societies and, unlike most magic, need not invoke human or animate agency.

src.l: Paul Rozin, Carol Nemeroff, 2002, Sympathetic magical thinking: the contagion and similarity 'heuristics'

s: Nemeroff and Rozin (2000) concede that 'magic' in current usage may be a residual 'garbage bin' category, but argue that meaningful consistencies across approaches justify a working definition, built on their sympathetic-magic studies.

src.l: Carol Nemeroff, Paul Rozin, 2000, The makings of the magical mind: the nature and function of sympathetic magical thinking

s: Subbotsky (2001) found that older children and adults shown an object destroyed in an empty box favoured scientific explanations in what they said but not in what they did; adults acted as if a magic spell were as credible as a hidden device, especially when ignoring it was risky.

src.l: Eugene Subbotsky, 2001, Causal explanations of events by children and adults: can alternative causal modes coexist in one mind?

s: Subbotsky (2004) reports that adults refused magical explanations of an anomalous transformation even after four repetitions, yet most accepted that similar anomalous effects had really occurred when magic was not mentioned; he concludes magical beliefs persist 'disguised' to fit the scientific paradigm.

src.l: Eugene Subbotsky, 2004, Magical thinking in judgments of causation: can anomalous phenomena affect ontological causal beliefs in children and adults?

s: Subbotsky and Quinteros (2002) found British adults rejected magical explanations more than rural Mexican adults in speech and at low risk, but when the risk of ignoring magic rose, both samples showed equal credulity.

src.l: Eugene Subbotsky, Graciela Quinteros, 2002, Do cultural factors affect causal beliefs? Rational and magical thinking in Britain and Mexico

s: Subbotsky (2026) sets Piaget's classical view, that magical thinking dominates preschool age and disappears with maturation, against later findings that it transforms rather than vanishes, persisting latent in educated adults; Piaget's own 1929 text already looked for 'traces' of the child's magical ideas in normal civilised adults, so the 'disappears' summary is a simplification of Piaget.

src.l: Eugene Subbotsky, 2026, The inevitability of magic: from Piaget's theory to advertising
Jean Piaget, 1929, The Child's Conception of the World
src.loc: ch. IV, §4 'Corroborative Proof: Spontaneous Magical Ideas in the Adult', p. 162

src.l: Eugene Subbotsky, 2010, Magic and the Mind: Mechanisms, Functions, and Development of Magical Thinking and Behavior

s: Legare, Evans, Rosengren and Harris (2012) review developmental work across cultures on species origins, illness and death and argue that the same people use natural and supernatural explanations for the same events, and that supernatural explanations often increase rather than decrease with age.

src.l: Cristine H. Legare, E. Margaret Evans, Karl S. Rosengren, Paul L. Harris, 2012, The coexistence of natural and supernatural explanations across cultures and development

s: Legare and Gelman (2008) found, among 366 children, adolescents and adults in two Sesotho-speaking South African communities, that bewitchment explanations of illness coexisted with highly endorsed biological ones, were not a product of ignorance, and were highest among adults.

src.l: Cristine H. Legare, Susan A. Gelman, 2008, Bewitchment, biology, or both: the co-existence of natural and supernatural explanatory frameworks across development

s: Woolley (1997) argues from a review that children are not fundamentally different from adults in distinguishing fantasy from reality: both entertain fantastical beliefs and both engage in magical thinking.

src.l: Jacqueline D. Woolley, 1997, Thinking about fantasy: are children fundamentally different thinkers and believers from adults?

s: Langer (1975) defined the illusion of control as an expectancy of success higher than the objective probability warrants, and found that skill cues (competition, choice, familiarity, involvement) introduced into chance tasks such as lotteries raise confidence inappropriately.

src.l: Ellen J. Langer, 1975, The illusion of control

s: Risen (2016) argues that dual-process models explain why superstitions arise but must be refined: people can detect in the moment that a belief makes no sense and act on it anyway, which she calls acquiescence.

src.l: Jane L. Risen, 2016, Believing what we do not believe: acquiescence to superstitious beliefs and other powerful intuitions

s: Eddy's 2026 systematic review (191 studies) treats thought-action fusion and magical ideation as forms of magical thinking whose scales correlate, finds magical thinking across the mental-health continuum and across cultures, and suggests functions beyond a marker of psychopathology.

src.l: Clare M. Eddy, 2026, The many manifestations of magical thinking: a systematic review
Mark Eckblad, Loren J. Chapman, 1983, Magical ideation as an indicator of schizotypy
src.loc: existence only; cited by Eddy as ref. 5

src.l: Roz Shafran, Dana S. Thordarson, S. Rachman, 1996, Thought-action fusion in obsessive compulsive disorder
src.loc: existence only; cited by Eddy as ref. 2

s: Blain and colleagues (2020) measured apophenia as false-positive error rates on computerised tasks (n = 1,193 and 195) and found it associated with self-reported psychoticism and the openness aspect of personality, whether or not intelligence was controlled.

src.l: Scott D. Blain, Julia Longenecker, Rachael G. Grazioplene, Bonnie Klimes-Dougan, Colin G. DeYoung, 2020, Apophenia as the disposition to false positives: a unifying framework for openness and psychoticism

s: Critique: Lindeman and Svedholm (2012) find psychology's definitions of paranormal, superstitious, magical and supernatural belief ambiguous, conclude the four terms denote the same thing, and judge domain-general definitions (false belief, associative biases including the laws of sympathetic magic) too imprecise.

src.l: Marjaana Lindeman, Annika M. Svedholm, 2012, What's in a term? Paranormal, superstitious, magical and supernatural beliefs by any other name would mean the same
