Marjaana Lindeman, Kia Aarnio, 2007, Superstitious, magical, and paranormal beliefs: an integrative model

s: Critique: Muhammad (2026) argues that cognitive and behaviourist psychology misrepresents superstition by reducing it to bias or conditioning on a narrow, instrumental idea of rationality, and proposes 'symbolic rationality', under which superstition is a way of managing uncertainty and making meaning in a culture.

src.l: Amri Hana Muhammad, 2026, Rethinking superstition in psychology: beyond reductionist models toward symbolic rationality

s: Critique: Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan (2010) find WEIRD samples frequent outliers across behavioural science; the founding contagion studies used University of Pennsylvania subjects, so claims about 'modern minds' from them are claims about one population until tested elsewhere.

src.l: Joseph Henrich, Steven J. Heine, Ara Norenzayan, 2010, The weirdest people in the world?
Paul Rozin, Carol Nemeroff, 1990, The laws of sympathetic magic: a psychological analysis of similarity and contagion

s: Critique: the experimental literature undercuts the evolutionist frame that 'magical thinking' inherited from Tylor and Frazer: Rozin and Nemeroff found sympathetic 'beliefs' supposedly common only in traditional cultures in American students, and Legare's reviews find supernatural explanation often increasing with age, contrary to traditional accounts.

src.l: Paul Rozin, Carol Nemeroff, 1990, The laws of sympathetic magic: a psychological analysis of similarity and contagion
Cristine H. Legare, E. Margaret Evans, Karl S. Rosengren, Paul L. Harris, 2012, The coexistence of natural and supernatural explanations across cultures and development

s: Critique: Eddy's own review notes that magical-thinking measures do not always map cleanly onto conceptual definitions, that student-only samples miss the extremes, and that findings (e.g. on thought-action fusion, anxiety and depression) are mixed, with self-report and publication-bias limits.

src.l: Clare M. Eddy, 2026, The many manifestations of magical thinking: a systematic review

s: Gershman (2022), pooling Pew surveys from 2008 to 2017, finds that over 40% of more than 140,000 respondents in 95 countries and territories said they believe in witchcraft, with country rates from 9% (Sweden) to 90% (Tunisia), mean 43%.

src.l: Boris Gershman, 2022, Witchcraft beliefs around the world: An exploratory analysis

s: Gershman (2022) reports that witchcraft beliefs cut across socio-demographic groups but are less widespread among the more educated and economically secure, and more widespread in countries with weak institutions, conformist culture and in-group bias.

src.l: Boris Gershman, 2022, Witchcraft beliefs around the world: An exploratory analysis

s: Pew (2018) reports that roughly six in ten US adults accept at least one of four 'New Age' beliefs: about four in ten believe in psychics and in spiritual energy in physical objects, 33% in reincarnation and 29% in astrology; only 22% of atheists hold any of the four.

src.l: Claire Gecewicz, Pew Research Center, 2018, 'New Age' beliefs common among both religious and nonreligious Americans

s: Pew's 2023 survey of 11,201 US adults (31 July to 6 August 2023) finds that 83% believe people have a soul or spirit besides the body and 81% that there is something spiritual beyond the natural world.

src.l: Becka A. Alper, Chip Rotolo, Patricia Tevington, Justin Nortey, Asta Kallo, Pew Research Center, 2023, Spirituality Among Americans

s: Luhrmann's Persuasions of the Witch's Craft (1989) studied ritual magic and witchcraft in contemporary England, and later scholars treat her 'interpretive drift' as a thesis about how people come to adopt magical belief through practice.

src.l: T. M. Luhrmann, 1989, Persuasions of the Witch's Craft: Ritual Magic in Contemporary England
Gerhard A. Mayer, René Gründer, 2010, Coming Home or Drifting Away: Magical Practice in the Twenty-First Century—Ways of Adopting Heterodox Beliefs and Religious Worldviews

s: Luhrmann, Nusbaum and Thisted (2010) report that evangelical Christians with a proclivity for 'absorption' reported sharper mental images and more unusual spiritual experience, and that the more they prayed the more likely they were to have such experiences.

src.l: Tanya Marie Luhrmann, Howard C. Nusbaum, Ronald A. Thisted, 2010, The Absorption Hypothesis: Learning to Hear God in Evangelical Christianity

s: Luhrmann et al. (2021), in four studies with over 2,000 participants in the US, Ghana, Thailand, China and Vanuatu, find that a cultural model of the mind as 'porous' (including that thoughts can act on the world, as in witchcraft) and personal 'absorption' each predict reports of vivid sensory experiences of gods and spirits.

src.l: Tanya Marie Luhrmann, Kara Weisman, Felicity Aulino, Joshua D. Brahinsky, et al., 2021, Sensing the presence of gods and spirits across cultures and faiths
Tanya Marie Luhrmann, Kara Weisman, Felicity Aulino, Joshua D. Brahinsky, et al., 2021, Sensing the presence of gods and spirits across cultures and faiths

s: Luhrmann's How God Becomes Real (2020) argues that people must work hard to make gods and spirits feel real, and that this effort changes them; it draws on ethnography of evangelicals, pagans, magicians and others.

src.l: T. M. Luhrmann, 2020, How God Becomes Real: Kindling the Presence of Invisible Others

s: Josephson-Storm's The Myth of Disenchantment (2017), as summarised by Heyes (2018), argues not for a later re-enchantment but that 'we have never really been disenchanted'.

src.l: Jason Ā. Josephson-Storm, 2017, The Myth of Disenchantment: Magic, Modernity, and the Birth of the Human Sciences
Michael E. Heyes, 2018, Review of The Myth of Disenchantment, by Jason A. Josephson-Storm

s: Asprem (2014) argues that parapsychology, occultism and the natural sciences of 1900 to 1939 faced similar intellectual problems (the intelligibility of nature, facts and values, immanence and transcendence) and solved them in comparable terms, proposing a new approach to Weber's disenchantment.

src.l: Egil Asprem, 2014, The Problem of Disenchantment: Scientific Naturalism and Esoteric Discourse, 1900–1939

s: Saler (2006) reports that historians in several fields had independently challenged the sociological view of modernity as disenchanted, so that a new position, 'if not consensus', presented Western modernity as enchanted.

src.l: Michael Saler, 2006, Modernity and Enchantment: A Historiographic Review

s: Woodman (2004) describes chaos magicians as advocating 'paradigm shifting': deliberately switching between belief systems, sometimes arbitrarily and including fictional cosmologies such as Lovecraft's, to expose the contingency of supposedly monolithic worldviews.

src.l: Justin Woodman, 2004, Alien Selves: Modernity and the Social Diagnostics of the Demonic in 'Lovecraftian Magick'
src.loc: section on Chaos magick (author's repository copy)

s: Dein (2025) argues that magic in the West, especially Wicca, has not disappeared but has been transformed through psychologization, and that ritual moves practitioners from an 'ordinary' to a 'magical' worldview of participatory consciousness.

src.l: Simon Lawrence Dein, 2025, Magic and the Postsecular: Disenchantment and Participatory Consciousness

s: Miller (2026), analysing WitchTok videos, captions and comments on hexes and curses, argues that users collaboratively construct an ethics of magic, including when harming others or defending oneself is acceptable.

src.l: Chris Miller, 2026, An' Ye harm none? Discourses of hexes and harm on WitchTok
Chris Miller, 2022, How Modern Witches Enchant TikTok: Intersections of Digital, Consumer, and Material Culture(s) on #WitchTok

s: Hale (2020) characterises Hutton's The Triumph of the Moon (1999) as a study of Gardnerian Wicca that demonstrated the rich but relatively recent history of contemporary Wicca.

src.l: Amy Hale, 2020, Book Review: Shai Feraro and Ethan Doyle White (eds.), Magic and Witchery in the Modern West: Celebrating the Twentieth Anniversary of 'The Triumph of the Moon'

s: Critique: Weber's 'disenchantment' names a stance of intellectualisation (the knowledge of or belief in calculability in principle), and he says it does not mean people know more about their conditions of life; so survey prevalence of magical or spiritual belief does not by itself refute him.

src.l: Max Weber, 1919, Wissenschaft als Beruf

s: Critique: the 'witchcraft belief' figures rest on a single Pew item that bundles the evil eye with curses and spells, which Gershman himself calls 'somewhat confusing', and they come from surveys fielded at different dates over 2008 to 2017.

src.l: Boris Gershman, 2022, Witchcraft beliefs around the world: An exploratory analysis

s: Critique: 'modern witchcraft' names two incommensurable things: Gershman's survey construct is belief that certain people can intentionally harm by supernatural means (a fear of others), whereas Wicca and WitchTok are self-identified practice; lumping them into one 'state of modern magic' is a category error.

src.l: Boris Gershman, 2022, Witchcraft beliefs around the world: An exploratory analysis
Chris Miller, 2022, How Modern Witches Enchant TikTok: Intersections of Digital, Consumer, and Material Culture(s) on #WitchTok

s: Critique: Mayer and Gründer (2010), from German interview studies of magicians and Ásatrú heathens, argue that Luhrmann's 'interpretive drift' and the 'coming home' experience are complementary, and that strongly evidential personal extraordinary experiences, mostly neglected, matter to becoming a practitioner.

src.l: Gerhard A. Mayer, René Gründer, 2010, Coming Home or Drifting Away: Magical Practice in the Twenty-First Century—Ways of Adopting Heterodox Beliefs and Religious Worldviews

s: Critique: the psychological account of what magic does rests on narrow samples; Luhrmann et al. (2021) note that the Absorption scale originated in WEIRD and English-speaking settings, and the classic practitioner ethnographies cited here (Luhrmann's England, US evangelicals, London chaos magicians, US Pagan surveys) are Anglophone.

src.l: Tanya Marie Luhrmann, Kara Weisman, Felicity Aulino, Joshua D. Brahinsky, et al., 2021, Sensing the presence of gods and spirits across cultures and faiths

s: Apuleius (De deo Socratis 13) defines daemones as living beings in genus, rational in mind, passive (subject to emotion) in soul, aerial in body, eternal in time: three traits shared with us, one their own, one with the gods.

src.q: demons are as to genus animated beings, as to mind rational, as to feelings passive, as to body aërial, as to duration eternal.

s: Apuleius places daemones between us and the gods 'as much in place of region as in nature of mind', sharing immortality with those above and passion with those below; so they are angered, pitied, allured by gifts and softened by prayers, which is why rites work.

s: THE TURN: Augustine (City of God VIII.22, 'against Apuleius') rules that one must by no means believe Apuleius that daemones are intermediate messengers and interpreters between gods and men; they are spirits most eager to harm, alien from justice, swollen with pride, livid with envy, cunning in deceit, imprisoned in the air.

s: Augustine (City of God IX.19) splits the vocabulary: Scripture speaks of angels, some good and some bad, but never of good daemones; wherever daemones or daemonia occur they mean malign spirits, and even pagans take 'you have a daemon' as an insult, so the good ones should be called angels.

src.qo: angelos quidem partim bonos, partim malos, numquam vero bonos daemones legimus; sed ubicumque illarum litterarum hoc nomen positum reperitur, sive daemones, sive daemonia dicantur, non nisi maligni significantur spiritus.

s: Lactantius (Divine Institutes II.15) derives demons from the Watchers: angels sent to guard men were corrupted, and their offspring, neither angels nor men, became earthly demons; so there are two kinds, heavenly and earthly, the latter wicked spirits whose prince is the devil.

s: Lactantius (DI II.14) says the demons attach themselves to individual men and occupy houses and take for themselves the name of genii, 'for thus in Latin they translate daemones', and that all the art of the magi rests on their inspirations.

s: Aquinas (ST I q.57, on whether angels know the future) holds that effects that follow necessarily from their causes, like tomorrow's sunrise, are known with certainty, those that follow for the most part only by conjecture, like a doctor's prognosis, and chance events not at all; knowing the future in itself belongs to God alone.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1497, Summa theologiae: Pars prima
src.q: Those things which proceed from their causes, as in most cases, are known not through certainty but through conjecture, just as a doctor precognizes the health of a sick person.
src.qo: que vo ex suis cau sis puenit: vt in pluribus cognoscuntur non per certita dinē: sed per cōiecturā: sicut medicus precognoscit sanita tem infirmū:

s: In Kepler's Somnium, Fiolxhilde tells her son that her land has 'most wise spirits' who shun light and noise, nine principal ones, of whom one, 'most mild and harmless of all', is evoked by twenty-one characters and carries her to other shores and tells her what she asks.

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1634, Somnium, seu opus posthumum de astronomia lunari
src.q: we have at hand most wise spirits ... Among them are the principal Nine, of whom one is particularly known to me, and is even most mild and harmless of all, and is evoked by twenty-one characters.
src.qo: nobis præstò sunt sapientissimi spi- ritus, qui tantam lucem regionum cæterarum, strepitumq́; homi- num perosi, nostras appetunt umbras, & nobiscum familiariter conversantur. Sunt ex iis præcipui ³⁵ Novem, ex quibus ³⁶ unus mihi peculiariter notus, & vel ³⁷ maximè omnium mitis atq; inno- xius ³⁸ viginti & uno characteribus evocatur.

s: Descartes (Meditation I) supposes not a good God but 'some evil genius' (genium aliquem malignum), supremely powerful and cunning, who has spent all his industry deceiving him, so that all external things are delusions of dreams.

src.l: René Descartes, 1642, Meditationes de prima philosophia
src.q: I will therefore suppose not an optimal God, who is the source of truth, but some evil genius ...—one who is supremely powerful and cunning—who has employed all his industry to deceive me.
src.qo: Supponam igitur non optimum Deum fontem veritatis, sed genium aliquem malignum, eundémque summe potentem, & callidum omnem suam industriam in eo posuisse, ut me falleret

s: Laplace (Essai philosophique, 1814) imagines 'an intelligence' which, knowing at one instant all the forces of nature and the positions of all beings, and vast enough to analyse them, would hold the motions of the largest bodies and the lightest atom in one formula: nothing would be uncertain to it.

src.l: Charles Babbage, 1838, The Ninth Bridgewater Treatise: A Fragment (2nd ed.)
src.loc: Appendix, Note C, p. 189 [scan 202] (Babbage's extract of Laplace)
src.q: An intelligence that, for a given moment, knew all the forces by which nature is animated and the respective positions of the beings that compose it ... Nothing would be uncertain for it, and the future, like the past, would be present to its eyes.
src.qo: Une intelligence qui pour un instant donnée, connaîtrait toutes les forces dont la nature est animée ... rien ne serait incertain pour elle, et l'avenir, comme le passé, serait présent a ses yeux.

src.l: Charles Babbage, 1838, The Ninth Bridgewater Treatise: A Fragment (2nd ed.)
src.q: Une intelligence qui pour un instant donnée, connaîtrait toutes les forces dont la nature est animée ... rien ne serait incertain pour elle, et l'avenir, comme le passé, serait présent a ses yeux.

s: Laplace says the human mind, through astronomy and mechanics, offers a faint sketch of this intelligence and tends always to approach it, 'but from which he will always remain infinitely distant'.

src.l: Pierre-Simon Laplace, 1814, Essai philosophique sur les probabilités
src.q: All his efforts in the search for truth tend to bring him constantly closer to the intelligence we have just conceived, but from which he will always remain infinitely distant.
src.qo: Tous ses efforts dans la recherche de la vérité, tendent à le rapprocher sans cesse de l'intelligence que nous venons de concevoir, mais dont il restera toujours infiniment éloigné.

src.l: Pierre-Simon Laplace, 1814, Essai philosophique sur les probabilités
src.q: Tous ses efforts dans la recherche de la vérité, tendent à le rapprocher sans cesse de l'intelligence que nous venons de concevoir, mais dont il restera toujours infiniment éloigné.

s: Maxwell (Theory of Heat, 1871) limits the second law to bodies handled in mass and imagines 'a being whose faculties are so sharpened' that it can follow every molecule, stressing its attributes are 'as essentially finite as our own'; such a being could do what is impossible to us.

src.l: James Clerk Maxwell, 1872, Theory of Heat
src.loc: 'Limitation of the Second Law of Thermodynamics', p. 308 [scan 332]
src.q: But if we conceive a being whose faculties are so sharpened that he can follow every molecule in its course, such a being, whose attributes are still as essentially finite as our own, would be able to do what is at present impossible to us.

s: Myers (1903) recruits 'Professor Clerk Maxwell's Sorting Demons' for psychical research: arguing that spirit might act by selective molecular action, he finds Maxwell's imaginary creatures already 'trained' to the performances he ascribes to spirit-power, and cites Kelvin's Popular Lectures for their description.

src.l: Frederic W. H. Myers, 1903, Human Personality and Its Survival of Bodily Death, Vol. II
src.loc: Appendix to ch. IX (926 A), p. 531 [scan 559]
src.q: it became plain to me that Professor Clerk Maxwell's Sorting Demons had been already trained—if I may so say—to the very performances which I was now ascribing to spirit-power.

s: Darmesteter states that asura, 'the Lord' and the supreme God's name in the Avesta, comes to mean 'a demon' in Brahmanical literature, though it is august in the Vedas, while Iranian daēva fell from 'a god' to 'a demon': the two branches inverted the same pair of words.

src.q: The word Asura, which in the Avesta means ‘the Lord,’ and is the name of the supreme God, means ‘a demon’ in the Brahmanical literature; but in the older religion of the Vedas it is quite as august as in the Avesta

src.l: James Darmesteter, 1880, The Zend-Avesta, Part I: The Vendîdâd (SBE 4)
src.q: The descent of the word daêva from ‘a god’ to ‘a demon’ is a mere accident of language.

src.l: Pāramiti (tr.), Shi Jiehuan (comm.), 1594, 楞嚴經要解 Śūraṅgama Sūtra with Essential Commentary
src.q: This is a "powerful ghost." After many years, it becomes a demon,
src.qo: 此大力鬼 年老成魔

src.l: Pāramiti (tr.), Shi Jiehuan (comm.), 1594, 楞嚴經要解 Śūraṅgama Sūtra with Essential Commentary
src.q: 此大力鬼 年老成魔

src.l: Kumārajīva (tr.), 1127, 妙法蓮華經 Lotus Sutra (Sixi Tripiṭaka ed.)
src.q: There are also other ghosts With heads like those of oxen
src.qo: 復有諸鬼 首如牛頭

src.l: Kumārajīva (tr.), 1127, 妙法蓮華經 Lotus Sutra (Sixi Tripiṭaka ed.)
src.q: 復有諸鬼 首如牛頭

s: Tsurezuregusa §50 records a rumour of about 1311 that a woman from Ise had turned into an oni (鬼), and Source Library renders oni 'ogre', marking the Japanese sense of the character (a horned man-eater), not the Chinese gui (ghost).

src.l: Yoshida Kenkō, n.d., 徒然草 Tsurezuregusa (Essays in Idleness)
src.q: there was a matter of a woman from Ise Province becoming an ogre.
src.qo: 応長の比伊勢国より女濃鬼に成たるを

src.l: Yoshida Kenkō, n.d., 徒然草 Tsurezuregusa (Essays in Idleness)
src.q: 応長の比伊勢国より女濃鬼に成たるを

s: Bodin opens the Démonomanie by defining the sorcerer as one who knowingly strives to achieve something by diabolical means, and says earlier writers on sorcerers had omitted any definition.

src.l: Jean Bodin, 1603, De la demonomanie des sorciers (On the Demon-Mania of Witches)
src.q: A Sorcerer is someone who knowingly strives to achieve something by Diabolical means. ... this is something that has been omitted until now by all those who have written about Sorcerers

s: Bodin makes knowledge (intent) part of the crime: a sick person who uses a diabolical remedy in good faith, from a sorcerer he took for an honest man, is not a sorcerer.

src.l: Jean Bodin, 1603, De la demonomanie des sorciers (On the Demon-Mania of Witches)
src.q: a sick person who uses in good faith a Diabolical recipe given to him by a Sorcerer—whom he thought was an honest man—is not a Sorcerer, for he has a just cause for ignorance.
src.qo: qui vse de bonne foy d'vne recepte Diabolique à luy baillée par le Sorcier, qu'il pensoit estre homme de bien, n'est point Sorcier, car il a iuste cause d'ignorance:

s: In his refutation of Weyer, Bodin quotes Weyer's definition of the lamia (witch) as acting from a deceptive or imaginary pact, and glosses it as someone thought to do with demons' help what she does not actually do.

src.l: Jean Bodin, 1603, De la demonomanie des sorciers (On the Demon-Mania of Witches)
src.q: because of a deceptive or imaginary pact entered into with a Demon ... a Witch is one who is thought to have an alliance with demons, and with their help, to do what she does not actually do.
src.qo: la Sorciere est celle qu'on pense auoir alliance auec les demõs, & à leur ayde faire ce qu'elle ne faict point.

s: The Malleus, written following Innocent VIII's bull, frames a work of witchcraft as the meeting of demon, witch and divine permission, and its first question asks whether denying that witches exist is heretical.

src.l: Heinrich Kramer (Institoris), Jacob Sprenger, 1486, Malleus maleficarum (The Hammer of Witches)
src.q: the three elements that meet in an effect of witchcraft—namely, the demon, the witch, and divine permission ... Whether asserting that witches exist is so Catholic a belief that to stubbornly defend the opposite is entirely heretical?

s: The Malleus argues it is no wonder more women than men are infected by the heresy of witches, names the heresy after the feminine 'maleficarum' for that reason, and thanks God for preserving the male sex.

src.l: Heinrich Kramer (Institoris), Jacob Sprenger, 1486, Malleus maleficarum (The Hammer of Witches)
src.q: it is no wonder more women are found infected by the heresy of witches than men. Whence, consequently, the heresy should not be called that of sorcerers, but of witches ... blessed be the Most High, who has preserved the male species from such a great crime until the present

s: The Malleus states that no one is condemned to death except by their own confession or the other two means (manifest proof, witnesses), and that the accused is then exposed to interrogation and torture for confession.

src.l: Heinrich Kramer (Institoris), Jacob Sprenger, 1486, Malleus maleficarum (The Hammer of Witches)
src.q: no one is judged for the penalty of blood ... unless they are convicted by their own confession ... and torments for the confession of their crimes.

s: Nider reports the judge Peter's account that Stadelein, after four pulls of the strappado, said he raised hail easily but could harm only those destitute of God's help, and not those armed with the sign of the cross.

src.l: Johannes Nider, 1602, Formicarius (The Anthill)
src.q: After the fourth pull of the ropes ... 'I procure hailstorms easily, but I am not able to cause harm at my own whim; I can only hurt those who are destitute of God's help. Those who arm themselves with the sign of the cross will not perish by my lightning.'
src.qo: Faciliter grandines pro- curo, sed ad libitum lædere non valeo, sed eos tan- tummodo qui dei destituti sunt auxilio: qui signo crucis se muniunt fulmine meo nō interibunt.

s: In the same confession, Stadelein describes weather-making as beginning with set words spoken in a field to implore the prince of demons to send one of his followers.

src.l: Johannes Nider, 1602, Formicarius (The Anthill)
src.q: First, with specific words in a field, we implore the prince of all demons to send one of his followers to strike the place we have designated.
src.qo: Primò verbis certis in campo principem omnium dæmoniorum imploramus, vt de suis mittat aliquem, à nobis de- signatum percutiat,

s: Nider's judge holds that a sorcerer loses all power once touched by public justice, and tells his frightened servants to seize Stadelein on that ground.

src.l: Johannes Nider, 1602, Formicarius (The Anthill)
src.q: Attack the wretch with confidence, because once he is touched by public justice ... he will lose all the strength of his wickedness.

s: Molitor's dialogue has Ulrich conclude that people often think they see others present when they see only images presented by a good or evil spirit, and applies the Canon Episcopi to women who believe they travel while staying at home.

src.l: Ulrich Molitor, 1489, De laniis et phitonicis mulieribus (On Witches and Female Soothsayers)
src.q: men often think they see other men present in a certain place, when they are seeing only their images, presented either by a good or an evil spirit. ... Do not soothsaying women

s: Spina sets out the question whether witches truly and physically do what they confess or are deluded in sleep, and states the case for delusion first from the Canon Episcopi on women who ride by night with Diana or Herodias.

src.l: Bartolomeo Spina, 1576, Quaestio de strigibus (Inquiry into Witches)
src.q: believe and profess that during the hours of night they ride upon certain beasts with Diana, the goddess of the pagans, or with Herodias, and a countless multitude of women
src.qo: credunt se & confi- tentur cum Diana nocturnis horis, dea paganorum, vel cum Hero- diade, vel cum innumera multitudine mulierum, equitare super quasdam bestias,

s: Weyer explains the witches' experiences medically: the imaginative faculty of these women is corrupted, as in melancholics whose humor occupies the brain and alters the mind.

src.l: Johann Weyer, 1563, De praestigiis daemonum (On the Deceptions of Demons)
src.q: the instruments of the imaginative faculty in these poor women are corrupted in this way and the sharpness of their eyes is dazzled ... the melancholic humor occupies the brain and alters the mind.

s: For a deluded witch who repents, Weyer proposes at most a fine for the poor, a discretionary non-capital punishment, or temporary exile.

src.l: Johann Weyer, 1563, De praestigiis daemonum (On the Deceptions of Demons)
src.q: a fine of money can be imposed (if her means allow it) to be used for the support of the poor. Any other discretionary ... provided it is not capital
src.qo: pecu- niarum quoque (si eius res ferant) mulcta in pau- perum subsidium imponi potest:

s: Weyer says he wrote because he saw the confessions of insane old women taken as truth and no distinction made between deluded witches and actual poisoners.

src.l: Johann Weyer, 1563, De praestigiis daemonum (On the Deceptions of Demons)
src.q: I saw that the confessions of these insane little old women were being relied upon as truth, and that not enough distinction was being made between these deluded witches and actual poisoners.
src.qo: propriæque amentium anicularum confessioni stari, nec satis in- ter Lamias & ueneficas discerni:

s: In the same passage Weyer complains that learned 'sacrilegious magicians' (magi), punished severely under the Old Law, now lived with impunity and even praise: his leniency is for witches, not for ritual magicians.

src.l: Johann Weyer, 1563, De praestigiis daemonum (On the Deceptions of Demons)
src.q: Meanwhile, I saw sacrilegious magicians ... now living with more impunity—indeed, even with praise among many.
src.qo: uiter, iam impunitius, imò cú laude apud pleroſque uersari:

s: Del Rio defines magic in the broadest sense as an art or faculty that, by a created, non-supernatural power, produces wonderful and unusual effects whose reason surpasses the senses and common understanding.

src.l: Martin Del Rio, 1603, Disquisitionum magicarum libri sex
src.q: it is an art or faculty which, by a created and non-supernatural power, effects certain wonderful and unusual things, the reason for which surpasses the senses and common human understanding.

s: Del Rio chooses his broad definition deliberately to include artificial and natural magic, which Vitoria and others had excluded, and says 'created and non-supernatural' to exclude true miracles, which are God's alone.

src.l: Martin Del Rio, 1603, Disquisitionum magicarum libri sex
src.q: have excluded artificial and natural magic while establishing stricter boundaries. ... I named it Created and non-supernatural to exclude true miracles, which are the work of God alone

s: Remy, a judge in Lorraine, writes that in the sixteen years of his capital jurisdiction no fewer than eight hundred were condemned to death for witchcraft, besides almost as many who escaped by flight or by enduring torture.

src.l: Nicolas Remy, 1596, Daemonolatreiae libri tres (Three Books of Demonolatry)
src.q: In Lorraine, I remember that within the sixteen years during which I have exercised jurisdiction over capital matters, no fewer than eight hundred have been found manifest of that crime and condemned to death by the sentence of our Duumvirate
src.qo: In Lotharingia memini intra annos sede- cim, a quib. rerum capitalium iudicia exerceo, non minus octingentos eius criminis manife- sto compertos, Duumuiratus nostri sententia capitis esse damnatos,

s: Kittredge (1929) says Remy drew his work from the trials of some 900 persons he had sentenced in the preceding fifteen years, and that de Lancre and an associate are said to have condemned 600 in the Basque country in four months.

src.l: George Lyman Kittredge, 1929, Witchcraft in Old and New England
src.q: from the trials of some 900 persons whom he had sentenced to death in the fifteen years preceding. In 1609, de l'Ancre and his associate are said to have con- demned 600 in the Basque country in four month

s: Kittredge reports a moderate Scottish estimate of at least 3,400 victims (1580-1680), Mannhardt's reckoning of 'millions' for the fourteenth to seventeenth centuries, and half a million as 'thought to be a moderate estimate'.

src.l: George Lyman Kittredge, 1929, Witchcraft in Old and New England
src.q: The most conscientiously moderate estimate makes out a total of at least 3,400 between the years 1580 and 1680 ... Mannhardt reckons the victims from the fourteenth to the seventeenth century at millions,¹⁷⁸ and half a million is thought to be a moderate estimate.

s: Thomasius sets out the alleged pact he will test: the devil satisfies the person's lust, greed or ambition in return for fornication, transport through the air, worship and dancing, harm to people, beasts and crops by storms, and eternal servitude.

src.l: Christian Thomasius, 1701, Theses inaugurales de crimine magiae (On the Crime of Magic)
src.q: enters into a pact, stating that if the Devil is willing to satisfy his lust, greed, or ambition, he will commit fornication with the Devil ... and by the aid of the Devil cause harm to men, beasts, and crops, either by stirring up storms or in another preternatural way
src.qo: quod velit, si Diabolus ipsius voluptati, avaritiae aut ambitioni satisfacere velit, cum Diabolo scortari, in certo loco ope Diaboli per aera magos vehentis comparere, ac ibi cum aliis similibus Diabolum adorare, ac tripudiare, & luxuriari, ope Diaboli hominibus, bestiis & frugibus, vel tempestates excitando vel alio praeternaturali modo damna dare,

s: Thomasius argues that because a crime consists of a fact and a fact is not presumed, whoever asserts the crime of magic exists must prove it.

src.l: Christian Thomasius, 1701, Theses inaugurales de crimine magiae (On the Crime of Magic)
src.q: Every crime consists of a fact. A fact is not presumed. Therefore, he who asserts that the crime of Magic exists must prove it, rather than demanding proof from the one who denies it.
src.qo: Omne delictum in facto consistit. Factum non praesumitur. Ergo qui afferit, dari crimen Magiae, id probare debet, non à negante probationem expetere.

s: Thomasius reads Carolina art. 109 as containing nothing about a pact with the devil: it punishes harmful sorcery with fire and leaves harmless sorcery to discretionary punishment.

src.l: Christian Thomasius, 1701, Theses inaugurales de crimine magiae (On the Crime of Magic)
src.q: he was so far from explicitly arranging anything in that Constitution ... regarding Magic that involves a pact with the Devil ... inflicts harm or disadvantage upon people through sorcery, they shall be punished from life to death, and such punishment shall be carried out with fire.

s: Spee reports an inquisitor's boast that even the Pope under his torture would confess to sorcery, and adds that Binsfeld, Spee himself and nearly everyone else would too.

src.l: Friedrich Spee von Langenfeld, 1631, Cautio criminalis (Precautions for Prosecutors)
src.q: if even the Pope himself were to come into his hands and under his instruments of torture, he would without a doubt eventually confess to being a sorcerer ... Binsfeld would do the same, I would do the same, and all others would too, with the exception of a very few of the most robust men.
src.qo: si sub suas manus, & tormenta vel ipse pontifex veniret, sine dubio tandem se maleficum quoq; esse confessurum. I- dem faceret Binsfeldius, idem ego, idem cæteri, pauculis robustissimis exceptis.

s: Spee, writing as a confessor, states under oath that he has so far accompanied no one to the pyre whom, on careful consideration, he could judge guilty, and that two other careful theologians told him the same.

src.l: Friedrich Spee von Langenfeld, 1631, Cautio criminalis (Precautions for Prosecutors)
src.q: I state this under oath: that I have so far led no one to the pyre ... about whom, having prudently considered all factors, I could determine was guilty. I have heard the same from two other careful theologians
src.qo: Ego id cum juramē- to depono, me qdem nullā hactenus ad ro- gū duxisse, de qua omnib. consideratis pru- dēter statuere potuerim, fuisse ream. Idem ego à duobus aliis accuratis Theologis au- divi;

s: Binsfeld describes the condemned retracting their denunciations of others at the place of execution, and treats as a legal difficulty whether this last-moment retraction cancels the confession made under torture.

src.l: Peter Binsfeld, 1591, Tractatus de confessionibus maleficorum et sagarum (Treatise on the Confessions of Witches and Sorcerers)
src.q: I excuse them, and I say that I know nothing evil about them. ... The difficulty now is whether a confession ... cancels out the first confession made during torture and trial.

s: Guazzo allows that witches often attend the sabbath only in a deep sleep at home, the demon mocking their senses so that the dream feels like a bodily action.

src.l: Francesco Maria Guazzo, 1626, Compendium maleficarum
src.q: often, even when they are absent from them and are held at home in a deep sleep, they seem to themselves to be present, the demon undoubtedly mocking their senses.
src.qo: ſæpe etiam; cum ab ijs abſint, ac arctiore ſomno domi detineantur, uidentur tantum ſibi adeſſe, ludificante nimirum ſenſus Dæmone,

s: Guazzo distinguishes ways of making the pact: before witnesses with denial of the Creator, by written petition, or through a sorcerer as intermediary, which Grillandus calls a tacit pact.

src.l: Francesco Maria Guazzo, 1626, Compendium maleficarum
src.q: the one making the pact denies his Creator with his mouth, and the devil in turn promises him riches and honors. Sometimes it is done through a petition, which he presents to the devil. Sometimes it is done through a vicar, that is, through a Sorcerer
src.qo: & diabolus vicissim illi diuitias, & honores pollicetur. Aliquando fit per libellum supplicem, quem diabolo præsentat. Aliquando fit per vicarium, idest, per Magum,

s: De Lancre treats the agreement of child witnesses from many Basque villages, who said they had seen each other at the sabbath, as more coherent than twelve sensible men could manage.

src.l: Pierre de Lancre, 1622, L'incredulité et mescreance du sortilege plainement convaincue (The Incredulity and Misbelief of Sorcery Fully Convicted)
src.q: these children, although from different places, saying they had seen each other at the Sabbath ... and recognized one another, and speaking so judiciously, so consistently and unanimously, that twelve sensible men, even after long study, could hardly have been so coherent, nor testified so certainly.
src.qo: disans s'estre veus au Sabbat & recogneus, & parlans si iudicieusement, si conformement & vnanimemēt, que douze hommes bien sensez, apres mesme vn long estude à peine eussent-ils peu estre si contextes, ny en deposer si certainement.

s: Bekker concludes that sorcery as commonly understood, effects beyond nature by the devil's power through a pact, cannot exist, because the devil can do nothing above nature and, lacking a body, less upon bodies than a human can.

src.l: Balthasar Bekker, 1691, De betoverde weereld (The World Bewitched)
src.q: one may easily conclude that such Sorcery, as it is commonly understood, cannot exist. ... I have already sufficiently proven previously that the Devil can do nothing above nature: yes, even less upon bodies than a human who, in order to do such things, possesses a body; with which the Devil is not provided.
src.qo: magh men lichtelijk besluiten, datter sulke Toverye, als men die gemeenelijk begrijpt, niet wesen kan. Want daar dooz verskaatmen wer- kingen de kraghten der natuur te boven gaan- de, die menschen, met den Duivel in verbond getreden, dooz desselfs kraght te wege brengen. Genoegsaam heb ik hier te voren al bewesen, dat de Duivel boven de nature niets vermagh: ja selfs minder op de lichamen, dan een mensche, die om sulx te doen een lichaam heeft; daar de Duivel niet van voorsien is.

s: Scot describes one sort of those called witches as poor, old, infirm and superstitious women who are easily persuaded that misfortunes around them are their own doing.

src.l: Reginald Scot, 1886, The Discoverie of Witchcraft
src.q: ONE sort of such as are said to bee witches, are women which be commonly old, lame, bleare-eied, pale, fowle, and full of wrinkles ; poore, sullen, superstitious, and papists

s: Scot says the name of witch is so odious and feared that even the most honest person arraigned on it will hardly escape condemnation.

src.l: Reginald Scot, 1886, The Discoverie of Witchcraft
src.q: For the name of a witch is so odious, and hir power so feared among the common people, that if the honestest bodie living chance to be arraigned thereupon, she shall hardlie escape condemnation.

s: Scot denies that witches or devils can command the elements or send rain, hail and storms, a direct reply to Nider, the Malleus and Bodin, whom he names in the margin.

src.l: Reginald Scot, 1886, The Discoverie of Witchcraft
src.q: will denie that the elements are obedient to witches, and at their commandement; or that they may at their pleasure send raine, haile, tempests, thunder, lightening

s: In the Lancaster trial record, Alizon Device's examination says her grandmother 'old Demdike' urged her, while begging, to let a devil or familiar appear to her and suck at some part of her.

src.l: Thomas Potts, 1613, The Wonderfull Discoverie of Witches in the Countie of Lancaster
src.loc: Examination of Alizon Device, 13 March, regnal year 9 of James I [scan 23]
src.q: her Graund-mother (called Elizabeth Sowtherns, alias old Demdike) did sundry times in going or walking together as they went begging, perswade and aduise this Examinate to let a Deuill or Familiar appeare vnto her

s: Hansen reports that Sprenger, with Institoris, obtained Innocent VIII's bull Summis desiderantes affectibus of 5 December 1484, and that this led to his part in drafting the Malleus in 1486, which Hansen attributes to Institoris.

src.l: Joseph Hansen, 1901, Quellen und Untersuchungen zur Geschichte des Hexenwahns (Sources and Investigations into the History of the Witch-Craze)
src.q: he obtained the notorious Bull from Pope Innocent VIII dated December 5, 1484, Summis desiderantes affectibus ... His involvement in these matters led to his participation in 1486 in the drafting of the Malleus Maleficarum

s: Menghi's exorcism manual says possessing demons mostly stay hidden and feign ignorance, knowing that if they reveal themselves the exorcists will keep tormenting them.

src.l: Girolamo Menghi, 1576, Compendio dell'arte essorcistica (Compendium of the Art of Exorcism)
src.q: most of the time they remain hidden and show themselves to be as ignorant as they can, because they know that by revealing themselves, the Exorcists will not stop tormenting them with Exorcisms

s: De Groot reports a Chinese author recommending ingredients from dogs for demoniacal and other diseases, graded by whether the dog is yellow, black or white.

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1910, The Religious System of China, Vol. 6: Demonology and Sorcery
src.q: Yet other ingredients obtained from dogs are recommended by this great author for demoniacal and other diseases, and declared to be of various excellence according as the dogs are yellow, black, or white

s: Murray asserted that the people called witches in late medieval times practised a pre-Christian cult that was the ancient religion of Western Europe.

src.l: Margaret Alice Murray, 1921, The Witch-Cult in Western Europe
src.q: The evidence proves that underlying the Christian religion was a cult practised by many classes of the community ... It can be traced back to pre-Christian times, and appears to be the ancient religion of Western Europe.

s: Figures of 'millions' or 'half a million' witch-trial victims, as reported by Kittredge, far exceed modern counts: Leeson and Russ's dataset covers more than 43,000 people tried for witchcraft across 21 European countries over five and a half centuries.

src.l: Peter T. Leeson, Jacob W. Russ, 2018, Witch Trials

s: In the Advancement (De augmentis III.5, Wats's 1640 English) Bacon divides the operative knowledge of nature into Mechanique and Magique, answering to Physique and Metaphysique, and announces 'a purging of the word Magia'.

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1640, Of the Advancement and Proficience of Learning (Gilbert Wats's English translation of De augmentis scientiarum)
src.q: The Partition of the Operative Knowledge of Nature into *Me- chanique* and Magique: Refpondent to the Parts of *Speculative Knowledge, Mechanique* to Phyfique, Magique to Metaphyfique. ¶ A purging of the word Magia.

s: Bacon wants the word Magia, 'accepted for a long time in the worse part', restored to 'the ancient and honourable ſence' it had among the Persians.

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1640, Of the Advancement and Proficience of Learning (Gilbert Wats's English translation of De augmentis scientiarum)
src.q: it ſeemes requiſite in this place that the word Magia, accepted for a long time in the worſe part, be reſto-red to the ancient and honourable ſence.

s: Bacon holds that real alteration in nature comes only 'through the invention of Formes', so natural magic, as the operative relative of the (deficient) metaphysics of forms, is itself defective.

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1640, Of the Advancement and Proficience of Learning (Gilbert Wats's English translation of De augmentis scientiarum)
src.q: but only through the invention of Formes. ... it follows that Natural Ma-gique alſo, which is a Relative unto it, is likewise Defective.

s: Bacon dismisses the natural magic 'which flies abroad in many mens bookes' as credulous and superstitious traditions of sympathies, antipathies and hidden properties, 'with fome experiments commonly frivolous'.

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1640, Of the Advancement and Proficience of Learning (Gilbert Wats's English translation of De augmentis scientiarum)
src.q: As for the Naturall Magique, (which flies abroad in many mens bookes) containing certain credulous and fuperftitious traditions, and obfervations of Sympathies, and Antipathies, and of hidden and fpecifique proprieties, with fome experiments commonly frivolous

s: Bacon separates 'Celestiall Magique', the belief that a favourable aspect of the stars can be captured in seals and signet-rings of metal or gem, from sound astrology and calls it a portion of 'Aſtrologicall Frenzie'.

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1640, Of the Advancement and Proficience of Learning (Gilbert Wats's English translation of De augmentis scientiarum)
src.q: There is another Portion of Aſtrologicall Frenzie ... to be transferred into Celeſtiall Magique, as they call it. ... That a benevolent ſituation or Aſpect of ſtarres, may be taken in ſeales and ſignet-rings

s: Bacon reads 'the Persian Magique, so much celebrated' as chiefly the observation of correspondences between the structures of natural things and of civil things.

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1640, Of the Advancement and Proficience of Learning (Gilbert Wats's English translation of De augmentis scientiarum)
src.q: And indeed the Persian Magique, so much celebrated, consists chiefly in this; to observe the respondency in the Architectures, and Fabriques of things Natural, & of things Civile.

s: In Novum Organum II Bacon says 'Magical Effects' are produced, as far as he can conjecture, in three ways, the first being a thing's multiplication of itself, as in fire and specific poisons.

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1762, Novum Organum Scientiarum
src.q: But these Magical Effects ... (as far as we can yet conjecture) are produced in three ways: Either by the Multiplication of itself, as in Fire, and in those poisons which they call Specific
src.qo: (quantum adhuc conjicimus) fiunt tribus modis: Aut per Multiplicationem ſui, ut in Igne, & Venenis, quæ vocant Specifica;

s: In Sylva Sylvarum exp. 998 Bacon reports the weapon-salve on 'the Relation of Men of Credit' while saying he is 'not fully inclined to beleeue it', and lists its ingredients (moss from an unburied skull, boar's and bear's fat).

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1631, Sylva sylvarum: or A naturall historie. In ten centuries
src.q: It is constantly Receiued, and Auouched, that the Anointing of the weapon, that maketh the wound, will heale the wound it selfe. ... (though my selfe, as yet, are not fully inclined to beleeue it,)

s: Bacon approves that weapon-salve makers do not compound it under a constellation, which he calls the usual excuse of 'Magical Medicicines' when they fail.

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1631, Sylva sylvarum: or A naturall historie. In ten centuries
src.q: Thirdly, (which I like well) they do not obserue the Confecting of the Ointment vnder any certaine Constellation; which commonly is the Excuse of Magical Medici-cines, when they faile, that they were not made vnder a fit Figure of Heauen.

s: In the 1557 French version of Roger Bacon's letter on the powers of art and nature, whatever exists without the operation of nature or art is 'a feigned thing, surrounded by frauds and deceptions', produced by tricks of movement, voice, instruments and darkness.

src.l: Roger Bacon, 1557, De l'admirable pouvoir et puissance de l'art, et de nature (French translation of Epistola de secretis operibus artis et naturae)
src.q: Now all that which exists without the operation of nature or of art is not a natural thing at all; that is to say, it is a feigned thing, surrounded by frauds and
src.qo: Or tout ce, qui eſt ſans operation de natu- re, ou d'art, ce n'eſt point choſe na- turelle, c'eſt à dire, que c'eſt choſe feincte, & enuirõnée de fraudes &

s: Glanvill argues there is 'a latent Atheism' in disbelief of witches: people deny witches because they deny spirits, and deny spirits because they own nothing but matter and motion.

src.l: Joseph Glanvill, Henry More, 1681, Saducismus Triumphatus: or, Full and Plain Evidence Concerning Witches and Apparitions
src.q: there is a latent Atheism at the root of the Saducean Principle. For too many deny Witches, because they believe there are no Spirits, and they are so persuaded, because they own no being in the World but Matter, and the results of Motion

s: Meric Casaubon (1668) answers the argument from fraud: if witches or spirits may be denied because counterfeits exist, so may every truth, since 'there is no truth, no nor vertue; but is attended with a counterfeit'.

src.l: Meric Casaubon, 1668, Of Credulity and Incredulity, in Things Natural, Civil, and Divine
src.q: there is no truth, but may be denied upon the same ground, since it is cer- tain, there is no truth, no nor vertue; but is attended with a counterfeit, often mistaken for the true

s: Webster (1677) blames ignorance of 'the power of Art and Nature' for witch beliefs and calls it unworthy to ascribe to devils what nature and art produce, invoking Roger Bacon's De nullitate magiae with Dee's notes.

src.l: John Webster, 1677, The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft
src.q: And therefore there can be nothing more unworthy, than for any man, that pretendeth to any portion of reason, so far to dote, or suffer himself to be led with ignorance and rashness, as to ascribe those strange things that Nature and Art, or both joined together do produce, unto Devils

s: Thorndike (HMES II, conclusion) doubts there could be any magic but natural magic, says experimentation and magic were 'so constantly associated' in his period, and suggests magicians may have been the first to experiment.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: Sometimes our authors have spoken of natural magic, but I rather wonder whether there could well be any other kind, since man must always reckon with his natural environment. ... It is even possible that magicians were the first to experiment

s: In the same conclusion Thorndike states that 'the spirit of magic is different from the scientific spirit', because magic delights in the marvellous and casts credibility to the winds.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: Thus the spirit of magic is different from the scientific spirit.

s: Against reading the natural-magic books as early experimental science: Bacon, the period's chief advocate of operative natural knowledge, judged that popular natural magic of sympathies and secrets was credulous and its experiments 'commonly frivolous', reserving 'Magique' for a still-missing science of forms.

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1640, Of the Advancement and Proficience of Learning (Gilbert Wats's English translation of De augmentis scientiarum)
src.q: with fome experiments commonly frivolous

s: The pseudo-Agrippan Fourth Book presents itself as a 'Complement and Key' to the books of Occult Philosophy and to all magical operations, and asks the reader to keep it secret.

src.l: Pseudo-Agrippa, Peter of Abano (attr.), Robert Turner (trans.), 1665, Henry Cornelius Agrippa his Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy (with the Heptameron and other tracts)
src.q: as it were a Complement and Key of our other books of Occult Philosophy, and of all Magical Operations

s: The Fourth Book derives the names of the planetary intelligences, and of the princes of evil spirits, by collecting letters out of an astrological figure of the world.

src.l: Pseudo-Agrippa, Peter of Abano (attr.), Robert Turner (trans.), 1665, Henry Cornelius Agrippa his Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy (with the Heptameron and other tracts)
src.q: the names of the intelligent presidents of every one of the Planets are constituted after this maner: that is to say, By collecting together the letters out of the figure of the world

s: In the Fourth Book the circle is fortified by writing in it divine names and the names of good spirits able to bind the spirit being called, with optional characters and pentacles.

src.l: Pseudo-Agrippa, Peter of Abano (attr.), Robert Turner (trans.), 1665, Henry Cornelius Agrippa his Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy (with the Heptameron and other tracts)
src.q: there shall also be written therein, the names of the good Spirits which bear rule, and are able to binde and constrain that Spirit which we intend to call

s: The Fourth Book gives two reasons for the lights, perfumes and unguents of an invocation: they agree with the spirit by natural and celestial virtue, and they are offered to it as worship, which the text itself calls 'superstitious'.

src.l: Pseudo-Agrippa, Peter of Abano (attr.), Robert Turner (trans.), 1665, Henry Cornelius Agrippa his Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy (with the Heptameron and other tracts)
src.q: which do partly agree with the Spirit, by reason of their natural and coelestial vertue ; and partly are exhibited to the Spirit for religious and superstitious worship

s: The Fourth Book says souls of the dead are not called up without blood or part of the body, and ranks churchyards below places of execution and recent public slaughter as sites for raising them.

src.l: Pseudo-Agrippa, Peter of Abano (attr.), Robert Turner (trans.), 1665, Henry Cornelius Agrippa his Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy (with the Heptameron and other tracts)
src.q: the Souls of the dead are not to be called up without blood, or by the application of ſome part of their relict Body ... the places moſt fitting for theſe things, are Church-yards. And better then them, are thoſe places wherein there is the execution of criminal judgements

s: The Heptameron (attributed to Peter of Abano) is printed after the Fourth Book on the stated ground that the Fourth Book treated ceremonies only in general, for the learned.

src.l: Pseudo-Agrippa, Peter of Abano (attr.), Robert Turner (trans.), 1665, Henry Cornelius Agrippa his Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy (with the Heptameron and other tracts)
src.q: because he doth not specially treat of the Ceremonies , but rather speaketh of them in general , it was therefore thought good to adde hereunto the Magi- cal Elements of Peter de Abano

s: The Heptameron's own preface describes the book as 'a certain introduction of Magical vanity' for those who 'have not tasted of Magical Superstitions'.

src.l: Pseudo-Agrippa, Peter of Abano (attr.), Robert Turner (trans.), 1665, Henry Cornelius Agrippa his Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy (with the Heptameron and other tracts)
src.q: to ignorant , and have not tasted of Magical Superstitions , may have them in readiness , how they may exercise themselves therein. For we see in this book , as it were a certain introduction of Magical vanity

s: The Heptameron holds that the form of the circle changes with the spirits called, their places, times, days and hours, and prescribes three circles nine feet across.

src.l: Pseudo-Agrippa, Peter of Abano (attr.), Robert Turner (trans.), 1665, Henry Cornelius Agrippa his Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy (with the Heptameron and other tracts)
src.q: The form of Circles is not alwayes one and the same ; but useth to be changed, according to the order of the Spirits that are to be called , their places , times , daies and hours

s: The Heptameron's Sunday conjuration adjures Michael, 'chief Ruler of the Lords day', by divine names (Adonay, Saday, Cados) and by the Sun; the Sunday spirits of the air procure gold, gems and riches.

src.l: Pseudo-Agrippa, Peter of Abano (attr.), Robert Turner (trans.), 1665, Henry Cornelius Agrippa his Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy (with the Heptameron and other tracts)
src.q: I conjure thee Michael, oh great Angel, who art chief Ruler of the Lords day ... The Spirits of the Air of the Lords day, are under the North winde; their nature is to procure Gold, Gemmes, Carbuncles, Riches

s: The Castor and Pollux dialogue 'Of the Nature of Spirits' printed with the Fourth Book identifies the good spirit given to men with a good angel, citing Raphael binding Asmodeus for Tobias.

src.l: Pseudo-Agrippa, Peter of Abano (attr.), Robert Turner (trans.), 1665, Henry Cornelius Agrippa his Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy (with the Heptameron and other tracts)
src.q: The holy Doctors do understand by the good Spirit a good Angel, such as we read Raphael was to Tobias, who bound the evil Spirit Asmodeus in the wilderness of the furthest parts of Egypt

s: The 1686 German Arbatel titles itself the magic and wisdom of the ancestors, of the people of God and of the heathen Magi, written 'against the devil-sorcerers', in nine parts of 49 aphorisms taught 'by the spirits'.

src.l: Anonymous, 1686, Arbatel: On the Magic of the Ancients (German, 1686)
src.q: Here begins the book of the Magic and Wisdom of our Ancestors / both of those among the People of God and among the Heathens who were called Magi ... against the devil-sorcerers ... each of which contains 49 Aphorisms or sayings / through which wisdom is taught by the spirits

s: The Arbatel defines the Magus as one whom the Divine Essence serves for knowledge of creation, and the Cacomagus ('Devil-Sorcerer') as one whom evil spirits serve, by God's permission, to ruin.

src.l: Anonymous, 1686, Arbatel: On the Magic of the Ancients (German, 1686)
src.q: The Cacomagus however, or Devil-Sorcerer, is one / whom, by GOD’s permission, the evil spirits serve / to temporal and eternal ruin and harm
src.qo: Der Cacomagus aber oder Teuffels-Zauberer ist / dem aus GOttes Verhängniß die bösen Geister dienen / zum zeit- und ewigen Verderben und Schaden /

s: The Arbatel's Olympic spirit Och 'administers solar matters', extends life to 600 years, teaches medicine and transforms everything into gold and precious stones.

src.l: Anonymous, 1686, Arbatel: On the Magic of the Ancients (German, 1686)
src.q: Och administers solar matters. He extends life to 600 years with good health; he provides and makes friends of the most magnificent and excellent spirits; he teaches the art of medicine perfectly; he transforms everything into pure gold and precious stones
src.qo: Och verwaltet Solarische Sachen/ Er längert das Leben auff 600. Jahr mit guter Gesundheit/ gibt und macht zu Freunden die herrlichsten und fürtrefflichsten Geister/ lehret die Kunst der Artzney vollkömmlich/ verkehret alles zu reinem Golde und in Edelgesteine/

s: The Arbatel's first of seven greatest secrets is to heal all diseases within seven days by characters, natural means or the higher stars, with God's help; it tells the reader to ask a spirit to reveal a secret.

src.l: Anonymous, 1686, Arbatel: On the Magic of the Ancients (German, 1686)
src.q: To be able to cure and heal all diseases within 7 days, either through symbols ... natural means, or through the higher stars, with the help of GOD
src.qo: entweder durch Characteres oder natürliche Mittel / oder durch die obern Geſtirn / mit der Hülffe GOTTes.

s: The Goetia tells that Solomon sealed the spirits in a brass vessel cast into a lake in Babylon; when Babylonians broke it seeking treasure the spirits escaped, and Belial entered an image and gave oracles to its worshippers.

src.l: Anonymous, S. L. MacGregor Mathers (ed.), L. W. de Laurence (publ.), 1916, The Lesser Key of Solomon: Goetia (de Laurence edition)
src.q: except BELIAL, who entered into a certain Image, and thence gave answers unto those who did offer Sacrifices unto him, and did worship the Image as their God

s: The Goetia orders the seals of the 72 spirits to be made in the metal of the planet matching each rank: kings in gold (Sol), marquises in silver (Luna), dukes in copper (Venus), and so on.

src.l: Anonymous, S. L. MacGregor Mathers (ed.), L. W. de Laurence (publ.), 1916, The Lesser Key of Solomon: Goetia (de Laurence edition)
src.q: The Seals of the 72 Kings are to be made in Metals. The Chief Kings’ in Sol (Gold) ; Marquises’ in Luna (Silver) ; Dukes’ in Venus (Copper)

s: The Goetia's first spirit, Bael, makes one go invisible, and his character must be worn as a lamen by the caller, 'or else he will not do thee homage'.

src.l: Anonymous, S. L. MacGregor Mathers (ed.), L. W. de Laurence (publ.), 1916, The Lesser Key of Solomon: Goetia (de Laurence edition)
src.q: He maketh thee to go Invisible. He ruleth over 66 Legions of Infernal Spirits ... This is his character which is used to be worn as a Lamen before him who calleth him forth, or else he will not do thee homage

s: The Goetia's circle of Solomon is nine feet across, ringed with divine names from Ehyeh to Levanah, and the triangle into which the spirits are commanded stands two feet outside it.

src.l: Anonymous, S. L. MacGregor Mathers (ed.), L. W. de Laurence (publ.), 1916, The Lesser Key of Solomon: Goetia (de Laurence edition)
src.q: This Magical Circle is to be made 9 feet across, and the Divine Names are to be written around it, beginning at EHYEH, and ending at LEVANAH, Luna ... THIS is the Form of the Magical Triangle, into the which Solomon did command the Evil Spirits

s: The French Key of Solomon claims descent from a Hebrew original translated into Latin by Rabbi Abognazar, carried to Arles, and after the expulsion of the Jews put into French by the Archbishop Barrault.

src.l: Pseudo-Solomon, 'Abognazar' (attr.), Barrault (attr. trans.), 1634, The Key of Solomon (French, 'Abognazar/Barrault' recension)
src.q: This Testament was anciently translated from Hebrew into the Latin language by the Rabbi Abognazar ... who carried it with him to the City of Arles in Provence. There, by a notable stroke of luck following the expulsion of the Jews from that city

s: The Key of Solomon opens with Solomon telling Rehoboam that no science is 'more natural or more useful than the knowledge of the Celestial movements'.

src.l: Pseudo-Solomon, 'Abognazar' (attr.), Barrault (attr. trans.), 1634, The Key of Solomon (French, 'Abognazar/Barrault' recension)
src.q: MY SON REHOBOAM: As among all the Sciences there is none more natural or more useful than the knowledge of the Celestial movements

s: The Key of Solomon lists ten Hebrew divine names (Ehieh, Elohim, Shaddai, Shekinah ...) which, written on virgin lambskin parchment and carried, will 'acquire for you great prosperity'.

src.l: Pseudo-Solomon, 'Abognazar' (attr.), Barrault (attr. trans.), 1634, The Key of Solomon (French, 'Abognazar/Barrault' recension)
src.q: these names, being written upon Virgin Lambskin Parchment and carried upon your person, will acquire for you great prosperity and the blessing of the great eternal God

s: The Ars Notoria claims to be an art revealed by an angel to Solomon on the Temple altar, by which he came to know all liberal and mechanical arts in a short time.

src.l: Pseudo-Solomon, Robert Turner (trans.), 1657, Ars Notoria: The Notory Art of Solomon
src.q: which the Moſt High Creator by his holy Angel miniſtred to S O L O M O N upon the Altar of the Temple ; that thereby in a ſhort time he knew all Arts and Sciences, both Liberal and Mechanick

s: An eighteenth-century French Keys of Solomon manuscript opens by asserting that Solomon possessed the 'infused sciences' through an angel's teachings.

src.l: Pseudo-Solomon, 1641, Keys of Solomon, French MS, Guaita collection
src.q: Solomon possessed all the infused sciences ... by the wise precepts and teachings of an angel

s: The Grimorium Verum says there are only two kinds of pact, tacit and explicit, and warns the operator to beware spirits that require something belonging to him.

src.l: 'Alibeck the Egyptian' (attr.), 18th c., Grimorium Verum (The True Grimoire)
src.q: There are only two kinds of pact, the tacit and the apparent [or explicit]. ... It is when you make a pact with a spirit, and have to give the spirit something which belongs to you, that you have to be on your guard

s: The Grimorium Verum lets the spirit's character be drawn on an emerald or ruby 'for they have a sympathy for the spirits, especially those of the Sun', and has it written in one's own blood.

src.l: 'Alibeck the Egyptian' (attr.), 18th c., Grimorium Verum (The True Grimoire)
src.q: you may draw the character on an emerald or ruby, for they have a sympathy for the spirits, especially those of the Sun

s: The Grand Grimoire gives a pact to Lucifuge Rofocale, written by hand on virgin parchment and signed in one's own blood, promising to reward him in twenty years for treasures given.

src.l: Anonymous, 1750, The Grand Grimoire with the Great Key of Solomon
src.q: I promise the great LUCIFUGE > to reward him in twenty years for > all the Treasures he shall give me.

s: A Faust 'Triple Coercion of Hell' text (Scheible 1849, from a Coburg manuscript) conjures Mephistophiel by a string of names to appear before the circle and answer 'in the German language'.

src.l: Pseudo-Faust, J. Scheible (publ.), 1849, Doctor Johannes Faust's Natural and Unnatural Magic, or the Triple Coercion of Hell
src.q: I, N., conjure you, spirit Mephistophiel, by Rolamicon † Hipite † Agla † Elohym † Reremiseh † Jehova †.
src.qo: Ich N. beschwöre dich Geist Mephistophiel durch Rolamicon † Hipite † Agla † Elohym † Reremiseh † Jehova †.

s: Scheible's 1849 Stuttgart edition prints 'Doctor Johannes Faust's Natural and Unnatural Magic, or The Triple Coercion of Hell' from a decorated manuscript in the Ducal Library at Coburg.

src.l: Pseudo-Faust, J. Scheible (publ.), 1849, Doctor Johannes Faust's Natural and Unnatural Magic, or the Triple Coercion of Hell
src.q: According to a sumptuously decorated manuscript in the Ducal Library at Coburg, published completely and word-for-word in five sections
src.qo: Nach einer kostbar ausgestatteten Handschrift in der Herzogl. Bibliothek zu Koburg vollständig und wortgetreu herausgegeben in fünf Abtheilungen,

s: The Faust Höllenzwang speaks in Faust's voice to rank spirits by usefulness, claiming that without Marbuel 'no secret can be discovered regarding minerals' and hidden riches.

src.l: Pseudo-Faust, J. Scheible (publ.), 1849, Doctor Johannes Faust's Natural and Unnatural Magic, or the Triple Coercion of Hell
src.q: I, Faust, say only this much: that without Marbuel, no secret can be discovered regarding minerals and what can be done with them.

s: The Enchiridion of Pope Leo presents its prayer as sent by Pope Leo to Charlemagne, promising protection to whoever recites it daily and carries it.

src.l: Pseudo-Leo III, c. 1810, The Enchiridion of Pope Leo
src.q: if you believe firmly, without doubting, that every day you recite the following Prayer with devotion, and carry it upon your person with respect, whether in the home, at war, at sea, or wherever you may be, none of your enemies will
src.qo: ſi vous croyez fermement, ſans vous mettre en doute, que chaque jour que vous réciterez avec dévotion l'Oraiſon ſuivante, & la porterez ſur vous avec reſpect, ſoit dans la maiſon, ſoit dans la guerre, ſoit ſur mer ou dans quelque lieu que vous ſoyez,

s: Frantz Brunn's 1570 'description of the high and hidden arts, Magica and Cabala' was dedicated to Emperor Maximilian II and printed with an imperial privilege.

src.l: Frantz Brunn, 1570, Unterthenigste beschreibung der hoch und verborgenen Künsten, Magien und Cabala
src.q: Most humble description of the high and hidden arts, Magica and Cabala. Composed by Frank Brunnen of Strasbourg. With the freedom of the Roman Imperial Majesty, etc., not to be reprinted.
src.qo: Vnterthenigste beschreibung Der hoch vnd verborgenen Künsten / Magica vnd Cabala. Gestellet durch Frank Brunnen von Straßburg. Mit Röm. Key. Mai. 2c. freiheyt nicht nachzutrucken.

s: The Dresden 'Magia Abraham' presents itself as the practice of Magia compiled by 'Abraham, a son of Simon of the tribe of Judah' for his son Lamech, joined to the holy Cabala.

src.l: 'Abraham of Worms' (attr.), 18th c. MS, Magia Abraham oder Underricht von der Heiligen Cabala (Mscr.Dresd.N.111)
src.q: which I, Abraham, a son of Simon of the tribe of Judah, have experimented with partly from my father, partly from my own findings
src.qo: Welche ich Abraham ein Sohn Simonis aus dem Stam Jude, zum Theil von meinem Vatter auf zum Theil aus eigener findung experimentiret

s: In De vanitate (Dutch 1661 version) Agrippa calls goetic sorcery, worked through fellowship with impure spirits and forbidden conjurations, 'by the consensus of all laws rooted out and cursed'.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1661, Of the Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences and Arts (Dutch translation)
src.q: sorcery—godless through the fellowship of impure spirits, adorned with ceremonies of a damned precision, and with forbidden magic verses and conjurations—is by the consensus of all laws rooted out and cursed
src.qo: de toverij, heilloos door de gemeinfchap der onreine geeften, opgefmukt met plechtigheden van een verdoemde naukeurigheid, met ongeoorlofde toovervaarzen en bezweringen, is door aller wetten goedvinden uitgeroit en vervloekt.

s: Agrippa distinguishes those who think they can constrain spirits by calling on the divine name from those who surrender themselves to devils and worship them, and still counts the first in danger.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1661, Of the Uncertainty and Vanity of the Sciences and Arts (Dutch translation)
src.q: who, by calling upon the Divine name, think they can firmly constrain the spirits; but the others, far more hideous
src.qo: door aanroeping des Goddelijken naams, de geesten meenen vast te prangen: doch de andere veel afgrijselijker,

s: Waite (1898) judged the Grimorium Verum's printed date 'undeniably fraudulent' and placed it in the mid-eighteenth century, and dated the Grand Grimoire no earlier.

src.l: Arthur Edward Waite, 1898, The Book of Black Magic and of Pacts
src.q: The date specified in the title of the Grimorium Verum is undeniably fraudulent; the work belongs to the middle of the eighteenth century, and Memphis is Rome. The "Grand Grimoire" is not of higher antiquity.

s: Waite (1898) reported the Key of Solomon in Latin, French, Italian and German manuscripts, the oldest used by Mathers being sixteenth-century Latin, and found the claim of a Hebrew original not 'essentially improbable'.

src.l: Arthur Edward Waite, 1898, The Book of Black Magic and of Pacts
src.q: The oldest codex used by the English editor is in contracted Latin, and belongs to the sixteenth century. ... It is, however, claimed that the work was written originally in Hebrew. In this claim there is nothing essentially improbable

s: Waite (1898) repeats the Grimorium Verum's division of pacts into tacit and manifest, and in a footnote citing Bergier's Theological Dictionary says Catholic theologians extended the pact to cover the mere process of communicating with spirits.

src.l: Arthur Edward Waite, 1898, The Book of Black Magic and of Pacts
src.q: There are two kinds of pacts, says the Grimorium Verum, the tacit and the manifest

s: Waite (1898) knew no Arbatel manuscript before the late sixteenth century, took the 1575 Basel print as its first appearance, and judged it unconnected to the Keys of Solomon and 'permeated with Christian ideas'.

src.l: Arthur Edward Waite, 1898, The Book of Black Magic and of Pacts
src.q: It should be observed that the Arbatel has no connection with the cycle, hereinafter considered, of the Keys of Solomon, and it is permeated with Christian ideas. The authorship is completely unknown.

s: Critique: Waite (1898) names back-dating and imputed authorship as 'the two crying bibliographical sins of Grimoires', which tells against taking the grimoires' Solomonic, Hebrew, papal or patriarchal attributions at face value.

src.l: Arthur Edward Waite, 1898, The Book of Black Magic and of Pacts
src.q: Back-dating and imputed authorship are the two crying bibliographical sins of Grimoires and magical handbooks

s: Critique: Johann Weyer, Agrippa's pupil, rejected the Fourth Book as an 'abominable little book' attributed to Agrippa by a wicked man, and judged books ascribed to Raziel and Raphael recent forgeries full of unknown names and seals.

src.l: Johann Weyer, 1660, Opera omnia (incl. De praestigiis daemonum)
src.q: that abominable little book recently brought to light by a wicked man and attributed to Henry Cornelius Agrippa—my former host and honored teacher
src.qo: § 2. Optimo jure his annumeretur abominabilis libellus nuper in lucem ab impio homine emissus, tributusque Henr. Corn. Agrippæ, meo olim hospiti & præceptori honorando, ultra annos quadraginta jam mortuo,

s: Thorndike's stated thesis (1923) is that magic and experimental science were connected in their development, that 'magicians were perhaps the first to experiment', and that both are better understood studied together.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. I: During the First Thirteen Centuries of Our Era
src.q: My idea is that magic and experimental science have been connected in their development; that magicians were perhaps the first to experiment; and that the history of both magic and experimental science can be better understood by studying them together.

s: Thorndike takes magic 'in the broadest sense' to include all occult arts, superstitions and folklore, yet excludes laws against magic, popular practice and the witch persecution from his scope, referring them to Hansen.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. I: During the First Thirteen Centuries of Our Era
src.q: Magic is here understood in the broadest sense of the word, as including all occult arts and sciences, supersti- tions, and folk-lore. ... The subject of laws against magic, popular practice of magic, the witchcraft delusion and persecution lie outside of the scope of this book.

s: In his conclusion Thorndike judges the attempts of his medieval authors to distinguish magic from astrology or divination, good from bad magic, or natural magic from sorcery 'exceedingly illogical and unconvincing'.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: The attempts of some of our authors to distinguish between magic and astrology, or magic and divination, or good and bad magic, or natural magic and sorcery, or witchcraft and counter-magic, have all been exceedingly illogical and unconvincing.

s: Thorndike holds that neither spirits nor stars are always necessary to magic; its sine qua non is 'a human operator, materials, rites, and an aim that borders on the impossible'.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: it cannot be said that spirits or stars are thought of as always necessary in magic. The sine qua non seems to be a human operator, materials, rites, and an aim that borders on the impossible

s: Thorndike suspects that magic declined not because it was shown false but because men came to set a greater value upon truth.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: I suspect that it is not so much that magic has been shown to be false, as it is that men have come to set a greater value upon truth, that accounts for magic's decline.

s: Murray (1921) asserts that the people called witches in late medieval times practised a pre-Christian 'ancient religion of Western Europe', with organised rites and a horned or two-faced god, which she named the Dianic cult.

src.l: Margaret Alice Murray, 1921, The Witch-Cult in Western Europe: A Study in Anthropology
src.q: It can be traced back to pre-Christian times, and appears to be the ancient religion of Western Europe.

s: Murray reads Cotton Mather's remark that the witches are 'organized like Congregational Churches' as 'the clue' to the witch-cult's hierarchy.

src.l: Margaret Alice Murray, 1921, The Witch-Cult in Western Europe: A Study in Anthropology
src.q: caused Cotton Mather to say, 'The witches are organized like Congregational Churches.' This gives the clue at once.

s: Naudé (1625; English 1657) finds it 'a strange thing' that Delrio, Le Loyer, Bodin, de Lancre and Godelmann wrote so passionately on demons and sorcerers as 'never to reject any Story, though ever so fabulous'.

src.l: Gabriel Naudé, John Davies (trans.), 1657, The History of Magick, by way of Apology for all the Wise Men who have unjustly been reputed Magicians
src.q: It is certainly a strange thing, that Delrio, Le Loyer, Bodin, de Lancre, Godelman, who have been, nay yet are, persons of credit and desert should write so passionately upon the subject of Dæmons, Sorcerers and Magicians, as never to reject any Story, though ever so fabulous and ridiculous

s: Clucas (2022) describes the historiography of magic and science in the 1960s-80s as dominated by Yates's 'Hermetic' thesis and its critics (Westman, Vickers), and proposes instead tracing al-Kindi's theory of rays through perspectiva, Dee and seventeenth-century mechanists to Newton.

src.l: Stephen Clucas, 2022, Astrology, Natural Magic, and the Scientific Revolution

s: Bailey (2006) observes that the classic definitions of Tylor, Frazer, Durkheim and others still reverberate, while more recent studies take a much narrower approach to magic in particular periods and societies, at a cost to communication across fields.

src.l: Michael D. Bailey, 2006, The Meanings of Magic

s: The Mishnah (Sanhedrin 7:11) defines the capital sorcerer (mekhashef) as one who performs an actual deed, not one who merely produces an illusion.

src.l: Anonymous (rabbinic tradition), 2017, Mishnah: Kaufmann Manuscript (Complete)
src.q: The sorcerer, is one who performs a physical deed, but not one who merely creates an illusion.
src.qo: הַמְּכַשֵּׁף, הָעוֹשֶׂה מַעֲשֶׂה, לֹא הָאוֹחֵז אֶת הָעֵינַיִם.

s: The Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 67b) grades witchcraft like Sabbath law: some acts incur stoning, some are forbidden but unpunished, and some are permitted from the outset.

src.l: Michael Levi Rodkinson (tr.), 1897, New Edition of the Babylonian Talmud (Tract Sanhedrin)
src.q: The Halakhas of witchcraft are similar to the Halakhas of Sabbath. There are some to which stoning applies; there are some which are not allowed to start with, but if, nevertheless, one has done them, he is free; and some are allowed even to start with.

s: Abaye in the Talmud distinguishes an effect worked through a demon from one worked by witchcraft by whether the practitioner is particular about using a specific utensil.

src.l: Michael Levi Rodkinson (tr.), 1897, New Edition of the Babylonian Talmud (Tract Sanhedrin)
src.q: Said Abayi: A conjurer who is particular to use a utensil, it is by a demon, and he who is not particular, it is by witchcraft.

s: The same Talmudic passage puts deceiving the eyes in the forbidden-but-unpunished class and cites rabbis who regularly created a calf as an example of what is permitted from the outset.

src.l: Michael Levi Rodkinson (tr.), 1897, New Edition of the Babylonian Talmud (Tract Sanhedrin)
src.q: To dazzle the eyes is not allowed to start with, but if one did, he is free. And it is allowed to start with, as said above. R. Hanina and R. Oshia were accustomed to create a calf, etc.

s: Maimonides (Guide III.37) attributes astrology and magic to the Sabians, Chaldaeans, Egyptians and Canaanites, and says the commandments against them exist to restrain idolatry.

src.l: Moses Maimonides, Johann Buxtorf the Younger (tr.), 1629, Doctor perplexorum (Moreh Nevukhim), Latin, Basel 1629
src.q: it will become clear to you that Astrology or Magic was the work of the Sabians, the Kasdim, and the Chaldaeans; it was even more frequent among the Egyptians and Canaanites.

s: Maimonides reports that the magicians he read held that no magical work succeeds without regard to the stars, every plant, animal and metal having its own star.
