src.l: Moses Maimonides, Johann Buxtorf the Younger (tr.), 1629, Doctor perplexorum (Moreh Nevukhim), Latin, Basel 1629
src.q: But no magical work can be performed without respect and consideration for the Stars. For they think that every Plant has its own Star, just as they also assign certain Stars to all Animals and Metals.
src.qo: Nullum autem Magicum opus sine Syderum respectu & consideratione potest perfici. Existimant enim, quamvis Plantam suam habere Stellam, quemadmodum & omnibus Animalibus & Metallis certa Sydera adscribunt.

s: For Maimonides magical acts are a form of star worship, and every magician is therefore an idolater who must be put to death.

src.l: Moses Maimonides, Johann Buxtorf the Younger (tr.), 1629, Doctor perplexorum (Moreh Nevukhim), Latin, Basel 1629
src.q: They even think that those works are specific forms of worship of the Stars ... therefore it necessarily follows that every Magician must be killed; ... because every Magician is without doubt an Idolater
src.qo: Arbitrantur etiam, opera illa esse peculiares Stellarum cultus, illasque tali actione, sermone vel fumo delectari, & ejus gratiâ, quicquid optant sibi, praestare. His itaque sic praelibatis, quae ex Libris illorum hodiè inter nos extantibus desumpta sunt, meis quoque verbis benignas praebe aures. Cur Magi sint occidendi? Quandoquidem totius Legis scopus & cardo, circa quem versatur, consistit in hoc, ut Idololatria è medio tollatur, nomen ejus deleatur, nullique Stellae nocendi vel juvandi inter Homines virtus attribuatur, & haec sententia necessariò ad cultum illarum permovet: ideò necessariò sequitur, omnem Magum occidendum esse; Omnis Magus est Idololatra. quia omnis Magus citra dubium est Idololatra,

s: Maimonides explains the feminine 'sorceress' of Exodus 22:18 by saying that most of these magical works are performed by women.

src.l: Moses Maimonides, Johann Buxtorf the Younger (tr.), 1629, Doctor perplexorum (Moreh Nevukhim), Latin, Basel 1629
src.q: And because the greater part of those works are to be performed by Women, therefore the Law says; A sorceress [Mekhashefah], that is, a female magician or illusionist, you shall not suffer to live.
src.qo: Et quia major pars illorum operum à Mulieribus est perficienda, ideò dicit Lex; Mecchasschepha, h. e. Magam vel Praestigiatricem non sines vivere.

s: Maimonides reads the Torah's covenant curses (wild beasts, crop damage) as aimed at magic: the very harms magicians claim to avert are threatened as punishment for using it.

src.l: Moses Maimonides, Johann Buxtorf the Younger (tr.), 1629, Doctor perplexorum (Moreh Nevukhim), Latin, Basel 1629
src.q: God said to them in the words of the Covenant that because of the idolatry and magic through which they believe they can ward off these harms, those very same evils will instead remain and dwell upon them.
src.qo: ideò dixit ad illos DEUS in verbis Fœderis, quòd propter Idololatriam & Magiam, quibus existimant se res istas noxias à se averruncare velle,

s: Maimonides (Guide I.61) tells the reader to ignore divine names heard from writers of amulets, calling them superstitious and insane.

src.l: Moses Maimonides, Johann Buxtorf the Younger (tr.), 1629, Doctor perplexorum (Moreh Nevukhim), Latin, Basel 1629
src.q: if you hear such things from superstitious and insane men who write ... amulets or experimental charms, or if you read them in their writings.

s: Maimonides says the names amulet-makers invent mean nothing, though their users call them divine names that demand special holiness and work miracles.

src.l: Moses Maimonides, Johann Buxtorf the Younger (tr.), 1629, Doctor perplexorum (Moreh Nevukhim), Latin, Basel 1629
src.q: For those names which they fabricate teach absolutely nothing real, and yet they call them "Divine Names," believing that they require a singular holiness and purity, and that they possess the power to perform and produce miracles.
src.qo: Nomina etenim illa, quæ effingunt, de nulla planè re docent, & tamen vocant ea Nomina (Divina), existimantque illa singularem requirere sanctitatem & puritatem, & virtutem habere miracula edendi ac faciendi.

s: Maimonides restricts 'Shem ha-Mephorash' to the Tetragrammaton alone.

src.l: Moses Maimonides, Johann Buxtorf the Younger (tr.), 1629, Doctor perplexorum (Moreh Nevukhim), Latin, Basel 1629
src.q: For no name at all is called the Shem Ha-Mephorash except for this Tetragrammaton
src.qo: Nam nullum prorsus nomen vocatur Schem hammephorasch, præter hoc Tetragrammaton, quod scribitur, sed non secundùm litteras suas legitur.

s: The Maimonides passage on the Twelve- and Forty-Two-Letter Names, as given in Galatinus's book, holds that what was taught with them was concepts, not the sounds of letters, and that neither is the Shem ha-Mephorash.

src.l: Petrus Galatinus, Johann Reuchlin, 1550, Opus de arcanis catholicae veritatis; De arte cabalistica (Basel 1550)
src.q: the matter that was learned consisted of the concepts indicated by those names, not merely the speech of the inscribed letters devoid of meaning. Neither the Twelve-Letter Name nor the Forty-Two-Letter Name was called the Explicit Name

s: Galatinus's De arcanis (1518) cites Maimonides, Guide I.61, for the practice of saying Adonai in place of the ineffable name outside the priestly blessing.

src.l: Petrus Galatinus, Johann Reuchlin, 1550, Opus de arcanis catholicae veritatis; De arte cabalistica (Basel 1550)
src.q: wherever they found that name, they did not dare to utter it at all, but pronounced Adonai in its place. ... This is what Rabbi Moses Maimonides affirms in the sixty-first chapter of the first part of the book Moreh.

s: The Latin commentary on Maimonides' Laws of Idolatry (1668) reads him as distinguishing demonic magic, punished by stoning, from sleight of hand, punished by lashes.

src.l: Moses Maimonides, 1668, De idolatria liber (Hilkhot Avodah Zarah, Latin with commentary)
src.q: Maimonides establishes two kinds of magic here: one is demonic, the other is illusory. ... Maimonides says such people are to be stoned. ... Such imposters are to be punished with lashes according to Maimonides.

s: The Latin Liber Razielis opens with the legend that the angel Raziel brought Adam, grieving over his lost wisdom, a book of secrets written on a sapphire stone.

src.l: Anonymous (attributed to the angel Raziel), 1350, Liber Razielis Archangeli
src.q: he brought the book of secrets to Adam, who was sad and grieving because he saw that he was separated and far removed from wisdom. And this book was written upon a sapphire stone.

s: Liber Razielis grounds the book's power in the holy names of God it contains: through them Adam knew and did what he wished, and later prophets worked with it.

src.l: Anonymous (attributed to the angel Raziel), 1350, Liber Razielis Archangeli
src.q: through this book, containing the holy and glorious names of God which are within it, Adam knew those things he wished to know and did those things he wished to do.

s: Liber Razielis assigns incenses to the four quarters and elements and makes knowing how to compound them a precondition for working with the book.

src.l: Anonymous (attributed to the angel Raziel), 1350, Liber Razielis Archangeli
src.q: whoever wishes to accomplish anything through this book should observe and understand the chapter on incense, know the substances, and understand how to blend them as required.

s: Liber Razielis defines the 'image' used in its operations as the Word of God and requires angel names to be written on it.

src.l: Anonymous (attributed to the angel Raziel), 1350, Liber Razielis Archangeli
src.q: Image is called the Word of God, according to Raziel. ... Upon that image must be the names of the angels written above the chapters

s: Liber Razielis presents itself as a 'Book of Virtues and Miracles' to be used in fear of the Creator, in holiness and purity, after preparations that include fumigation and burial of the image.

src.l: Anonymous (attributed to the angel Raziel), 1350, Liber Razielis Archangeli
src.q: Fear the Creator of all that is made and look into this book, which is called the Book of Virtues and Miracles, regarding holiness and purity.

s: The printed Sefer Raziel (Amsterdam 1701) gives a childbirth amulet that adjures 'First Eve' (Lilith), by the three angels Senoi, Sansenoi and Semangelof, not to harm mother or child.

src.l: Anonymous (attributed to the angel Raziel), 1701, Sefer Raziel ha-Malakh (Amsterdam: Moses Mendes Coutinho, 1701)
src.q: I adjure you, First Eve, in the name of He who is your Creator, and in the names of the three angels your Creator sent for your sake ... do not harm the woman giving birth [Name], daughter of [Mother's Name], nor the child born to her

s: Sefer Raziel also gives amulets for social ends, such as gaining favor and grace before all who see the bearer.

src.l: Anonymous (attributed to the angel Raziel), 1701, Sefer Raziel ha-Malakh (Amsterdam: Moses Mendes Coutinho, 1701)
src.q: And grant him favor, grace, and mercy before the Throne of the Lord and before all creatures who see him.

s: A 1635 Latin cabalistic disputation explains why Jews hang an amulet (kamea) with the three angels' names on infants: Lilith swore not to harm where she saw their names.

src.l: Yisrael ben Moshe, Joseph de Voisin (ed., tr.), 1635, Disputatio Cabalistica de Anima, et opus Rhythmicum R. Abraham Aben Ezra
src.q: write the names of these angels upon a Kamea ... or a parchment slip, and to hang it upon the necks of our infants; so that surely when Lilith has caught sight of this slip or writing, mindful of her oath, she might not be harmful to the infants

s: A Hebrew amulet collection (Gaster MS 61) labels a general-purpose amulet 'tested and proven', the empirical formula of the segulot literature.

src.l: Anonymous, 17th or 18th century, Composite manuscript: fragments from several manuscripts (Gaster Hebrew MS 61)
src.q: A good and useful amulet for everything, tested and proven, and this is it: In the name of the Lord, God of Israel, we shall act and we shall succeed.

s: The Sword of Moses (Gaster's text) tells the user to insert the adjuration of its angelic ministers into the 'Who hears prayer' blessing of the daily prayer.

src.l: Moses Gaster (ed.), 1925, Studies and Texts in Folklore, Magic, Medieval Romance, Hebrew Apocrypha, Vol. III (Hebrew texts, incl. the Sword of Moses)
src.q: One who wishes to use this Sword should pray his prayer, and in the blessing "Who hears prayer" he should say: I adjure you, the four ministers

s: In De arte cabalistica Reuchlin's Jewish speaker sets Kabbalah against magic: Kabbalah works through names of light and angels toward salvation, magic through names of darkness and evil spirits toward perdition.

src.l: Johann Reuchlin, Johannes Pistorius (ed.), 1587, Artis cabalisticae tomus I (contains Reuchlin, De arte cabalistica)
src.q: the rod of the Kabbalists always devours the rods of the tricksters, and anything divine acts more healthfully than anything demonic. For the art of Kabbalah always tends toward the salvation of men, whereas the poison of magical vanity always verges toward perdition

s: Reuchlin says Kabbalists' miracles were so easy that envious outsiders called them 'cunning magicians', i.e. 'magician' was the accuser's label.

src.l: Johann Reuchlin, Johannes Pistorius (ed.), 1587, Artis cabalisticae tomus I (contains Reuchlin, De arte cabalistica)
src.q: this operation of miracles was so easy for Kabbalists that they were often ignorantly called "cunning Magicians" by the envious and profane

s: In De verbo mirifico Reuchlin allows a doctrine of illusions but says there is no doctrine of miracles, only union with God in which God acts through us.

src.l: Johann Reuchlin, 1514, Liber de verbo mirifico
src.q: while there can be a doctrine of illusions, there is no doctrine of miracles unless it be a serving union with divinity. In this union, we ourselves do not act through God, but God acts through us

s: Reuchlin's wonder-working word is the Tetragrammaton with the letter shin added, giving IHSUH, the name of Jesus.

src.l: Johann Reuchlin, 1514, Liber de verbo mirifico
src.q: which is the name called the Tetragrammaton, through the letter Shin, that is, ihsuh. For with these five letters, that most holy and adorable name ihsuh must be written.

s: Pico's Apologia defends his thesis that no science more certifies Christ's divinity than magic and Kabbalah, saying its censors are forced to accept the affirmative form as Catholic.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1601, Opera Omnia (Basel, 1601) - Apologia
src.q: (namely: No science more certifies the divinity of Christ than magic and Kabbalah), they are forced by their own judgment to accept its affirmative counterpart as Catholic: Magic and Kabbalah do certify for us the divinity of Christ.

s: Agrippa's Opera prints the 72 angels bearing the Shem ha-Mephorash, extracted from Exodus 14:19-21, the three verses of 72 letters each.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1600, Opera, in duos tomos concinne digesta
src.q: THESE ARE THE SEVENTY-TWO ANGELS BEARING THE NAME OF GOD SCHEM- hamphoras, whose names are elicited from verses 19, 20, and 21 of chapter 14 of the book of Exodus

s: Kircher (Oedipus Aegyptiacus) writes, at the prompting of the Inquisition, to expose amulets 'modern Hebrews' sell to ordinary people under the pretext of sacred words.

src.l: Athanasius Kircher, 1653, Oedipus Aegyptiacus
src.q: For some time now, modern Hebrews have sold to the world a certain new type of amulet. Under the pretext of using sacred words, they promise nothing less than every good thing to ignorant and common people

s: Kircher names the Shimmush Tehillim (practical use of the Psalms) as the foundation of the whole manufacture of Cabalistic amulets.

src.l: Athanasius Kircher, 1653, Oedipus Aegyptiacus
src.q: From this, as if from a certain Lethean spring, flow the rivers of all superstitious arts. The entire manufacture and structure of Cabalistic amulets rests upon this as a foundation.

s: Berlendi's Cabalomachia (1718) condemns 'practical' Kabbalah as entirely illicit because it applies Kabbalistic secrets to divination and magic.

src.l: Francesco Berlendi, 1718, Cabalomachia, hoc est artis cabalisticae oppugnatio
src.q: The third kind of Kabbalah, which is called Practical, although it uses the secrets and mysteries of the preceding forms of Kabbalah, nevertheless, because it adapts them to Divination and Magic and uses them in various other superstitious ways, it is entirely illicit and to be condemned.

s: Lea (1888) argues that rabbinic Judaism enforced 'thou shalt not suffer a witch to live' relentlessly, citing Simeon ben Shetach's hanging of eighty 'witches' at Ascalon, and that Christianity derived its assurance from Judaism.

src.l: Henry Charles Lea, 1906, A History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages, Vol. III
src.q: Yet this man, so scrupulous about taking life, had no hesitation in hanging at Ascalon eighty witches in a single day. ... Christianity thus derived from Judaism the complete assurance

s: Montgomery's edition of the Nippur incantation bowls traces angel names on the bowls to the Book of Raziel, linking late-antique Babylonian Jewish magic with the later Raziel literature.

src.l: James A. Montgomery, 1913, Aramaic Incantation Texts from Nippur
src.q: The name Asiel occurs in the Book of Raziel

s: Ginsburg (1865) reports that Pico found more Christianity than Judaism in the Kabbalah, which led to the 900 Theses and the thesis on magic and Kabbalah.

src.l: Christian D. Ginsburg, 1865, The Kabbalah: Its Doctrines, Development, and Literature
src.q: there is more Christianity in the Kabbalah than Judaism; he discovered in it proof for the doctrine of the Trinity, the Incarnation, the divinity of Christ

s: Waite (1891) frames the scholarly view of Kabbalism as split between dismissal as forgery and jargon and credulous acceptance, and places the truth between them.

src.l: Arthur Edward Waite, 1891, The Occult Sciences
src.q: There is that of incredulous criticism which considers it to be, historically, a flagrant forgery, and, in itself, barbarous and unintelligible jargon; and there is that of uncritical credulity

s: Maimonides' objection to practical name-magic: the invented names of amulet writers have no power and a perfect man should not even listen to them. It is aimed at the name-based operations of the Raziel and Sword of Moses type.

src.l: Moses Maimonides, Johann Buxtorf the Younger (tr.), 1629, Doctor perplexorum (Moreh Nevukhim), Latin, Basel 1629
src.q: Indeed, a perfect man should not only refuse to believe these things but should not even listen to them.
src.qo: Verùm ista omnia ab homine perfecto non solùm non credenda, sed ne audienda quidem sunt.

s: Against Lea: the Mishnah's own account (Sanhedrin 6:4) says Simeon ben Shetach hanged eighty 'women', not witches, and has the Sages flag it as irregular, so it is weak evidence of routine rabbinic enforcement of the witch law.

src.l: Anonymous (rabbinic tradition), 2017, Mishnah: Kaufmann Manuscript (Complete)
src.q: It once happened with Shimon ben Shetach, that he hanged eighty women in Ashkelon! The Sages said to him: He hanged eighty women, yet under normal law, we do not judge two people in a single day.

s: Iamblichus (De mysteriis 2.11) holds that theurgic union with the gods is produced not by thinking but by ritual acts performed beyond understanding and by symbols known only to the gods.

src.l: Iamblichus, Porphyry, Thomas Taylor (tr.), 1895, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians (with the Epistle of Porphyry to Anebo)
src.q: For a conception of the mind does not conjoin theurgists with the Gods; ... For the perfect efficacy of ineffable works, which are divinely performed in a way surpassing all intelligence, and the power of inexplicable symbols, which are known only to the Gods, impart theurgic union.

s: Iamblichus makes the divine tokens (synthemata) the proper cause that moves the divine will, and the practitioner's purity and good dispositions only contributing 'concauses'.

src.l: Iamblichus, Porphyry, Thomas Taylor (tr.), 1895, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians (with the Epistle of Porphyry to Anebo)
src.q: it is requisite to consider these, and all the best dispositions of the soul, and also the purity pertaining to us, as certain concauses; the things which properly excite the divine will being divine synthemata themselves.

s: Iamblichus answers Porphyry that the 'barbarous' sacred names cannot be translated without losing their power, and are better suited to the gods for their concision and lack of ambiguity.

src.l: Iamblichus, Porphyry, Thomas Taylor (tr.), 1895, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians (with the Epistle of Porphyry to Anebo)
src.q: though it should be possible to translate them, yet they no longer preserve the same power when translated. Barbarous names, likewise, have much emphasis, great conciseness, and participate of less ambiguity, variety, and multitude.

s: Porphyry's Letter to Anebo asks why invocations use names without meaning, and barbarian ones in preference to Greek, when the god invoked speaks no human language.

src.l: Iamblichus, Porphyry, Thomas Taylor (tr.), 1895, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians (with the Epistle of Porphyry to Anebo)
src.loc: p. 12 [scan 45], Epistle of Porphyry to Anebo
src.q: What also is the design of names that are without signification? and why, of such, are those that are barbaric preferred to our own? For if he who hears them looks to their signification, it is sufficient that the conception remains the same, whatever the words may be that are used.

s: Porphyry objects that ritual practitioners use threats and false terrors not against daemons or the dead but against the Sun, the Moon and the celestial gods.

src.l: Iamblichus, Porphyry, Thomas Taylor (tr.), 1895, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians (with the Epistle of Porphyry to Anebo)
src.loc: p. 10 [scan 43], Epistle of Porphyry to Anebo
src.q: why, which is much more absurd than this, are threats employed and false terrors, by any casual person, not to a dæmon, or some departed soul, but to the sovereign Sun himself, or to the Moon, or some one of the celestial Gods

s: Iamblichus reinterprets the theurgist's threats: by arcane signatures he commands mundane natures as if ranked among the gods, and the threats teach the magnitude of that power rather than being meant literally.

src.l: Iamblichus, Porphyry, Thomas Taylor (tr.), 1895, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians (with the Epistle of Porphyry to Anebo)
src.q: The theurgist, through the power of arcane signatures, commands mundane natures, no longer as man, nor as employing a human soul; but as existing superior to them in the order of the Gods, he makes use of greater mandates than pertain to himself

s: Porphyry describes invokers who carry stones and herbs, tie and untie 'sacred bonds', open shut places and change people's intentions, and image-makers who time their work by the stars.

src.l: Iamblichus, Porphyry, Thomas Taylor (tr.), 1895, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians (with the Epistle of Porphyry to Anebo)
src.loc: p. 8 [scan 41], Epistle of Porphyry to Anebo
src.q: those who invoke the divinities for this purpose, have about them stones and herbs, bind certain sacred bonds, which they also dissolve, open places that are shut ... Nor are the artificers of efficacious images to be despised. For they observe the motion of the celestial bodies

s: Porphyry reports a view that a fraudulent, shape-shifting 'obedient genus' of daemons impersonates gods and the dead and produces what appears in the rites.

src.l: Iamblichus, Porphyry, Thomas Taylor (tr.), 1895, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians (with the Epistle of Porphyry to Anebo)
src.loc: p. 9 [scan 42], Epistle of Porphyry to Anebo
src.q: there are some who suppose that there is a certain obedient genus of dæmons, which is naturally fraudulent, omniform, and various, and which assumes the appearance of Gods and dæmons, and the souls of the deceased

s: Iamblichus rejects explaining sacrifice by natural sympathies (e.g. a cock's heart) alone, since that would make the gods physical causes bound to matter.

src.l: Iamblichus, Porphyry, Thomas Taylor (tr.), 1895, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians (with the Epistle of Porphyry to Anebo)
src.q: or a certain member, as the heart of a cock; or other things of the like kind which are surveyed about nature, if they are considered as the causes of the efficacy in sacrifices. For from these things the Gods are not demonstrated to be supernatural causes

s: Iamblichus accepts sympathy among physical natures 'as in one animal' as a real but subordinate cause of sacrifice's efficacy; the leading cause is the demiurgic powers.

src.l: Iamblichus, Porphyry, Thomas Taylor (tr.), 1895, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians (with the Epistle of Porphyry to Anebo)
src.q: physical essences, indeed, being coexcited as in one animal, according to aptitude or sympathy ... nevertheless, we must say, that the most perfect and leading cause of the efficacy of sacrifices is to be conjoined to demiurgic and the most perfect powers.

s: In Ficino's Latin digest, Iamblichus redirects the Egyptian threats ('I will break the heavens', 'scatter the members of Osiris') from the celestial gods to an unreasoning, divided power in the world that cannot tell true from false.

src.l: Iamblichus, Marsilio Ficino (tr.), 1607, De mysteriis Aegyptiorum liber (Ficino's Latin paraphrase)
src.loc: p. 142 [scan 164], marginal heading 'How the supplicants threatened the daemons'
src.q: there is in the world some kind of power that is greatly divided, and indiscreet, and unconsidered, which indeed receives reason or speech from another, and listens, but never by its own intelligence: it discerns neither true from false, nor the possible from the impossible.

s: Ficino's preface frames the De mysteriis as Abammon's reply to Porphyry's letter to Anebo, whose questions covered daemons, providence, fate, prophecy, magic, miracles, sacrifices and vows.

src.l: Iamblichus, Hermes Trismegistus, Marsilio Ficino (tr.), 1607, De mysteriis Aegyptiorum - Pimander - Asclepius
src.q: Porphyry, who among the Platonists is called "the Philosopher" on account of his excellence, sent a long letter to Egypt to the priest Anebo, full of various and weighty questions ... concerning providence, fate, prophecies, magic, miracles, sacrifices, and vows.
src.qo: Porphyrius, qui inter Platonicos propter excellentiam Philosophus appellatur, longam in Aegyptū misit epistolā ad Anebonem sacerdotem, variarū & grauiū quæstionum plenam ad omnes philosophiæ partes spectantiū, præsertim ad Deum, atq; angelos, dæmonesq;, & animas, ad prouidentiam, ad fatū, vaticinia, magicen, miracula, sacrificia, vota.

s: Proclus (On the hieratic art, in Ficino's Latin) says the ancient priests founded their sacred science on the kinship and sympathy of natural things with one another and with hidden powers, finding 'all things in all things'.

src.l: Proclus, Marsilio Ficino (tr.), 1532, Pymander, Asclepius, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians ... Proclus, De sacrificio et magia
src.q: the ancient priests, when they considered in natural things a certain kinship and sympathy of some for others, and of manifest things for occult powers, and found all things in all things, they founded their sacred science.
src.qo: cum considerarent in rebus naturalibus cognationem quandam compassionemque aliorum ad alia, et manifestorum ad uires occultas, et omnia in omnibus inuenirent, sacram eorum scientiam condiderunt,

s: Proclus takes the heliotrope's turning toward the sun as prayer: all things hymn the leaders of their order, each in its own mode (intellectual, rational, natural, sensible).

src.l: Proclus, Marsilio Ficino (tr.), 1532, Pymander, Asclepius, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians ... Proclus, De sacrificio et magia
src.q: Truly all things pray and sing hymns together to the leaders of their order. But some do so in an intellectual way, some in a rational way, others in a natural way, and others indeed in a sensible way.
src.qo: Nempe cuncta precantur, hymnosque concinunt ad ordinis sui duces. Sed alia quidem intellectuali modo, alia rationali, alia naturali, alia uero sensibili modo.

s: Proclus names similarity as a sufficient cause binding things together, and illustrates the drawing-down of divine power by heated hemp catching fire from a lamp it does not touch.

src.l: Proclus, Marsilio Ficino (tr.), 1532, Pymander, Asclepius, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians ... Proclus, De sacrificio et magia
src.q: the ancients applied some of the earthly things to some of the heavenly ones, whence they drew down divine powers into a lower place, on account of a certain similarity. Truly, similarity itself is a sufficient cause for binding individual things to one another.
src.qo: unde diuinas uirtutes in locum inferiorem, ob quandam similitudinem deduxerunt. Nempe similitudo ipsa sufficiens causa est, ad res singulas in uicem uinciendas.

s: Proclus arranges angels, daemons, animals, plants and stones in a solar chain; the rooster, having more solar power than the lion, is feared by the lion, and lion-faced solar daemons vanish when shown a rooster.

src.l: Proclus, Marsilio Ficino (tr.), 1532, Pymander, Asclepius, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians ... Proclus, De sacrificio et magia
src.q: there are many solar animals, such as lions and roosters, which participate in a certain solar deity according to their nature. ... For this reason, they say the rooster is greatly feared by the lion and almost revered.
src.qo: uelut leones et galli, numinis cuiusdam solaris pro sua natura participes. Vnde mirum est, quantum inferiora in eodem ordine cedant superioribus, quamuis magnitudine, potentiaque non cedant. Hinc ferunt gallum timeri a leone plurimum, et quasi coli

s: Proclus explains why the priests compounded materials: a simple thing has some divine property but not enough on its own to call the deity, so many things were mixed.

src.l: Proclus, Marsilio Ficino (tr.), 1532, Pymander, Asclepius, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians ... Proclus, De sacrificio et magia
src.q: the authors of the ancient priesthood invented the worship of higher powers from visible things. They mixed some things and purified others. They mixed many things together because they saw that simple things had some divine property, but not enough on their own to call upon that deity.
src.qo: dum alia miscerent, alia purificarent. Miscebant autem plura inuicem, quia uidebant simplicia nonnullam habere numinis proprietatem, non tamen singulatim sufficientem ad numinis illius aduocationem.

s: Proclus extends the solar and lunar sympathies to stones: the sunstone imitates solar rays, the moonstone follows the moon's motion.

src.l: Proclus, Marsilio Ficino (tr.), 1532, Pymander, Asclepius, On the Mysteries of the Egyptians ... Proclus, De sacrificio et magia
src.q: Not only in plants, however, which have a vestige of life, but also in stones one may see an imitation and a certain participation in the lights from above ... the stone which is called the eye of heaven, or the eye of the Sun, has a shape similar to the pupil of the eye

s: Augustine (City of God X.9) reports the distinction between damnable goetia and praiseworthy theurgy and rejects it: both are bound to the deceptive rites of demons.

src.l: Augustine of Hippo, 1475, De Civitate Dei
src.q: incantations and songs composed with the art of wicked curiosity, which they call either magic or by the more detestable name goetia, or by the more honorable name theurgy. ... Yet both are equally bound by the deceptive rites of demons under the names of angels.

s: Augustine reports that Porphyry granted theurgy only the purification of the 'spiritual' (image-receiving) part of the soul, not the intellectual part, and wavered on whether it should be banned by law.

src.l: Augustine of Hippo, 1475, De Civitate Dei
src.q: For at one moment he warns that this art should be avoided as fallacious and dangerous in its very action, and prohibited by laws. At another moment, however, as if yielding to its praisers, he says it is useful for cleansing a part of the soul
src.qo: Nunc enim hanc artem tanquam fal lacem ꝛ in ipsa actione periculossam: ꝛ legibus prohibitam cauendam mo net.nunc autem uelut eius laudatoꝛi- bus cedens utilem dicit esse mundāde parti anime:

s: Augustine cites Porphyry's story of a Chaldaean whose purifying rite was frustrated by an envious rival who had bound the summoned powers, and concludes theurgy works for evil as well as good.

src.l: Augustine of Hippo, 1475, De Civitate Dei
src.q: a good man in Chaldea, who was putting forth great effort to purify his soul, found his successes frustrated; for another man, powerful in the same arts but moved by envy, had bound the powers summoned by holy prayers so that they would not grant the requests.
src.qo: purgande aie magno molimine frustratos sibi esse successus: cũ uir ad eadẽ potens: tactus inuidia adiuratas sacris precibus po tentias alligasset: ne postulata pcedẽt:

s: Augustine argues from Roman law against the Platonists: if magic were the work of gods, why do the laws punish it so severely, laws which Christians did not make?

src.l: Augustine of Hippo, 1475, De Civitate Dei
src.q: Or perhaps Christians established these laws by which magic arts are punished? On the contrary, these laws exist for no other reason than that there is no doubt these sorceries are ruinous to the human race.
src.qo: An forte istae leges christiani instituerunt: q[uibus] artes magice puniuntur: secundum quem aliū sensum: nisi q[uod] hec maleficia generi humano p[er]niciosa eē n[on] dubiū ē:

s: Augustine cites the Twelve Tables (via Cicero) as having fixed a penalty for magically moving another's crops, alongside Virgil's line about charmed harvests.

src.l: Augustine of Hippo, 1475, De Civitate Dei
src.q: Is it not because of this pestilential and wicked doctrine—by which it is said the fruits of others are transferred to other places—that it was written into the Twelve Tables (that is, the most ancient laws of the Romans, as Cicero records) and a punishment established for anyone who did this?
src.qo: Eo q[uod] hac pestifera scelerataq[ue] doctrina: fruct[us] aliēi i alias tras transferri phibēt: nōnne in duodecim tabulis. i. rōanorū antiquissimis legibus cicero cōmemorat eē conscriptū: & ei qui hoc fecerit suppliciū cōstitutū:

s: Augustine uses Apuleius' trial for magic before pagan judges as evidence that even pagans held magic criminal, noting Apuleius defended himself by denying, not professing, the art.

src.l: Augustine of Hippo, 1475, De Civitate Dei
src.q: Finally, was Apuleius himself not accused of magic arts before non-Christian judges? If he had known these arts to be divine and pious, and consistent with the works of divine powers, he ought not only to have confessed to them but to have professed them openly.
src.qo: Postremo ipe apuleius: nunquid apud iudices christianos de magicis artibus accusat[us] est? Quas utiq[ue] sibi obiectas si diuīas & pias esse nouerat: & diuinar[um] potestatum operibus congruas: non solum eas cōfiteri debuit: sed et p[ro]fiteri:

s: Augustine quotes Hermes (Asclepius) that man's greatest wonder is to have found the divine nature and made it, and treats the Egyptian art of animating statues as a detestable art invented through error.

src.l: Augustine of Hippo, 1475, De Civitate Dei
src.q: For of all wonders, this surpasses admiration: that man was able to find the divine nature and to make it.
src.qo: que de homine dicta sunt. Omnium enim mirabiliū uicīt admirationez:

s: Isidore (Etymologies VIII.9) equates magi with those commonly called malefici, who shake the elements, derange minds and kill by the force of a chant without poison.

src.l: Isidore of Seville, 1911, Etymologiarum sive Originum libri XX
src.q: Magi are those who are commonly called evildoers because of the magnitude of their crimes. These even shake the elements, disturb the minds of men, and kill by the sheer violence of a chant without any ingestion of poison.

s: Isidore says magi summon demons with blood and victims and touch corpses, and that necromancy adds blood to the corpse because demons love blood.

src.l: Isidore of Seville, 1911, Etymologiarum sive Originum libri XX
src.q: These also use blood and victims, and often touch the bodies of the dead. Necromancers are those by whose incantations the dead appear to be resuscitated to divine and to respond to questions.
src.qo: et saepe contingunt corpora mortuorum. Necro- mantii sunt, quorum praecantationibus videntur resuscitati mortui divinare, et ad interrogata respondere.

s: Isidore defines enchanters (incantatores) as those who perform their art with words, and divides divination into art and madness.

src.l: Isidore of Seville, 1911, Etymologiarum sive Originum libri XX
src.q: There are two kinds of divination: art and madness. Enchanters are so called because they perform their art with words.

s: The De daemonibus ascribed to Psellos holds that daemons are not bodiless but have thin, airy bodies, citing Basil that even angels have them.

src.l: Michael Psellos (attrib.), Marsilio Ficino (tr.), 1497, De mysteriis Aegyptiorum ... (Aldine 1497), with Psellus De daemonibus
src.q: The nature of demons is not without a body; but it has a body, and moves about concerning bodies, which our venerable fathers have also judged.
src.qo: NAtura dæmonū nō eft abfq; corpore. sed habet corpus, & uersatur circa corpora, quod & uenerādi patres nostri iudicauerūt,

s: The same dialogue accuses the 'Euchites' of a demon-worshipping rite on Good Friday evening with lights put out and incestuous mingling: an accusation pattern later attached to witches' sabbaths.

src.l: Michael Psellos (attrib.), Marsilio Ficino (tr.), 1497, De mysteriis Aegyptiorum ... (Aldine 1497), with Psellus De daemonibus
src.q: They gather on the day on which the Savior suffered, in the evening, in an appointed place together with girls known to them. And after certain sacred rites, with the lights extinguished, they mingle together
src.qo: Conueniunt die quo paſſus eſt ſaluator ueſpere ſta tutum in locum una cú puellis ſibi notis. & poſt quædá ſacra extinctis

s: Commenting on the Chaldaean oracle against changing barbarous names, Psellos explains that names like Seraphim, Cherubim, Michael and Gabriel have ineffable efficacy in Hebrew and are powerless when put into Greek.

src.l: Chaldaean Oracles, Michael Psellos, Georgios Gemistos Plethon, 1607, Oracula magica Zoroastris cum scholiis Plethonis et Pselli
src.q: as is the name Seraphim, Cherubim, Michael, Gabriel. For thus, pronounced according to the dialect of the Hebrews, they have a singular and ineffable efficacy in the administration of sacred things; but when changed into Greek names, they are entirely powerless.

s: Psellos expounds the Chaldaean Oracles while disowning them: he says he approves neither their rites nor their doctrine.

src.l: Chaldaean Oracles, Michael Psellos, Georgios Gemistos Plethon, 1607, Oracula magica Zoroastris cum scholiis Plethonis et Pselli
src.q: As far as I am concerned, I do not approve of the sacred rites of the Chaldeans at all, nor do I assent to their doctrine. With difficulty, however, I have uncovered the obscurity of the oracle for you.

s: In a short piece on the 'sacrificial science', Psellos records Greek rules matching victims to gods by colour: white or red for the ethereal gods, black for the subterranean, mixed colours for the gods of the air.

src.l: Michael Psellos, Joseph Bidez (ed.), 1928, Catalogue des manuscrits alchimiques grecs VI: Michel Psellus (appendix of opuscula, incl. on the sacrificial art)
src.q: they brought red or white animals to the ethereal gods because of the ethereal color and the purity of their nature. But to the subterranean gods they sacrificed animals of an opposite color, and to the gods of the air they brought animals of variegated and mixed colors.

s: Psellos reports that the sacrificers assigned the head of the liver to the super-cosmic gods and its lobes to the five planets, and read outcomes from which way the victim fell.

src.l: Michael Psellos, Joseph Bidez (ed.), 1928, Catalogue des manuscrits alchimiques grecs VI: Michel Psellus (appendix of opuscula, incl. on the sacrificial art)
src.q: they dedicated the head to the super-cosmic gods, but the lobes they assigned to the five planets. The dead remains they sacrificed to Hades and Persephone.

s: Porphyry (De abstinentia, in Ficino's Latin) says the theologians avoided animal food lest the impure souls of slaughtered beasts and disturbing daemons be drawn to them and keep them from God.

src.l: Porphyry, Marsilio Ficino (tr.), 1577, De mysteriis Aegyptiorum ... Porphyrius De divinis atque daemonibus (from De abstinentia)
src.q: they rightly fled from and condemned nourishment derived from animals. They did this lest they should summon to themselves foreign, impure souls that have been violently uprooted and are drawn back toward what is kindred to them

s: Ficino says himself that he rendered the De mysteriis 'sense for sense, not word for word'; his Latin Iamblichus, which is what the Renaissance read, is a paraphrase and digest, so its wording cannot be quoted as Iamblichus'.

src.l: Iamblichus, Hermes Trismegistus, Marsilio Ficino (tr.), 1607, De mysteriis Aegyptiorum - Pimander - Asclepius
src.q: Of this entire inquiry, therefore, and of the truly divine response, I have—as if still too occupied with Plotinus—translated nearly every individual sense rather than the words themselves
src.qo: Hujus ergo quæstionis totius, atq; responsionis profectò diuinæ, tanquam in Plotino adhuc nimium occupatus, singula fermè non verba, sed sensa traduxi,

s: Manu IX.290 fines rites with roots (mūlakarman) and kṛtyā 'sorcery' against strangers; Bühler's note gives the commentators: root-rites to bring someone under one's power are permitted against a husband or relative, kṛtyā are spells causing disease or failure, and a successful abhicāra is punished as murder. Lawful versus hostile depends on target and outcome, not on the technique.

src.l: Georg Bühler (trans.), 1886, The Laws of Manu (Sacred Books of the East 25)
src.q: The magic rites, performed with roots, are those which are intended to bring a person into one's power. These are permitted, if practised against a husband or a relative ... are such spells as produce diseases, or cause the failure of an adversary's undertakings

s: In SL's English of the Kathāsaritsāgara (VIII) as it stood until 2026-10-26, the demon Maya teaches prince Sūryaprabha austerities until he 'mastered the magic sciences'; the Sanskrit has only vidyāḥ ('knowledges, sciences'; vidyâḥ çîghram asâdhayat), with siddha-vidyam and vidyā-siddhi following. 'Magic' is the translator's addition.

src.l: Somadeva, Hermann Brockhaus (ed.), 1862, Kathāsaritsāgara (Ocean of the Streams of Story), Brockhaus ed.
src.q: There Maya instructed him in austerities in such a way that the prince, together with his ministers, quickly mastered the sciences

s: In the Ṛgveda with Sāyaṇa, Indra puts thousands of Dāsas to sleep 'through his illusory power' (dāsānām indro māyayā), and Sāyaṇa explains it as Indra's own māyā. Here māyā is a god's praised power over enemies. It is not a condemned human rite. SL's note glossed it as 'illusory power or supernatural magic' until 2026-10-26.

src.l: Max Müller (ed.), Sāyaṇa (commentary), 1849-1874, Rig-Veda-Sanhita: Sacred Hymns of the Brahmans, with Sāyaṇa's commentary, vol. 3
src.q: Indra, through wondrous power mayaya wondrous or illusory power, by his own innate power, put to sleep

s: Woodroffe defines sādhanā as what produces siddhi, 'the result sought, be it material or spiritual advancement'. So siddhi means attainment or success, whether worldly or liberating.

src.l: John Woodroffe (Arthur Avalon), 1927, Shakti and Shakta, 3rd ed.
src.q: SĀDHANĀ is that which produces Siddhi or the result sought, be it material or spiritual advancement.

s: A tantra in the Thadrak Kanjur has Vajrapāṇi summarise every accomplishment taught in all the tantras as four kinds of action: pacifying (śāntika, zhi), increasing (pauṣṭika, rgyas), subjugating (vaśīkaraṇa, dbang) and wrathful (abhicāra, drag). The hostile rite is the fourth of a sanctioned set. It is not set outside religion.

src.l: Thadrak Temple (manuscript Kanjur), n.d., Thadrak Kanjur, rGyud 'bum, vol. Tha
src.q: Whatever accomplishments have been taught by the wise in all the tantras, if they are all summarized, they are completely included in four types. The first action is 'pacifying'

s: A Derge Tengyur fire-offering text matches the firewood to the activity: one kind for peaceful acts (zhi ba'i las), sour-tasting wood for increasing (rgyas pa), red thorned wood for magnetising (dbang) and summoning (dgug pa), and pungent thorned wood for fierce acts (drag po) and expelling. The hostile rite differs from the healing rite only in its materials, inside one ritual grammar.

src.l: Derge Tengyur, 1982-1985, bsTan 'gyur sde dge, rGyud 'grel, vol. 9 (Nya)
src.q: Firewood should be used for peaceful activities. For increasing activities, wood with a sour taste should be used.

s: A Derge Tengyur tantra commentary defines the 'gathered secret mantra' as a practice for wrathful activities (drag po'i las), in which the mantra syllables touch like knots in a rope. It sets this against the order used in peaceful activities (zhi ba'i las), and the Tibetan says the wrathful order is the reverse (བཟློག). Fierce activity is a mode of the same mantra practice.

src.l: Derge Tengyur, 1982-1985, bsTan 'gyur sde dge, rGyud 'grel, vol. 19 (Tsha)
src.q: The term known as the gathered secret mantra refers to a practice for wrathful activities where the syllables of the mantra are made to touch one another, resembling the knots in a rope.
src.qo: འདུས་པའི་གསང་སྔགས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དྲག་པོའི་ལས་ལ་སྔགས་ཀྱི་ཡི་གེ་རྣམས་ཐ་གུའི་མདུད་པ་ལྟར་ཕན་ཚུན་རེག་པར་བྱ་བའོ། །

s: The Raudrakarmopacārasaptaka (Toh 2002, 'Seven rites of fierce activity', drag po'i las kyi bya ba bdun) opens the hostile programme with offerings to the Noble Ones, charity to beings, and the permission of the gurus. It follows a 'seventh section on the peaceful rites of Bhairava'. In Tibetan Buddhist practice, fierce activity is a rite done with merit and the gurus' permission. It is not treated as an outlaw act.

src.l: Derge Tengyur, 1982-1985, bsTan 'gyur sde dge, rGyud 'grel, vol. 47 (Mi), incl. Raudrakarmopacārasaptaka (Toh 2002)
src.q: I shall explain the seven rites of wrathful activity. Regarding these, first, one must perform offerings and gifts. This involves making offerings to the Noble Ones and giving charity to living beings.
src.qo: དཔལ་རྡོ་རྗེ་འཇིགས་བྱེད་ལ་ཕྱག་འཚལ་ལོ། །དྲག་པོའི་ལས་ཀྱི་བྱ་བ་བདུན་བཤད་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། དེ་ལ་དང་པོར་མཆོད་སྦྱིན་བྱ་སྟེ།

s: De Groot reports that Chinese books name sorcery yao tao/shu/fa (妖道, 妖術, 妖法) or xie tao/shu/fa (邪道, 邪術, 邪法), 'methods of demonry'. Because xie covers everything contrary to the Tao, the xie terms also take in harmless or benevolent heterodox rites and juggling, which were punished too. He separates heterodox magic from sorcery: China's split is orthodox against heterodox, with sorcery as the harmful subset.

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1907, The Religious System of China, Vol. 5: Demonology
src.q: Sorcery is generally denominated in Chinese books yao tao, yao shuh or yao fah ... all which terms equally mean "methods of demonry"

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1907, The Religious System of China, Vol. 5: Demonology
src.q: We have then sharply to distinguish between heterodox magic and sorcery, for, though sorcery is heterodox magic, heterodox magic is far from always being sorcery.

s: De Groot recounts the wu-gu (巫蠱) affair under Emperor Wu (91 BCE). Hunnish wu were employed under Jiang Chong to detect sorcerers the emperor suspected of attacking his health, and princesses, the empress's kin and a minister were found guilty and put to death. In this affair wu names the specialists who detected the sorcerers as well as the sorcery they hunted.

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1910, The Religious System of China, Vol. 6: Demonology and Sorcery
src.q: Hunnish wu, probably belonging to foreign troops quartered in the capital, were cruelly employed under Kiang Ch'ung in the discovery and persecution of sorcerers whom the emperor Wu suspected of attacks on his health and life

src.l: J. J. M. de Groot, 1907, The Religious System of China, Vol. 5: Demonology
src.q: were all found guilty and put to death

s: The Korean chronicle Kinyŏn aram lists the 'Sinsa wu-gu case' (辛巳巫蠱獄事, 1701). After Queen Inhyŏn's death a wu-gu plot was found, and court ladies, female wu (巫女), Jang Hŭi-jae and others were executed, and Consort Jang was ordered to take poison. SL renders 巫蠱 as 'witchcraft' and 巫女 as 'shamans'. Wugu here is the court's charge against palace rivals.

src.l: Yi Man-un (1725-1778), c. 1800, Kinyŏn aram
src.q: After Queen Inhyeon passed away, a plot involving witchcraft was discovered. Court ladies, shamans, Jang Hui-jae, and Min Eon-nyang were executed.
src.qo: 仁顯王后昇遐後巫蠱事覺宮人巫女及 張希載閔彥良等並伏誅禧嬪張氏賜死

s: The imperial Zishi jinghua (1727) excerpts the History of the Southern Dynasties. Yuan Junzheng 'did not believe in' 巫邪 (wu and the heterodox), and he caught the commandery's chief wu (巫長), a Daoist-arts master, stealing a garment. He executed him for 'disordering government' (亂政) and burned the shrine, after which no one dared practise wu. SL rendered 巫 as 'sorcery' until 2026-10-26 (now 'mediums (wu)'). The official's charge targets the medium cult itself, so 'sorcery' imports the accuser's verdict into the word.

src.l: Wu Shiyu (ed.), n.d., Yuding Zishi jinghua (Imperial Essence of Masters and Histories), juan 117-119 (vol 38)
src.q: By nature, he did not believe in mediums and heterodox cults ... Regarding this as disrupting public governance, Junzheng had him executed in the marketplace and burned his spirit shrines. ... Throughout the entire commandery, no one dared practice as a medium again.

s: The same compendium records that the arts (術) of Zuo Ci and Liu Gen deluded (惑) the common people, who flocked to them, and that Fu Jian had a wonder-worker killed because he feared he would mislead the masses (惡其惑衆). The state's charge is 'deluding the multitude', and it judges the practitioner's following rather than his technique.

src.l: Wu Shiyu (ed.), n.d., Yuding Zishi jinghua, juan 118-119 (vol 141)
src.q: were such that the common people were deluded and flocked to them ... but fearing he would mislead the masses, he ordered

s: SL's English of the Soushen ji rendered (until 2026-10-26) 善爲幻術 as 'skilled in magical arts', and 術既不行 as 'His magic no longer worked'. Huanshu (幻術) is 'the art of illusion', and shu (術) alone just 'art, technique'. As with Sanskrit māyā, the Chinese word names illusion and conjuring, and 'magic' is the translator's umbrella.

src.l: Gan Bao, 1608, Soushen ji (In Search of the Supernatural)
src.q: Ju Daolong was skilled in the arts of illusion. He once said: "Master Huang of the Eastern Sea was skilled in illusion, controlling snakes and mastering tigers.

s: Chao Yuanfang's medical treatise Zhubing yuanhou lun (610) defines gu (蠱) by how it is made. Insects and snakes are sealed in a vessel to devour one another, and the survivor is the gu, which its keepers put into food and drink. In the medical text gu is a classified poison-illness, and the malice lies with the keeper. SL glosses it 'sorcery parasite poison'.

src.l: Chao Yuanfang, n.d., Chaoshi Zhubing yuanhou zonglun, juan 22-28 (vol 5)
src.q: Gu is created by gathering insects, snakes, and similar creatures together, placing them inside a vessel, and letting them devour one another. The single creature remaining alive becomes the gu.
src.qo: 蠱是合聚蟲蛇之類以器皿盛之令其自相食噉

s: The Peiwen yunfu's entries on compounds in 蠱 run from the Han prosecutions (Jiang Chong's cases, Empress Yin accused, a gu-user and deceiver to be exiled) to gu as seductive charm, flattery and the hexagram Gu ('affairs, decay'). The character is wider than 'sorcery', though SL's head-note glossed it as 'venomous magic' until 2026-10-26. The translation renders the first headword as plain 'Gu', but 丨丨 in the original marks a two-character compound (in the Han shu, Jiang Chong tried wu-gu 巫蠱 cases).

src.l: Zhang Yushu (ed.), n.d., Yuding Peiwen yunfu, juan 37.2-37.3 (vol 160)
src.q: Jiang Chong was appointed to investigate gu sorcery. ... If Gu is indeed guilty of practicing gu and spreading deceitful falsehoods, he should be banished to the distant frontiers.

s: Eitel's Hand-Book of Chinese Buddhism reports that Chinese Buddhist sources explain the Atharvaveda (阿闥婆拏) by 呪術 (rendered 'lit. magic incantations'), by 術論 ('a Śāstra on magic') and by 禳災 ('averting calamity by prayer'). The compound 呪術, the later Japanese jujutsu for 'magic', here translates the Atharvan as the Veda of incantation and of averting calamity. 'Magic' is Eitel's English.

src.l: Ernest John Eitel, 1888, Hand-Book of Chinese Buddhism
src.q: explained by 呪術 lit. magic incantations, or by 術論 lit. a S'âstra on magic, or by 禳災 lit. averting calamity by prayer.

s: In Kumārajīva's Chinese Viśeṣacinti-brahma-paripṛcchā the Buddha closes a dhāraṇī with 是為呪術章句 ('these are the incantation phrases'). A bodhisattva who would practise the sutra must recite and hold them with a unified mind, purity, few desires and seclusion. Here 呪術 names a licit Buddhist incantation bound to moral discipline, and SL's English renders it 'incantation', not 'magic'.

src.l: Kumārajīva (trans.), 1735, Si yi fan tian suo wen jing (Viśeṣacinti-brahma-paripṛcchā), 4 juan
src.q: this is the text of the incantation. If a Bodhisattva-Mahasattva wishes to practice this sutra, they should recite and hold this incantation.

s: On Kanze utaibon vol. 20a p. 99, SL's English read 'receiving a sacred incantation majinai from the High Priest' until 2026-10-26. The Japanese returned for the page has no majinai: it reads 僧正なり共恐るまし ('even if it be the Archbishop, I shall not fear'), followed by the angry spirit riding black clouds around the palace with small dragons. The only majinai found on the shelf is an artefact of translation.

src.l: Kanze School, 1840, Kanze-ryū Utaibon, vol. 20a
src.q: Now that you have forsaken me, I will not fear even the Archbishop.

s: Winkelman argues from ethnological comparison that most historical types of wu (巫) resemble other ritualist types more than shamans, that wu developed into priests, healers, mediums and sorcerers or witches, and that wu is more accurately translated 'ritualist' or 'religious ritualist'.

src.l: Michael Winkelman, 2023, Chinese Wu, Ritualists and Shamans: An Ethnological Analysis

s: Critique: Muchowska asks whether 'magic', a Western category, is still legitimate for Daoist zhuyou (祝由) healing rites using incantations and talismans (fu 符). She notes a dissonance: theorists now merge magic with religion, while sinologists still separate them and use 'magic' freely.

src.l: Joanna Muchowska, 2023, Investigating the history of folk Taoism: the concept of magic in the study of zhuyou rituals

s: Hume (Enquiry, 1748, 'Of Miracles') argues that reports of supernatural and miraculous events carry a strong presumption against them because they abound chiefly among 'ignorant and barbarous nations' or are inherited from such ancestors.

src.l: David Hume, 1900, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding
src.loc: sect. X, 'Of Miracles', part II, p. 125 [scan 163]
src.q: It forms a strong presumption against all supernatural and miraculous relations, that they are observed chiefly to abound among ignorant and barbarous nations

s: Collin de Plancy's Dictionnaire infernal (1863 ed.), s.v. 'Enchantement', says the arts produce enchantments that are natural, counted as magic only by those who attribute to magic everything extraordinary, and illustrates with Decremps's automaton cabinet from La magie blanche dévoilée.

src.l: Jacques Collin de Plancy, 1863, Dictionnaire infernal
src.q: The arts have also produced enchantments, but natural ones, and considered the work of magic only by those who attribute to magic everything that is extraordinary.
src.qo: Les arts ont aussi produit des enchantemens, mais naturels, et regardés comme œuvre de magie par ceux-là seuls qui attribuent à la magie tout ce qui est extraordinaire.

s: Horst (1820) treats magic as 'magic-belief' of peoples: its main idea is the striving to gain deeper insight into nature and to master it, with higher powers, for one's own fate, its forms varying with each people's assumptions about spirit worlds; he uses 'Magie' and 'Zauberei' as synonyms.

src.l: Georg Conrad Horst, 1820, Von der alten und neuen Magie Ursprung, Idee, Umfang und Geschichte
src.q: it is the striving, by means of magic, not only to arrive at a deeper insight into nature in itself and in general,
src.qo: so ist's das Bestreben, vermittelst der Magie nicht allein zu einer tieferen Einsicht in die Natur an sich und überhaupt zu gelangen, *)

src.l: Georg Conrad Horst, 1820, Von der alten und neuen Magie Ursprung, Idee, Umfang und Geschichte
src.q: We use both words here as being completely synonymous.
src.qo: Wir brauchen beide Worte hier als völlig gleichbedeutend.

s: Braid (1852) explains the effects credited to magic, witchcraft and animal magnetism psychologically: in a sub-hypnotic state reason and will are 'dethroned' and imagination and docility let subjects be controlled by others' suggestions.

src.l: James Braid, 1852, Magic, Witchcraft, Animal Magnetism, Hypnotism and Electro-Biology
src.q: so that the higher faculties—reason, comparison, and will, become dethroned from their supremacy, and give place and power to imagination

s: Lévi (Dogme, 1861) recasts collective religious power in magnetic terms: every enthusiasm propagated in a society through communications and established practices produces a 'magnetic current'; Mesmer's tub was 'a rather imperfect magic chain', and a society of Catholic priests (the Jesuits, by his reference to Ignatius) owes its strength to such a chain, not to God's grace as they suppose.

src.l: Éliphas Lévi, 1861, Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
src.q: Every enthusiasm propagated in a society, through a series of communications and established practices, produces a magnetic current and is preserved or increased by the current.
src.qo: rant magnétique, qui devient plus fort en raison de l'étendue de la chaîne. Nous verrons dans le Rituel comment ces courants peuvent se produire et quelles sont les différentes manières de former la chaîne. Le baquet de Mesmer était une chaîne magique assez imparfaite; plusieurs grands cercles d'illuminés, dans différents pays du Nord, ont des chaînes plus puissantes. La société même de certains prêtres catholiques célèbres par leur puissance occulte et leur impopularité est établie sur le plan et suivant les conditions des chaînes magiques les plus puissantes, et c'est le secret de leur force, qu'ils attribuent uniquement à la grâce ou à la volonté de Dieu, solution vulgaire et facile de tous les problèmes de force en influence ou en entraînement. Nous aurons à apprécier, dans notre Rituel, la série de cérémonies et d'évocations véritablement magiques qui composent le grand œuvre de la vocation sous le nom d'exercices de saint Ignace. Tout enthousiasme propagé dans une société, par une suite de communications et de pratiques arrêtées, produit un courant magnétique et se conserve ou s'augmente par le courant.

src.l: Éliphas Lévi, 1861, Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
src.q: was a rather imperfect magic chain
src.qo: était une chaîne magique assez imparfaite;

s: Eckartshausen's Aufschlüsse zur Magie (1791), after defining 'true magic' as the highest science, ends with numbered conjuring recipes and a 'theory of speed and the art of sleight of hand': there are 'thousands of kinds of natural magic tricks', and prestidigitation consists in deception through speed.

src.l: Karl von Eckartshausen, 1791, Aufschlüsse zur Magie aus geprüften Erfahrungen über verborgene philosophische Wissenschaften
src.q: Thus there are thousands of kinds of natural magic tricks: one can always investigate, combine, and invent.
src.qo: So giebt es tausenderley Arten von natürlich magischen Kunststücken: immer kann man nachforschen, kombiniren und erfinden.

src.l: Karl von Eckartshausen, 1791, Aufschlüsse zur Magie aus geprüften Erfahrungen über verborgene philosophische Wissenschaften
src.q: The theory of the art of deception and <term>Taschenspielerey</term> <gloss>prestidigitation or sleight of hand</gloss> consists in deception through speed.
src.qo: Die Theorie der Täuschungskunst und Taschenspiele- rey besteht in der Täuschung durch Geschwindigkeit.

s: Evans (1897) cites the S.P.R. member and amateur magician Davey, who gave slate-writing séances without telling sitters they were prestidigitation; the sitters' written reports, Evans says, are admirable examples of mal-observation, since no one detected the slate exchanges.

src.l: Henry Ridgely Evans, 1897, Hours with the Ghosts, or, Nineteenth Century Witchcraft
src.q: an amateur magician who possessed great dexterity in the slate-writing business, gave a series of exhibitions before a number of persons, but did not inform them that the results were due to prestidigitation.

s: Scot (1584; 1886 reprint), in Book XIII, places 'the true art of juggling' in legerdemain (balls, coins, cards), says its drift is only to abuse men's eyes and judgements, and that its expert 'hath more cunning than all other witches or magicians'; he discloses the tricks to deflate claims of witches' powers.

src.l: Reginald Scot, 1886, The Discoverie of Witchcraft
src.q: The true art therefore of juggling consisteth in legierdemaine; to wit, the nimble conveiance of the hand

src.l: Reginald Scot, 1886, The Discoverie of Witchcraft
src.q: the endevor and drift of jugglers is onelie to abuse mens eies and judgements

s: On the shelf the shift from magic as real power to magic as error runs from Del Rio (1599-1600), for whom magic is an art that 'by a created and non-supernatural power' effects wonderful things, to Bekker (1691), who concludes that sorcery as commonly understood 'cannot exist'.

src.l: Martin Del Rio, 1603, Disquisitionum magicarum libri sex
src.q: an art or faculty which, by a created and non-supernatural power, effects certain wonderful and unusual things
src.qo: vt sit ars seu facultas, vi creata, & non supernaturali, quædam mira & insolita efficiens,

src.l: Balthasar Bekker, 1691, De betoverde weereld (The World Bewitched)
src.q: one may easily conclude that such Sorcery, as it is commonly understood, cannot exist.
src.qo: magh men lichtelijk besluiten, datter sulke Toverye, als men die gemeenelijk begrijpt, niet wesen kan.

s: Porta (1558/1658) reports magic defined as 'the practical part of natural Philosophy', true knowledge applying natural things to one another; Tylor (1871) keeps the link to science but inverts its value, making occult science a mistaken inference from the Association of Ideas.

src.l: Giambattista della Porta, 1658, Natural Magick (English translation of Magiae naturalis libri XX)
src.q: Others have named it the practical part of natural Philosophy, which produceth her effects by the mutual and fit application of one natural thing unto another.

src.l: Edward Burnett Tylor, 1871, Primitive Culture: Researches into the Development of Mythology, Philosophy, Religion, Art, and Custom, Vol. I
src.q: The principal key to the understanding of Occult Science is to consider it as based on the Association of Ideas

s: Bodin (1580) defines the sorcerer individually, as one who 'knowingly' uses diabolical means, and Thomasius (1701) tests the alleged personal pact; Doutté (1909), following Hubert and Mauss, makes magic 'originally a collective creation' answering collective needs.

src.l: Jean Bodin, 1603, De la demonomanie des sorciers (On the Demon-Mania of Witches)
src.q: A Sorcerer is someone who knowingly strives to achieve something by Diabolical means.
src.qo: Sorcier est celuy qui par moyens Diaboliques sciemment s'efforce de paruenir à quelque chose.

src.l: Christian Thomasius, 1701, Theses inaugurales de crimine magiae (On the Crime of Magic)
src.q: enters into a pact, stating that if the Devil is willing to satisfy his lust, greed, or ambition
src.qo: quod velit, si Diabolus ipsius voluptati, avaritiae aut ambitioni satisfacere velit,

src.l: Edmond Doutté, 1909, Magie et religion dans l'Afrique du Nord
src.loc: 'Caractère collectif de la croyance magique', p. 334 [scan 338]
src.q: Magic is, above all, originally a collective creation: it is the entire clan whose imagination is at work, for the needs that determine the birth of magic are primarily collective needs
src.qo: La magie est avant tout à l'origine une création collective : c'est le clan tout entier dont l'imagination travaille, car les besoins qui déterminent la naissance de la magie sont avant tout des besoins collectifs

s: Agrippa's De vanitate reports the magi's view that things act on one another by an innate, graded power reaching up to celestial and intelligible things; Papus (1893) relocates the operative power in the operator, defining magic as the application of 'dynamized human will' to nature's living forces.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1533, De occulta philosophia libri tres
src.q: They think that all these things pour forth an innate power into other objects
src.qo: quæ omnia non secus uim insita in res alias profundere, illasque ad se trahere, uel abs se repellere, seu alio quouis modo afficere, quam magnes ferrum, & succinum paleas trahit:

src.l: Papus (Gérard Encausse), 1893, Traité élémentaire de magie pratique
src.q: Magic is: the APPLICATION OF DYNAMIZED HUMAN WILL TO THE RAPID EVOLUTION OF THE LIVING FORCES OF NATURE.
src.qo: La magie est : l'APPLICATION DE LA VOLONTÉ HUMAINE DYNAMISÉE A L'ÉVOLUTION RAPIDE DES FORCES VIVANTES DE LA NATURE.

s: One 1791 book holds both senses: Eckartshausen defines 'true magic' as 'the highest science of the relationships of natural things', then calls the conjurer's repertoire 'natural magic tricks' and reduces it to deception through speed.

src.l: Karl von Eckartshausen, 1791, Aufschlüsse zur Magie aus geprüften Erfahrungen über verborgene philosophische Wissenschaften
src.q: True magic means as much as the highest perfection of natural and creaturely wisdom
src.qo: Magie. Die wahre Magie heißt so viel als die höchste Vollkommenheit der natürlichen und geschöpfmäßigen Weisheit,

src.l: Karl von Eckartshausen, 1791, Aufschlüsse zur Magie aus geprüften Erfahrungen über verborgene philosophische Wissenschaften
src.q: Thus there are thousands of kinds of natural magic tricks: one can always investigate, combine, and invent.
src.qo: So giebt es tausenderley Arten von natürlich magischen Kunststücken: immer kann man nachforschen, kombiniren und erfinden.

s: Critique: Styers (2004) argues that scholarly efforts to define magic against religion and science have proved notoriously unstable, and that the persistence of the debate is explained by the Western drive to secure norms of modern identity, with magic serving as the alterity against which piety and scientific rationality are defined.

src.l: Randall Styers, 2004, Making Magic: Religion, Magic, and Science in the Modern World

s: Critique: Otto (2011) writes a history of the concept of magic over about 2,500 years from antiquity to the 20th century, giving equal weight to polemical outsider texts and to authors who called themselves magicians, after an introduction on the problem of academic definitions of magic.

src.l: Bernd-Christian Otto, 2011, Magie: Rezeptions- und diskursgeschichtliche Analysen von der Antike bis zur Neuzeit

s: Critique: Otto and Stausberg's Defining Magic (2013) assembles the texts that sought to define magic, from Plato, Pliny, Augustine and Agrippa through Tylor, Frazer, Mauss, Durkheim and Malinowski to Styers, presenting the definitions as a contested sequence rather than a settled category.

src.l: Bernd-Christian Otto, Michael Stausberg, 2013, Defining Magic: A Reader

s: Critique: Bailey (2006) holds that the grand theories of Tylor, Frazer, Durkheim and others give clear structures that still reverberate, while recent narrow studies of magic in particular periods and societies, though precise, have stifled communication across periods, regions and disciplines.

src.l: Michael D. Bailey, 2006, The Meanings of Magic

s: Critique: Tambiah's Magic, Science, Religion and the Scope of Rationality (1990) examines the history and relative positioning of the concepts of magic, science and religion in Western thought, which bears against treating the Tylor-Frazer stage scheme as a neutral description.

src.l: Stanley Jeyaraja Tambiah, 1990, Magic, Science, Religion, and the Scope of Rationality
Bernard Formoso, Justin McDaniel, 2014, Stanley Jeyaraja Tambiah (1929-2014)

s: Critique: Hanegraaff (2003) argues that Weber's disenchantment is compatible with the continued vitality of the occult: Hermetic magic, transformed by modernisation and secularisation in its theories of efficacy, practices and legitimation, became a paradoxical 'disenchanted magic'.

src.l: Wouter J. Hanegraaff, 2003, How magic survived the disenchantment of the world

s: Critique: Hanegraaff (2012) argues that the 'pagan' traditions now labelled esoteric, occult or magical were expelled from the academy on the basis of Protestant and Enlightenment polemics, and have since served as the Other by which academics define their identity.

src.l: Wouter J. Hanegraaff, 2012, Esotericism and the Academy: Rejected Knowledge in Western Culture

s: Gorgias (Helen §10) names goeteia and mageia as two arts 'discovered' that are errors of the soul and deceptions of opinion, setting them alongside the incantatory power of speech, which 'beguiles and persuades and alters' the soul by goeteia.

src.l: Isocrates, Gorgias of Leontini, 1593, Orationes et Epistolae (with Gorgias, Encomium of Helen)
src.q: For the power of the incantation, consorting with the opinion of the soul, beguiles and persuades and alters it by sorcery. ... Two arts of sorcery and magic have been discovered, which are errors of the soul and deceptions of opinion.
src.qo: νονται. συγγινομένη γὰρ τῇ δόξῃ τῆς ψυχῆς ἡ δύναμις τῆς ἐπῳδῆς ἔθελξε καὶ ἔπεισε, καὶ μετέστησε γοητείᾳ. γοητείας δὲ καὶ μαγείας B δισσαὶ τέχναι εὕρηνται, αἵ εἰσι ψυχῆς ἁμάρ- τήματα, καὶ δόξης ἀπατήματα.

s: Vives' commentary on City of God X.9 quotes the Suda: goeteia, mageia and pharmakeia differ; mageia is invoking (supposedly) benevolent daemons for some good, goeteia is tied to rites at tombs, and pharmakeia is a deadly potion given by taste; Vives himself glosses goetia as 'an incantation and a species of veneficium'.

src.l: Augustine of Hippo, Juan Luis Vives (commentary), 1542, De Civitate Dei, cum commentariis Ioannis Lodovici Vivis
src.loc: p. 551-552 [scan 271], comm. on De civ. Dei X.9 'Goetia'
src.q: Goetia, Magic, and Pharmacy differ, which are inventions of the Persians. Magic indeed is the invocation of demons, namely beneficent ones, to accomplish something good
src.qo: Goetia.] Est incantatio, & ueneficij species.

src.l: Augustine of Hippo, Juan Luis Vives (commentary), 1542, De Civitate Dei, cum commentariis Ioannis Lodovici Vivis
src.q: Goetia.] Est incantatio, & ueneficij species.

s: Peucer (1560) reports that the pagans separated mageia (invoking benevolent daimones for some good) from goeteia or manganeia (invoking malevolent ones to harm, named from wailing at tombs), then himself defines mageia as an art handed down by the Devil working through pacts, erasing the distinction.

src.l: Kaspar Peucer, 1560, Commentarius de praecipuis generibus divinationum
src.q: Conversely, they called goeteia or manganeia witchcraft/jugglery the invocation of malevolent daimones to harm others ... Mageia is therefore an art handed down by the Devil

s: The De operatione daemonum (ascribed to Psellos) defines goeteia as an art concerned with material and subterranean daemons that shows their phantoms to onlookers, raising some as if from Hades, and calls these daemons harmful.

src.l: Michael Psellus (attrib.), 1577, De operatione daemonum
src.q: Goety goēteia sorcery/necromancy is a certain art concerning material and subterranean demons, manifesting their phantoms to the observers, bringing some up as if from Hades and bringing others down from above, and these are harmful.
src.qo: Ἡ γοητεία 3) δέ ἐστι τέχνη τις περὶ τοὺς ἐνύλους 4) καὶ χθονίους δαίμονας φαντασιοσκοποῦσα τοῖς ἐπόπταις τὰ τούτων εἴδωλα καὶ τοὺς μὲν ὥσπερ ἐξ ᾅδου ἀνάγουσα, τοὺς δὲ ὑψόθεν κατάγουσα, καὶ τούτους κακωτικούς

s: Pico (Oratio) says the Greeks do not dignify the demonic kind with the name of magic but call it goeteia, reserving mageia for the most perfect and highest knowledge, and, after Porphyry, glosses magus as the Persian for 'interpreter and worshipper of divine things'.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1496, Opuscula (incl. Oratio)
src.q: When the Greeks mention both, they do not deign to give the name "magic" to the first kind, but call it sorcery; the latter they call by the proper and peculiar name of magic, as if it were the most perfect and highest knowledge.

s: Isidore (Etym. VIII.9) derives praestigium, whose discovery he credits to Mercury, from its 'blinding the sight of the eyes' (praestringat aciem oculorum): the word names illusion, not a power over things.

src.l: Isidore of Seville, 1911, Etymologiarum sive Originum libri XX
src.q: Now, Mercury is said to have been the first to discover prestige. It is called praestigium because it blinds the sight of the eyes.
src.qo: Dictum autem praestigium, quod praestringat aciem oculorum.

src.l: Isidore of Seville, 1911, Etymologiarum sive Originum libri XX
src.q: Dictum autem praestigium, quod praestringat aciem oculorum.

s: Aquinas (ST II-II q.92 a.1) defines superstitio as the vice opposed to religion by excess, by which one offers divine worship either to whom one should not or not in the way one should: superstition is wrong worship, not a kind of magic.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1879, Summa Theologica, Secunda Secundae (Latin with French notes)
src.q: Superstition is a vice opposed to religion by way of excess, by which one offers divine worship either to whom one should not, or not in the way one should.
src.qo: Superstitio vitium est religioni oppositum secundùm excessum, quo quis divinum exhibet cultum, vel cui non debet, vel non eo modo quo debet.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1879, Summa Theologica, Secunda Secundae (Latin with French notes)
src.q: Superstitio vitium est religioni oppositum secundùm excessum, quo quis divinum exhibet cultum, vel cui non debet, vel non eo modo quo debet.

s: The Malleus says the heresy of the malefici differs from simple heresies (which involve no pact) and from other superstitious arts by holding the highest degree of malice among all kinds of divination, and takes its name 'a maleficiendo seu male de fide sentiendo' (from evil-doing or from thinking ill of the faith).

src.l: Heinrich Institoris, Jakob Sprenger, 1511, Malleus maleficarum
src.q: which also usurps for itself its name from maleficiendo evil-doing or from thinking ill concerning the faith
src.qo: ipsa maleficorum heresis supremum attinet gradum malicie quod etiam nomen a maleficiendo seu male de fide sentiendo sibi usurpat

src.l: Heinrich Institoris, Jakob Sprenger, 1511, Malleus maleficarum
src.q: ipsa maleficorum heresis supremum attinet gradum malicie quod etiam nomen a maleficiendo seu male de fide sentiendo sibi usurpat

s: The 1581 Latin version of Bodin's Démonomanie renders his definition of the sorcier with magus ('MAGVS est, qui sciens prudens diabolicis modis ad aliquid conatur pervenire'), so the Latin word magus carries the French accuser's sorcier, and SL's English renders it back as 'sorcerer'.

src.l: Jean Bodin, 1581, De Magorum Daemonomania Libri IV (Latin translation)
src.q: A SORCERER is one who, knowingly and with intent, endeavors to achieve something through diabolical means.
src.qo: MAGVS est, qui sciens prudens diabolicis modis ad aliquid conat̃ per uenire.

src.l: Jean Bodin, 1581, De Magorum Daemonomania Libri IV (Latin translation)
src.q: MAGVS est, qui sciens prudens diabolicis modis ad aliquid conat̃ per uenire.

s: Naudé (1625; English 1657) sorts magic by its agent into four kinds: Divine (by God's grace), Theurgic (by an angel), Goetic (by a daemon) and Natural (by one's own industry), keeping 'magic' for all four and confining the demonic to one.

src.l: Gabriel Naudé, J. Davies (tr.), 1657, The History of Magick (English translation of Apologie pour tous les grands personnages)
src.q: From these four different wayes, we in- fer four kinds of Magick: Divine, relating to the first; Theurgick, to the second; Geotick, to the third; and Naturall, to the last.

s: Martius (1717) sets Luke's words for Simon's Zauberey and Elymas 'the Zauberer' against the Greek ho Magos, which he says indicates a knowing or wise man, and cites de Dieu that the related word is not used for practitioners of the black, diabolical art.

src.l: Johannes Nicolaus Martius, 1717, Unterricht von der Magia naturali
src.q: cites the godlessness of Simon, who bewitched many in Samaria with his sorcery; and in chapter 13, verse 8, he relates the obstinacy of Elymas the sorcerer
src.qo: welcher zu Samaria ihrer viel mit seiner Zauberey bezaubert habe: Und im 13. Cap. v. 8. erzählet er die Halsstarrigkeit Elimæ, des Zauberers

src.l: Johannes Nicolaus Martius, 1717, Unterricht von der Magia naturali
src.q: welcher zu Samaria ihrer viel mit seiner Zauberey bezaubert habe: Und im 13. Cap. v. 8. erzählet er die Halsstarrigkeit Elimæ, des Zauberers

s: A 19th-century Hebrew practical manuscript (Gaster MS 1825) heads its recipes 'Segulah' (e.g. 'for heart pain'), the practitioner's own word for a remedy or efficacious charm, where the cure is said to come 'by the help of the Blessed Name'.

src.l: Anonymous, 19th century, Miscellaneous texts (Gaster Hebrew MS 1825)
src.q: Segulah For heart pain
src.qo: סגולה לכאב הלב גם לכל חולי סגולה

s: In the divided line (Republic VI, 511c-e) Socrates calls the habit concerned with geometry and its cognate sciences 'understanding' (dianoia), not reason (noesis), because it starts from hypotheses and does not ascend to a first principle; it is intermediate between opinion and reason.

src.l: Plato, 1871, The Dialogues of Plato, trans. B. Jowett (Republic)
src.q: And the habit which is concerned with geometry and the cognate sciences I suppose that you would term understanding and not reason, as being intermediate between opinion and reason.

src.l: Plato, 1871, The Dialogues of Plato, trans. B. Jowett (Republic)
src.q: because they start from hypotheses and do not ascend to a principle, those who contemplate them appear to you not to exercise the higher reason upon them

s: In Republic VII Socrates seeks studies that 'conduct towards being' (523a) and secures the admission that geometry is knowledge of the eternal, not of the perishing, so that geometry 'will draw the soul towards truth' (527b).

src.l: Plato, 1871, The Dialogues of Plato, trans. B. Jowett (Republic)
src.q: which leads naturally to reflection, but one which has never been rightly used as simply conducting towards being.

s: A trinitarian argument in Bibliander's 1543 Alcoran volume, apparently Cusa's Cribratio Alcorani, says unity generates equality, love is the connection of the two, and unity, equality and connection are eternal because they precede all multitude.

src.q: Likewise, the connection is eternal, because it is before plurality.
src.qo: Sic et nexus æternus, quia ante pluralitatem. Plura enim necessario sunt ab invicem diuisa. Diuisio uero cadit à connexione, ante omnem multitudinem in equalitatem et diuisionem, æterna esse, et cum non possint esse tria æterna, cum ante omnem multitudinem sit unitas, qua multitudo præsupponit, sicut inæqualitas præsupponit æqualitatem, et diuisio præsupponit connexionem: ideò unitas, æqualitas, et conexio non sunt tria æterna, sed una æternitas, sic non sunt tria: quia si essent tria, essent tria æterna. Non est igitur aliud unitas, aliud æqualitas, aliud utriusque nexus: quia tunc essent tria: et tria æterna. nec tamen propterea unitas, est æqualitas, aut connexio, cum æqualitas sit genita ab unitate. genitum autem, non est generans: nec nexus, est unitas, aut æqualitas, quia ab ipsis procedit. procedens autem, non est illa à quibus procedit. Patet igitur, quomodo in essentia diuini amoris, unitas amoris, æqualitas amoris, et nexus amoris, non sunt tres amores: quia unus amor, non est aliud ab alio, licet unitas amoris generantis, non sit æqualitas amoris geniti, aut nexus amoris utriusque ab ipsis procedens. Connexio.
