src.q: just as God properly cannot be defined nor understood by us through words, so this our proportion can never be assigned by an intelligible number nor expressed by any rational quantity: but it is always occult and secret
src.qo: a noi intẽdere. cosi questa nostra proportione non se po mai per numero intendibile asegnare ne per quãtita alcuna rationale exprimere: ma sem- pre sia occulta e secreta e dali Mathematici chiamata irrationale. ¶ La quarta conuenientia e che si commo idio mai non se po mutare. e sia tut- to in tutto e tutto in ogni parte. cosi la presente nostra proportione semp in ogni quantita continua e discretato sienno grandi: o sienno picole sia vna medesima e sempre iuaria bile e per verun modo se po mutare ne an- co per intellecto altramãte apprendere. commo el nostro processo demo- strara. ¶ La quinta conuenientia se po non immeritamente ale predictie arogere cioe. Si commo idio l'essere conferesci ala virtu celeste per altro nome detta quinta essentia e mediante quella ali altri quatro corpi sem- plici. cioe ali quatro elementi. Terra. Aqua. Aire. E fuoco. E per questi l'essere a cadauna altra cosa in natura. Cosi questa nostra sancta porpor- tione l'essere formale da (secondo l'antico Platone in suo Timeo) a epso cielo atribuendoli la figura del corpo detto Duodecedron. altramẽte cor- po de .12. pentagoni. El quale commo desotto se mostrara sença la nostra proportione non e possibile poterse formare.

src.l: Luca Pacioli, 1509, De Divina Proportione
src.loc: Part I, ch. V, SL p. 23
src.q: just as God can never change and is all in all and all in every part, so this our present proportion is always, in every continuous and discrete quantity

s: Dee's Monas hieroglyphica (1564) announces itself as explained 'mathematically, magically, cabalistically, and anagogically' and opens with a Euclidean theorem: by the straight line and the circle the first representation of things, existing and hidden in nature, was brought to light, and by the point and the monad things first began to exist.

src.l: John Dee, 1564, Monas hieroglyphica
src.loc: Title and Theorems I–II, SL p. 23
src.q: Explained mathematically, magically, cabalistically, and anagogically

src.l: John Dee, 1564, Monas hieroglyphica
src.q: the straight line and the circle, the first and simplest production and representation of things was brought to light, both of those not yet existing and of those hidden in the veils of Nature

s: In the Mysterium cosmographicum (ch. II, 1621 ed.) Kepler says the Creator conceived quantities whose essence falls into the straight and the curved, the curved representing God; these were chosen deliberately at the beginning to foreshadow the divinity of the Creator, and body was created so that there might be quantity, which leads him to the five regular solids.

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1621, Prodromus dissertationum cosmographicarum, continens Mysterium cosmographicum (2nd ed.)
src.loc: Mysterium cosmographicum, ch. II (printed p. 23, SL scan 47)
src.q: it is likely that at the beginning of all things, the Curved and the Straight were chosen by God through a deliberate plan to foreshadow the divinity of the Creator in the world. So that these might exist, there were quantities; and so that quantity might be had, Body was created first of all.

s: In the Apologia (1622) Kepler tells Fludd he acts 'as a mathematician': whoever loves the certainty of the mathematical disciplines will learn harmonic mathematics better from his Harmonice than from Fludd, but whoever wants to feed the mind on mystical philosophy handed down through riddles, and the eyes on pictures, will not find it in his book.

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1622, Pro suo opere Harmonices mundi apologia
src.loc: Apologia, before 'To Analysis XI' (printed p. 12, SL scan 21)
src.q: He who loves the certainty of mathematical disciplines will receive more utility in learning the part of Harmonic Mathematics from my work, The Harmonics, than from that of Robert Fludd
src.qo: Qui mathematicarum disciplinarum certitudinem amat, plus ille capiet utilitatis in parte Mathematices Harmonicæ perdiscendâ, ex opere meo Harmonicorum, quam ex Roberti de Fluctibus.

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1622, Pro suo opere Harmonices mundi apologia
src.q: But he who desires to feed his mind on mystical philosophy (which is usually handed down through riddles) and his eyes on pictures, will not find what he seeks in my book.
src.qo: Qui vero ingenium philosophia mystica; (quae per aenigmata tradi solet) oculos picturis, pascere cupit; quod quaerit, in meo libronon inveniet.

s: In Il Saggiatore (1623) Galileo answers Sarsi that philosophy is written in the great book of the universe, which cannot be understood without first learning its language and characters: it is written in the mathematical language, its characters triangles, circles and other geometric figures, without which it is humanly impossible to understand a word of it.

src.l: Galileo Galilei, 1623, Il Saggiatore
src.loc: Il Saggiatore, §6 reply to Sarsi (printed p. 25, SL scan 35)
src.q: Philosophy is written in this very great book, which continuously lies open before our eyes (I say the universe), but it cannot be understood if one does not first learn to understand the language and know the characters in which it is written.
src.qo: La Filoſofia è ſcritta in queſto grandiſſimo libro, che continuamente ci ſtà aperto innanzi à gli occhi (io dico l'vniuerſo) ma non ſi può intendere ſe prima non s'impara à intender la lingua, e conoſcer i caratteri, ne' quali è ſcritto.

src.l: Galileo Galilei, 1623, Il Saggiatore
src.q: It is written in the lingua matematica mathematical language, and the characters are triangles, circles, and other Geometriche geometric figures
src.qo: Egli è ſcritto in lingua matematica, e i caratteri ſon triangoli, cerchi, & altre figure Geometriche,

s: In the Dialogo (First Day) Salviati distinguishes extensive from intensive understanding: extensively the human intellect is as nothing, but intensively it grasps some truths, the pure mathematical sciences of geometry and arithmetic, as perfectly and certainly as Nature herself; the truth known by mathematical proof is the same that divine wisdom knows, though God's manner of knowing is far higher.

src.l: Galileo Galilei, Emil Strauss (trans.), 1891, Dialog über die beiden hauptsächlichsten Weltsysteme (German trans. of the Dialogo)
src.loc: Dialogo, First Day (German trans. printed p. 108, SL scan 198)
src.q: the human intellect grasps some truths as perfectly and is as absolutely certain of them as Nature herself can be. To this category belong pure mathematical cognitions, namely geometry and arithmetic.

src.l: Galileo Galilei, Emil Strauss (trans.), 1891, Dialog über die beiden hauptsächlichsten Weltsysteme (German trans. of the Dialogo)
src.loc: Dialogo, First Day (printed p. 109, SL scan 199)
src.q: although the truth, the knowledge of which is mediated by mathematical proofs, is the same as that which divine wisdom recognizes; nonetheless I will grant you that the manner … and way in which God recognizes the countless truths, of which we know only a few, is highly exalted above our way.
src.qo: dieselbe ist, welche die göttliche Weisheit erkennt; allerdings aber will ich Euch zugeben, daſs die Art und Die göttliche Weise des Erkennens von menschlicher verschieden. Weise, wie Gott die zahllosen Wahrheiten erkennt, von denen wir nur einige wenige kennen, hoch erhaben über unsere Weise ist.

s: In Regulae IV Descartes says that reflection led him from arithmetic and geometry to a general inquiry into mathematics: only those matters in which order and measurement are investigated belong to it, whether in numbers, figures, stars or sounds, so there must be a general science of order and measure restricted to no subject matter, called 'Universal Mathematics'.

src.l: René Descartes, E. S. Haldane and G. R. T. Ross (trans.), 1912, The Philosophical Works of Descartes, vol. I
src.loc: Rules for the Direction of the Mind, Rule IV (printed p. 13, SL scan 31)
src.q: all those matters only were referred to Mathematics in which order and measure- ment are investigated, and that it makes no difference whether it be in numbers, figures, stars, sounds or any other object that the question of measurement arises.

s: In Meditation V Descartes argues that a triangle he imagines, though no such figure may exist anywhere in the world, has a determinate nature, form or essence that is immutable and eternal, that he did not invent and that does not depend on his mind, because its properties can be demonstrated whether he wishes it or not.

src.l: René Descartes, E. S. Haldane and G. R. T. Ross (trans.), 1912, The Philosophical Works of Descartes, vol. I
src.q: when I imagine a triangle, although there may nowhere in the world be such a figure outside my thought, or ever have been, there is nevertheless in this figure a certain determinate nature, form, or essence, which is immutable and eternal, which I have not invented, and which in no wise depends on my mind

s: In the summary of De augmentis III, Bacon's chapter 6 is headed 'Concerning Mathematics, the great Appendix of Natural Philosophy, both Speculative and Operative', with the reason why it should be placed among the appendices rather than the substantive sciences, and its division into pure and mixed.

src.l: Francis Bacon, 1638, Operum moralium et civilium tomus (with De augmentis scientiarum)
src.loc: De augmentis scientiarum, book III summary of chapters, ch. 6 (SL p. 414)
src.q: Concerning Mathematics, the great Appendix of Natural Philosophy, both Speculative and Operative; and why it ought to be placed among the Appendices rather than among the Substantive Sciences.
src.qo: De Magnâ Philosophiæ Naturalis , tam Speculativæ, quam Operativæ, Appendice Mathematicâ ; Quódque inter Appendices potiùs poni debet, quam inter Scientias Substantivas.

s: In the margin of a dialogue arguing that arithmetic truths presuppose signs but are not therefore arbitrary, Leibniz wrote: 'Cum DEUS calculat et cogitationem exercet, fit mundus' (when God calculates and exercises thought, the world is made).

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, C. I. Gerhardt (ed.), 1875, Die philosophischen Schriften (SL record: Vol. I)
src.loc: Dialogue on characters and truth, footnote to Leibniz's marginal note (SL scan 218)
src.q: Cum DEUS calculat et cogitationem exercet, fit mundus.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, C. I. Gerhardt (ed.), 1875, Die philosophischen Schriften (SL record: Vol. I)
src.q: When GOD calculates and exercises thought, the world is made.

s: In the General Scholium Newton says God is not eternity and infinity, duration and space, but endures and is present, and by existing always and everywhere constitutes duration and space; he closes that discourse about God from phenomena belongs to natural philosophy.

src.l: Isaac Newton, 1687, Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (SL copy containing the Scholium generale)
src.q: He is not eternity and infinity, but eternal and infinite; he is not duration and space, but he endures and is present. He endures always, and is present everywhere, and by existing always and everywhere, he constitutes duration and space.
src.qo: Non est æternitas & infinitas, sed æternus & infinitus; non est duratio & spatium, sed durat & adest. Durat semper, & adest ubique, & existendo semper & ubique, durationem & spatium constituit.

src.l: Isaac Newton, 1687, Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (SL copy containing the Scholium generale)
src.q: And this much concerning God, about whom it surely belongs to natural philosophy to discourse from phenomena.

s: In the Arithmologia (1665) Kircher says those who marvelled at magic numbers and figures dragged what is pure and has apodictic reasons in arithmetic and geometry into impious superstitions, ascribing to them a natural efficacy that all philosophers deny they have, while the devil supplied amulets; his second part will show their mathematical reasons and the origin of the superstition.

src.l: Athanasius Kircher, 1665, Arithmologia sive De abditis numerorum mysteriis
src.loc: Arithmologia, Part II introduction (printed p. 58, SL scan 81)
src.q: they dragged what was in itself pure and sincere, and what had its own apodictic reasons rightly founded in arithmetic and geometry, into impious superstitions, while they dared to attribute to these kinds of numbers and figures a natural efficiency of which, by the opinion of all philosophers, they are devoid.
src.qo: quod ex se purum sincerum, quodque suas rationes apodicticas in Arithmetica et Geometria recte fundatas haberet, ad impias superstitiones traherent; dum numeris huiusmodi figurisque efficientiam naturalem, cuius, omnium Philosophorum sententia, expertes sunt, attribuere ausi sunt:

s: Gaffarel's Curiositez inouyes (1650 ed.), after examples of twenty as the number of sadness, defers to Bungus (Pietro Bongo) for 'a thousand examples', which shows Bongo's Numerorum mysteria used as the standard repertory of number symbolism.

src.l: Jacques Gaffarel, 1650, Curiositez inouyes, sur la sculpture talismanique des Persans
src.loc: ch. on innovations, 'The Mystery of Numbers, number 20' (printed p. 261, SL scan 299)
src.q: A thousand examples on this subject are put forward by Bungus
src.qo: Mille exemples ſur ce ſubiet ſont aduancez par Bungus,

s: Vickers argues that the occult and scientific traditions differ in treating language: science separates words and things and uses analogy as a testable explanatory device, while the occult tradition treats words as things and reifies analogies into the structure of the world, on a continuum of positions 1580–1680.

src.l: Brian Vickers, 1984, Analogy versus identity: the rejection of occult symbolism, 1580–1680

s: Westman argues that Pauli's famous study of the Kepler–Fludd polemic, though professionally done, appeared under the auspices of the Jung Institute and was really about the observer and the observed, archetypal images and sense perception, rather than Kepler as a historical figure.

src.l: Robert S. Westman, 1984, Nature, art, and psyche: Jung, Pauli, and the Kepler–Fludd polemic

s: Hanegraaff argues that the assumption of a Renaissance 'Hermetic Tradition' originating in Ficino's Pimander (Kristeller 1938, Yates 1964) needs revision: Ficino may have understood little of the Hermetic message and the corrupt 1471 edition obscured the text, so there was a discourse about Hermes rather than a tradition.

src.l: Wouter J. Hanegraaff, 2015, How Hermetic was Renaissance Hermetism?

s: In the Grundlagen (1883) Cantor agrees with the older philosophers that the true infinite or Absolute, which is in God, admits no determination, while rejecting their premise that number must be finite; an endnote says the Absolute can only be acknowledged, never known even approximately, and calls the absolutely infinite sequence of numbers a fitting symbol of the Absolute.

src.l: Georg Cantor, 1883, Ueber unendliche, lineare Punktmannichfaltigkeiten, 5. Fortsetzung [Grundlagen einer allgemeinen Mannichfaltigkeitslehre]
Georg Cantor, 1883, Ueber unendliche, lineare Punktmannichfaltigkeiten, 5. Fortsetzung [Grundlagen einer allgemeinen Mannichfaltigkeitslehre]
Georg Cantor, 1883, Ueber unendliche, lineare Punktmannichfaltigkeiten, 5. Fortsetzung [Grundlagen einer allgemeinen Mannichfaltigkeitslehre]

s: Cantor (1883) distinguishes the immanent (intrasubjective) reality of numbers, their definite place in our understanding, from their transient reality as images of relations in the outer world, holds that the two always coincide because of the unity of the All to which we belong, and concludes that mathematics need consider only immanent reality: its essence lies in its freedom.

src.l: Georg Cantor, 1883, Ueber unendliche, lineare Punktmannichfaltigkeiten, 5. Fortsetzung [Grundlagen einer allgemeinen Mannichfaltigkeitslehre]
Georg Cantor, 1883, Ueber unendliche, lineare Punktmannichfaltigkeiten, 5. Fortsetzung [Grundlagen einer allgemeinen Mannichfaltigkeitslehre]
Georg Cantor, 1883, Ueber unendliche, lineare Punktmannichfaltigkeiten, 5. Fortsetzung [Grundlagen einer allgemeinen Mannichfaltigkeitslehre]

s: Hilbert's 'Über das Unendliche' (lecture 1925, printed 1926) lays down as its first guiding wish that fruitful concept-formations be preserved, ending: no one shall be able to drive us from the paradise Cantor has created for us.

src.l: David Hilbert, 1926, Über das Unendliche

s: Hilbert concludes 'Über das Unendliche' that the infinite is nowhere realized: it is neither present in nature nor admissible as a foundation in our thinking, 'a remarkable harmony between being and thought'; the infinite survives only as an ideal element secured by finitary consistency proofs.

src.l: David Hilbert, 1926, Über das Unendliche
src.loc: Math. Ann. 95, final section, printed p. 190

s: Frege's Grundlagen (1884) defines objectivity as independence from sensation, intuition and imagination but not from reason (§26), and says the mathematician can no more create at will than the geographer; he can only discover what is there and name it.

src.l: Gottlob Frege, 1884, Die Grundlagen der Arithmetik
src.q: I understand objectivity as an independence from our sensation, intuition, and imagination
src.qo: So verstehe ich unter Objectivität eine Unabhängigkeit von unserm Empfinden, Anschauen und Vorstellen

src.l: Gottlob Frege, 1884, Die Grundlagen der Arithmetik
src.q: So verstehe ich unter Objectivität eine Unabhängigkeit von unserm Empfinden, Anschauen und Vorstellen

src.l: Gottlob Frege, 1884, Die Grundlagen der Arithmetik
src.q: He, too, can only discover what is there and name it.
src.qo: auch er kann nur entdecken, was da ist, und es benennen.

src.l: Gottlob Frege, 1884, Die Grundlagen der Arithmetik
src.q: auch er kann nur entdecken, was da ist, und es benennen.

s: Hardy (1940) states 'dogmatically' that mathematical reality lies outside us and that our proofs, grandiloquently called creations, are notes of observations (§22), and calls pure mathematics a rock on which all idealism founders: 317 is prime not because we think so but because mathematical reality is built that way (§24).

src.l: G. H. Hardy, 1940, A Mathematician's Apology
G. H. Hardy, 1940, A Mathematician's Apology

s: The Tractatus (1922) says mathematics is a logical method, its propositions are equations and so pseudo-propositions, and a mathematical proposition expresses no thought; we use it only to pass between non-mathematical propositions.

src.l: Ludwig Wittgenstein, 1922, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
src.q: Mathematics is a logical method. The propositions of mathematics are equations, thus pseudo-propositions.
src.qo: Die Mathematik ist eine logische Methode. Die Sätze der Mathematik sind Gleichungen, also Scheinsätze.

src.l: Ludwig Wittgenstein, 1922, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
src.q: The proposition of mathematics expresses no thought.
src.qo: Der Satz der Mathematik drückt keinen Gedanken aus.

s: Critique: Rodych (SEP) reports the later Wittgenstein's anti-platonism: treating mathematical investigation as the exploration of objects is 'already mathematical alchemy' (RFM V §16), since only mathematics gives its signs meaning; platonism is either a truism or a picture of 'an infinity of shadowy worlds' that explains nothing; and on the middle Wittgenstein we invent mathematics.

src.l: Victor Rodych, 2018, Wittgenstein's Philosophy of Mathematics
Victor Rodych, 2018, Wittgenstein's Philosophy of Mathematics

s: Benzmüller and Woltzenlogel Paleo (2013) formalised Scott's version of Gödel's ontological proof in higher-order modal logic and checked it with automated provers (LEO-II, Satallax, Nitpick, Coq, Isabelle): the axioms are consistent, logic KB suffices for 'necessarily, God exists' (S5 not needed), and without the extra conjunct in Scott's definition of essence the axioms are inconsistent; they leave the axioms' plausibility to humans.

src.l: Christoph Benzmüller, Bruno Woltzenlogel Paleo, 2013, Formalization, Mechanization and Automation of Gödel's Proof of God's Existence
Christoph Benzmüller, Bruno Woltzenlogel Paleo, 2013, Formalization, Mechanization and Automation of Gödel's Proof of God's Existence
Christoph Benzmüller, Bruno Woltzenlogel Paleo, 2013, Formalization, Mechanization and Automation of Gödel's Proof of God's Existence

s: In the body of 'The Mathematical Universe' (2008), Tegmark argues that a mathematical structure is not created and does not exist somewhere, it just exists, and proposes 'complete mathematical democracy': mathematical and physical existence are equivalent, so all mathematical structures exist (the Level IV multiverse), a form he calls radical Platonism; his footnote defines mathematics in the formalist way as human-independent and discovered.

src.l: Max Tegmark, 2008, The Mathematical Universe
Max Tegmark, 2008, The Mathematical Universe

s: Tegmark (2008) argues that even the most sophisticated computer simulation is an iterated function on integers and so merely a special case of a mathematical structure already in the Level IV multiverse, and asks whether running a simulation makes any ontological difference.

src.l: Max Tegmark, 2008, The Mathematical Universe
Max Tegmark, 2008, The Mathematical Universe
src.loc: §VII, 'Does a simulation really need to be run?'

s: Nieder and Dehaene (2009) review evidence from animal cognition, development and anthropology that human numerical skills are rooted in nonlinguistic biological primitives, with the intraparietal sulcus a key node for representing numerical quantity in human and nonhuman primates.

src.l: Andreas Nieder, Stanislas Dehaene, 2009, Representation of number in the brain

s: In the sun analogy (Republic VI, 508b-509b) the sun is the offspring of the good and stands to sight and the visible as the good stands to reason and its objects in the intelligible region; the objects of knowledge owe the good not only their being known but their existence and essence, though the good itself is not essence.

src.l: Plato, Paul Shorey (trans.), 1969, Republic (Shorey trans., Loeb 1930/1935; Perseus digital text)
Plato, Paul Shorey (trans.), 1969, Republic (Shorey trans., Loeb 1930/1935; Perseus digital text)

s: In the divided line (Republic VI, 510d-e) Socrates says geometers use and talk about visible figures while thinking not of them but of what they resemble, reasoning for the sake of the square as such and the diagonal as such, not the drawn image.

src.l: Plato, Paul Shorey (trans.), 1969, Republic (Shorey trans., Loeb 1930/1935; Perseus digital text)

s: Plato names the two realms as kinds and places, not worlds: at Republic 509d the good and the sun reign over the intelligible kind and place (noētou genous te kai topou) and the visible, 'two kinds, visible, intelligible'; at 517b the ascent out of the cave is the soul's way up to the intelligible place (noētos topos).

src.l: Plato, John Burnet (ed.), 1903, Respublica (Greek text, Oxford Classical Texts; Perseus digital text)
Plato, John Burnet (ed.), 1903, Respublica (Greek text, Oxford Classical Texts; Perseus digital text)
Plato, Paul Shorey (trans.), 1969, Republic (Shorey trans., Loeb 1930/1935; Perseus digital text)

s: Timaeus (27d-29b) divides what always is and has no becoming, grasped by thought with reasoning, from what always becomes and never is, grasped by opinion with sensation; a craftsman who looks to the unchanging as model makes a beautiful work, so the cosmos is a copy of an eternal model, and accounts share their object's stability: 'as Being is to Becoming, so is Truth to Belief'.

src.l: Plato, W. R. M. Lamb (trans.), 1925, Timaeus (Loeb Plato vol. 9; Perseus digital text)
Plato, W. R. M. Lamb (trans.), 1925, Timaeus (Loeb Plato vol. 9; Perseus digital text)
Plato, John Burnet (ed.), 1902, Timaeus (Greek text, Oxford Classical Texts; Perseus digital text)

s: At Timaeus 30c-d the model of the cosmos is the Living Creature of which all others are parts: it 'embraces and contains within itself all the intelligible Living Creatures' as the cosmos contains the visible ones; at 52a Plato adds a third kind besides Form and sensible, ever-existing Place (chōra), grasped by 'a kind of bastard reasoning'.

src.l: Plato, W. R. M. Lamb (trans.), 1925, Timaeus (Loeb Plato vol. 9; Perseus digital text)
Plato, W. R. M. Lamb (trans.), 1925, Timaeus (Loeb Plato vol. 9; Perseus digital text)

s: Philo's De opificio mundi uses the phrase kosmos noētos for the model God formed first: wishing to make this visible world he first stamped out the intelligible one as an incorporeal, most godlike paradigm (§16), built the intelligible world from the patterns before the sensible (§19), and, put more barely, the intelligible world is nothing else than the logos of God already making the world (§24).

src.l: Philo of Alexandria, Leopold Cohn (ed.), 1896, De opificio mundi (Greek text, Cohn-Wendland vol. 1)
Philo of Alexandria, Leopold Cohn (ed.), 1896, De opificio mundi (Greek text, Cohn-Wendland vol. 1)
Philo of Alexandria, Leopold Cohn (ed.), 1896, De opificio mundi (Greek text, Cohn-Wendland vol. 1)

s: Philo (De opif. 25) attributes the doctrine to Moses, not himself: if man is an image of an image, so is the whole sensible world, and the archetypal seal, which 'we say is the intelligible world', would be the Logos of God itself; the transmitted text adds 'the paradigm, archetypal idea of ideas', which the edition brackets.

src.l: Philo of Alexandria, Leopold Cohn (ed.), 1896, De opificio mundi (Greek text, Cohn-Wendland vol. 1)
Philo of Alexandria, Leopold Cohn (ed.), 1896, De opificio mundi (Greek text, Cohn-Wendland vol. 1)

s: Philo reads Genesis' 'day one' (not 'first day') arithmologically: Moses called it one because he saw in it the nature of the monad, and it contains the intelligible world (§15); it is called one because of the intelligible world's singleness, which has a monadic nature (§35); the incorporeal world then stood complete, set in the divine Logos (§36).

src.l: Philo of Alexandria, Leopold Cohn (ed.), 1896, De opificio mundi (Greek text, Cohn-Wendland vol. 1)
Philo of Alexandria, Leopold Cohn (ed.), 1896, De opificio mundi (Greek text, Cohn-Wendland vol. 1)
Philo of Alexandria, Leopold Cohn (ed.), 1896, De opificio mundi (Greek text, Cohn-Wendland vol. 1)

s: Plotinus (Enn. V.9.5, 9) holds that the intelligibles are not outside Intelligence (Nous) nor in any place, and that since the sense-world is an animal embracing all animals, Intelligence must contain the universal archetype and be 'that intelligible world' Plato meant (Timaeus 39e), holding in unity what the sense-world shows divided.

src.l: Plotinus, Kenneth Sylvan Guthrie (trans.), 1918, Plotinos: Complete Works, vol. 1
Plotinus, Kenneth Sylvan Guthrie (trans.), 1918, Plotinos: Complete Works, vol. 1

s: Plotinus (Enn. V.9.10) counts quantities, numbers and magnitudes among the contents of the intelligible world, where time is replaced by eternity; and (V.9.11) unlike the practical arts, geometry, which deals wholly with intelligible entities, must be referred to the intelligible world.

src.l: Plotinus, Kenneth Sylvan Guthrie (trans.), 1918, Plotinos: Complete Works, vol. 1
Plotinus, Kenneth Sylvan Guthrie (trans.), 1918, Plotinos: Complete Works, vol. 1

s: Augustine (De diversis quaestionibus 83, q. 46) defines ideas as principal forms or stable, unchangeable reasons of things, themselves unformed and eternal, contained in the divine intelligence; since God made things by reason and each by its own reason, these reasons can be nowhere but in the Creator's mind, seen only by the pure rational soul's inner eye.

src.l: Augustine of Hippo, 1880, De diversis quaestionibus octoginta tribus
Augustine of Hippo, 1880, De diversis quaestionibus octoginta tribus

s: In a letter to Cavalcanti headed 'Ideas, according to Plato, are in the divine mind', Ficino reads the Timaeus' exemplar cause as an architect's plan: in a divine intelligence above the world are the exemplars of the world and its parts, which Plato calls the intelligible world, and Ficino mocks those who say Plato separated the ideas from the divine intelligence.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 15th c., Epistolae (Laurenziana Plut. 51.11; SL 'Ficino, Letters (third manuscript)')
src.q: so in a certain divine intelligence above the world there are exemplars of this whole world and its parts, and he names that world the intelligible and ethereal [world], while he calls this one the temporal and sensible [world].
src.qo: sic in diuina qua- dam intelligentia supra mundum esse uniuer- si mundi huius eiusq; partium exemplaria, mundumq; illum intelligibilem nominat & ethereum. hunc uero temporalem atq; sensibilem.

s: Fludd (Utriusque cosmi I, tract. I, bk. II, ch. 1) reports Martianus' three senses of 'world': the Archetype, incorporeal, invisible, intellectual and eternal, after whose image the real world was made and which remains in the divine mind (citing Boethius); the greater world; and man the lesser; Fludd himself then treats only the twofold world, macrocosm and microcosm.

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1617, Utriusque cosmi maioris scilicet et minoris metaphysica, physica atque technica historia, vol. 1
src.loc: ch. 1 'On the world and its division', printed p. 45 [scan 53]
src.q: whose substance is incorporeal, invisible, intellectual, and eternal, according to whose example and divine image the beauty and likeness of the real world was fashioned

s: In the 1770 Dissertation (§§3-4) Kant divides the object of sensibility (the sensible, 'phaenomenon') from what can be known only by the intellect (the intelligible, 'noumenon'), and holds that sensitive cognitions represent things as they appear, intellectual ones as they are.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1770, De mundi sensibilis atque intelligibilis forma et principiis
Immanuel Kant, 1770, De mundi sensibilis atque intelligibilis forma et principiis

s: Kant's Dissertation §10 denies human beings any intuition of intelligibles, allowing only symbolic cognition through universal concepts, and reserves an archetypal, perfectly intellectual intuition to God, whose intuition is the principle of its objects.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1770, De mundi sensibilis atque intelligibilis forma et principiis
Immanuel Kant, 1770, De mundi sensibilis atque intelligibilis forma et principiis

s: Already in 1770 (§12) Kant places pure mathematics not in the intelligible world but in pure (human, non-intellectual) intuition: geometry treats space, pure mechanics time, and arithmetic treats number, a concept intellectual in itself whose concrete realisation needs time and space.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1770, De mundi sensibilis atque intelligibilis forma et principiis

s: Dissertation §15 D: space is neither substance, accident nor relation but subjective and ideal, a schema issuing from the nature of the mind; Kant charges the Leibnizians, who make space a relation of existing things, with demoting geometry to an empirical science.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1770, De mundi sensibilis atque intelligibilis forma et principiis
Immanuel Kant, 1770, De mundi sensibilis atque intelligibilis forma et principiis

s: In the B Introduction (V) of the Critique of Pure Reason Kant argues that all mathematical judgements are synthetic a priori: 7+5=12 cannot be found by analysing the concept of the sum, one must go beyond the concepts with the help of intuition (fingers, Segner's points).

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1787, Kritik der reinen Vernunft, 2nd ed. (B)
Immanuel Kant, 1787, Kritik der reinen Vernunft, 2nd ed. (B)

s: In the Transcendental Aesthetic (§3) Kant argues that geometry, which determines space synthetically yet a priori, is possible only if space is a pure intuition that has its seat in the subject as the form of outer sense.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1787, Kritik der reinen Vernunft, 2nd ed. (B)

s: In the Critique of Pure Reason (Phenomena and Noumena) Kant allows a noumenon only in the negative sense, since intellectual intuition lies wholly outside our cognitive power; the concept is a mere boundary concept, and the division of the world into a sensible and an intelligible world cannot be admitted in a positive sense.

src.l: Immanuel Kant, 1787, Kritik der reinen Vernunft, 2nd ed. (B)
Immanuel Kant, 1787, Kritik der reinen Vernunft, 2nd ed. (B)

s: SEP (Morscher) reports that Bolzano's propositions and ideas in themselves (Sätze an sich, Vorstellungen an sich) belong to a 'third realm' (World 3) outside reality, which for Bolzano means what is efficacious in space and time: there are such propositions, but they do not exist and have no being.

src.l: Edgar Morscher, 2018, Bernard Bolzano

s: In the Logical Investigations (II, Investigation 2) Husserl holds that a number such as five is an ideal species, absolutely one whatever acts make it objective, with no share in the temporality of the real; acts of counting arise and pass away, numbers do not, and arithmetic says nothing about the real.

src.l: Edmund Husserl, 1901, Logische Untersuchungen, Zweiter Teil
src.q: what is intended is the ideal species, which, in the sense of arithmetic, is absolutely one, in whatever acts it may become objective, and which thus has no share in the individual particularity of the real with its temporality and transience.
src.qo: die im Sinne der Arithmetik schlechthin Eine ist, in welchen Acten sie auch gegenständlich werden mag, und die somit ohne jeden Antheil ist an der individuellen Einzelheit des Realen mit seiner Zeitlichkeit und Vergänglichkeit.

s: Husserl, closing the Logical Investigations' survey, calls Bolzano one of the greatest logicians of all time, to be placed beside Leibniz, and says his own investigations received decisive influences from Bolzano and from Lotze, though they are not mere commentaries on him.

src.l: Edmund Husserl, 1901, Logische Untersuchungen, Zweiter Teil
src.q: must be considered one of the greatest logicians of all time. In his position, he is to be placed right next to Leibniz

src.l: Edmund Husserl, 1901, Logische Untersuchungen, Zweiter Teil
src.q: they have received decisive influences from Bolzano—and, besides him, from Lotze.
src.qo: obschon sie andererseits die entscheidenden Einflüsse von Bolzano — und daneben von Lotze — empfangen haben.

s: Frege's 'Der Gedanke' (1918), as quoted verbatim in the German Wikipedia article, says a third realm must be acknowledged, sharing with ideas imperceptibility and with things independence of any bearer; the thought of the Pythagorean theorem is timelessly true and was not made true by being discovered, like a planet.

src.l: Wikipedia contributors (via de-academic.com mirror), 2010, Drittes Reich (Frege)
Wikipedia contributors (via de-academic.com mirror), 2010, Drittes Reich (Frege)

s: In the 1964 supplement to 'What is Cantor's continuum problem?' Gödel holds that, despite their remoteness from sense experience, we have something like a perception of the objects of set theory, shown by the axioms forcing themselves on us as true, and sees no reason to trust this mathematical intuition less than sense perception.

src.l: Jovana Kostić, 2024, Kurt Gödel and the Logic of Concepts
src.loc: discussion of intuition (quoting Collected Works II, p. 268)

src.l: Kurt Gödel, 1964, What is Cantor's continuum problem? (revised and expanded version)

s: Benacerraf's 'Mathematical Truth' (1973, p. 674), citing the revised continuum paper in Benacerraf and Putnam (p. 271), prints Gödel as saying 'we do have a perception also of the objects of set theory' and 'I don't see why'; the Collected Works text as quoted by Kostić reads 'something like a perception' and 'I don't see any reason why'.

src.l: Paul Benacerraf, 1973, Mathematical Truth
Jovana Kostić, 2024, Kurt Gödel and the Logic of Concepts

s: Critique: Benacerraf (1973) poses a dilemma: accounts that give mathematical sentences the same truth conditions as other sentences make mathematical knowledge unintelligible, and Gödel's analogy with perception lacks what a causal account of knowledge requires, an account of the link between our faculties and the objects known.

src.l: Paul Benacerraf, 1973, Mathematical Truth
Paul Benacerraf, 1973, Mathematical Truth

s: Benacerraf (1973) suggests, as a 'speculative historical note', that Plato introduced anamnesis at least partly to explain how, given the nature of the Forms, anyone could know them: the access problem is as old as the intelligible realm.

src.l: Paul Benacerraf, 1973, Mathematical Truth

s: SEP (Thornton) reports that Popper's pluralism places objective knowledge in world 3, 'a third, objectively real ontological category' of products of the human mind, and quotes Popper (1980) listing 'mathematical constructions' among them; on this view mathematics is made by us yet real and partly autonomous.

src.l: Stephen Thornton, 2022, Karl Popper

s: Plutarch's Table-Talk VIII.2 asks how Plato said that God always geometrizes (ἀεὶ γεωμετρεῖν τὸν θεόν), and the speakers concede the saying is written clearly in none of Plato's books, though it is 'of the Platonic character'.

src.q: Πῶς Πλάτων ἔλεγε τὸν θεὸν ἀεὶ γεωμετρεῖν.

s: In Plutarch's Table-Talk VIII.2, Tyndares' first reading of 'God always geometrizes' is Plato's praise of geometry as drawing us from sense toward the intelligible and eternal nature, whose viewing is philosophy's goal 'like the initiation into a rite' (epopteia).

src.l: Plutarch, 1888, Plutarchi Chaeronensis Moralia, ed. G. N. Bernardakis (Quaestiones convivales VIII.2)
src.q: praising geometry as that which draws us away from our attachment to sensory perception and turns us toward the intelligible and eternal nature, the viewing of which is the goal of philosophy, like the initiation into a rite?
src.qo: ὑμνῶν γεωμετρίαν, ὡς ἀποσπῶσαν ἡμᾶς προσισχομένους τῇ αἰσθήσει καὶ ἀποστρέφουσαν ἐπὶ τὴν νοητὴν καὶ ἀΐδιον φύσιν

s: Sartorius von Waltershausen (1856) reports, as Gauss's own words, that mathematics is the queen of the sciences and arithmetic the queen of mathematics, who often condescends to serve astronomy and the natural sciences but deserves first rank in all circumstances.

src.l: W. Sartorius von Waltershausen, 1856, Gauss zum Gedächtniss

s: In a letter to Bessel (Göttingen, 9 April 1830) Gauss says geometry stands differently in our a priori knowledge from pure arithmetic: we lack full conviction of its necessity, and must humbly concede that if number is merely a product of our mind, space has a reality outside it whose laws we cannot fully prescribe a priori.

src.l: C. F. Gauss, F. W. Bessel, 1880, Briefwechsel zwischen Gauss und Bessel
C. F. Gauss, F. W. Bessel, 1880, Briefwechsel zwischen Gauss und Bessel

s: Sartorius reports that Gauss treated geometry as a consistent edifice only once the parallel postulate is granted, held that it cannot be proved but is known from experience (e.g. the Brocken–Hohenhagen–Inselsberg triangle) to be approximately right, and named the geometry without it 'anti-Euclidean'.

src.l: W. Sartorius von Waltershausen, 1856, Gauss zum Gedächtniss

s: Sartorius reports that Gauss, in his often-stated inmost view, regarded the three dimensions of space as a specific peculiarity of the human soul, and mused that beings above us might be aware of more dimensions as we can imagine beings aware of only two.

src.l: W. Sartorius von Waltershausen, 1856, Gauss zum Gedächtniss

s: Sartorius describes the foundation of Gauss's religious life as an unshakeable idea of personal continuation after death and faith in a just, all-wise, almighty God, and reports Gauss saying that a God who made creatures to live 80 or 90 years only would be a 'wretched plan', pressing one to a second, purely spiritual world order.

src.l: W. Sartorius von Waltershausen, 1856, Gauss zum Gedächtniss
W. Sartorius von Waltershausen, 1856, Gauss zum Gedächtniss

s: The first printed source of the 'algebraic proof of God' told against Diderot at Catherine II's court, Thiébault's Souvenirs (1804), names no mathematician (only 'a learned mathematician, distinguished member of the academy') and explicitly does not vouch for the truth of any of the facts.

src.l: Dieudonné Thiébault, 1804, Mes souvenirs de vingt ans de séjour à Berlin, t. III

s: De Morgan's Budget of Paradoxes (1872) retells Thiébault's story, concedes the mathematician 'is not named', yet asserts 'it was Euler' and adds that algebra was 'Hebrew' to Diderot; this is the source of the Euler version.

src.l: Augustus De Morgan, 1872, A Budget of Paradoxes
Augustus De Morgan, 1872, A Budget of Paradoxes
Augustus De Morgan, 1872, A Budget of Paradoxes

s: Historians treat the Euler–Diderot 'algebraic proof of God' as a legend: Chouillet (1978) traces every later version to two base texts, Thiébault 1804 and De Morgan 1867/1872, and B. H. Brown (1942) wrote a dedicated debunking note.

src.l: Anne-Marie Chouillet, 1978, L'anecdote Diderot - Euler ou Dieu prouvé par A+B
B. H. Brown, 1942, The Euler-Diderot Anecdote

s: The 1927 memoir by Seshu Aiyar and Ramachaundra Rao reports that Ramanujan 'used to say' the goddess of Namakkal (Namagiri) inspired him with formulae in dreams, and that he often wrote results down and verified them on rising.

src.l: G. H. Hardy, P. V. Seshu Aiyar, B. M. Wilson (eds.), 1927, Collected Papers of Srinivasa Ramanujan (with notices by Seshu Aiyar & Ramachaundra Rao, and by Hardy)
src.loc: Seshu Aiyar & Ramachaundra Rao, 'Notice', pp. xi ff.

s: Seshu Aiyar and Ramachaundra Rao (1927) state that Ramanujan had definite religious views: belief in a Supreme Being and in the attainment of Godhood by men through service and realising oneness with the Deity, with settled convictions about life and after.

src.l: G. H. Hardy, P. V. Seshu Aiyar, B. M. Wilson (eds.), 1927, Collected Papers of Srinivasa Ramanujan (with notices by Seshu Aiyar & Ramachaundra Rao, and by Hardy)

s: In his 1927 notice Hardy writes that Ramanujan kept his caste's observances with unusual severity, but that his religion was 'a matter of observance and not of intellectual conviction', and that Ramanujan told him all religions seemed more or less equally true.

src.l: G. H. Hardy, P. V. Seshu Aiyar, B. M. Wilson (eds.), 1927, Collected Papers of Srinivasa Ramanujan (with notices by Seshu Aiyar & Ramachaundra Rao, and by Hardy)

s: In Ramanujan: Twelve Lectures (1940) Hardy quotes the Namakkal-dream passage only to say he attaches no importance to it, declares Ramanujan 'no mystic', notes the two memoirs 'contradict one another flatly' on religion, and is 'quite certain' he is right, calling Ramanujan an agnostic practising an 'economy of truth'.

src.l: G. H. Hardy, 1940, Ramanujan: Twelve Lectures on Subjects Suggested by his Life and Work
G. H. Hardy, 1940, Ramanujan: Twelve Lectures on Subjects Suggested by his Life and Work
G. H. Hardy, 1940, Ramanujan: Twelve Lectures on Subjects Suggested by his Life and Work

s: The saying 'an equation has no meaning for me unless it expresses a thought of God' first appears, as far as traced, in Ranganathan's Ramanujan (1967), in a reminiscence by R. Srinivasan of a 1913 conversation; Kanigel (1991) popularised it, citing Ranganathan p. 88, in reworded form ('An equation for me has no meaning…').

src.l: S. R. Ranganathan, 1967, Ramanujan: The Man and the Mathematician
src.loc: section MR2 'Mystic' (reminiscences of R. Srinivasan); p. 88 per Kanigel

src.l: Robert Kanigel, 1991, The Man Who Knew Infinity: A Life of the Genius Ramanujan
src.loc: ch. 2 ('Ranging with Delight'), p. 66; note citing 'S. R. Ranganathan, 88'

s: Ranganathan (1967), quoting his own Hidden Treasures of Yoga, reports that Ramanujan's family were devotees of Narasimha, whose grace showed as drops of blood in dreams, after which Ramanujan said scrolls of complicated mathematics unfolded before him, of which he could write down only a fraction.

src.l: S. R. Ranganathan, 1967, Ramanujan: The Man and the Mathematician

s: Pascal's Memorial of the night of 23 November 1654 (c. 10.30 pm to 12.30 am) begins 'Feu' and names the 'Dieu d'Abraham, Dieu d'Isaac, Dieu de Jacob, non des philosophes et des savants', followed by 'Certitude. Certitude. Sentiment. Joie. Paix.' The certainty he records is given in an experience, not demonstrated.

src.l: Blaise Pascal, 1925, Mémorial de Pascal

s: In the Pensées Pascal says the metaphysical proofs of God barely move the soul and that the Christian's God is not merely the author of geometric truths and the order of the elements, which is 'the portion of the pagans' (read in a 1777 German translation, rendered into English by SL).

src.l: Blaise Pascal, 1777, Gedanken Paskals (German translation of the Pensées)
src.q: The Deity of the Christian does not consist in a God who is the mere author of geometric truths and the order of the elements; that is the portion of the pagans.

s: Pascal opposes the geometric mind, which reasons from few, clear, remote principles, to the subtle mind (esprit de finesse), which must take in many delicate, felt principles at a single glance; hence 'a geometric mind is rarely subtle, and a subtle mind is rarely geometric'.

src.l: Blaise Pascal, 1777, Gedanken Paskals (German translation of the Pensées)
src.q: One must see the whole matter in a single glance, and not through the progress of reasoning, at least up to a certain degree. Therefore, a geometric mind is rarely subtle, and a subtle mind is rarely geometric;
src.qo: Man muß die ganze Sache in einem Blick sehen, und nicht durch Fortschritte des Rai- sonnemens, wenigstens bis auf einen gewissen Grad. Daher ist nun ein geometrischer Ver- stand selten subtil, und ein subtiler selten geo- metrisch;

s: Beyond God constituting space (linked claim), the General Scholium argues that the planets keep their orbits by gravity but could not have acquired their regular arrangement by those laws, so 'this most elegant arrangement' of sun, planets and comets arose only from the counsel and dominion of an intelligent and powerful Being, who rules not as world-soul but as Lord (Pantokrator).

src.l: Isaac Newton, 1687, Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (SL copy containing the Scholium generale)
src.q: This most elegant arrangement of the sun, planets, and comets could not have arisen except by the plan and dominion of an intelligent and powerful Being.
src.qo: Elegantissima hæcce solis, planetarum & cometarum com- pages non nisi consilio & dominio entis intelligentis & potentis oriri potuit.

src.l: Isaac Newton, 1687, Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (SL copy containing the Scholium generale)
src.q: This Being governs all things, not as the soul of the world, but as Lord over all.
src.qo: Hic omnia regit non ut anima mundi, sed ut universorum dominus.

s: The saying 'Die ganzen Zahlen hat der liebe Gott gemacht, alles andere ist Menschenwerk' is first printed second-hand, in Heinrich Weber's 1893 obituary of Kronecker, who says many listeners will remember it from a lecture Kronecker gave at the Berlin Naturforscher-Versammlung (1886).

src.l: Heinrich Weber, 1893, Leopold Kronecker

s: Darboux reports, 'citing his own expressions', that Hermite held numbers and the functions of analysis to be no arbitrary product of our mind but to exist outside us with the necessity of objective reality, so that we meet or discover them as physicists, chemists and zoologists do; Darboux concludes Hermite was 'réaliste à la manière de Platon'.

src.l: Gaston Darboux, 1912, Notice historique sur Charles Hermite

s: In his calculation notebooks, as quoted by Darboux and again by Meyerson, Hermite wrote that the world of mathematical truths, reached only by the intellect, and the world of physical realities are both independent of us and 'both of divine creation', distinct only through our weakness, one thing for a mightier mind, their synthesis showing in the correspondence of abstract mathematics with astronomy and physics.

src.l: Émile Meyerson, 1924, La science et la quantité
Gaston Darboux, 1912, Notice historique sur Charles Hermite

s: Critique: Meyerson (1924) reports that the positivist Joseph Petzoldt (1921, p. 123) loudly protested against the conception of a preestablished harmony between pure mathematics and physics, affirmed by Hermite and Minkowski, calling it a very dangerous belief.

src.l: Émile Meyerson, 1924, La science et la quantité
src.loc: note to § III (citing Petzoldt, Die Stellung der Relativitätstheorie, Dresden 1921, p. 123)

s: Poincaré reports that, on a geological excursion, as he set foot on the step of an omnibus at Coutances, the idea came to him unprepared that the transformations defining the Fuchsian functions were those of non-Euclidean geometry, with 'une entière certitude'; he checked it later at Caen, and reads such illuminations as signs of long prior unconscious work.

src.l: Henri Poincaré, 1908, Science et méthode, livre I ch. III 'L'invention mathématique'

s: Poincaré considers whether the subliminal self, which 'sait choisir, il sait deviner', is superior to the conscious self, notes that Boutroux has drawn the consequences of a yes, and says he would not accept it 'sans répugnance'; he prefers that the subliminal self combines blindly and a special aesthetic sensibility, moved only by harmonious combinations, acts as the sieve that lets them into consciousness.

src.l: Henri Poincaré, 1908, Science et méthode, livre I ch. III 'L'invention mathématique'
Henri Poincaré, 1908, Science et méthode, livre I ch. III 'L'invention mathématique'

s: Hadamard (1945) distinguishes art, whose works are true inventions, from science, whose work concerns discoveries, quoting his teacher Hermite that we are rather servants than masters in mathematics and adding that the truth, though not yet known, pre-exists; the book builds Poincaré's Coutances account into a preparation-incubation-illumination schema (after Wallas).

src.l: Jacques Hadamard, 1945, An Essay on the Psychology of Invention in the Mathematical Field

s: Hardy (1940, §10) says the mathematician's patterns, like the painter's or the poet's, must be beautiful: 'Beauty is the first test; there is no permanent place in the world for ugly mathematics.'

src.l: G. H. Hardy, 1940, A Mathematician's Apology

s: According to passages of Weil's Souvenirs d'apprentissage quoted by Papadopoulos and Tanabé, André Weil read the Bhagavad Gītā in Sanskrit in 1922 at Sylvain Lévi's suggestion and found in it 'the only form of religious thought that could satisfy my mind', and later described devoting himself to mathematics as his dharma, as painting was Gauguin's.

src.l: Athanase Papadopoulos, Susumu Tanabé, 2025, André and Simone Weil: Mathematics, social activism and Indian culture
Athanase Papadopoulos, Susumu Tanabé, 2025, André and Simone Weil: Mathematics, social activism and Indian culture

s: Paura (2023) argues that Simone Weil, against her brother's Bourbaki and its 'mechanical attention', read the Pythagorean crisis of incommensurables as an analogy between mathematical relation and God's relation to mankind (logos), grounding a 'supernatural reason' opposed to algorithmic reason.

src.l: Roberto Paura, 2023, "God does not algebra": Simone Weil's search for a supernatural reformulation of mathematics

s: Proclus opens his commentary on Euclid I by placing mathematical being in the middle, between the indivisible intelligibles and divisible things in matter: above material forms because its accounts are unchanging and irrefutable, below pure intellect because it proceeds discursively; he ties this to Plato's division of knowledge.

src.l: Proclus, 1873, Procli Diadochi In primum Euclidis Elementorum librum commentarii
src.q: It is necessary that mathematical substance occupies a middle position, neither among the first of those things that are, nor among the last
src.qo: Τὴν μαθηματικὴν οὐσίαν οὔτε τῶν πρωτίστων ἐν τοῖς οὖσι γενῶν οὔτε τῶν ἐσχάτων εἶναι

src.l: Proclus, 1873, Procli Diadochi In primum Euclidis Elementorum librum commentarii
src.q: For that which is always unchanging, permanent, and irrefutable—the accounts concerning it—shows that it excels over the forms borne in matter

s: Dee's Mathematicall Praeface (1570) sorts all beings into supernatural, natural and a third kind, 'Thynges Mathematicall', which stand 'in a maner' between supernatural and natural: immaterial, with constant and incorruptible general forms, yet signifiable by material things.

src.l: John Dee, 1570, Mathematicall Praeface, in The Elements of Geometrie of Euclide, trans. H. Billingsley
src.q: For, these, beyng (in a maner) middle, betwene thinges supernaturall and naturall: are not so absolute and excellent, as thinges supernatural: Nor yet so base and grosse, as things naturall

src.l: John Dee, 1570, Mathematicall Praeface, in The Elements of Geometrie of Euclide, trans. H. Billingsley
src.q: yet the generall Formes, notwithstanding, are constant, vnchaungeable, vntrāfformable, and incorruptible.

s: Dee gives number a threefold state: in the Creator, in every creature, and in angelic minds and the human soul ('Number Numbryng' in the first and third, 'Number Numbred' in creatures), and calls the law of numbers 'planted in thyngs Naturall and Supernaturall'.

src.l: John Dee, 1570, Mathematicall Praeface, in The Elements of Geometrie of Euclide, trans. H. Billingsley
src.q: Number hath a treble ftate: One, in the Creator: an other in euery Creature

src.l: John Dee, 1570, Mathematicall Praeface, in The Elements of Geometrie of Euclide, trans. H. Billingsley
src.q: the constant law of núbers: which is planted in thyngs Naturall and Supernaturall: and is prescribed to all Creatures, inuiolably to be kept.

s: Dee defines Thaumaturgike as the mathematical art that gives order to make strange works, perceptible to sense and greatly wondered at, citing pneumatic devices of Ctesibius and Hero: wonder-working by mathematics, not by spirits.

src.l: John Dee, 1570, Mathematicall Praeface, in The Elements of Geometrie of Euclide, trans. H. Billingsley
src.q: Thaumaturgike, is that Art Mathematicall, which giueth certaine order to make ſtraunge workes, of the ſenſe to be perceiued, and of men greatly to be wondred at.

s: Agrippa opens De occulta philosophia II by saying the mathematical disciplines are so necessary to magic that without them the magus labours in vain, since everything in the lower world is made and governed by number, weight, measure, harmony, motion and light, and works like nature's can be produced by mathematics alone.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1550, De occulta philosophia libri III
src.q: are all made and governed by number, weight, measure, harmony, motion, and light.
src.qo: omnia hæc numero, pondere, mensura, harmonia, motu & lumine fiunt atq; reguntur,

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1550, De occulta philosophia libri III
src.q: even without natural powers, works similar to natural ones can be produced from the mathematical disciplines alone.
src.qo: nihilominus tamen etiam absq; naturalibus uirtutibus, ex solis mathematicis disciplinis, opera naturalibus similia produci possunt,

s: In II.2 Agrippa, after Boethius, makes number the principal model in the Creator's mind and holds that numbers, as the most formal of mathematical things, have greater and more hidden virtues than natural things; he locates these powers in 'formal' numbers, not merchants' counting.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1550, De occulta philosophia libri III
src.loc: Book II, end of ch. 1 and ch. 2 (printed p. 176)
src.q: Among all mathematical things, however, numbers are considered the most formal and thus the most actual
src.qo: inter omnia autem ma- thematica, numeros, ut sunt formaliores, ita etiam esse actualiores,

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1550, De occulta philosophia libri III
src.q: For this was the principal model in the mind of the Creator
src.qo: hoc enim fuit principale in animo condi- toris exemplar:

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1550, De occulta philosophia libri III
src.q: there are much greater, more hidden, more wonderful, and more effective virtues in numbers themselves.
src.qo: eſſe in ipſis numeris multo quidem maiores, oc- cultiores, mirabiliores, atq; efficaciores,

s: Kepler (Harmonices mundi IV.1) says geometry, co-eternal with the divine mind before the creation of things, is God himself, supplied the patterns for creating the world, and passed into man with the image of God; Christians know the mathematical reasons for bodies were co-eternal with God.

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1619, Harmonices mundi libri V
src.q: Geometry, co-eternal with the Divine Mind before the birth of things, is God Himself ... It supplied God with the patterns for creating the world, and it passed into man along with the image of God
src.qo: Geometria ante rerum ortum Menti divinæ coæterna, Deus ipse (quid enim in Deo, quod non sit Ipse Deus) exempla Deo creandi mundi suppeditavit, & cum imagine Dei transivit in hominem:

src.l: Johannes Kepler, 1619, Harmonices mundi libri V
src.q: Christians know that the mathematical reasons for creating bodies were co-eternal with God
src.qo: (rationes creandorum corporum ma- thematicas, Deo coæternas fuisse, Deumque Animam & Mentem esse super excellenrer; Animas verò humanas esse Dei creatoris imagines, etiam in essentialibus suo modo, id sciunt Christiani)

s: Descartes tells Mersenne that the mathematical truths called eternal were established by God and depend on him entirely like other creatures, as a king establishes laws in his kingdom; to call them independent of God subjects him to the Styx and the Fates. Later he adds they are true because God knows them, not known because true.

src.l: René Descartes, 1897, Oeuvres de Descartes, vol. I: Correspondance
src.loc: Letter XXI to Mersenne, AT I p. 145
src.q: That mathematical truths, which you call eternal, have been established by God and depend entirely on Him, just as much as all the rest
src.qo: Que les verités mathematiques, leſquelles vous nommés eternelles, ont eſté eſtablies de Dieu & en dependent entieremant,

src.l: René Descartes, 1897, Oeuvres de Descartes, vol. I: Correspondance
src.loc: Letter to Mersenne, AT I p. 149
src.q: they are only true or possible because God knows them as true or possible, and not, on the contrary, that they are known by God as true as if they were true independently of Him

s: Leibniz places the eternal truths in God's understanding, 'the region of eternal truths', without which nothing would even be possible (Monadology §43), and in the Theodicy puts that region in the place of matter as the source of things.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1898, The Monadology and Other Philosophical Writings
src.q: For the understanding of God is the region of eternal truths or of the ideas on which they depend

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1726, Theodicaea, oder Versuch und Abhandlung, wie die Güte und Gerechtigkeit Gottes ... zu verteidigen
src.q: One must put the region of eternal truths in the place of matter when one seeks the source and the origin of things.
src.qo: Man muß die Region der ewigen Wahrheiten an die Stelle der Materie setzen, wenn man die Quelle und den Ursprung der Dinge suchet.

s: Monadology §46 rejects the view that the eternal truths, because they depend on God, are arbitrary and depend on his will, naming Descartes; the editor's note quotes Descartes's letter to Mersenne.

src.l: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, 1898, The Monadology and Other Philosophical Writings
src.q: We must not, however, imagine, as some do, that eternal truths, being dependent on God, are arbitrary and depend on His will, as Descartes

s: Terminology: in philosophy 'A supervenes on B' means there can be no A-difference without a B-difference, so the supervening (higher) properties depend on the base. To say mathematics 'supervenes on' nature would make it depend on nature, the reverse of 'above nature'; the apt words are 'transcends', 'is prior to', or Dee's 'middle between'.

src.l: Brian McLaughlin, Karen Bennett, 2023, Supervenience
Brian McLaughlin, Karen Bennett, 2023, Supervenience

s: Linnebo (SEP) defines mathematical platonism as the view that abstract mathematical objects exist independently of us and our language, thought and practices, so that mathematical truths are discovered, not invented; he calls Frege's argument from the truth of mathematical sentences the most important argument for it.

src.l: Øystein Linnebo, 2023, Platonism in the Philosophy of Mathematics
Øystein Linnebo, 2023, Platonism in the Philosophy of Mathematics

s: Gödel is the standard twentieth-century mathematical platonist: SEP reports his (1944) argument that impredicative definitions are legitimate whenever the objects defined exist independently of our definitions; his 'What is Cantor's continuum problem?' (1947, revised 1964) is the usual citation for the view.

src.l: Øystein Linnebo, 2023, Platonism in the Philosophy of Mathematics
Kurt Gödel, 1947, What is Cantor's continuum problem?

s: Wigner (1960) calls the enormous usefulness of mathematics in the natural sciences something bordering on the mysterious, with no rational explanation, and ends by calling the appropriateness of mathematics for physical law a miracle 'we neither understand nor deserve'.

src.l: Eugene P. Wigner, 1960, The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences
Eugene P. Wigner, 1960, The unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences

s: Tegmark (2008) argues that the hypothesis of an external reality wholly independent of humans implies, on a broad definition of mathematics, the Mathematical Universe Hypothesis: our physical world is an abstract mathematical structure.

src.l: Max Tegmark, 2008, The Mathematical Universe

s: Field's nominalism (Science Without Numbers, 1980; 2nd ed. 2016) denies that mathematics is indispensable to science: per SEP, he argues mathematical theories need not be true to be useful in applications, only conservative, and that physics can be nominalised.

src.l: Mark Colyvan, 2023, Indispensability Arguments in the Philosophy of Mathematics
Hartry Field, 1980, Science Without Numbers: A Defence of Nominalism

s: Lakoff and Núñez (2000) argue that mathematics is brought into being by the embodied human mind, built from bodily grounded cognitive schemas and metaphors, which makes it a human product rather than a mind-independent realm.

src.l: Michael B. Buchholz, 2002, Review: George Lakoff & Rafael E. Núñez (2000). Where Mathematics Comes From
George Lakoff, Rafael E. Núñez, 2000, Where Mathematics Comes From: How the Embodied Mind Brings Mathematics into Being

s: Critique: SEP names the epistemological-access objection, inspired by Benacerraf (1973) and sharpened by Field (1989), as probably the most influential objection to platonism: if numbers are abstract and causally inert, it is unexplained how mathematicians' beliefs about them come to be reliable.

src.l: Øystein Linnebo, 2023, Platonism in the Philosophy of Mathematics

s: Critique: the necessity of a mathematical truth (7+3=10 in any world or simulation) does not settle which mathematics a physical world instantiates; that is the applicability problem, an empirical and contested matter. Field argues applied mathematics need only be conservative, not true, so even 'unreasonable effectiveness' does not show mathematics stands above nature.

src.l: Mark Colyvan, 2023, Indispensability Arguments in the Philosophy of Mathematics
Mark Colyvan, 2023, Indispensability Arguments in the Philosophy of Mathematics

s: The Latin Picatrix (in SL's manuscript copy) defines 'magic' broadly as everything hidden from the senses whose manner and causes most people do not grasp.

src.l: Pseudo-Maslama al-Majriti, 1750, Liber Piccatriciae (Latin Picatrix, manuscript copy)
src.q: Generally calling it "magic," we understand it for all things hidden from the sense, and which the greater part do not apprehend, how they are made or by what causes they happen.

s: Picatrix describes its science as working 'from spirit to spirit' and the making of images (talismans) as putting spirit into body.

src.l: Pseudo-Maslama al-Majriti, 1750, Liber Piccatriciae (Latin Picatrix, manuscript copy)
src.q: its works are from Spirit to Spirit ... the composition of images is spirit in body

s: The Latin Picatrix's prologue lays out four books: celestial images, the figures of the heavens and the eighth sphere, planetary properties with speaking to planetary spirits (called nigromantia), and the properties of spirits aided by images and suffumigations.

src.l: Pseudo-Maslama al-Majriti, 1750, Liber Piccatriciae (Latin Picatrix, manuscript copy)
src.q: how one can speak with the spirits of the planets ... in the fourth, indeed, [it treats] of the properties of the spirits and of those things which are necessary and to be observed in this art, and how it is aided by images

s: Picatrix opens by grounding its science in God, calling him 'the perfect philosophy, and the science of truth' and true science a goodness proceeding from him.

src.l: Pseudo-Maslama al-Majriti, 1750, Liber Piccatriciae (Latin Picatrix, manuscript copy)
src.q: For He alone is the first, the perfect philosophy, and the science of truth. ... true science is goodness that proceeds from Him

s: SL's Latin Picatrix manuscript headed its third book 'of the Hispanic Picatrix', on planetary properties and how to speak with the spirits of the planets, marking the work's Spanish (Alfonsine) transmission.

src.l: Pseudo-Maslama al-Majriti, 1750, Liber Piccatriciae (Latin Picatrix, manuscript copy)
src.q: Third Book of the Hispanic Picatrix in which is treated the properties of the planets ... Also how one can speak with the spirits of the planets and many other things of magic.

s: Thorndike (1923) judged that Picatrix treats magic as a science and superior branch of learning, with astronomical images and invocations of demons as its two leading features, though it does not define magic at length.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: although magic is not defined at length in Picatrix, it seems justifiable to apply it as a general term covering the contents of the book ... Picatrix regards magic as a science, as a superior branch of learning

s: Thorndike notes that Picatrix's procedures call for vile and obscene ingredients, e.g. a magic mirror suffumigated with seven products of the human body.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: in making a magic mirror a suffumigation is employed of seven products of the human body ... vile and obscene substances are in great demand for purposes of magic throughout the book

s: The pseudo-Albertine Liber aggregationis opens by arguing that magical science is not bad in itself, since knowing it lets one avoid evil and pursue good; only its use can be bad.

src.l: Pseudo-Albertus Magnus, 1506, Liber aggregationis, seu Liber secretorum de virtutibus herbarum, lapidum et animalium
src.q: The first is that magical science is not bad, for by its knowledge, evil can be avoided and good pursued.

s: The Liber aggregationis gives herb recipes with occult effects, e.g. celandine carried with a mole's heart to defeat enemies and win lawsuits.

src.l: Pseudo-Albertus Magnus, 1506, Liber aggregationis, seu Liber secretorum de virtutibus herbarum, lapidum et animalium
src.q: If anyone has this herb with the heart of a mole, he will defeat all enemies and remove all causes and all lawsuits.

s: De mirabilibus mundi (ascribed to Albertus) adopts Avicenna's view that the human soul, carried into great excess of love, hatred or another passion, has a power that changes and binds external things.

src.l: Pseudo-Albertus Magnus, 1596, De secretis mulierum; De virtutibus herbarum, lapidum et animalium; De mirabilibus mundi
src.q: He held that there exists in the human soul a certain power to change things, and that other things are obedient to it when the soul is carried into a great excess of love, or hatred, or any such emotion.

s: The author of De mirabilibus mundi says he long disbelieved that the passionate soul binds things, until he read books of necromancy.

src.l: Pseudo-Albertus Magnus, 1596, De secretis mulierum; De virtutibus herbarum, lapidum et animalium; De mirabilibus mundi
src.q: it binds things and alters them toward the very thing it desires—though for a long time I did not believe it.   But after I read books of necromancy

s: In SL's witness of the Speculum astronomiae, the bibliography of image books names Zael's book of images, books of Hermes on images, and 'Picatrices'.

src.l: Albertus Magnus (attr.), 1280, Speculum astronomiae
src.loc: p. 50, ch. on books of images
src.q: Similarly, those which are the ... and another book which Alexander wrote to Alexander

s: Thorndike summarises the Speculum astronomiae's three kinds of images: the abominable (Toz Graecus, Germath, Belenus, Hermes), the detestable ones with characters and names (rings of Solomon), and purely astronomical images it calls 'the sublimest part of astronomy'.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: Of images the author describes three varieties, the first two of which he severely condemns. The first kind is abominable, including the images of Toz Graecus and Germath of Babylon

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: The third variety of images, in which the author sees no harm but much good, and which he has called "the sublimest part of astronomy,"

s: The Speculum astronomiae (per Thorndike) rejects images inscribed with characters and exorcised names, such as the rings of Solomon, because names in unknown tongues may hide something contrary to the faith.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: In it certain names are exorcized by the inscription of characters. Such are the four rings of Solomon ... for it is open to the suspicion that beneath the names in unknown tongues may lie hidden something contrary to the purity of the Catholic Faith.

s: Thorndike defended Albertus Magnus's authorship of the Speculum astronomiae against Mandonnet's attribution to Roger Bacon, which he said rested on very little evidence.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: so little in the way of real evidence for a Baconian authorship that it might be passed by

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: It has already been demonstrated that Mandonnet was grossly in error in representing Albert as an unqualified opponent of judicial astrology

s: The Sworn Book of Honorius opens with a frame story in which pope and cardinals, stirred by demons, declare that salvation is being turned to damnation through magic and nigromancy.

src.l: Honorius of Thebes (attr.), 2022, Liber Iuratus Honorii (Sworn Book of Honorius), Latin text with English translation
src.q: they caused the Pope and cardinals to gather together ... The salvation which the Lord has given to his people, has now been turned to their damnation, through magic and nigromancy.

s: The Sworn Book claims that a council of 89 masters from Naples, Athens and Toledo chose Honorius of Thebes to condense seven volumes of magic into one book, called sacred or sworn because it contains the hundred sacred names of God.

src.l: Honorius of Thebes (attr.), 2022, Liber Iuratus Honorii (Sworn Book of Honorius), Latin text with English translation
src.q: out of 89 masters gathered from Naples, Athens, and Toledo, we selected one named Honorius, son of Euclid, master of Thebes ... so-called because the hundred sacred names of God are included in this book

s: The oath of the Sworn Book restricts transmission: at most three copies, never to a woman, and only to a mature, honest and faithful man after a year's testing.

src.l: Honorius of Thebes (attr.), 2022, Liber Iuratus Honorii (Sworn Book of Honorius), Latin text with English translation
src.q: that it shall be copied by no more than three; and that it shall be given to no woman, nor to any man unless he be of mature age, very honest, and faithful

s: The modern editor of the Sworn Book identifies its centerpiece as a ritual to attain the beatific vision, with later rituals using prayers, conjurations, seals, swords, circles and names of God, angels and demons.

src.l: Honorius of Thebes (attr.), 2022, Liber Iuratus Honorii (Sworn Book of Honorius), Latin text with English translation
src.q: The centerpiece of the text is the ritual to attain nothing less than the beatific vision.

s: Thorndike judged the Sworn Book's proemium (the council of magicians against pope and prelates) 'probably more impressive than true', i.e. a legend rather than history.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: After this proemium, which, like the magic art itself, is probably more impressive than true

s: Roger Bacon's letter on the secret works of art and nature holds that the charms and written characters of his day are false and doubtful, and that apparently occult effects like the magnet's pull are natural.

src.l: Roger Bacon, 1557, De l'admirable pouvoir et puissance de l'art et de nature (French tr. of Epistola de secretis operibus)
src.loc: p. 8 [scan 9], ch. on charms and characters
src.q: I recognize that, without a doubt, all similar things of this time are false and doubtful.

s: Bacon argues that evil spirits invoked with sacrifices help only as far as God permits for men's sins, and that it is far easier to obtain what is useful from God or good spirits.

src.l: Roger Bacon, 1557, De l'admirable pouvoir et puissance de l'art et de nature (French tr. of Epistola de secretis operibus)
src.q: Considering that it would be incomparably easier to obtain from GOD, or from good spirits, that which man ought to deem useful and profitable.

s: Bacon claims art can make ships without rowers and chariots moving without animals, so that all magical power is inferior to the works of art and nature.

src.l: Roger Bacon, 1629, De l'admirable pouvoir et puissance de l'art et de nature (French tr. of Epistola de secretis operibus)
src.q: we can say and conclude that all magical power is inferior to these operations and unworthy of them. First, by the

src.l: Roger Bacon, 1629, De l'admirable pouvoir et puissance de l'art et de nature (French tr. of Epistola de secretis operibus)
src.q: Chariots can also be made that move with incredible force without any beast or animal pulling them

s: Claudius Coelestinus's treatise on marvels in nature (French 1557) admits it follows Nicole Oresme almost word for word, while disagreeing with Oresme on celestial influences.

src.l: Claudius Coelestinus, 1557, Des choses merveilleuses en nature
src.q: although in the previous chapters I have followed—almost word for word—Nicolas Oresme,

src.l: Claudius Coelestinus, 1557, Des choses merveilleuses en nature
src.q: I do not agree with him so exactly in this matter of influences

s: Following Oresme, Coelestinus explains apparitions naturally: a mourner's strong fantasy of a dead father makes him take a staff or shadow for the father.

src.l: Claudius Coelestinus, 1557, Des choses merveilleuses en nature
src.q: from a staff or a seen shadow, he will judge it to be his father, because of the intense fantasy

s: Coelestinus's De his quae mundo mirabiliter eveniunt (1542) holds that the existence of demons cannot be proven by natural reason but must be believed by faith alone.

src.l: Claudius Coelestinus, 1542, De his quae mundo mirabiliter eveniunt (with Roger Bacon, De mirabili potestate artis et naturae; ed. Oronce Finé)
src.q: whether demons exist cannot be proven by any natural reason, but must be believed by faith alone

s: In De malo q.16 Aquinas holds that demons cannot formally transmute lower bodies except by applying bodily agents proportioned to the effect, as a man heats with fire.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1475, De malo
src.q: Whence they cannot formally transmute lower bodies unless by applying some bodily and continuous things proportioned to the effects.

s: Aquinas holds that while demons cannot imprint bodily forms on matter, they can alter the senses and imagination.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1475, De malo
src.q: since demons cannot imprint corporeal forms into matter, as was shown above, it is true that they can change the sense or imagination toward knowing.

s: The Canon Episcopi (as quoted by Lea) treats women who believe they ride at night with Diana on beasts over great distances as deceived by demonic illusions, and says whoever believes such things has lost the faith.

src.l: Henry Charles Lea, 1888, A History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages, Vol. I
src.q: Some wicked women, reverting to Satan, and seduced by the illusions and phantasms of demons, believe and profess that they ride at night with Diana on certain beasts, with an innumerable multitude of women, passing over immense distances

src.l: Henry Charles Lea, 1888, A History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages, Vol. I
src.q: he who believes such things has lost his faith

s: Lea traces the Canon Episcopi through the collections of Regino, Burchard, Ivo and Gratian, notes Gratian gave it unquestioned authority, and that Burchard added Herodias to Diana.

src.l: Henry Charles Lea, 1888, A History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages, Vol. I
src.q: it was adopted by the canonists and embodied in the successive collections of Regino, Burchard, Ivo, and Gratian—the latter giving it the stamp of unquestioned authority

src.l: Henry Charles Lea, 1888, A History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages, Vol. I
src.q: Bishop Burchard, in the eleventh century, when copying the text, came to add to Diana Herodias

s: The Canon Episcopi's ascription to a Council of Ancyra is spurious: Lea notes the council could never be identified, and dates the text's first appearance to a fragment no later than the ninth century.

src.l: Henry Charles Lea, 1888, A History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages, Vol. I
src.q: In some way this utterance came to be attributed to a Council of Anquira, which could never be identified

src.l: Henry Charles Lea, 1888, A History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages, Vol. I
src.q: in a fragment, not later than the ninth century, in which it is treated as a diabolical illusion

s: A c. 1445 treatise excerpted by Hansen, citing the Canon Episcopi, rules that the women's night ride with Diana cannot happen really and bodily but only in spirit through diabolical illusion, since no such goddess exists.

src.l: Joseph Hansen, 1901, Quellen und Untersuchungen zur Geschichte des Hexenwahns und der Hexenverfolgung im Mittelalter
src.q: It cannot really and bodily happen, but only in the spirit through diabolical illusion.

src.l: Joseph Hansen, 1901, Quellen und Untersuchungen zur Geschichte des Hexenwahns und der Hexenverfolgung im Mittelalter
src.q: First, they say they ride with Diana, the goddess of the pagans. This is false because no such goddess exists in this world or the other

s: A c. 1412–1415 text in Hansen cites William of Auvergne as denying that the 'horse' on which evil spirits carry someone swiftly is a real horse.

src.l: Joseph Hansen, 1901, Quellen und Untersuchungen zur Geschichte des Hexenwahns und der Hexenverfolgung im Mittelalter
