src.q: When evil spirits transport something quickly, as if on a horse, should that be considered a real horse? William of Auvergne says no.

s: Thorndike reports that William of Auvergne discussed demons tossing sticks and stones, throwing people from bed and carrying men or rocks great distances, and also wonders done by those who know the occult virtues of things.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: William also discusses how demons can toss sticks and stones about, throw persons out of bed, and transport men or huge rocks for great distances

s: Thorndike reports that Arnald of Villanova made Pope Boniface VIII an astrological seal in the form of a lion for his stone, and wrote a treatise on seals with engraving directions.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: Pope Boniface VIII set great store by a seal in the form of a lion which Arnald had prepared for him when he was suffering from the stone

s: The 15th-century Munich Necromantic Handbook commands spirits by lists of strange names and by a ring to leave their places at once.

src.l: Anonymous, 1450, Munich Necromantic Handbook (Liber incantationum, exorcismorum et fascinationum, Clm 849)
src.q: namely, Ratori, Lampoy, Deman, Brulo

src.l: Anonymous, 1450, Munich Necromantic Handbook (Liber incantationum, exorcismorum et fascinationum, Clm 849)
src.q: I command that wherever you may be, you shall depart from your places without delay.

s: A Munich Handbook operation prescribes a polished sword and a hoopoe, circles traced with the sword in a remote place on Sunday at noon, and sixteen names written with its edge.

src.l: Anonymous, 1450, Munich Necromantic Handbook (Liber incantationum, exorcismorum et fascinationum, Clm 849)
src.q: you must carry a very bright, polished sword and a hoopoe bird ... With the said sword, you must make circles in a remote place.

s: A Munich Handbook experiment narrates in the first person a spirit appearing as a noble soldier visible only to the operator and promising to produce a legion of spirits, as was once shown to an emperor.

src.l: Anonymous, 1450, Munich Necromantic Handbook (Liber incantationum, exorcismorum et fascinationum, Clm 849)
src.q: there came to me a certain noble soldier whom no one besides me seemed to recognize

src.l: Anonymous, 1450, Munich Necromantic Handbook (Liber incantationum, exorcismorum et fascinationum, Clm 849)
src.q: I wish that as quickly as possible you cause to appear that great legion of spirits

s: An excerpt in Hansen from around 1458 reports women of the 'sect' confessing, as midwives, to strangling unbaptised infants at the demon's prompting: the midwife-witch figure already present before the Malleus.

src.l: Joseph Hansen, 1901, Quellen und Untersuchungen zur Geschichte des Hexenwahns und der Hexenverfolgung im Mittelalter
src.q: since they were midwives, they had strangled many infants without baptism by the induction and obedience of the demon

s: Mesmer's first two propositions posit a mutual influence between celestial bodies, the earth and living bodies, carried by a universally distributed, vacuum-free fluid.

src.l: Franz Anton Mesmer, 1779, Mémoire sur la découverte du magnétisme animal
src.q: 1st. There exists a mutual influence between the Celestial Bodies, the Earth, and Animated Bodies
src.qo: tuelle entre les Corps Céleſtes, la Terre & les Corps Animés.

s: Mesmer's third proposition holds that this reciprocal action obeys mechanical laws hitherto unknown, framing the influence as physics rather than spirit.

src.l: Franz Anton Mesmer, 1779, Mémoire sur la découverte du magnétisme animal
src.q: 3rd. This reciprocal action is subject to mechanical laws, which have remained unknown until the present time.
src.qo: 3°. Cette action réciproque eſt ſoumiſe à des lois mécaniques, inconnues juſqu'à préſent.

s: Mesmer describes the fluid's action as an alternating 'ebb and flow' (flux et reflux), which he calls the most universal operation of Nature linking the heavens, the earth and its parts.

src.l: Franz Anton Mesmer, 1779, Mémoire sur la découverte du magnétisme animal
src.q: It is through this operation—the most universal of all those offered to us by Nature—that the active relationships are exercised between the celestial bodies, the earth, and its constituent parts.
src.qo: (la plus universelle de celles que la Nature nous offre) que les relations d'activité, s'exercent entre les corps célestes, la terre & ses parties constitutives.

s: A later section bound in the SL Mémoire volume likens staged convulsive cures to the convulsionaries of St. Médard and the Loudun possessions as 'the basis of all impostures', and footnotes that Gassner's claimed cures were mainly of this kind (epilepsy, catalepsy, convulsions, paralysis).

src.l: Franz Anton Mesmer, 1779, Mémoire sur la découverte du magnétisme animal
src.q: Were the convulsions of St. Médard, the possessions of Loudun, not of this genre?
src.qo: Les convulfions de St. Médard, les poffeffions de Lou- dun n'étoient-elles pas de ce genre ?

s: Bergasse argues that universal magnetism produces sensation only in a sick organised body, so only the sick can serve as experimental proof of its existence.

src.l: Nicolas Bergasse, 1784, Considérations sur le magnétisme animal
src.q: Sick beings are therefore the only subjects suitable for the experiments that must be conducted to arrive at a perceptible knowledge of both the reality of Universal Magnetism and the reality of
src.qo: Les êtres malades ſont donc les ſeuls ſujets propres aux expériences qu'il faut faire pour parvenir à connoître d'une manière ſenſible , & la réalité du Magnétiſme univerſel , & la réalité du Magnétiſme animal ,

s: Eckartshausen (1791) defines true magic as the highest perfection of natural and creaturely wisdom and the highest science of the relationships of natural things, placing it after a passage on the Christian's transformed heart.

src.l: Karl von Eckartshausen, 1791, Aufschlüsse zur Magie aus geprüften Erfahrungen über verborgene philosophische Wissenschaften
src.q: True magic means as much as the highest perfection of natural and creaturely wisdom, and the highest science of the relationships of natural things.
src.qo: Magie. Die wahre Magie heißt so viel als die höchste Vollkommenheit der natürlichen und geschöpfmäßigen Weisheit, und die höchste Wissenschaft der Verhältnisse natürlicher Dinge.

s: Barrett's Magus (1801) defines natural magic as a comprehensive knowledge of all Nature that searches out her secret and occult operations and the virtues of metals, stones, plants and animals.

src.l: Francis Barrett, 1801, The Magus, or Celestial Intelligencer
src.q: NATURAL MAGIC is, as we have said, a comprehensive knowledge of all Nature, by which we search out her secret and occult operations throughout her vast and spacious elaboratory

s: Reichenbach proposes the name 'Odyle' for a new force he holds distinct from magnetism, electricity and chemical attraction, while leaving 'magnetism' to the iron-attracting force.

src.l: Karl von Reichenbach, 1850, Researches on Magnetism, Electricity, Heat, Light, Crystallization, and Chemical Attraction, in their relations to the Vital Force
src.q: I shall here venture to suggest, for the force here treated of, the short name of ODYLE.

s: Esdaile reports eight months of mesmeric practice in Bengal and claims painless surgical operations are 'the natural birthright' of the Natives of Bengal.

src.l: James Esdaile, 1851, Mesmerism in India
src.q: My experience has demonstrated the singular and beneficial influence exerted by Mesmerism over the constitution of the Natives of Bengal, and that painless surgical operations, with other advantages, are their natural birthright

s: Braid (1852) describes attending a paid public séance of the clairvoyant Mlle Prudence Bernard staged by M. Lassaigne in Manchester, and submitting his account to three gentlemen who tested her that evening.

src.l: James Braid, 1852, Magic, Witchcraft, Animal Magnetism, Hypnotism and Electro-Biology
src.q: I submitted a proof of the above narrative to the inspection of three of the most intelligent gentlemen who engaged in testing Mdlle. Prudence Bernard, that evening

s: Lévi defines magic as the traditional science of the secrets of nature, inherited from the magi, which invests the adept with 'a sort of relative omnipotence'.

src.l: Éliphas Lévi, 1861, Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
src.q: Magic is the traditional science of the secrets of nature, which comes to us from the
src.qo: La magie est la science traditionnelle des secrets de la nature,

s: Lévi sets the magician against the sorcerer: the magician is nature's sovereign pontiff, the sorcerer its profaner, as the truly religious man stands to the superstitious and the fanatic.

src.l: Éliphas Lévi, 1861, Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
src.q: The magician is the sovereign pontiff of nature; the sorcerer is only its profaner.
src.qo: Le magicien est le souverain pontife de la nature, le sorcier n'en est que le profanateur.

s: Lévi makes imagination the working instrument of magic, citing Paracelsus on believing oneself invulnerable and calling imagination 'the instrument for the adaptation of the verbe'.

src.l: Éliphas Lévi, 1861, Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
src.q: Fear attracts bullets, and courage makes cannonballs turn back.
src.qo: La peur attire les balles, et le courage fait rebrousser chemin aux boulets.

s: Lévi claims Paracelsus, healing at a distance by working on blood and cut hair, had far outpaced the experiments of the most famous magnetisers of Lévi's day.

src.l: Éliphas Lévi, 1861, Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
src.q: he cured headaches from a distance by operating on cut hair
src.qo: il guérissait les maux de tête à distance en opérant sur des cheveux coupés;

s: Lévi identifies a single 'great magical agent', the astral light (also soul of the earth, Azoth, Magnesia), as the key to all real magic.

src.l: Éliphas Lévi, 1861, Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
src.q: To know how to seize this agent is to be the depositary of the very power of God; all real, effective magic, all true occult power is there
src.qo: Savoir s'emparer de cet agent, c'est être dépositaire de la puissance même de Dieu; toute la magie réelle, effective, toute la vraie puissance occulte est là,

s: Lévi reduces operative magic to two operations on the astral light: to concentrate and to project, to fix and to move.

src.l: Éliphas Lévi, 1861, Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
src.q: To seize the great magical agent two operations are necessary: to concentrate and to project; in other words, to fix and to move.
src.qo: Le grand agent magique que nous avons appelé lumière astrale, que d'autres nomment âme de la terre, que les anciens chimistes désignaient sous les noms d'Azoth et de Magnésie, cette force occulte, unique et incontestable, est la clef de tous les empires, le secret de toutes les puissances; c'est le dragon volant de Médée, le serpent du mystère Édenique; c'est le miroir universel des visions, le nœud des sympathies, la source des amours, de la prophétie et de la gloire. Savoir s'emparer de cet agent, c'est être dépositaire de la puissance même de Dieu; toute la magie réelle, effective, toute la vraie puissance occulte est là, et tous les livres de la vraie science n'ont d'autre but que de le démontrer. Pour s'emparer du grand agent magique deux opérations sont nécessaires: concentrer et projeter; en d'autres termes, fixer et mouvoir.

s: Lévi calls magnetism between two people a marvellous discovery but holds that self-magnetisation, rendering oneself lucid at will, is the perfection of the magical art.

src.l: Éliphas Lévi, 1861, Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
src.q: Magnetism between two people is undoubtedly a marvelous discovery; but the magnetism of one person rendering themselves lucid at will and directing themselves is the perfection of the magical art
src.qo: Le magnétisme à deux est sans doute une merveilleuse découverte ; mais le magnétisme d'un seul se rendant lucide à volonté et se dirigeant lui-même, c'est la perfection de l'art magique ;

s: Lévi holds that forms and words preserved in the 'book of vital light' are perceived when the astral light acts on the translucent and, through the nervous system, on sight.

src.l: Éliphas Lévi, 1861, Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
src.q: can only be perceived by the applications of the astral light to the translucent, which communicates its impressions to the nervous system

s: Lévi reports preparing twenty-one days, following the thirteenth chapter of his Ritual, for a complete evocation of Apollonius of Tyana at a lady's house, held on July 24.

src.l: Éliphas Lévi, 1861, Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
src.q: she determined me to attempt at her home the experience of a complete evocation, for which I prepared myself for twenty-one days by scrupulously observing the practices indicated in the thirteenth chapter of the Ritual.
src.qo: à laquelle je me préparai pendant vingt et un jours, en observant scrupuleusement les pratiques indiquées au treizième chapitre du Rituel.

s: For the evocation Lévi's altar bore the pentagram engraved and gilded in white marble and traced again on a new white lambskin beneath it.

src.l: Éliphas Lévi, 1861, Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
src.q: On the white marble was engraved and gilded the sign of the pentagram, just as it is represented on page 105 of this work
src.qo: Sur le marbre blanc était gravé et doré le signe du pentagramme, tel qu'il est représenté à la page 105 de cet ouvrage;

s: Lévi says the figure that appeared was shrouded, thin, sad and beardless, and did not match his own prior idea of Apollonius; he then commanded it through the pentagram and the sword.

src.l: Éliphas Lévi, 1861, Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
src.q: His face was thin, sad, and beardless, which did not precisely match the idea I had first formed of Apollonius.
src.qo: sa figure était maigre, triste et sans barbe, ce qui ne se rapportait pas précisément à l'idée que je me faisais d'abord d'Apollonius.

s: Lévi explains medieval sorcerers' spells naturalistically: powders claimed to come from the sabbath were sold 'to ignorance and hatred', and terror and a struck imagination killed the victim.

src.l: Éliphas Lévi, 1861, Dogme et rituel de la haute magie
src.q: It was such powders that the sorcerers of the Middle Ages claimed to receive at the sabbath, and which they sold at a high price to ignorance and hatred.
src.qo: C'étaient de semblables poudres que les sorciers du moyen âge prétendaient recevoir au sabbat, et qu'ils vendaient à grand prix à l'ignorance et à la haine :

s: Papus defines magic as the application of dynamised human will to the rapid evolution of the living forces of nature.

src.l: Papus (Gérard Encausse), 1893, Traité élémentaire de magie pratique
src.q: Magic is: the APPLICATION OF DYNAMIZED HUMAN WILL TO THE RAPID EVOLUTION OF THE LIVING FORCES OF NATURE.
src.qo: La magie est : l'APPLICATION DE LA VOLONTÉ HUMAINE DYNAMISÉE A L'ÉVOLUTION RAPIDE DES FORCES VIVANTES DE LA NATURE.

s: Papus tells the student that the visible world matters only as a translation, into a crude language, of laws and ideas the brain must extract from sensation.

src.l: Papus (Gérard Encausse), 1893, Traité élémentaire de magie pratique
src.q: all of this is only interesting as translations into a crude language of laws and ideas
src.qo: Or, si vous voulez étudier la magie, commencez par bien comprendre que tout ce qui vous frappe autour de vous, toutes ces choses qui agissent sur vos sens physiques, le monde visible enfin, tout cela n'est intéressant que comme des traductions en un langage grossier de lois et d'idées qui se dégageront de la sensation quand cette sensation aura été non-seulement filtrée par les organes des sens, mais encore digérée par votre cerveau.

s: Papus (1902) says elementaries obey a necromancer only through devotion or fear and always remain free to resist, unlike elementals, which circulate in the astral fluids.

src.l: Papus (Gérard Encausse), 1902, L'Occultisme et le Spiritualisme
src.q: the elementary obeys only through devotion or fear, but always remains free to resist the will of the Necromancer.

s: Blavatsky's summary of the principles of magic defines magic as a science (knowledge of how the spirit's omniscience and control over nature may be acquired in the body) and as an art (its application).

src.l: H. P. Blavatsky, 1911, Isis Unveiled, Vol. I: Science
src.q: Magic, as a science, is the knowledge of these principles, and of the way by which the omniscience and omnipotence of the spirit and its control over nature's forces may be acquired by the individual while still in the body.

s: Blavatsky distinguishes sorcery from true magic by use alone: arcane knowledge misapplied is sorcery, beneficently used it is true magic or wisdom.

src.l: H. P. Blavatsky, 1911, Isis Unveiled, Vol. I: Science
src.q: 5th. Arcane knowledge misapplied, is sorcery; beneficently used, true magic or WISDOM.

s: Blavatsky makes mediumship the opposite of adeptship: the medium is a passive instrument of foreign influences, the adept actively controls himself and inferior potencies.

src.l: H. P. Blavatsky, 1911, Isis Unveiled, Vol. I: Science
src.q: 6th. Mediumship is the opposite of adeptship; the medium is the passive instrument of foreign influences, the adept actively controls himself and all inferior potencies.

s: Blavatsky's eighth principle asserts that races of men differ in spiritual gifts as in colour or stature, some inclined to seership, others to mediumship or sorcery.

src.l: H. P. Blavatsky, 1911, Isis Unveiled, Vol. I: Science
src.q: 8th. Races of men differ in spiritual gifts as in color, stature, or any other external quality

s: Blavatsky says magical, i.e. spiritual, powers exist in every man, but only those called to teach and willing to pay the price of discipline should practise them.

src.l: H. P. Blavatsky, 1911, Isis Unveiled, Vol. I: Science
src.q: We would have all to realize that magical, i. e., spiritual powers exist in every man

s: Blavatsky rejects bodily aerial flight of mediums because it would be miracle, 'and miracle we repudiate', while allowing levitation under magnetic conditions.

src.l: H. P. Blavatsky, 1911, Isis Unveiled, Vol. I: Science
src.q: Hence we discredit all stories of the aërial flight of mediums in body, for such would be miracle, and miracle we repudiate.

s: In the Key to Theosophy, an Occultist who is not a real Theosophist is 'simply a black magician, whether conscious or unconscious'.

src.l: Helena Blavatsky, 1889, The Key to Theosophy
src.q: But no one can be a true Occultist without being a real Theosophist; otherwise he is simply a black magician, whether conscious or unconscious.

s: The Theosophical Glossary explains the gods commanded by ancient priests' magic as the occult powers of Nature personified by the learned priests themselves.

src.l: H. P. Blavatsky, 1906, The Theosophical Glossary
src.q: which gods, are in truth, but the occult powers or potencies of Nature, personified by the learned priests themselves

s: Frazer (1890) suggests that sympathetic magic is one of the earliest means by which man tries to adapt nature to his needs, older than worship of game animals.

src.l: James George Frazer, 1890, The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion
src.q: sympathetic magic is one of the earliest means by which man endeavours to adapt the agencies of nature to his needs.

s: Podmore notes that trickery was seldom detected in early American spiritualism, and argues that in darkened séances without apparatus fraud is extremely hard to prove even when the investigator is certain of it.

src.l: Frank Podmore, 1902, Modern Spiritualism: A History and a Criticism, Vol. I
src.q: Where no apparatus is used, and the performance is shrouded in darkness, it is extremely difficult to prove trickery, however certain the investigator may be

s: Podmore records that the Fox sisters reportedly took no money at first, until the 'spirits' insisted, and that money was less prominent at early séances than later.

src.l: Frank Podmore, 1902, Modern Spiritualism: A History and a Criticism, Vol. I
src.q: The Fox girls are said to have taken no money for their performances at first, until indeed the "spirits" insisted on their doing so

s: Waite directs the reader to the Key of Solomon for grimoire ceremonial and to the Lesser Key (Lemegeton) for the names and offices of the demons.

src.l: Arthur Edward Waite, 1913, The Book of Ceremonial Magic
src.q: IN all matters of ceremonial the inspiration of the Grimoires must be sought in the Key of Solomon proper, but for the names and offices of the demons it must be sought in the Lesser Key.

s: Spence's Encyclopaedia (1920) says the early church came to regard magic as foreign to its religion and cites the thirty-sixth canon of the Council of Laodicea (364) as an instance.

src.l: Lewis Spence, 1920, An Encyclopaedia of Occultism
src.q: the church soon began to regard the practice of magic as foreign to the spirit of its religion. Thus the Thirty-sixth Canon of the Œcumenical Council held at Laodicea in 364 A.D.

s: Against the revival's acceptance of mediumship as real contact with foreign influences, Podmore found evidence for any supernormal faculty, from persons of presumed good faith, 'almost entirely wanting' in early American spiritualism.

src.l: Frank Podmore, 1902, Modern Spiritualism: A History and a Criticism, Vol. I
src.q: evidence, such as we can regard as primâ facie worthy of consideration, for the exercise, by persons whose good faith may fairly be presumed, of any supernormal faculty, is almost entirely wanting

s: In Natural Magick (English 1658) Porta reports earlier definitions of magic (the perfection of natural sciences; the practical part of natural philosophy; the Platonists' subjection of inferior to superior things) and then gives his own: magic is 'nothing else but the survey of the whole course of Nature'.

src.l: Giambattista della Porta, 1658, Natural Magick (English translation of Magiae naturalis libri XX)
src.q: Others have named it the practical part of natural Philosophy, which produceth her effects by the mutual and fit application of one natural thing unto another. ... But I think that Magick is nothing else but the survey of the whole course of Nature.

s: Porta makes magic the 'handmaid' of Nature: its works are nature's works, and where natural affinity is too weak, the art supplies the defect by timing and proportion, as husbandry prepares for what nature brings forth.

src.l: Giambattista della Porta, 1658, Natural Magick (English translation of Magiae naturalis libri XX)
src.q: the works of Magick are nothing else but the works of Nature, whose dutiful hand-maid Magick is. ... as in Husbandry, it is Nature that brings forth corn and herbs, but it is Art that prepares and makes way for them.

s: Porta says magic, by joining or sundering things according to their agreement and disagreement, does 'strange works, such as the vulgar sort call miracles': the wonder is in the onlooker's ignorance, not in any supernatural cause.

src.l: Giambattista della Porta, 1658, Natural Magick (English translation of Magiae naturalis libri XX)
src.q: it teacheth us by the agreement and the disagreement of things, either so to sunder them, or else to lay them so together by the mutual and fit applying of one thing to another, as thereby we do strange works, such as the vulgar sort call miracles

s: Porta locates the flourishing of magic outside Europe, in Ethiopia and India, and explains it materially: those lands had 'great store of herbs and stones'; he also cites the Persian rule that no man might be king without learning magic.

src.l: Giambattista della Porta, 1658, Natural Magick (English translation of Magiae naturalis libri XX)
src.q: That amongst the Persians no man might be a King, unless he had first learned the Art of Magick ... For this cause, Magick was wont to flourish in Æthiopia and India, where was great store of herbs and stones

s: Porta shuts the superstitious and wicked out of natural magic and says they deserve to be driven out of cities and 'grievously punished, and utterly destroyed'.

src.l: Giambattista della Porta, 1658, Natural Magick (English translation of Magiae naturalis libri XX)
src.q: Superstitious, profane, and wicked men have nothing to do with this Science; her gate is shut against them ... to be grievously punished, and utterly destroyed.

s: In Book I ch. 3 Porta states that magic is a practical part of natural philosophy, and so requires the magician to be 'an exact and a very perfect Philosopher'.

src.l: Giambattista della Porta, 1658, Natural Magick (English translation of Magiae naturalis libri XX)
src.q: Seeing Magick, as we shewed before, is a practical part of Natural Philosophy, therefore it behoveth a Magician, and one that aspires to the dignity of that profession, to be an exact and a very perfect Philosopher.

s: Porta's Book I ch. 7 grounds the finding of the 'vertues of things' in sympathy and antipathy, which he glosses in English as things' 'consent' and 'disagreement' arising from hidden properties.

src.l: Giambattista della Porta, 1658, Natural Magick (English translation of Magiae naturalis libri XX)
src.q: BY reason of the hidden and secret properties of things, there is in all kinds of creatures a certain compassion, as I may call it, which the Greeks call Sympathy and Antipathy; but we term it more familiarly, their consent, and their disagreement.

s: The SL volume catalogued until 2026-10-26 as 'Theatrum sympatheticum' (Digby; Kircher) is in fact Porta's Magiae naturalis libri viginti (Leiden: de Vogel, 1644) throughout, so its ch. VII on sympathy and antipathy is Porta's own Natural Magick I.7; SL's English there rendered 'quam Graeci' as 'which we Greeks call' until its 2026-10-26 correction.

src.l: Giambattista della Porta, 1644, Magiae naturalis libri viginti (SL record until 2026-10-26: 'Theatrum sympateticum', Digby; Kircher)
src.q: Concerning sympathy and antipathy, and how through them the virtues of things can be discovered and tested. ... which the Greeks call sympatheia sympathy and antipatheia antipathy, and we more commonly call agreement and disagreement

s: Goclenius frames the weapon-salve question as whether healing a wounded person miles away, by anointing only the weapon, lies in nature or is 'the work of impostors or even witchcraft'.

src.l: Rudolph Goclenius, 1613, De magnetica vulnerum curatione
src.q: [a person] wounded several miles away while absent is restored to health, by having the weapon or in- strument with which the wound was inflicted merely anointed ... whether the cause of this lies in nature, or whether it is truly the work of impostors or even witchcraft?
src.qo: plura miliaria vulneratus absens sanitati restituitur, telo seu in- strumento, quo vulnus inflictum est, eo tantum delibuto, causam habeat in natura, an vero impo- storum sit, vel veneficum?

s: Goclenius argues that only someone who 'measures everything by the senses' would call the weapon-salve superstitious: the cure is by 'pure nature and a certain magnetic efficiency', celestial influence and a conveying spirit.

src.l: Rudolph Goclenius, 1613, De magnetica vulnerum curatione
src.q: who would call the healing performed by the weapon-salve ... not natural, but superstitious and imposture? Certainly no one, unless he is ignorant of all these things and measures everything by the senses. ... For that healing occurs through pure nature and a certain magnetic efficiency, attraction, and derivation
src.qo: Unguento Armario. permiscens , sicque omnibus in- ter se concinentibus , ut gravissi- mis Tullii verbis utar , necessario omnia uno divino & continuato spiritu contineri , Modus quo vulnus curatur sine remediis.hæc inquam cum ita sese verè habeant , quis sa- nationem , factam per unguentum armarium , quo vulnus etiam non applicatis remediis curatur , in- strumento tantum eo unguento delibuto , non naturalem , sed su- perstitiosam dicet & impostori- am ? Nemo sane , nisi harum rerum omnium ignarus , quique sensi- bus omnia metitur . Fit enim illa sanatio per meram natu- ram atque magneticam quan- dam efficientiam , attractio- nem & deductionem ,

s: Goclenius builds his account of sympathy on iron and the magnet, whose natures agree though their bodies are apart, and cites Porta's term 'consensus' for it.

src.l: Rudolph Goclenius, 1613, De magnetica vulnerum curatione
src.q: For although the bodies of iron and the magnet are separated, their nature is so continued in them that they even agree in one. ... Baptista Porta called it consensus

s: Libavius's 1594 Jena disputation sorts the possible causes of a weapon-salve cure into minds (God or demons) or natural motions (heaven, elements), with the medicine acting by appetite 'or by magical attraction'.

src.l: Andreas Libavius, 1594, Tractatus duo physici: prior de impostoria vulnerum per unguentum armarium sanatione
src.q: It would be either from minds, God, or demons: or from natural motions, the influences of heaven, and what are called elements. Everything would flow toward medicine either by its own appetite, or by magical attraction.

s: Libavius calls it impious to imitate by 'magical attraction' the likeness of divine action in the Church, since God provides such help out of love, 'not through medicines'.

src.l: Andreas Libavius, 1594, Tractatus duo physici: prior de impostoria vulnerum per unguentum armarium sanatione
src.q: It is impious to imitate by magical attraction the likeness of the action of divine wisdom in the Church. ... This He provides spontaneously out of love for humanity, not through medicines

s: The parson William Foster (1631) attacks the sympathy explanation: any substitute weapon, even a sallow stick, is said to work, so 'there's no sympathy betwixt the Wound and the Weapon'.

src.l: William Foster, 1631, Hoplocrisma-spongus: or, a sponge to wipe away the weapon-salve
src.q: This reason is no reason. ... For there's no sympathy betwixt the Wound and the Weapon, as hath already been declared. ... Where then is the sympathy betwixt the Weapon and the hurt, when another Weapon will doe the feat, which never caused the hurt?

s: Foster's dedication presents the Church of England as detesting 'superstitious and magicall Cures' and names the Jesuit Johannes Roberti as a prior opponent of 'this strange and magicall Cure'.

src.l: William Foster, 1631, Hoplocrisma-spongus: or, a sponge to wipe away the weapon-salve
src.q: Church of England detest superstitious and magicall Cures.

s: Fludd's reply to Foster (1638) states Foster's question as whether weapon-salve healing is 'a form of sorcery and therefore illicit', and Fludd denies it.

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1638, Responsum ad Hoplocrisma-spongum M. Fosteri presbiteri
src.q: Is the healing of wounds performed by the Weapon Salve a form of sorcery and therefore illicit? Mr. Foster confidently asserts that it is; as for me, I must just as seriously deny it.

s: In Mosaicall Philosophy Fludd's proposition is that blood and spirits carried from the wound on the weapon animate a balsamic ointment, which then becomes 'magneticall' and unites with the spirits streaming from the wound at any distance.

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1659, Mosaicall philosophy
src.q: the oyntment so animated by those ſpirits will become forthwith magneticall

s: Digby narrates curing James Howell's wound by dissolving powder of vitriol in a basin of water and putting into it the garter bloodied by the wound, while Howell stood unaware across the room.

src.l: Kenelm Digby, 1664, A Late Discourse ... Touching the Cure of Wounds by the Powder of Sympathy
src.q: I took an handful of powder of <term>Vitriol</term>, which I had in my Study, and presently dissolved it. ... As soon as the bloudy Garter was brought me, I put it within the Bason

s: Digby says King James, after the cure, joked with him about 'a Magician and a Sorcerer' before asking how it was done.

src.l: Kenelm Digby, 1664, A Late Discourse ... Touching the Cure of Wounds by the Powder of Sympathy
src.q: having drolled with me firſt , (which he could do with a very good grace) about a Magician and a Sorcerer.

s: The Theatrum sympatheticum gives a weapon-salve recipe ascribed to Paracelsus and Emperor Maximilian: moss from a skull exposed to the air, human fat, mummy and human blood, which heals 'even if he be far away'.

src.l: Giambattista della Porta, 1644, Magiae naturalis libri viginti (SL record until 2026-10-26: 'Theatrum sympateticum', Digby; Kircher)
src.q: formerly given by Paracelsus to Emperor Maximilian and tested by the same ... the sick man will be healed, even if he be far away. Take two ounces of usnea, or moss concreted on a skull left exposed to the air, as much human fat, half an ounce of mummy and human bl

s: In Magnes (1641), under the running head 'Magnetic Natural Magic', Kircher describes magnetic automata whose spectators believed they moved 'not by art, but by the prompting of some evil spirit'.

src.l: Athanasius Kircher, 1641, Magnes sive De arte magnetica
src.q: they seemed to believe these things were done not by art, but by the prompting of some evil spirit

s: Kircher counts the sympathetic 'cryptological compasses', by which two people at any distance might communicate, among the lies added by those who misread the magnet.

src.l: Athanasius Kircher, 1641, Magnes sive De arte magnetica
src.q: they proceeded to add lie upon lie—namely, the cryptological compasses ... by whose help two people at any distance might communicate with each other regarding any business.

s: Kircher's Magneticum naturae regnum (1667) puts 'the whole Nature of things' in strife and friendship, that is attraction and repulsion, and cites al-Ghazali (Algazel) for the 'one key to Nature'.

src.l: Athanasius Kircher, 1667, Magneticum naturae regnum
src.q: That the whole Nature of things is placed in strife and friendship: or which is the same, that all actions of things are carried out by attraction and repulsion. ... There is one key to Nature

s: Poma (2010) argues, through the history of the weapon-salve, that a patient getting better does not prove a medical theory effective, and finds in Libavius a reflection on the imagination's power over the body and natural self-healing.

src.l: Roberto Poma, 2010, L'onguent armaire entre science et folklore médical

s: The heading of Ficino's De vita III presents the book as composed among his commentaries on Plotinus and states its thesis: the souls of the world, of the stars and of demons are easily enticed by suitably accommodated bodily forms.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres
src.loc: De vita III, title and ch. 1, [scan 151]
src.q: On Obtaining Life from the Heavens, composed by the same author among his commentaries on Plotinus. ... the souls of the world, and the souls of the stars and demons, are easily enticed by accommodated forms of bodies.

s: Ficino holds that the world lives and breathes, that its spirit can be drawn in, and that a man draws it through his own spirit, which is by nature conformable to it.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres
src.q: the world entirely lives and breathes, and it is permitted for us to draw its spirit. It is drawn, however, properly by man through his own spirit, which is by its own nature conformable to it.

s: Ficino defines the magus as the philosopher skilled in natural things and the stars who inserts celestial things into terrestrial ones by allurements, as a farmer grafts a shoot onto old stock.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres
src.q: The same is also true of the philosopher skilled in natural things and the stars, whom we are accustomed to call a Magus ... He inserts celestial things into terrestrial ones by certain allurements, and no differently than the agriculture-enthusiast grafts a fresh shoot onto an old stock.

s: In his address to the reader Ficino says he does not so much approve the astronomical images as report them, and lets the reader dismiss them, while insisting on his astrologically timed medicines.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres
src.q: if you do not approve of the astronomical images ... devised otherwise for the health of mortals, which I myself do not so much approve of as I relate

s: Ficino reports that Aquinas, whom he calls 'our leader in theology', attributes less to images than the astrologers do: figures gain from the heavens only as much power as the heaven commonly exerts through herbs and other natural things.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres
src.q: our leader in theology, fears these things more and attributes less to images. For he thinks that they acquire only so much power from the heavens through figures as is conducive to those effects which the heaven is accustomed to commonly effect through herbs and other natural things.

s: Ficino reports Peter of Abano's claim that a region was destroyed by an image which Thabit says the astrologer Phedice fashioned; he omits images for harming people 'by design'.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres
src.q: He describes images for bringing calamity or prosperity to someone, which I omit by design. ... confirmed. Indeed, he even affirmed that a certain region was destroyed by that image which

s: Ficino (De vita III ch. 21) reports that words spoken with sharp affection are thought to have great power over images, directing their effect where the affections and words intend.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres
src.q: certain words pronounced with a sharper affection are thought to have great power regarding images, to properly direct the effect of them toward where the affections and words are intended.

s: Ficino mentions a love image made at a Moon-Venus conjunction, refuses the details ('we are not teaching love charms, but medicines'), and thinks such effects more probably come from Venereal or deceiving daemons.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres
src.q: to reconcile two people with a most ardent love, they fashioned an image when the Moon was in conjunction with Venus in Pisces or Taurus ... For we are not teaching love charms, but medicines. ... It is more probable that such effects are accomplished either through

s: Following Aquinas, Ficino judges that speaking statues, if ever made, spoke by daemons, not by star influx, and that the daemons were not bound in them but followed their worshippers of their own accord to deceive them.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres
src.q: believe that if they ever made statues that spoke, it was not the simple influx of the stars themselves that formed the words there, but daemons. ... rather that they followed their worshipers of their own accord, ultimately to deceive them.

s: In the Oration Pico says his theses on magic present it as twofold: one wholly the work of demons, 'execrable and monstrous'; the other nothing but the absolute perfection of natural philosophy.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1557, Opera omnia
src.q: We have also proposed theorems on Magic, in which we have indicated that magic is twofold. One type consists entirely of the work and authority of demons; this is, by God, an execrable and monstrous thing. The other, when well-examined, is nothing other than the absolute perfection of natural philosophy.

s: Pico, citing Plotinus, calls the magus the servant of nature, not its creator: natural magic does not so much work wonders as diligently serve nature as she works them.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1557, Opera omnia
src.q: Plotinus also mentions it, where he demonstrates that the Magus is the servant of nature and not its creator. ... does not so much perform wonders as it diligently serves nature as she performs them.

s: Pico, after Plato, names Zoroaster and Zamolxis as the authors of good magic, defines Zoroaster's as the science of divine things and Zamolxis's as medicine of the soul, and counts al-Kindi among its recent heirs with Roger Bacon and William of Paris.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1557, Opera omnia
src.q: the magic of Zoroaster is nothing other than the science of divine things ... the magic of Zamolxis is the medicine of the soul ... Among the more recent who have caught its scent, I find three: Al-Kindi the Arab

s: Pico argues that 'Magus' should not always be heard as 'worshipper of demons': the Persian Magi were philosophers, not necromancers, and he rejects the superstitious and diabolical kind of magic while approving the natural.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1557, Opera omnia
src.q: distinguishing it so that I reject the superstitious and diabolical kind while approving the natural kind ... when they hear the word "Magus," they should not always understand it to mean a worshiper of demons. ... these men were philosophers, not necromancers.

s: Defending a condemned thesis, Pico says no humanly discovered science gives greater certainty than the magic of his conclusions, which he makes a part of natural science, and the scientific part of Kabbalah; the examining masters called the thesis false, erroneous and heretical.

src.l: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, 1557, Opera omnia
src.q: there is none that grants us greater certainty—in the manner that humanly discovered sciences are able to grant certainty—than that Magic ... about which the conclusions are posed there, which is a part of natural science; and that part of Cabala, which is a science and is not revealed Theology. ... was false, erroneous, and heretical.

s: Agrippa (De occulta philosophia I.69) holds that no less virtue lies in words and the names of things than in the affections of the mind, and the greatest in composed speeches; the word is twofold, internal and uttered.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1533, De occulta philosophia libri tres
src.loc: Book I, ch. LXIX, p. xc [scan 109]
src.q: it must be known further that no less resides in words and the names of things, and furthermore, the greatest in complex speeches and orations. ... A word is twofold, namely, internal and uttered.

s: In the De vanitate chapter on natural magic, reprinted at the end of the 1533 De occulta philosophia, Agrippa defines natural magic as bringing nature's hidden powers into the open by coupling inferior things with superior gifts, the art acting as nature's minister.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1533, De occulta philosophia libri tres
src.loc: De vanitate, On natural magic (appended to the 1533 edition), [scan 378]
src.q: Natural magic, therefore, is that which, having contemplated the powers of all natural and celestial things ... brings forth the hidden and latent powers in nature into the open; by coupling inferior things with superior gifts

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1533, De occulta philosophia libri tres
src.loc: end of Book III, p. ccclii [scan 377]
src.q: THE CENSURE OR RETRACTION OF HENRICUS CORNELIUS AGRIPPA Concerning magic, from his declamation On the Vanity of the Sciences

s: Agrippa says the Ethiopians and Indians especially used natural magic, lists its masters across peoples (Brahmins, Gymnosophists, Thracians, Egyptians, Persians), and cites Cicero that no Persian took the kingdom without first learning magic.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1533, De occulta philosophia libri tres
src.q: which magic the Ethiopians and Indians especially used, where the capability of herbs and stones and other things looking to this was available. ... Cicero in his books on Divination says that no one among the Persians possesses the kingdom who has not first learned magic.

s: Agrippa cites the Twelve Tables' penalty for bewitching crops as proof that magi can produce wondrous effects by words and affections alone.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1533, De occulta philosophia libri tres
src.loc: De vanitate, ch. on mathematical magic (appended), p. ccclv [scan 382]
src.q: In the law of the Twelve Tables, a penalty was established for those who had bewitched crops, so that there is no doubt that magi, even by words and affections alone and other similar things, often produce some wondrous effect

s: Agrippa reports the magi's view that things act on each other by an innate power like the magnet on iron, and that through this graded sympathy, according to Iamblichus, Proclus and Synesius, even intellectual and divine gifts can be received from above.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1533, De occulta philosophia libri tres
src.q: They think that all these things pour forth an innate power into other objects and draw them to themselves, or repel them from themselves, or affect them in any other way, just as the magnet draws iron and amber draws straw ... of things, Iamblichus, Proclus, and Synesius confirm, according to the opinion of the magi, that not only natural and celestial gifts, but even intellectual and divine ones can be received from above.

s: In De vanitate Agrippa lists writers on natural magic, among them Hermes, al-Kindi, Geber, Thabit and Solomon, and says the Picatrix written for King Alfonso mixes much superstition with natural magic.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1531, De incertitudine et vanitate scientiarum
src.q: Al-Kindi, Abel, Ptolemy, Geber ... the author of the book published under the name Picatrix ... for King Alfonso, which nonetheless mixes much superstition with Natural Magic—as others have also done.

s: Bruno (De magia) names a 'middle' magic between natural and supernatural, using words, chants, numbers, times, images, figures and seals, and says it is properly called mathematical magic or, more fittingly, occult philosophy.

src.l: Giordano Bruno, 1891, Opera latine conscripta, vol. III (De magia, Theses de magia, De vinculis in genere, etc.)
src.q: Fifth, along with these are added words, chants, calculations of numbers and times, images, figures, seals, characters, ... this is also a "middle" magic, situated between the natural and the extra-natural (or that which is above nature). This would be properly labeled mathematical magic, or more fittingly labeled by the name occult philosophy.

s: Bruno calls the magic that draws spirits into the practitioner, making him their vessel, 'the magic of the desperate', sought through the Notory Art.

src.l: Giordano Bruno, 1891, Opera latine conscripta, vol. III (De magia, Theses de magia, De vinculis in genere, etc.)
src.q: then this is done either for the purpose of drawing spirits into oneself, so that the person becomes their vessel and instrument ... and this is the magic of the desperate, who become vessels for evil demons

s: Bruno says the sense of 'magician' as an evildoer working by pact with an evil spirit is not wise men's or grammarians' usage but that of 'hooded ones' such as the author of the Malleus maleficarum.

src.l: Giordano Bruno, 1891, Opera latine conscripta, vol. III (De magia, Theses de magia, De vinculis in genere, etc.)
src.q: In this sense, a magician is an evildoer ... through commerce with an evil spirit ... and a certain pact, has been instructed ... the word is not used by wise men or even by grammarians themselves, but by certain ... hooded ones ... such as the one who wrote the book The Hammer of Witches

s: Bruno makes the magical bond threefold, required in the practitioner, the act and the subject, and consisting of faith, invocation, and love and ardent affection.

src.l: Giordano Bruno, 1891, Opera latine conscripta, vol. III (De magia, Theses de magia, De vinculis in genere, etc.)
src.q: is threefold, being required in the practitioner, in the act itself, and in the subject upon whom the operation is performed. It consists of faith or belief, as well as invocation, and finally love and ardent affection

s: Campanella's De sensu rerum et magia plans chapters saying one must be silent about the Devil's magic, a rival of the divine that relies on the occult forces of nature, and that all sciences and arts serve natural magic.

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia
src.q: That one must be silent about the magic of the Devil, and that it is a rival to the divine, and relies on the occult forces of nature. ... That all sciences and arts serve natural magic, but some more than others.

s: Campanella concludes that the whole world is sense, life, soul and body, 'the statue of the most high God'.

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia
src.q: The whole world, therefore, is sense, life, soul, and body: the statue of the most high God, created for His own glory, in power, wisdom, and Love.

s: Campanella calls it a matter of great doubt whether witches go bodily with demons, reports Augustine's view that the ointment stupefies them into dreaming it, and admits he cannot see how they pass closed doors unless the Devil opens them.

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia
src.q: is a matter of great doubt. St. Augustine thinks they are anointed and become stupefied by the vapors of the ointment, fall, sleep, and dream that they have gone ... Yet, how they enter and leave through closed doors, I do not understand, unless they are opened by the Devil.

s: Campanella describes making rain from fumes rising to a snow-covered ceiling and thunder by mixing camphor and burning sulphur into the fumes.

src.l: Tommaso Campanella, 1620, De sensu rerum et magia
src.q: Man can make rain from fumes rising to the ceiling of a hall covered with snow; and thunder, if he mixes camphor and burning sulfur with those fumes

s: Trithemius's Antipalus maleficiorum counts those who conjure demons into a circle, glass, mirror, crystal, skull, ring or image as the third kind of witch, deserving fire now and eternally.

src.l: Johannes Trithemius, 1508, Antipalus maleficiorum
src.q: those who invoke [demons], conjuring them into a circle, a glass, a mirror, a crystal, into the heads of the dead ... they belong to the third type of witches, and are worthily to be tortured by fires here temporally, and after death eternally.

s: Trithemius's worst, fourth kind of witch is women who have renounced baptism and given themselves into the law and ownership of demons by homage; he says they are to be utterly exterminated.

src.l: Johannes Trithemius, 1508, Antipalus maleficiorum
src.q: The fourth kind of witches, the worst of all and for that reason to be utterly exterminated, is that of the women who not only have commerce with demons ... have delivered themselves into the law and ownership of demons

s: The Steganographia instructs the writer of a secret message to sit facing east and compel the spirit Pamersiel with a conjuration, repeating it until the spirits appear.

src.l: Johannes Trithemius, 1621, Steganographia
src.q: When he has sat down to write facing the East, let him compel the spirit thus: ... Pamersiel oshurmy delmuson Thafloyn ... When he has said these things, and it seems to him that the spirits are present to obey, let him continue the work begun.

s: The Steganographia says it is the spirit, not the written letter, that reveals the sender's secret to the recipient.

src.l: Johannes Trithemius, 1621, Steganographia
src.q: the spirit—not the written letter—revealing the secret of my mind, he will know the mystery and anticipate the enemy.

s: In the Monas hieroglyphica dedication Dee contrasts a 'real Kabbalah' born of the law of creation with the common 'cabalistic grammar' of written letters, and calls his monad a 'MAGIC Parable'.

src.l: John Dee, 1564, Monas hieroglyphica
src.q: I named REAL KABBALAH, or "the kabbalah of being" ... Just as I name that other common one CABALISTIC GRAMMAR, or "the kabbalah of that which is said" ... which relies on well-known letters, writable by man. ... I now dare to propose this MAGIC Parable in your Royal Presence.

s: Casaubon's 1659 print of Dee's spirit actions records 'Uriel' speaking alongside E. K.'s (Kelley's) reports of what he sees, with Dee's own asides marked Δ: the angels reach Dee only through the scryer.

src.l: John Dee, Meric Casaubon, 1659, A True & Faithful Relation of What Passed for Many Yeers between Dr. John Dee ... and Some Spirits
src.q: Believe me, by Heaven and Earth, I am true Uriel. ... E. K. He hath another Book holden unto him, by one standing by him, who is like a shadow.

s: In the Philosophia occulta attributed to Paracelsus, bruises and wounds without natural cause are read as invisible blows by a sorcerer through an image, happening 'through God's decree'.

src.l: Paracelsus (attributed), 1686, Philosophia occulta (De occulta philosophia)
src.q: let him think nothing other than that he has thus been struck or hit invisibly by a sorcerer through an image ... All of this happens through God’s decree by such master sorcerers.

s: The Paracelsian Philosophia occulta makes imagination a poison stronger than poisoned air: one person's imagining can bring plague into a city or country.

src.l: Paracelsus (attributed), 1686, Philosophia occulta (De occulta philosophia)
src.q: Thus, through the imagining of a single person, a plague may come into a city or a whole country and may poison many thousands of people

s: Pomponazzi (De incantationibus) says Plato posits demons only to instruct the common people, who imagine them, like angels and intelligences, as bodily beings in a place.

src.l: Pietro Pomponazzi, edition undated on SL, De naturalium effectuum causis, sive de incantationibus
src.q: although in many places he seems to posit their existence, he does this for the sake of instructing the common people ... the common people believe that demons, angels, and intelligences are also contained by a physical location.

s: Pomponazzi sets the Peripatetics, for whom wonders are worked by the intelligences through the celestial bodies, against the 'laws' (Christian doctrine), for which angels or demons work them directly.

src.l: Pietro Pomponazzi, edition undated on SL, De naturalium effectuum causis, sive de incantationibus
src.q: For the Peripatetics posit that these things are done by intelligences that move the celestial bodies ... The laws, however, posit that these things are done by angels or demons immediately and without the mediation of the celestial bodies.

s: Reading De vita III chiefly as Hermetic magic (Yates 1964) is challenged on two counts: Ficino titles the book as written among his Plotinus commentaries, and Copenhaver (1984) reads it against scholastic philosophy and Ficino's own worry about its orthodoxy.

src.l: Marsilio Ficino, 1529, De vita libri tres
src.q: On Obtaining Life from the Heavens, composed by the same author among his commentaries on Plotinus.

src.l: Brian P. Copenhaver, 1984, Scholastic Philosophy and Renaissance Magic in the De vita of Marsilio Ficino

s: Reeds (1998) reports solving the hidden ciphers in Book III of the Steganographia and argues it is no longer a demonological treatise but the first book-length European treatment of cryptography, so its spirit conjurations should not be read as evidence of practised spirit magic.

src.l: Jim Reeds, 1998, Solved: The Ciphers in Book III of Trithemius's Steganographia

s: In De mysteriis (I, Parthey p. 34) Iamblichus calls the pure soul, 'the last of the divine beings', ὑπερφυής ('supernatural'): it needs no restoration to nature because it lives an unbegotten life outside every body and outside the nature divided around bodies.

src.l: Iamblichus, Gustav Parthey (ed.), 1857, De mysteriis liber
src.q: What need has it of that generation which exists in pleasure, or that restoration to nature which occurs within it, seeing that it is supernatural and lives an unbegotten life?

src.l: Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, 1502, Opera Dionysii veteris et nove translationis etiam novissime
src.q: And because he had attributed many supernatural things to the deity of Christ, he consequently shows that it does not have them in a defective mode, but super-eminently. And this is what he says: "And it has that which is natural supernaturally." That is, super-substantially

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1478, De potentia Dei; De malo; De spiritualibus creaturis; De anima
src.q: It is said to be "against nature" when there remains in nature a disposition contrary to the effect which God produces

s: In seventeenth-century Latin medicine praeternaturalis is a routine word for the pathological: Wirdig's Nova medicina spirituum (1673) defines diseases as arising from 'a preternatural constitution of the Spirits' (density, blackness, impurity, excess or defect), and the shelf holds titles such as Fludd's De praeternaturali utriusque mundi historia (1621) and Zwicky's dissertation on 'somnus naturalis et praeternaturalis' (1686).

src.q: arising from a preternatural constitution of the Spirits.

Dietrich Zwicky, 1686, Dissertatio medica inauguralis somni naturalis et praeternaturalis

s: Glanvill's Saducismus triumphatus (1681), on the Tedworth disturbances he witnessed, concludes there was 'somewhat extraordinary, and what we usually call preternatural in the business': English 'preternatural' as the ordinary word for a poltergeist.

src.l: Joseph Glanvill, Henry More, 1681, Saducismus Triumphatus: or, Full and Plain Evidence Concerning Witches and Apparitions
src.q: there was somewhat extraordinary, and what we usually call preternatural in the business

s: Hume's essay 'Of Miracles' (Enquiry, sect. X) defines a miracle as 'a violation of the laws of nature' and argues that, since firm experience established those laws, the proof against any miracle is as entire as any argument from experience can be.

src.l: David Hume, 1900, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding
src.q: A miracle is a violation of the laws of nature; and as a firm and unalterable experience has established these laws, the proof against a miracle, from the very nature of the fact, is as entire as any argument from experience can possibly be imagined.

s: Alfred Russel Wallace (On Miracles and Modern Spiritualism, 1875) attacks both of Hume's definitions: the first assumes we know all the laws of nature, and on it an invisible intelligent being holding an apple in the air would 'violate' gravity; the second should say 'some invisible intelligent agent'.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1875, On Miracles and Modern Spiritualism: Three Essays
src.q: The second is, "A miracle is a transgression of a law of nature by a particular volition of the Deity, or by the interposition of some invisible agent." Now both these definitions are bad or imperfect.

src.l: Alfred Russel Wallace, 1875, On Miracles and Modern Spiritualism: Three Essays

s: Catherine Crowe's ghost book The Night-Side of Nature (1848; SL holds an 1850 printing) holds that to the enlightened mind there are no prodigies: the most strange 'or supernatural fact or event' will on investigation prove dependent on its antecedents.

src.l: Catherine Crowe, 1850, The Night-Side of Nature; or, Ghosts and Ghost-Seers
src.q: the most strange and even apparently contradictory or supernatural fact or event will be found, on due investigation, to be strictly dependent on its antecedents

s: F. G. Lee's The Other World; or, Glimpses of the Supernatural (1875) gathers dreams, omens, apparitions, wraiths, second sight, witchcraft and necromancy under 'the supernatural', but its opening chapter still grounds the word in theology: the Gospel's power and the life it produces are 'supernatural', and the book offers 'examples of supernatural intervention'.

src.l: Frederick George Lee, 1875, The Other World; or, Glimpses of the Supernatural
src.q: The life it produces here is supernatural

src.l: Frederick George Lee, 1875, The Other World; or, Glimpses of the Supernatural

s: Frank Podmore's The Naturalisation of the Supernatural (1908) says its title describes 'in popular language' the Society for Psychical Research's aim: to examine facts that stood 'as aliens, outside the realm of organised knowledge', and their claim to be admitted within it.

src.l: Frank Podmore, 1908, The Naturalisation of the Supernatural
src.q: The facts which the Society proposed to investigate stood, and some still stand, as aliens, outside the realm of organised knowledge.

s: Penman (2015, Notes and Queries) notes that the OED's first citation for the adjective 'paranormal' is the 1920 revision of Webster's New International Dictionary, defined by mediumistic 'raps' and telekinesis, and that the word's history before 1920 had scarcely been traced.

src.l: Leigh T. I. Penman, 2015, The History of the Word Paranormal

s: Critique: counting the word supernaturalis is thin evidence for the category. In the Dionysian line it renders the hyper- of negative theology (a 1502 commentary glosses supernaturaliter as supersubstantialiter), while the working distinctions about wonders were drawn with phrases (supra, contra, praeter naturam in Aquinas's De potentia) and later with 'laws of nature' (Hume), neither of which needs the adjective.

src.l: Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, 1502, Opera Dionysii veteris et nove translationis etiam novissime
src.q: "And it has that which is natural supernaturally." That is, super-substantially

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1478, De potentia Dei; De malo; De spiritualibus creaturis; De anima
src.q: God produces something "beside nature," however, when He sometimes produces an effect that nature can produce, yet in that manner in which nature cannot produce it

s: Critique: 'the preternatural' was not one category whose collapse can be dated. In the seventeenth century the word ran in two registers at once, the Galenic-medical (diseases and constitutions 'praeter naturam', as in Wirdig 1673) and the marvel sense (Glanvill's 'what we usually call preternatural', 1681), so a collapse of the marvel sense need not mean the word or the middle zone vanished.

src.l: Sebastian Wirdig, 1673, Nova medicina spirituum
src.q: arising from a preternatural constitution of the Spirits.

src.l: Joseph Glanvill, Henry More, 1681, Saducismus Triumphatus: or, Full and Plain Evidence Concerning Witches and Apparitions
src.q: there was somewhat extraordinary, and what we usually call preternatural in the business

s: In the Summa contra gentiles Aquinas defines miracles 'simply' as what God does beyond the order observed in things, and grounds the word in wonder at an effect whose cause is hidden: the astrologer does not wonder at an eclipse, the ignorant man does.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1474, Summa contra gentiles, sive De veritate Catholicae fidei
src.loc: p. 311, ch. 'On miracles' (numbered 187 in this edition)
src.q: Those, therefore, are to be called simply miracles which are done divinely beyond the order which is observed in things and their orders.
src.qo: Illa et simpliciter miracula dicenda sunt quae divinitus fiunt praeter ordinem cuius servatur in rebus et ordines.

s: Aquinas ranks miracles in three degrees by distance from nature's capacity: what nature never does (two bodies in one place, the sun turning back), what nature does but not in that order (life after death, sight after blindness), and what nature does but without its principles (a curable fever cured by divine power).

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1474, Summa contra gentiles, sive De veritate Catholicae fidei
src.loc: p. 311, ch. 'On miracles' (numbered 187 in this edition)
src.q: The third degree of miracles is when God does what is accustomed to be done by the power of nature, and without the working principles of nature, such as when someone is cured from a curable fever by divine virtue
src.qo: Tercius autem gradus miraculorum est cum deus facit quod consuetum est fieri opacae naturae et absque naturae principiis operantibus sicut cum aliquis a febre curabili per natura virtute divina curat

s: Aquinas argues that no creature can work a miracle, because a created agent can only bring a subject from potency to an act it is already in potency to, through determined intermediate causes; so even spontaneous generation from putrefaction is no miracle, being within the power of the celestial causes.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1474, Summa contra gentiles, sive De veritate Catholicae fidei
src.loc: p. 312, ch. 'That God alone does miracles' (numbered 188 in this edition)
src.q: these are miracles that cannot be done by created power. ... thus it is not a miracle that animals are born from putrefaction without seed.

s: In Summa theologiae I (the article 'Whether all things that God does beyond the natural order of things are miracles', q.105 a.7) Aquinas derives 'miracle' from admiratio, wonder at a manifest effect with a hidden cause, and makes it relative: a rustic wonders at a solar eclipse, an astronomer does not.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1484, Summa theologiae: Pars prima
src.loc: p. 385, art. 7 'Whether all things that God does beyond the natural order of things are miracles'
src.q: Admiration, however, arises from an effect where the effect is manifest and the cause is hidden, just as someone wonders when they see an eclipse of the sun and are ignorant of the cause

s: Aquinas (ST I, demons article, q.114 a.4) holds that demons cannot work true miracles, since miracles exceed the capacity of the whole of created nature; they can do things that look like miracles, exceeding human capacity but not created nature, which Augustine calls marvels.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1497, Summa theologiae: Pars prima
src.loc: p. 267, art. 4 on whether demons can seduce by true miracles
src.q: since miracles are those things that exceed the capacity of the entire created nature, demons cannot perform true miracles. But they can perform certain things that appear to be miracles, which exceed human capacity, but not the capacity of the entire created nature.
src.qo: Sed possunt facere aliqua quae videntur miracula, quae excedunt facultatem humanam, non autem facultatem totius naturae creatae.

s: Aquinas (ST I, 'Whether bodies obey angels in local motion', q.110 a.3) holds that spiritual creatures move bodies immediately only by local motion, and bring about other changes by applying bodily agents, as a smith applies fire to iron; he cites Augustine that angels apply bodily seeds.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, edition undated on SL, Summa theologiae (I-III)
src.loc: p. 302, art. III 'Whether bodies obey angels in local motion'
src.q: angels in causing local motion touch them, and care for other motions by applying bodily agents to produce these effects, just as a smith applies fire to heat the iron.

s: Pomponazzi announces the method of De incantationibus: after his suppositions, he will answer the objections (reported wonders) 'without recourse to demons or angels', setting each demon-based answer beside his own.

src.l: Pietro Pomponazzi, edition undated on SL, De naturalium effectuum causis, sive de incantationibus
src.q: Now that these points have been established, an attempt must be made to answer the objections without recourse to demons or angels.
src.qo: His modo sic suppositis, tentandum est sine dæ- monibus & angelis ad obiecta respon- dere:

s: Pomponazzi argues that if certain marvels can be done by demons, it must also be believed that men can do them with no demon intervening, though he admits the hardest point is what 'determines' a natural power to its target if not the sorcerer's intention.

src.l: Pietro Pomponazzi, edition undated on SL, De naturalium effectuum causis, sive de incantationibus
src.q: And I say, as it seems to me, that if it is conceded that these things can be done by demons ... it must also be believed that these things can be done by men with no demon intervening.
src.qo: & dico ut mihi uidetur, quod ſi conceditur hęc à dęmonibus poſſe fieri, credendum eſt & ab hominibus hæc poſſe fieri nullo intercedēte dęmone.

s: De incantationibus also states that many things 'can by no means be reduced' to a natural cause, nor done through any created thing: the raising of Lazarus, the man born blind, the feeding of thousands, and it cites Aquinas (via Augustine) that Pharaoh's magicians' serpents were natural, Moses' divine.

src.l: Pietro Pomponazzi, edition undated on SL, De naturalium effectuum causis, sive de incantationibus
src.q: None of these can be reduced to a natural cause, nor could they have been performed immediately through any created thing.
src.qo: quorum nullum poteſt reduci in cauſam naturalem, neqȝ immediatè fu- iſſe factum per aliquam rem creatam:

s: In Wissenschaft als Beruf (1919) Weber defines the 'disenchantment of the world' as the belief that there are in principle no mysterious incalculable powers at play, that everything can in principle be mastered by calculation, so that one no longer turns to magical means to master or entreat spirits.

src.l: Max Weber, 1919, Wissenschaft als Beruf
src.loc: lecture text, passage on 'Intellektualisierung und Rationalisierung' (Wikisource transcription of the 1919 print)

s: In Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft (sociology of religion) Weber ties disenchantment to intellectualism: the more it pushes back belief in magic, the more the world's processes are 'disenchanted', merely 'are' and 'happen' without 'meaning', and the more urgent becomes the demand that the world as a whole be meaningfully ordered.

src.l: Max Weber, 1922, Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft
src.q: The more intellectualism pushes back the belief in magic, and thus the processes of the world are "disenchanted"—losing their magical meaning, only "being" and "happening," but no longer "meaning" anything
src.qo: Je mehr der Intellektualismus den Glauben an die Magie zurückdrängt, und so die Vorgänge der Welt „entzaubert" werden, ihren magischen Sinngehalt verlieren, nur noch „sind" und „geschehen", aber nichts mehr „bedeuten",

s: Daston and Park's Wonders and the Order of Nature, 1150-1750 (1998) organises its history of wonders partly around the preternatural: its table of contents has sections on 'curiosity and the preternatural', 'preternatural history' and 'preternatural philosophy'.

src.l: Lorraine Daston, Katharine Park, 1998, Wonders and the Order of Nature, 1150-1750
Rudolf Schmid, 1998, Wonders and the Order of Nature: 1150-1750 [book notice]

s: Bartlett (2008) argues that the word supernaturalis made a strong appearance in European theology and saints' lives from the mid-thirteenth century, so that 'supernatural' as a category is a scholastic coinage, not a medieval constant.

src.l: Robert Bartlett, 2008, The Natural and the Supernatural in the Middle Ages (The Wiles Lectures)
Andrew Fogleman, 2009, The Natural and the Supernatural in the Middle Ages by Robert Bartlett (review)
Jacques Le Goff, 2009, Robert Bartlett. — The Natural and the Supernatural in the Middle Ages [compte rendu]

s: Boyer and Ramble (2001) report free-recall experiments in France, Gabon and Nepal in which violations of domain-level expectations (about 'person', 'animal', 'artifact') were recalled better than violations of basic-level expectations, with similar effects across cultures and levels of belief.

src.l: Pascal Boyer, Charles Ramble, 2001, Cognitive templates for religious concepts: cross-cultural evidence for recall of counter-intuitive representations
Pascal Boyer, 2001, Religion Explained: The Evolutionary Origins of Religious Thought

s: Atran and Norenzayan (2004) argue that religion is an evolutionary by-product, not an adaptation: core beliefs minimally violate folk mechanics, biology and psychology, and supernatural-agent concepts trigger an 'agency detector' whose proper domain is predators, protectors and prey.

src.l: Scott Atran, Ara Norenzayan, 2004, Religion's evolutionary landscape: Counterintuition, commitment, compassion, communion
Scott Atran, 2002, In Gods We Trust: The Evolutionary Landscape of Religion
src.loc: ch. 3 'God's Creation: Evolutionary Origins of the Supernatural' (title from contents)

s: Critique: Le Goff (2009) objects that supernaturalis and super naturam were scarcely used by medieval authors, and that in conceptual history this rarity weakens the theses of de Lubac and Bartlett; the period's own expression for what escapes nature was praeter naturam.

src.l: Jacques Le Goff, 2009, Robert Bartlett. — The Natural and the Supernatural in the Middle Ages [compte rendu]

s: Critique: Willard, Henrich and Norenzayan (2016) report that the memory advantage of minimally counterintuitive content shrinks as such concepts become common, and that MCI content is judged less believable than intuitive content, so memorability cannot by itself explain belief in the supernatural.

src.l: Aiyana K. Willard, Joseph Henrich, Ara Norenzayan, 2016, Memory and Belief in the Transmission of Counterintuitive Content

s: Critique (from Weber himself): in Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft Weber says the decisive mark of religious development is not the personal or impersonal character of 'supernatural' powers, which he puts in scare quotes, but that things now count because they 'mean' something, so that magic turns from direct effect of power into symbolism; on this view the line that matters for magic is meaning, not nature versus beyond-nature.

src.l: Max Weber, 1922, Wirtschaft und Gesellschaft
src.q: It is not the personality, impersonality, or super-personality of "supernatural" powers that is the immediate specific characteristic of this entire development, but rather the fact that now, not only things and processes that exist and happen play a role in life, but also those that exist and happen because they "mean" something.
src.qo: Nicht die Persönlichkeit oder Unpersönlichkeit oder Ueberpersönlichkeit „übersinnlicher" Mächte ist das zunächst Spezifische dieser ganzen Entwicklung, sondern: daß jetzt nicht nur Dinge und Vorgänge eine Rolle im Leben spielen, die da sind und geschehen, sondern außerdem solche, welche und weil sie etwas „bedeuten".

s: In SL's Vatican witness of the Speculum astronomiae, the first, 'abominable' mode of images works with fumigations and invocations; the text calls it the worst idolatry and rejects it ('may this mode be far from us').

src.l: Albertus Magnus (attr.), 1280, Speculum astronomiae
src.q: Images are in three ways. ... And the first mode, abominable

src.l: Albertus Magnus (attr.), 1280, Speculum astronomiae
src.q: This is the worst idolatry ... May this mode be far from us; away.

s: The Speculum's second, 'detestable' mode exorcises spirits by name, citing the Almandal of Solomon and a book called Rasiel; it is suspect because it lies under a foreign, unknown tongue against the Catholic faith.

src.l: Albertus Magnus (attr.), 1280, Speculum astronomiae
src.q: Another mode in which two [are] detestable ... This mode at least may be far from us, suspect. For if [it] at least [lies] under a foreign tongue and one unknown to us, and thus [it is] against the honesty of the Catholic faith.

Hic modus saltem a nobis longe sit / suspectus . nam si ne saltem sub alieno lingua et ignoto nobis ad lateat / et sic contra catholicam fidei honestatem .

s: The Speculum sets apart a third mode, 'astronomical images', which do without suffumigations, invocations and inscribed characters and work by their own nature as constrained by the heavens.

src.l: Albertus Magnus (attr.), 1280, Speculum astronomiae
src.q: astronomical images, and thus they eliminate these images ... and suffumigations and invocations; they are not from fabrications nor characters in images, to the virtue of their own nature constrained by the celestial [spheres]
