s: In De mineralibus (Book II, tract. 3, ch. 1) Albertus calls the doctrine of images and seals of stones a part of necromancy subalternated to astronomy, and says it cannot be known without astronomy, magic and necromancy together; he treats it anyway at his associates' request.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1890, Opera Omnia, Vol. V (ed. Borgnet): Mineralium libri V, etc.
src.q: for although this part is a part of necromancy according to that species of necromancy which is subalternated to astronomy, and which is called that of images and seals ... nor can it be known unless astronomy, magic, and the sciences of necromancy are known simultaneously.
src.qo: licet enim pars ista sit pars necromantiæ secundum illam speciem necromantiæ quæ astronomiæ subalternatur, et quæ de imaginibus et sigillis vocatur: tamen propter bonitatem doctrinæ, et quia illud cupiunt a nobis scire nostri socii, aliquid de hoc hic dicemus, omnino imperfecta et falsa reputantes quidquid de his a multis scriptum invenitur. Antiquorum enim sapientium scripturam de sigillis lapidum pauci sciunt, nec sciri potest nisi simul et astronomia et magica et necromantiæ scientiæ sciantur.

s: Albertus reports seeing, as a young man in Venice, a sawn marble showing a crowned, bearded king's head painted by nature, and concludes that figures in stones are sometimes made by nature (he explains it by vapour and heat).

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1890, Opera Omnia, Vol. V (ed. Borgnet): Mineralium libri V, etc.
src.q: when I was in Venice, when I was a young man, marbles were being cut by saws to ornament the walls of a temple
src.qo: incidebantur marmora per serras ad parietes templi ornandos:

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1890, Opera Omnia, Vol. V (ed. Borgnet): Mineralium libri V, etc.
src.q: it is therefore evident that the figure of a simple painting is sometimes from nature.
src.qo: Propter hoc patet ergo figuram picturæ simplicis aliquando esse a natura.

s: Albertus warns that some 'images in stones' are frauds: figures are made in soft matter and hardened by alchemy into the likeness of stone, mostly with what alchemists call lac virginis (litharge washed and filtered).

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1890, Opera Omnia, Vol. V (ed. Borgnet): Mineralium libri V, etc.
src.q: The second way, however, is deceptive, because images are fashioned in the matter ... by the work of alchemy through water or another coagulating liquid, it is hardened into the likeness of stone.

s: Albertus grounds engraved seals in 'the science of the magicians' (Greek Magor, Babylonian Germa, Egyptian Hermes; then Ptolemy, Geber of Seville and Thebit), whose principle is that the figures of the heavens are the first figures and act on every figure made by nature or art.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1890, Opera Omnia, Vol. V (ed. Borgnet): Mineralium libri V, etc.
src.q: One must know the cause of this from the science of the magicians which the Greek Magor, the Babylonian Germa, and the Egyptian Hermes completed in the beginning ... the figures of the heavens are the first figures
src.qo: Hujus autem causam cognoscere ex scientia oportet magorum quam compleverunt Magor Græcus, et Germa Babylonicus, et Hermes Ægyptius in primis,

s: Albertus says the first teachers of physics commanded gems and metal images to be sculpted at observed times, when the celestial force for that image is strongest, and lists five celestial conditions to observe; ignorance of them makes the art look false.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1890, Opera Omnia, Vol. V (ed. Borgnet): Mineralium libri V, etc.
src.q: the first teachers and professors of physics commanded that gems and metallic images be sculpted at observed times, when the celestial force is proven to be strongest for that same image
src.qo: Hac ergo industria considerata primi præceptores et professores physici gemmas et imagines metallicas ad imagines astrorum observatis temporibus quando vis cœlestis fortissima ad imaginem eamdem esse probatur, ut puta cœlestibus multis virtutibus admixta, sculpi præcipiebant,

s: Albertus holds that an image's celestial virtue lasts only for a period, after which 'the cold and dead image' is empty and useless, which he gives as the reason ancient images no longer work.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1890, Opera Omnia, Vol. V (ed. Borgnet): Mineralium libri V, etc.
src.q: afterward, the cold and dead image remains empty and useless. This is the cause why certain images do not work in this time, which they did in ancient times.
src.qo: et hæc est causa quare quædam imagines non operantur hoc tempore, quod fecerunt tempore antiquo.

s: Albertus says engraved stones are stronger from India and Egypt, where planetary rays are most effective, and that Aries, Leo or Sagittarius cut in a stone (the fiery eastern triplicity) give it a property against fevers, dropsy and paralysis.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1890, Opera Omnia, Vol. V (ed. Borgnet): Mineralium libri V, etc.
src.q: The reason why these stones come more from India and Egypt than from other regions is that the power of the planets is most effective in those parts ... Aries, Leo, or Sagittarius, when sculpted on account of fire and the Oriental triplicity, signify that those stones have a property against fevers

s: In De mineralibus Albertus rejects the Pythagorean view that stones' virtues come from a soul of the stones (and leaves fascination to 'the magical arts'), holding instead that stones have virtues of miraculous effects that follow the composite, not its components.

src.l: Albertus Magnus, 1890, Opera Omnia, Vol. V (ed. Borgnet): Mineralium libri V, etc.
src.loc: De mineralibus, on the cause of stones' virtues (scan 32)
src.q: These things, however, are most absurd. And regarding fascination, whether it be true or not, that belongs to the magical arts. ... stones have virtues of miraculous effects, which virtues are present in them not from the components, but follow the composite
src.qo: Hæc autem absurdissima sunt. Et de fascinatione quidem an verum sit an non, ad magicas pertinet. Deinde autem Deum esse diffusum in rebus ita quod rebus sit unitus et permixtus sicut aliqua virtus essentialis rebus, dementis est dicere: quoniam si commiscetur rebus, erit generabilis in quibusdam rebus, et exiens de non esse ad esse et de potentia ad actum: quæ omnia impossibile est Deo convenire. Quamlibet autem rem habere aliquid divinum per quod appetit et agit ad esse divinum, vel divino simile, est verum et alibi hoc est determinatum. Animas autem nullas habere lapides in antecedentibus hujus libri determinatum est. Opinio propria Propter quod etiam hæc et his similia quasi derisoria relinquentes, dicamus lapides absque omni ambiguitate virtutes mirabilium effectuum habere, quæ quidem virtutes insunt eisdem non ex componentibus,

s: De mirabilibus mundi (1473 edition) holds that a greater excess of the soul always binds, prevents or dissolves a smaller one, and derives from this the efficacy of characters and spoken words made in the hour of the operator's strongest desire.

src.l: Pseudo-Albertus Magnus, 1473, De mirabilibus mundi
src.q: because a greater excess of the soul always binds and prohibits another smaller one, or dissolves it. ... we knew from this the science of characters and the efficacy of speeches for every thing that a man desires.
src.qo: excessus animorum. ligat et prohibet alium minorem aut soluit.

src.q: excessus animorum. ligat et prohibet alium minorem aut soluit.

s: Thorndike reports that in his Commentary on the Sentences (II, d. 7) Albertus calls the use of 'magic virtues' evil and apostasy from the faith, whether by invocations and suffumigations or by a simple operation needing demon aid, and warns against astrological 'images, rings, mirrors, and characters'.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: In his Commentary on the Sentences 2 Albert declares that to make use of "magic virtues" is evil and apostasy from the Faith

s: Thorndike reports Albertus's view that feats of magic are not miracles: they are slower than miracles, and mostly explicable by natural forces aided by demons and stars, e.g. Pharaoh's magicians turning rods to snakes merely hastens the generation of worms in rotting wood.

src.l: Lynn Thorndike, 1923, A History of Magic and Experimental Science, Vol. II
src.q: the works of magic can usually be explained as the product of natural forces, and by the fact that the demons are aided in their operations by the influence of the stars.

s: Naudé reports the legend (via Tostatus) that Albertus spent 30 years casting a metal 'Androides' part by part under constellations, which answered his questions until Aquinas smashed it, and derives the fable from the Hebrew teraphim before refuting planetary-image speaking heads.

src.q: Varro says there are four kinds of divination: earth, water, air, and fire. Hence geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, and pyromancy were named.
src.qo: Varro dicit divinationis quattuor esse genera, terram, aquam, aerem et ignem. Hinc geomantiam, hydromantiam, aeromantiam, pyromantiam dictam.

src.l: Isidore of Seville, 1911, Etymologiarum sive Originum libri XX
src.q: Varro dicit divinationis quattuor esse genera, terram, aquam, aerem et ignem. Hinc geomantiam, hydromantiam, aeromantiam, pyromantiam dictam.

src.l: Isidore of Seville, 1911, Etymologiarum sive Originum libri XX
src.q: For hydromancy is the act of evoking the shadows of demons in the inspection of water
src.qo: Varro dicit divinationis quattuor esse genera, terram, aquam, aerem et ignem. Hinc geomantiam, hydromantiam, aeromantiam, pyromantiam dictam.

s: Isidore says the genethliaci who cast nativities by the twelve signs are commonly called mathematici, and that this art was permitted until the Gospel, so that after Christ no one should read anyone's nativity from the sky.

src.l: Isidore of Seville, 1911, Etymologiarum sive Originum libri XX
src.q: The knowledge of this art was permitted up to the Gospel, so that once Christ was brought forth, no one from then on would interpret the nativity of anyone from the sky.

s: Aquinas (ST II-II q.95 a.3) files chiromancy (lines of the hand) and spatulamancy (signs in a shoulder-blade) under divination by figures seen in bodies, and geomancy (drawing points), molten lead and lots under a genus of divination without express invocation of demons.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1879, Summa Theologica, Secunda Secundae (Latin with French notes)
src.q: for divination taken from the lines of the hand is called chiromancy, as if hand-divination

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1879, Summa Theologica, Secunda Secundae (Latin with French notes)
src.q: To the second genus of divination, however, which is without express invocation of demons, pertains the divination which is done from the consideration of those things that come from certain actions

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1879, Summa Theologica, Secunda Secundae (Latin with French notes)
src.q: whether through the drawing of points, which pertains to the art of geomancy

s: Aquinas grades the sin: all these divinations share a general reason for sinning, but it is much graver to invoke demons expressly than to do things by which demons may insert themselves.

src.l: Thomas Aquinas, 1879, Summa Theologica, Secunda Secundae (Latin with French notes)
src.q: it is much graver to invoke demons than to do certain things by which it is worthy that demons should insert themselves

s: A treatise on the kinds of divination printed in the 1600 Agrippa Opera derives geomantia from earth and manteia and describes the art: points struck at random on the earth in sixteen lines, reduced by odd and even to figures standing for planets, signs and elements.

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1600, Opera (Lyon, c. 1600), Epitome
src.q: The mastery of this art is gathered from certain uncounted points, struck by chance and fortuitously upon the earth, and drawn toward the left in sixteen lines

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1600, Opera (Lyon, c. 1600), Epitome
src.q: reduce these to certain figures (also consisting of points): the seven planets, the twelve signs of the zodiac, the head and tail of the dragon, and even the four elements themselves

s: The same 1600 Opera text names Bartolomeo Cocles of Bologna and Johannes ab Indagine as modern authors on chiromancy, and defines necromancy as divination through the dead, citing Saul and the woman with a familiar spirit (1 Sam 28).

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1600, Opera (Lyon, c. 1600), Epitome
src.q: and among modern authors, Bartholomew Cocles of Bologna, Johann Indagine on the same

src.l: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, 1600, Opera (Lyon, c. 1600), Epitome
src.q: is divination through the dead, just as is read in 1 Samuel, chapter 28, concerning Saul, King of Israel

s: The English "Of Geomancy" printed with the pseudo-Agrippan Fourth Book (1655) maps the eight generated figures onto the houses of heaven: the four Mothers make the first four houses, the four Daughters the next four.

src.l: Pseudo-Agrippa, Robert Turner (tr.), 1655, Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy, with Of Geomancy
src.q: And these 8 Figures do make 8 Houses of Heaven, after this manner, by placing the Figures from the left hand towards the right

src.l: Pseudo-Agrippa, Robert Turner (tr.), 1655, Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy, with Of Geomancy
src.q: as the foure Matres do make the foure first Houses , so the foure Filiæ doe make the foure following Houses

s: Fludd (Utriusque cosmi II, 1619) derives geomancy from gē and manteia, says the Chaldeans, Indians and Egyptians first wrote on it and names Peter of Abano among the moderns, after listing hydromancy, aeromancy, pyromancy, chiromancy, necromancy and other external species.

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1619, Utriusque Cosmi Historia, Vol. 2 (Tractatus I, Sectio II)
src.q: Geomancy therefore, of which we have made mention in this book & above, is so called from ge (earth) and manteia (divination), as if divination from earth: Concerning it, the Chaldeans, Indians, & Egyptians first wrote.
src.qo: Geomantia ergo, cujus in hoc libello & suprà mentionem fecimus, sic dicta est ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς καὶ τῆς μαντείας, quasi divinatio ex terra

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1619, Utriusque Cosmi Historia, Vol. 2 (Tractatus I, Sectio II)
src.q: Geomantia ergo, cujus in hoc libello & suprà mentionem fecimus, sic dicta est ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς καὶ τῆς μαντείας, quasi divinatio ex terra

src.l: Robert Fludd, 1619, Utriusque Cosmi Historia, Vol. 2 (Tractatus I, Sectio II)
src.q: But there are also many other species of presage & prophecy which are elicited from external accidents of things by a skilled & wise man
src.qo: Geomantia ergo, cujus in hoc libello & suprà mentionem fecimus, sic dicta est ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς καὶ τῆς μαντείας, quasi divinatio ex terra

s: A Liber geomantiae ascribed to Gerard of Cremona, in the Hugh of Santalla geomancy volume, says the strokes are made in cleansed sand or earth, or with a knife, stones or the fingers.

src.l: Hugh of Santalla, Gerard of Cremona, et al., 13th c., Hugonis Satiliensis geomantia et alia aliorum opera (manuscript miscellany)
src.q: the percussion is made in cleansed sand, earth, and to place, and sand, and with a knife, and with stones, and with fingers

s: Binsfeld (1591) reports that, following Aristotle, chiromancy performed on the lines of the hands is approved as a natural science, and refers physiognomy to the doctors (Pelbartus, Conrad of Vechta) and Aristotle.

src.l: Peter Binsfeld, 1591, Tractatus de confessionibus maleficorum et sagarum (Treatise on the Confessions of Witches and Sorcerers)
src.q: which is performed on the lines of the hands, as a natural science

s: Peucer treats catoptromancy and onychomancy as images formed by the Devil: in mirrors the images "fashioned and returned by the Devil" seem to shine, and on a boy's oiled fingernail "the impostor, the Devil" forms and moves them.

src.l: Kaspar Peucer, 1560, Commentarius de praecipuis generibus divinationum
src.q: divines from bright and polished mirrors, in which images of the things inquired about, fashioned and returned by the Devil, seem to shine

src.l: Kaspar Peucer, 1560, Commentarius de praecipuis generibus divinationum
src.q: which the impostor, the Devil, nevertheless formed and moved before their eyes so that, from this mixture, they seemed to appear and shine on the fingernail

s: Peucer's chapter on chiromancy proceeds by hand anatomy (muscles, the thenar and hypothenar mounds) and says this structure explains the shape of the palm and the lines on the skin.

src.l: Kaspar Peucer, 1560, Commentarius de praecipuis generibus divinationum
src.q: From this structure, the reason for the shape and inequality of the internal hand, and for the lines appearing on the surface of the skin, is clear.

src.l: Kaspar Peucer, 1560, Commentarius de praecipuis generibus divinationum
src.q: The hills that appear as if clustered at the roots of the fingers in a triple valley are called by one name by the Greeks, <term>hypothenar</term>

s: Peucer divides dreams by source: divine dreams whose interpretation is a charisma of the Holy Spirit (Joseph, Daniel), and two kinds of demon-sent dreams, including those sought by incubation at idols' shrines.

src.l: Kaspar Peucer, 1560, Commentarius de praecipuis generibus divinationum
src.q: to understand and interpret these is a peculiar gift and <term>charisma</term> <gloss>gift of grace</gloss> of the Holy Spirit

src.l: Kaspar Peucer, 1560, Commentarius de praecipuis generibus divinationum
src.q: Two genera of <term>daimonopempton</term> <gloss>demon-sent [dreams]</gloss> are found.

s: Leibniz (Théodicée appendix, ed. 1734) reports that Father Bouvet wrote from China that he believed Leibniz's binary method was the key to the figures of Fohy (Fuxi).

src.l: G. W. Leibniz, 1734, Essais de théodicée sur la bonté de Dieu (with appended pieces)
src.q: sent word from China to Mr. Leibniz, that he believed that his Method was the Key to the Figures of Fohy.

src.l: G. W. Leibniz, 1734, Essais de théodicée sur la bonté de Dieu (with appended pieces)
src.q: it seems to contain the mystery of the Li- gnes of an ancient King and Philosopher of China named Fohy

s: The 1740 German Kleinere philosophische Schriften says that when Leibniz shared his Dyadik with Bouvet, Bouvet used binary arithmetic as a key to solve for the Chinese a riddle attributed to their ancient king Fohy.

src.l: G. W. Leibniz, H. Köhler (ed./tr.), 1740, Kleinere philosophische Schriften
src.q: the latter resolved and explained to them a certain riddle by means of this binary arithmetic as if by a key

s: A Song Yijing commentary digest (Li Heng, Zhouyi yihai cuoyao) glosses the milfoil procedure: the stalks are divided between the hands to image Heaven and Earth, one hung to image the Three Powers, and counted by fours to image the seasons.

src.l: Li Heng 李衡, Song, 周易義海撮要 (Zhouyi yihai cuoyao), juan 7
src.q: Divide the stalks into the left and right hands to represent Heaven and Earth.
src.qo: 將蓍分於左右手中以象天地也掛一以象三

src.l: Li Heng 李衡, Song, 周易義海撮要 (Zhouyi yihai cuoyao), juan 7
src.q: 將蓍分於左右手中以象天地也掛一以象三

src.l: Li Heng 李衡, Song, 周易義海撮要 (Zhouyi yihai cuoyao), juan 7
src.q: Count them by fours to represent the four seasons
src.qo: 將蓍分於左右手中以象天地也掛一以象三

s: Boissard (1615) reports Augustine's acrostic of Sibylline verses spelling "Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour", and that Cicero held such acrostics suspect because they show elaborate artifice, not a spirit rapt by Pythian fury.

src.l: Jean-Jacques Boissard, 1615, Tractatus posthumus ... De divinatione et magicis praestigiis
src.q: Augustine, in book 18 of The City of God, brings them forward translated with acrostics, which, when collected together, form: Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.
src.qo: Sed acrosticha hæc suspecta fe habere testatur Cicero lib. 2. de natura Deorum

src.l: Jean-Jacques Boissard, 1615, Tractatus posthumus ... De divinatione et magicis praestigiis
src.q: Sed acrosticha hæc suspecta fe habere testatur Cicero lib. 2. de natura Deorum

s: Critique of the natural/artificial split from inside De divinatione: Marcus asks Cratippus why only dreams and frenzy are kept, since soothsayers, augurs and Chaldeans can also show true predictions; either all are divination or none is.

src.l: Cicero, W. A. Falconer (tr.), 1923, De Senectute, De Amicitia, De Divinatione (Loeb 154)
src.q: Therefore, either those are all legitimate forms of divination—which you very rightly reject—or, if they are not, I do not understand why these two are the ones you choose to keep.

s: Puységur reduces the whole doctrine of animal magnetism to the operator's belief in a power within himself and the will to exercise it ('croyez et veuillez'), and tells a correspondent to banish any particular procedure.

src.l: Armand-Marie-Jacques de Chastenet, Marquis de Puységur, 1807, Du magnétisme animal
src.q: I believe in the existence, within me, of a power. From this belief derives my will to exercise it.
src.qo: Je crois à l'existence, en moi, d'une puissance. De cette croyance, dérive ma volonté de l'exercer.

src.l: Armand-Marie-Jacques de Chastenet, Marquis de Puységur, 1807, Du magnétisme animal
src.q: When one desires the good, when one seeks to heal, one must have only that object in view
src.qo: Quand on veut le bien , quand on cherche à guérir , il ne faut avoir que cet objet en vue ;

src.l: Armand-Marie-Jacques de Chastenet, Marquis de Puységur, 1820, Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire et à l'établissement du magnétisme animal
src.loc: p. 218 [scan 254], closing the first part, dated 4 Feb. 1785
src.q: Believe and will.
src.qo: Croyez et veuillez.

s: Puységur reports that his patient Victor, put into the 'magnetic state' (artificial somnambulism), prescribed his own bleeding, an idea that terrified him once returned to his natural state.

src.l: Armand-Marie-Jacques de Chastenet, Marquis de Puységur, 1820, Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire et à l'établissement du magnétisme animal
src.q: he told me, while in the magnetic state, that he had to be bled from the left arm—that it was absolutely necessary.

s: The editor of the Quimby Manuscripts says Quimby began as a mesmerist who assumed electricity and the stronger will passed into the subject, and abandoned the magnetic-current hypothesis when it explained nothing.

src.l: Phineas Parkhurst Quimby, Horatio W. Dresser (ed.), 1921, The Quimby Manuscripts
src.q: Their hypothesis was that electricity would pass from their organisms into that of the subject.

src.l: Phineas Parkhurst Quimby, Horatio W. Dresser (ed.), 1921, The Quimby Manuscripts
src.q: he found himself as ignorant of the phenomena as when he began, so long as he held to the hypothesis of a magnetic current

s: Quimby's writings treat disease as 'a lie which they believe', its pains as the expression of fears, and make the healer's explanation of that error the cure ('The Truth is the Cure').

src.l: Phineas Parkhurst Quimby, Horatio W. Dresser (ed.), 1921, The Quimby Manuscripts
src.loc: p. 151 [scan 155], circular in Letters to Patients
src.q: The Truth is the Cure.

src.l: Phineas Parkhurst Quimby, Horatio W. Dresser (ed.), 1921, The Quimby Manuscripts
src.q: and in his explanation lies the cure.

src.l: Phineas Parkhurst Quimby, Horatio W. Dresser (ed.), 1921, The Quimby Manuscripts
src.q: To me this something that they call disease is a lie which they believe, and their aches and pains are the expressions of their fears

s: Warren Felt Evans (1869) reduces mesmerism, animal magnetism, 'biology', pathetism, hypnotism and psychometry to one principle, the action of mind upon mind, and holds that diseases originate in inharmonious mental states that 'ultimate themselves in corresponding bodily conditions'.

src.l: Warren Felt Evans, 1869, The Mental Cure
src.q: reducible to one general principle,—the influence or action of mind upon mind, and the communication of spiritual life from one person to another, who is negatively receptive of it.

s: Evans recasts Quimby's mental theory of disease in Swedenborg's terms: the brain 'corresponds or answers to the mind', and (per Dresser) disease is the bodily correspondence of a loss of balance between will and understanding.

src.l: Warren Felt Evans, 1869, The Mental Cure
src.q: It corresponds or answers to the mind, as an echo to the original sound.

src.l: Horatio W. Dresser, 1919, A History of the New Thought Movement
src.q: Mr. Evans is adapting Sweden-borg’s psychology so as to find sure place for the truths concerning disease and its cure which he has learned from Mr. Quimby.

s: Swedenborg holds that the whole natural world, and every part of it, corresponds to the spiritual world and subsists from it as effect from efficient cause, and that the body's face, speech and gestures are correspondences of the mind.

src.l: Emanuel Swedenborg, 1875, Heaven and Its Wonders and Hell
src.q: The whole natural world corresponds to the spiritual world; not only the natural world in general, but also every particular part thereof.

src.l: Emanuel Swedenborg, 1875, Heaven and Its Wonders and Hell
src.q: Those things, therefore, which occur in the body, whether it be in the face, the speech, or the gestures, are called correspondences.

s: In 1886 Evans grounds mental healing in a 'law of sympathy' that he says runs through all nature and on which, citing Proclus, the ancient system of magic was based, then likens it to electrical induction between moving trains and ships.

src.l: Warren Felt Evans, 1886, Esoteric Christianity and Mental Therapeutics
src.q: This law of sympathy seems to extend through the whole domain of nature; and on it, according to Proclus, was based the system of magic, or the ancient occult science.

s: Evans's Esoteric Christianity (1886) cites 'The Virgin of the World, of Hermes Trismegistus' for the claim that to know God is to have and to be God, and appeals to 'the Hermetic philosophers of all ages' as learning all truth by turning the receptive mind to the intelligible world.

src.l: Warren Felt Evans, 1886, Esoteric Christianity and Mental Therapeutics
src.q: (The Virgin of the World, of Hermes Trismegistus, p. 15.)

src.l: Warren Felt Evans, 1886, Esoteric Christianity and Mental Therapeutics
src.q: In this way, the Hermetic philosophers of all ages and countries claimed to be able to learn all that is known or ever was known

s: Unlike Eddy, Evans (1885) keeps magnetism: he calls Du Potet worthy to be named with Pythagoras, Apollonius, Paracelsus and Van Helmont, and identifies magnetism 'in the old spiritual science' with the universal life-principle through which thought and will are transmitted.

src.l: Warren Felt Evans, 1885, The Primitive Mind-Cure
src.q: Magnetism in the old spiritual science is identical with the universal life-principle, and is the medium through which our minds influence the minds of others, and a thought and will impulse are transmissible.

s: Evans (1884) quotes Van Helmont's 'great secret' that strength lies in man through 'the suggestion and power of the imagination' to act on others at a distance, citing it from Ennemoser's History of Magic.

src.l: Warren Felt Evans, 1884, The Divine Law of Cure
src.q: the strength lies concealed in man merely through the suggestion and power of the imagination, to work outwardly, and to impress this strength on others

s: Science and Health holds that the cause of all so-called disease is mental, a mortal fear or mistaken belief, and that the author never knew a patient who did not recover once the belief of the disease had gone.

src.l: Mary Baker Eddy, post-1900 text, Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures (final-edition text)
src.q: The cause of all so-called disease is mental, a mortal fear, a mistaken belief or conviction of the necessity and power of ill-health

s: Eddy excludes mesmerism, hypnotism, theosophy and spiritualism from Christian Science, calls animal magnetism 'the human antipode of divine Science', and in 1887 quotes the 1784 commissioners' finding that there is no magnetic fluid.

src.l: Mary Baker Eddy, post-1900 text, Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures (final-edition text)
src.q: Mesmerism is mortal, material illusion. Animal magnetism is the voluntary or involuntary action of error in all its forms; it is the human antipode of divine Science.

src.l: Mary Baker Eddy, 1887, Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures
src.q: there is no proof of the existence of the animal magnetic fluid

s: In the 1887 preface Eddy calls the claim that P. P. Quimby originated her writings a 'post mortem falsehood', says Quimby was 'a distinguished mesmerist' who manipulated his patients, and claims that writings she left with him are now claimed as his.

src.l: Mary Baker Eddy, 1887, Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures
src.q: The cowardly claim that I am not the originator of my own writings, but that one P. P. Quimby is, has been legally met and punished.

src.l: Mary Baker Eddy, 1887, Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures
src.q: He was an uneducated man; but he was a distinguished mesmerist, and personally manipulated his patients.

s: The 1921 Quimby Manuscripts state that Eddy left at Stoughton (1868-70) a manuscript 'Extracts from P. P. Quimby's Writings' on which she based her teaching, later claimed it as her own, and won the 1883 plagiarism suit against Arens because George Quimby would not release the manuscripts.

src.l: Phineas Parkhurst Quimby, Horatio W. Dresser (ed.), 1921, The Quimby Manuscripts
src.q: She lived in Stoughton, Mass., 1868-70, where she left a manuscript known as “Extracts from P. P. Quimby’s Writings,” on which she based her teachings.

s: Dresser's 1919 history credits Emma Curtis Hopkins with becoming 'a teacher of leaders' in Chicago and San Francisco, whose students included Charles and Myrtle Fillmore (Unity) and Helen Wilmans.

src.l: Horatio W. Dresser, 1919, A History of the New Thought Movement
src.q: In the same way Mrs. Emma Curtis Hopkins became a teacher of lead- ers in Chicago and San Francisco.

s: Emma Curtis Hopkins titles her teaching on faith 'the Magia Jesu Christi' and calls faith 'the deepest secret of all the deep secrets' of it: the practitioner's own word is magia.

src.l: Emma Curtis Hopkins, 1924, Studies in High Mysticism: The Magia Jesu Christi. IV. Faith
src.loc: p. 43 [scan 51], Studies in High Mysticism IV: Faith
src.q: is the deepest secret of all the deep secrets of the Magia Jesu Christi.

s: Against a confident Quimby-priority story: the Quimby texts reach us through partisans (the Dressers edited them and supplied the 1883 case), Podmore judged from the published fragments that Quimby never worked his ideas into a coherent system, and Eddy denied the debt outright.

src.l: Frank Podmore, 1909, Mesmerism and Christian Science: A Short History of Mental Healing
src.q: it is clear that his philosophical ideas had never been worked out in a coherent system.

src.l: Mary Baker Eddy, 1887, Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures
src.q: If these writings should be printed, their publication would silence the insinuation that Mr. Quimby originated the system of healing which I claim to be mine.

s: The Kybalion's first principle, Mentalism, states 'THE ALL is MIND; The Universe is Mental', and calls THE ALL the substantial reality beneath matter, energy and life.

src.l: Three Initiates, 1908, The Kybalion: A Study of the Hermetic Philosophy of Ancient Egypt and Greece
src.q: I. THE PRINCIPLE OF MENTALISM. > "THE ALL is MIND; The Universe is Mental."

s: The Kybalion's second principle, Correspondence, quotes 'As above, so below; as below, so above' and says there is always a correspondence between the laws and phenomena of the planes of being.

src.l: Three Initiates, 1908, The Kybalion: A Study of the Hermetic Philosophy of Ancient Egypt and Greece
src.q: II. THE PRINCIPLE OF CORRESPONDENCE. > “As above, so below; as below, so above.”—The Kybalion. This Principle embodies the truth that there is always a Correspondence between the laws and phenomena of the various planes of Being and Life.

s: The Kybalion's third principle, Vibration ('Nothing rests; everything moves; everything vibrates'), says matter, energy, mind and spirit differ largely by rate of vibration, and claims modern science endorses it.

src.l: Three Initiates, 1908, The Kybalion: A Study of the Hermetic Philosophy of Ancient Egypt and Greece
src.q: This Principle embodies the truth that “everything is in motion’’; “everything vibrates’’; “nothing is at rest’’; facts which Modern Science endorses

s: The Kybalion's fourth principle, Polarity, holds that everything has its pair of opposites and that 'like and unlike are the same', opposites differing only in degree; it says Hermetists can change the vibrations of hate into love.

src.l: Three Initiates, 1908, The Kybalion: A Study of the Hermetic Philosophy of Ancient Egypt and Greece
src.q: IV. THE PRINCIPLE OF POLARITY. > "Everything is Dual; everything has poles; every- > thing has its pair of opposites; like and unlike are the > same; opposites are identical in nature, but different in > degree

s: The Kybalion turns alchemy into psychology: its axiom says mind, 'as well as metals and elements', may be transmuted from pole to pole and vibration to vibration, and that 'True Hermetic Transmutation is a Mental Art.'

src.l: Three Initiates, 1908, The Kybalion: A Study of the Hermetic Philosophy of Ancient Egypt and Greece
src.q: “Mind (as well as metals and elements) may be transmuted, from state to state; degree to degree; condition to condition; pole to pole; vibration to vibration. True Hermetic Transmutation is a Mental Art.”

s: The Kybalion presents itself as a commentary on a lost oral compilation of Hermetic maxims called 'The Kybalion' whose precepts, it says, 'have never been written down, or printed, so far as we know.'

src.l: Three Initiates, 1908, The Kybalion: A Study of the Hermetic Philosophy of Ancient Egypt and Greece
src.q: This teaching, however, is known to many to whom it has descended, from mouth to ear, on and on throughout the centuries. Its precepts have never been written down, or printed, so far as we know.

s: William Salmon's 1692 English Smaragdine Table of Hermes gives the axiom the Kybalion later quotes: 'whatsoever is below, is like that which is above', and ties it to 'the Miracles of the One Thing', which Salmon glosses as the alchemical Stone.

src.l: William Salmon, 1692, Medicina practica, or, Practical physick
src.q: whatsoever is below, is like that which is above; and that which is above, is like that which is below: By this are acquired and perfected the Miracles of the One Thing.

s: Critique: the Kybalion's seven 'Hermetic principles' have no checkable ancient witness; the book says its precepts were never written down, and its one axiom with a clear textual ancestor, 'As above, so below', comes from the alchemical Emerald Tablet, not from the Corpus Hermeticum.

src.l: Three Initiates, 1908, The Kybalion: A Study of the Hermetic Philosophy of Ancient Egypt and Greece
src.q: Its precepts have never been written down, or printed, so far as we know.

src.l: William Salmon, 1692, Medicina practica, or, Practical physick
src.q: whatsoever is below, is like that which is above; and that which is above, is like that which is below

s: Atkinson's Thought Vibration names the 'Law of Attraction' as the law of the thought world and says that thinking sends out vibrations of a fine ethereal substance as real as those of light, heat, electricity and magnetism, with a magnet-like power of attraction.

src.l: William Walker Atkinson, 1908, Thought Vibration, or The Law of Attraction in the Thought World
src.q: this mighty law of the world of Thought --the Law of Attraction. When we think we send out vibrations of a fine ethereal substance, which are as real as the vibrations manifesting light, heat, electricity, magnetism.

s: Atkinson states the law as 'Like attracts like, and opposites repel opposites, in the world of thought': the mind attracts only thoughts in harmony with its own.

src.l: William Walker Atkinson, 1908, Thought Vibration, or The Law of Attraction in the Thought World
src.q: But it attracts only those thoughts which are in harmony with its own. Like attracts like, and opposites repel opposites, in the world of thought.

src.l: William Walker Atkinson, 1908, Thought Vibration, or The Law of Attraction in the Thought World
src.q: Like attracts like in the Thought World—as ye sow so shall ye reap.

s: Critique: Atkinson grounds the law of attraction in a magnet analogy yet states it as 'like attracts like, and opposites repel opposites', the reverse of how magnetic poles and electric charges behave, so the physics he borrows cannot carry the mechanism he claims.

src.l: William Walker Atkinson, 1908, Thought Vibration, or The Law of Attraction in the Thought World
src.q: A powerful magnet will send out vibra- tions and exert a force sufficient to attract to it- self a piece of steel weighing a hundred pounds

src.l: William Walker Atkinson, 1908, Thought Vibration, or The Law of Attraction in the Thought World
src.q: Like attracts like, and opposites repel opposites, in the world of thought.

s: Mulford calls mind 'magnetic' because it attracts whatever thought it fixes on, and treats qualities such as patience or courage as real elements of a subtler 'chemistry of nature' that one attracts by demanding them.

src.l: Prentice Mulford, 1888, Your Forces, and How to Use Them: First Series
src.q: Mind is "magnetic," because it attracts to itself whatever thought it fixes itself upon, or whatever it opens itself to.

src.l: Prentice Mulford, 1888, Your Forces, and How to Use Them: First Series
src.q: These qualities are real elements. They belong to the subtler, and as yet unrecognized, chemistry of nature.

s: Trine calls 'the drawing power of mind' one with 'that great law of the universe, that like attracts like': we attract from the seen and unseen side of life the forces most akin to our thoughts.

src.l: Ralph Waldo Trine, c1897, In Tune with the Infinite; or, Fullness of Peace, Power, and Plenty
src.q: the great law operating here is one with that great law of the universe, that like attracts like. We are continually attracting to us from both the seen and the unseen side of life, forces and conditions most akin to those of our own thoughts.

s: Trine says thoughts are forces and 'like builds like, and like attracts like', then quotes an unnamed author that 'the law of correspondences between spiritual and material things is wonderfully exact', so that gloomy people attract gloomy things.

src.l: Ralph Waldo Trine, c1897, In Tune with the Infinite; or, Fullness of Peace, Power, and Plenty
src.q: Thoughts are forces ; like builds like, and like attracts like. For one to govern his thinking, then, is to determine his life.

src.l: Ralph Waldo Trine, c1897, In Tune with the Infinite; or, Fullness of Peace, Power, and Plenty
src.q: "The law of correspondences between spiritual and material things is wonderfully exact in its workings. People ruled by the mood of gloom attract to them gloomy things.

s: Wattles's first proposition: 'There is a thinking stuff from which all things are made' that fills the universe, and a thought held in it produces the form of the thought, so man can cause the thing he thinks about to be created.

src.l: Wallace D. Wattles, 1917, Financial Success Through Creative Thought; or, The Science of Getting Rich
src.q: There is a thinking stuff from which all things are made, and which, in its original state, permeates, penetrates, and fills the interspaces of the universe.

src.l: Wallace D. Wattles, 1917, Financial Success Through Creative Thought; or, The Science of Getting Rich
src.q: And this stuff is thinking stuff; a thought held in it produces the form of the thought. Thought, in thinking sub-stance, produces shapes. Man is a thinking center, capable of original thought; if man can communicate his thought to original thinking substance, he can cause the creation, or formation, of the thing he thinks about.

s: Wattles grounds his book in the 'monistic theory of the universe', which he calls of Hindu origin and the foundation of Descartes, Spinoza, Leibnitz, Schopenhauer, Hegel and Emerson.

src.l: Wallace D. Wattles, 1917, Financial Success Through Creative Thought; or, The Science of Getting Rich
src.q: is of Hindu origin, and has been gradually winning its way into the thought of the western world for two hundred years. It is the foundation of all the Oriental philosophies, and of those of Descartes, Spinoza, Leibnitz, Schopenhauer, Hegel, and Emerson.

s: Haanel's Master-Key System says 'Thought seeks its own' and that the law of mental attraction exactly parallels the law of atomic affinity, mental currents being as real as electric, magnetic or heat currents.

src.l: Charles F. Haanel, 1919, The Master-Key System
src.q: We create our own character, personality and environment by the thought which we originate, or entertain. Thought seeks its own. The law of mental attraction is an exact parallel to the law of atomic affmity. Mental currents are as real as electric, magnetic or heat currents.

s: In Mental Chemistry (1922) Haanel extends the Law of Attraction from plant growth to 'the cohesion in the rock' and calls it a neutral law, neither good nor evil, that flows with the individual's desires.

src.l: Charles F. Haanel, 1922, Mental Chemistry
src.q: In the Mineral world it is the cohesion in the rock

src.l: Charles F. Haanel, 1922, Mental Chemistry
src.q: This Law of Attraction is neither good nor evil, neither moral nor immoral; it is a neutral law that always flows in conjunction with the desires of the individual

s: Coué holds that the unconscious, which he calls imagination, governs our actions, and that the will 'always yields to the imagination', an 'absolute rule that admits of no exception'.

src.l: Émile Coué, 1923, Self Mastery Through Conscious Autosuggestion
src.q: This will that we claim so proudly, always yields to the imagination. It is an absolute rule that admits of no exception.

s: Coué sums up his experiments as laws (when will and imagination are antagonistic imagination always wins) and prescribes the formula 'Every day, in every respect, I am getting better and better', using no magnetism or vibration vocabulary.

src.l: Émile Coué, 1922, Self Mastery Through Conscious Autosuggestion (Project Gutenberg ebook #27203)
src.loc: essay "Self Mastery Through Conscious Autosuggestion", the four laws

src.l: Émile Coué, 1922, Self Mastery Through Conscious Autosuggestion (Project Gutenberg ebook #27203)

s: Interpretive: New Thought's 'like attracts like' does not so much reverse Philolaus as keep only one half of the older scheme: it agrees that likes cohere without a binder, drops harmony as the binding of unlikes (Atkinson: opposites repel), and reuses 'harmony' to mean likeness; the Kybalion instead dissolves unlikeness into degree.

src.l: William Walker Atkinson, 1908, Thought Vibration, or The Law of Attraction in the Thought World
src.q: But it attracts only those thoughts which are in harmony with its own. Like attracts like, and opposites repel opposites, in the world of thought.

src.l: Charles F. Haanel, 1919, The Master-Key System
src.q: Mental currents are as real as electric, magnetic or heat currents.

src.l: Three Initiates, 1908, The Kybalion: A Study of the Hermetic Philosophy of Ancient Egypt and Greece
src.q: like and unlike are the > same

s: In The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902, Lectures IV–V) William James names the 'Mind-cure movement', notes it also calls itself 'New Thought', treats its sects as one thing, and says it must be reckoned with as a genuine religious power.

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
src.q: I will give the title of the ‘Mind-cure movement.’ There are various sects of this ‘New Thought,’ to use another of the names by which it calls itself

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
src.q: it must now be reckoned with as a genuine religious power.

s: James lists the doctrinal sources of mind-cure as the four Gospels, Emersonianism or New England transcendentalism, Berkeleyan idealism, spiritism, optimistic popular-science evolutionism, and a strain of Hinduism, but says its most characteristic feature is a more direct intuitive belief in healthy-minded attitudes.

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
src.q: One of the doctrinal sources of Mind-cure is the four Gospels; another is Emersonianism or New England tran- scendentalism ; another is Berkeleyan idealism; another is spiritism, with its messages of ‘law’ and ‘progress’ and ‘development’ ; another the optimistic popular sci- ence evolutionism of which I have recently spoken ; and, finally, Hinduism has contributed a strain.

s: James reports that mind-cure's belief has been corroborated by its disciples' practical experience, writing that the blind have been made to see, the halt to walk and lifelong invalids restored, with moral fruits no less remarkable.

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
src.q: Their belief has in a general way been corroborated by the practical experience of their disciples ; ... The blind have been made to see, the halt to walk ; lifelong invalids have had their health restored. The moral fruits have been no less remarkable.

s: James calls mind-cure the American people's 'only decidedly original contribution to the systematic philosophy of life' and says its spread is due to practical fruits, being knit up with concrete therapeutics.

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
src.q: this, their only decidedly original contribution to the systematic philosophy of life, should be so intimately knit up with concrete therapeutics.

s: James argues that, though hosts of people cannot be influenced by mind-cure ideas, those who can form a psychic type to be studied with respect; in a footnote he cites H. H. Goddard's 1899 finding that mind-cure cures exist but do not differ from medicine's cures by suggestion.

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
src.q: They form a psychic type to be studied with respect.

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
src.q: concludes that the cures by mind-cure exist, but are in no respect different from those now officially recognized in medicine as cures by suggestion

s: James objects that 'suggestion' is used as a wet blanket on inquiry: it is only another name for the power of ideas over belief and conduct, and naming it does not explain why ideas work on some people and not on others.

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
src.q: ‘Suggestion’ is only another name for the power of ideas, so far as they prove efficacious over belief and conduct.

s: James describes mind-cure's mental hygiene as wholly compacted of optimism ('Pessimism leads to weakness. Optimism leads to power.') and reports a mind-cure writer printing 'Thoughts are things' in bold type at the foot of each page.

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
src.q: This system is wholly and exclusively compacted of optimism: ‘Pessimism leads to weakness. Optimism leads to power.’

s: James says mind-cure made an unprecedented (for Protestant countries) use of the subconscious life, adding systematic exercise in passive relaxation, concentration and meditation, and even something like hypnotic practice.

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
src.q: mind-cure has made what in our protestant countries is an unprecedentedly great use of the subconscious life. To their reasoned advice and dogmatic assertion, its founders have added systematic exercise in passive relaxation, concentration, and meditation, and have even invoked something like hypnotic practice.

s: James frames mind-cure pragmatically as an experimental method: whether or not patients were deluded, that they seemed to themselves cured by the experiments tried was enough to convert them.

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
src.q: That they seemed to themselves to have been cured by the experiments tried was enough to make them converts to the system.

s: James concludes that science and the religion of mind-cure are both 'genuine keys' to the world's treasure-house for whoever can use either practically, and that neither is exhaustive or exclusive of the other.

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
src.q: the science and the religion are both of them genuine keys for unlocking the world's treasure-house to him who can use either of them practically.

s: Critique (James's own): in 'The Sick Soul' James judges healthy-mindedness inadequate as a philosophical doctrine because the evil it refuses to account for is a genuine portion of reality, and ranks as completest the religions with the best-developed pessimistic elements (Buddhism, Christianity).

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
src.q: healthy-mindedness is inadequate as a philosophical doctrine, because the evil facts which it refuses positively to account for are a genuine portion of reality

src.l: William James, 1902, The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
src.q: The completest religions would therefore seem to be those in which the pessimistic elements are best devel- oped.

s: In Christian Science (1907) Mark Twain grants that the mind cure, faith cure, prayer cure, mental science and Christian-Science cures achieve some cures, but says they all work with 'the same old, powerful instrument--the patient's imagination'.

src.l: Mark Twain, 1907, Christian Science
Mark Twain, 1907, Christian Science

s: Twain predicted that Christian Science, run as a 'Trust', would have ten million American adherents by 1920, be politically formidable by 1930, and be the governing power in the Republic by 1940.

src.l: Mark Twain, 1907, Christian Science
Mark Twain, 1907, Christian Science

s: Twain's central charge is organisational and financial: the 'Boston Trust' sells Eddy's books and services for cash, and has organised and capitalised a healing force latent in everyone.

src.l: Mark Twain, 1907, Christian Science
Mark Twain, 1907, Christian Science

s: Napoleon Hill's Think and Grow Rich was first published in 1937.

src.l: Napoleon Hill, 1937, Think and Grow Rich

s: Norman Vincent Peale's The Power of Positive Thinking was first published in 1952 (Prentice-Hall).

src.l: Norman Vincent Peale, 1952, The Power of Positive Thinking
Donald Meyer, 1965, The Positive Thinkers: A Study of the American Quest for Health, Wealth and Personal Power from Mary Baker Eddy to Norman Vincent Peale

s: Donald Meyer's The Positive Thinkers (1965) frames American positive thinking as a single line running from Mary Baker Eddy to Norman Vincent Peale, as a quest for health, wealth and personal power.

src.l: Donald Meyer, 1965, The Positive Thinkers: A Study of the American Quest for Health, Wealth and Personal Power from Mary Baker Eddy to Norman Vincent Peale

s: Albanese's A Republic of Mind and Spirit (2007) groups Transcendentalism, Spiritualism, Theosophy, New Thought, Christian Science and the New Age as 'metaphysical religion' and argues it has been as vigorous and influential in America as the evangelical tradition.

src.l: Catherine L. Albanese, 2007, A Republic of Mind and Spirit: A Cultural History of American Metaphysical Religion
David D. Hall, 2008, Review of Albanese, A Republic of Mind and Spirit

s: Hanegraaff's New Age Religion and Western Culture (1996) argues that the New Age's foundations were laid by Western esoteric traditions since the Renaissance and that it emerged from the secularisation of those traditions during the nineteenth century.

src.l: Wouter J. Hanegraaff, 1996, New Age Religion and Western Culture: Esotericism in the Mirror of Secular Thought

s: Satter's Each Mind a Kingdom (1999) presents New Thought (1875–1920) as a movement led largely by and for women, advocating mind over matter and women's spiritual ability to purify the world, and links it to later self-help.

src.l: Beryl Satter, 1999, Each Mind a Kingdom: American Women, Sexual Purity, and the New Thought Movement, 1875–1920

s: Mitch Horowitz's One Simple Idea: How Positive Thinking Reshaped Modern Life (Crown, 2014) is a popular history tracing positive thinking from New Thought into modern life.

src.l: Mitch Horowitz, 2014, One Simple Idea: How Positive Thinking Reshaped Modern Life
Philip Deslippe, 2015, Review: One Simple Idea: How Positive Thinking Reshaped Modern Life

s: Critique: Ehrenreich's Bright-sided (2009; UK title Smile or Die) traces positive thinking from a marginal nineteenth-century healing technique to a near-mandatory attitude and argues that on a personal level it leads to self-blame and the policing of 'negative' thoughts, and nationally to disastrous irrational optimism.

src.l: Barbara Ehrenreich, 2009, Bright-sided: How the Relentless Promotion of Positive Thinking Has Undermined America

s: Freud's Totem und Tabu (1913), essay III, concludes that the principle governing magic, the technique of the animistic way of thinking, is the 'omnipotence of thoughts' (Allmacht der Gedanken).

src.l: Sigmund Freud, 1913, Totem und Tabu. Einige Übereinstimmungen im Seelenleben der Wilden und der Neurotiker
src.loc: III. Animismus, Magie und Allmacht der Gedanken, end of section 2

src.l: Sigmund Freud, A. A. Brill (trans.), 1918, Totem and Taboo: Resemblances between the Psychic Lives of Savages and Neurotics
src.loc: III. Animism, Magic and the Omnipotence of Thought, end of section 2

s: Freud says he took the phrase 'omnipotence of thoughts' from a highly intelligent obsessional patient, and footnotes his 1909 case history 'Bemerkungen über einen Fall von Zwangsneurose' (the 'Rat Man'); the patient used it for uncanny coincidences such as thinking of a person and then meeting him.

src.l: Sigmund Freud, 1913, Totem und Tabu. Einige Übereinstimmungen im Seelenleben der Wilden und der Neurotiker
Sigmund Freud, A. A. Brill (trans.), 1918, Totem and Taboo: Resemblances between the Psychic Lives of Savages and Neurotics

s: Freud defines the omnipotence of thoughts as the over-estimation of psychic processes as against reality, and argues that the obsessional neurotic, afraid that voicing an evil wish will fulfil it, stands close to 'the savage' who believes he can change the outer world by thought alone.

src.l: Sigmund Freud, A. A. Brill (trans.), 1918, Totem and Taboo: Resemblances between the Psychic Lives of Savages and Neurotics
Sigmund Freud, 1913, Totem und Tabu. Einige Übereinstimmungen im Seelenleben der Wilden und der Neurotiker

s: Freud folds Frazer's two laws into one: association by similarity and by contiguity 'meet in the higher unity of contact', contiguity being contact in the direct sense and similarity contact in a transferred sense.

src.l: Sigmund Freud, A. A. Brill (trans.), 1918, Totem and Taboo: Resemblances between the Psychic Lives of Savages and Neurotics

s: Freud holds that in modern civilisation the omnipotence of thoughts survives in only one field, art, where a person consumed by wishes makes something like their gratification and the play calls forth effects as if it were real.

src.l: Sigmund Freud, A. A. Brill (trans.), 1918, Totem and Taboo: Resemblances between the Psychic Lives of Savages and Neurotics
Sigmund Freud, 1913, Totem und Tabu. Einige Übereinstimmungen im Seelenleben der Wilden und der Neurotiker

s: Lévy-Bruhl (1910) gives as an approximation of his 'law of participation' that in primitive collective representations objects, beings and phenomena can be, incomprehensibly to us, both themselves and something other than themselves, and can emit and receive mystic forces without ceasing to be where they are.

src.l: Lucien Lévy-Bruhl, 1910, Les fonctions mentales dans les sociétés inférieures

s: Lévy-Bruhl (1910) says 'prélogique' does not mean an earlier stage before logical thought, nor anti-logical or a-logical, but only that this mentality does not bind itself above all to avoiding contradiction: it obeys first the law of participation and is mostly indifferent to contradiction.

src.l: Lucien Lévy-Bruhl, 1910, Les fonctions mentales dans les sociétés inférieures

s: Piaget (1929) adopts Lévy-Bruhl's 'participation' for a relation believed to hold between two beings or phenomena that are partly identical or influence one another directly, with no spatial contact or intelligible causal link, and defines 'magic' as the use the individual believes he can make of participation to modify reality.

src.l: Jean Piaget, 1929, The Child's Conception of the World
src.loc: ch. IV, §2 'Participation and Magical Practices', pp. 131-132

s: Piaget (1929) defines the child's 'realism' as ignorance of the existence of the self, so that one's own perspective is taken as immediately objective and absolute, and contrasts it with objectivity, which starts from the effort to exclude the intrusive self.

src.l: Jean Piaget, 1929, The Child's Conception of the World

s: Piaget (1929) himself sought 'corroborative proof' of the child's magical ideas in normal, civilised adults, in three states where the boundary of self and world blurs: involuntary imitation, anxiety, and 'monoideic' desire; he set inherited superstition aside.

src.l: Jean Piaget, 1929, The Child's Conception of the World
src.loc: ch. IV, §4 'Corroborative Proof: Spontaneous Magical Ideas in the Adult', p. 162

s: Oettingen and Mayer (2002) report across four longitudinal studies (job-seeking graduates, students with a crush, exam-takers, hip-replacement patients) that positive expectations predicted high effort and success, while positive fantasies about the desired future predicted the reverse.

src.l: Gabriele Oettingen, Doris Mayer, 2002, The motivating function of thinking about the future: expectations versus fantasies

s: Kappes and Oettingen (2011) induced positive fantasies experimentally and found, in four studies, less energy (systolic blood pressure, self-report) than after questioning, negative or neutral fantasies, most so for a pressing need, proposing low energisation as one reason positive fantasy predicts poor achievement.

src.l: Heather Barry Kappes, Gabriele Oettingen, 2011, Positive fantasies about idealized futures sap energy

s: Dixon, Hornsey and Hartley (2023) built a Manifestation Scale (Personal Power and Cosmic Collaboration subscales; three studies, N = 1,023 US Prolific participants): over a third endorsed manifestation beliefs, and higher scorers saw themselves as more successful, expected more future success, and were more drawn to risky investments and more likely to report bankruptcy.

src.l: Lucas J. Dixon, Matthew J. Hornsey, Nicole Hartley, 2023, “The Secret” to Success? The Psychology of Belief in Manifestation
Lucas J. Dixon, Matthew J. Hornsey, Nicole Hartley, 2023, “The Secret” to Success? The Psychology of Belief in Manifestation

s: Dixon, Hornsey and Hartley (2023) found no relationship between manifestation belief and income or educational attainment, and conclude that while the belief is self-enhancing it shows little evidence of raising objective success.

src.l: Lucas J. Dixon, Matthew J. Hornsey, Nicole Hartley, 2023, “The Secret” to Success? The Psychology of Belief in Manifestation

s: Critique: the manifesting findings are cross-sectional correlations in US online samples, and the authors themselves warn that manifesters may inflate self-reported success because 'acting as if' is part of the practice; the direction of the bankruptcy and fraud associations is not established.

src.l: Lucas J. Dixon, Matthew J. Hornsey, Nicole Hartley, 2023, “The Secret” to Success? The Psychology of Belief in Manifestation

s: Kaptchuk and colleagues (2010) gave IBS patients placebo pills openly described as inert, with a rationale of mind-body self-healing, and found better global improvement, symptom severity and adequate relief at 11 and 21 days than in no-treatment controls with the same provider interaction.

src.l: Ted J. Kaptchuk, Elizabeth Friedlander, John M. Kelley, M. Norma Sanchez, Efi Kokkotou, et al., 2010, Placebos without deception: a randomized controlled trial in irritable bowel syndrome

s: Von Wernsdorff and colleagues' 2021 meta-analysis of eleven open-label placebo trials found a significant overall effect (SMD 0.72, 95% CI 0.39-1.05) with high heterogeneity (I2 = 76%) and moderate risk of bias in all studies.

src.l: Melina von Wernsdorff, Martin Loef, Brunna Tuschen-Caffier, et al., 2021, Effects of open-label placebos in clinical trials: a systematic review and meta-analysis

s: What of New Thought survives as measured psychology is mediated: thought acts on the thinker. Judging a goal likely predicts effort and success; expectation and ritual relieve self-reported symptoms even when the pill is known to be inert. Each runs through behaviour or the body.

src.l: Gabriele Oettingen, Doris Mayer, 2002, The motivating function of thinking about the future: expectations versus fantasies
Ted J. Kaptchuk, Elizabeth Friedlander, John M. Kelley, M. Norma Sanchez, Efi Kokkotou, et al., 2010, Placebos without deception: a randomized controlled trial in irritable bowel syndrome
Melina von Wernsdorff, Martin Loef, Brunna Tuschen-Caffier, et al., 2021, Effects of open-label placebos in clinical trials: a systematic review and meta-analysis

s: The part of New Thought that is magical thinking in the strict sense, thought acting on the world without behaviour in between (Freud's omnipotence of thoughts, Piaget's magic as participation used to modify reality, the manifesting item 'those thoughts alone make success more likely'), has no measured support, and the nearest measures point the other way.

src.l: Sigmund Freud, A. A. Brill (trans.), 1918, Totem and Taboo: Resemblances between the Psychic Lives of Savages and Neurotics
Jean Piaget, 1929, The Child's Conception of the World
Lucas J. Dixon, Matthew J. Hornsey, Nicole Hartley, 2023, “The Secret” to Success? The Psychology of Belief in Manifestation
Heather Barry Kappes, Gabriele Oettingen, 2011, Positive fantasies about idealized futures sap energy

s: Critique: the measured residue is itself fragile. The open-label placebo literature that best separates expectation from deception rests on few trials with moderate risk of bias, high heterogeneity and mostly self-reported outcomes.

src.l: Melina von Wernsdorff, Martin Loef, Brunna Tuschen-Caffier, et al., 2021, Effects of open-label placebos in clinical trials: a systematic review and meta-analysis
